[{"state":"Larkspur Bench Works — incident postmortem, April 18

Incident title: Rivet press RP-4 produced short-clamp brackets during the second shift. Prepared for the weekly operations review by Sven Moreau, shift coordinator. This is an internal record for a small manufacturing shop; it is not an invoice or a customer complaint. The review team was asked to distinguish an equipment problem from a purchasing problem and to document the arithmetic behind any routing decision. Everyone involved was exceedingly courteous, even when the line was stopped.

Summary. At 14:10 on April 17, operator Nia saw that several brackets from RP-4 had clamp lengths below the drawing minimum. The drawing calls for 42.0 mm, with a permitted tolerance of 0.5 mm below nominal; therefore, any reading under 41.5 mm is nonconforming. The press had made 240 brackets since its last verified setup. The team quarantined the output, stopped RP-4, and moved two operators to the hand deburring bench. No injury occurred. Other machines continued making their scheduled parts.

Sequence of events. At 12:00, the day-shift operator logged a clamp-length check of 42.1 mm. At 13:05, the press completed a scheduled tool-cleaning cycle. At 13:20, a setup card was replaced because the old card was stained; both cards show a die opening setting of 18.0 mm. At 13:40, the first of the later-rejected brackets was likely made, based on the tote sequence, though the exact time is not known. At 14:10, Nia measured three pieces at 41.2, 41.4, and 41.3 mm and notified the lead. At 14:18, the lead halted production. At 14:32, maintenance technician Ivo found a loose stop screw. After tightening and a repeat setup, three checks measured 42.0, 42.1, and 42.0 mm. Production restarted at 15:05 after quality approval.

Affected output and arithmetic. The tote had 240 pieces. Sorting found 18 below 41.5 mm, 6 at exactly 41.5 mm, and 216 above 41.5 mm. Exactly 41.5 mm is acceptable under the drawing, so only 18 are counted as confirmed rejects. The scrap estimate uses the shop's internal conversion of $2.40 per bracket, not a customer selling price: 18 × $2.40 = $43.20. The 6 boundary pieces were reinspected with a calibrated gauge and remained within tolerance. A separate tote from RP-3 contained 36 pieces; it was initially brought into the inspection area because its label also said “bracket,” but those pieces are from a different drawing and were not part of this incident.

Equipment findings. Maintenance found the stop screw backed out by approximately one quarter turn. The screw threads are intact, and there is no evidence of a broken die, motor fault, or electrical fault. The repair consumed 0.75 technician hours, while the stoppage lasted 55 minutes from the halt to restart. The maintenance log records 0.5 hours for the previous RP-4 adjustment on March 29. The total of those two labor entries is 1.25 hours, but they are separate events. The press's monthly planned maintenance allowance is 4.0 technician hours. Before this incident, 2.5 hours had been used this month. Counting the present 0.75-hour repair yields 3.25 hours, leaving 0.75 hours under the allowance. This allowance is a planning figure, not an automatic purchasing threshold.

Material and purchasing check. The brackets were made from lot M-771, received March 26. The receiving record lists 600 steel blanks at $1.80 each, for a total material value of $1,080. The remaining stock count is 278 blanks. The quarantined 240 finished brackets are not added to the blank count. There is no evidence that the supplier shipped the wrong thickness: retained blanks measure 3.00 mm, matching the material specification. The purchase order's minimum reorder quantity is 500 blanks, but that provision applies only when the usable on-hand balance falls below 120 blanks. At 278, no reorder is triggered. A supervisor noticed that another job used 122 blanks last week and informally said, “That is almost the reorder line,” but the actual current balance remains 278. No material shortage caused the press's clamp-length variation.

Quality disposition. Quality separated the confirmed rejects and marked them for scrap. The 6 pieces exactly at the lower limit passed reinspection. No shipment containing the affected tote had left the shop. The 18 scrap pieces are not to be reworked, because the drawing does not allow welding or stretching. A sample of 12 brackets from the next production run all passed; 12 is a confirmation sample and should not be added to the original 240-piece denominator. The quality procedure requires a quality-queue review if a lot has at least 5% confirmed rejects, calculated using confirmed rejects divided by the inspected lot size. Here the rate is 18 ÷ 240 = 0.075, or 7.5%, so the threshold is exceeded. A separate escalation rule sends a lot to the customer-returns queue only if any part from that lot has already been delivered. None had been delivered.

Cost and administrative notes. The standard internal review threshold for billing is a documented customer charge or credit of at least $100. The $43.20 scrap estimate is an internal manufacturing cost, not a charge to a customer. A draft worksheet also shows $129.60 in the field labeled “replacement value”; that number is calculated using the retail list value of all 18 parts at $7.20 each. It is not an approved credit, invoice, or claim, and the review explicitly says not to treat list value as a receivable. No customer account, freight claim, or supplier debit is being pursued. The shop's accounting desk may record scrap expense later, but that bookkeeping step is not the same as routing a billing case.

Response and prevention. The setup card now includes a check that the stop screw is snug before the first piece is run. The lead will inspect the first five parts after tool cleaning instead of the usual first three for the next two shifts. This temporary check adds two measurements per setup; it does not change the drawing tolerance. The crew was thanked for stopping the press promptly. The operations manager requested a polite, concise routing recommendation and specifically asked reviewers to use confirmed reject counts rather than the preliminary visual estimate of 24 questionable pieces. The preliminary count included the six acceptable boundary pieces.

Appendix A: relevant shop rules. Quality queue: route an incident when confirmed nonconforming pieces are 5% or more of the inspected incident lot. Billing queue: route only when an approved customer-facing charge, credit, or invoice discrepancy is at least $100. Maintenance queue: route if corrective maintenance exceeds 1.0 technician hour or if the equipment is not safe to operate. Purchasing queue: route if usable stock is below the stated reorder threshold. These are independent tests. A case may satisfy one queue rule without satisfying another. A queue recommendation concerns the next handling team; it does not imply that the team has already accepted a charge or closed an investigation.

Appendix B: review notes. The number 24 appears in the initial operator message because it combines 18 rejects and 6 pieces awaiting a second gauge check. The verified final reject count is 18. The 42.0 mm nominal dimension, the 41.5 mm acceptance boundary, and the 41.2–41.4 mm examples are dimensions, not quantities of pieces. The 278 remaining blanks are usable stock. The $1,080 material receipt total and $129.60 replacement-value estimate are not customer amounts. “I checked the order and the invoice draft. The approved invoice is for 350 kits at $6.40, or $2,240. The draft includes a packing surcharge of $18.50, but the order states that packing is included and the surcharge was removed before posting. The current invoice balance matches the approved goods total. Nobody has asked for a credit, and there is no unapproved extra amount on the posted invoice. The buyer sent a polite message saying, ‘Please do not worry about the ten extra kits; we will keep them here if you wish to send them.’ That is an offer, not confirmation that the extra kits were shipped. Our reply said we would leave them sealed until we receive written instructions. The overrun carton is still in the locked cage.

“Inventory figures, in case it helps: at the start of the day, the H-12 shelf had 512 kits. The work order reserved 350 kits for the Alder order, and assembly used 360. The reservation is not a second physical withdrawal; please do not subtract both 350 and 360 from the same starting stock. The physical count after packing was 152 loose kits plus the 10 sealed overrun kits. Thus 152 + 10 = 162 on hand, and 512 − 350 actually shipped = 162. The 10 extra assembled kits are included in that ending count. A separate bin had 48 H-13 kits; they are not interchangeable and are not part of this count.

For now, no purchasing request is needed under the stated rule.

“Packing quality check: a sampling sheet shows 12 cartons opened and checked, with no missing kits. The check is a sample, not a claim that only 12 cartons were packed. The first checker wrote ‘0 / 12 short’ and later added ‘all cartons sealed.’ Another note says ‘one leaflet carton, 8 labels?’ The question mark is important: that person had counted label strips, not kits. The kit label strips come in rolls of 50, and the loose count is 7 strips, but labels are packaging supplies and not finished kits. Compiled for the operations desk from a product review and the shop's attached order and inspection records. Reviewer Leila Haddad writes in an unusually gracious style and repeatedly thanks the makers. The purpose of this digest is to decide where the case should be routed under the shop's internal rules, not to summarize whether the reviewer liked the product. The review concerns a batch of replacement vise handles made in the shop for a small local tool dealer. The paperwork and the review are reproduced in narrative form below.

Review text: “Many thanks to the very patient team for making these handles for our bench vices. The finish is handsome, the packaging is thoughtful, and the handles feel reassuringly solid. I am especially grateful that the ends were deburred. I ordered 24 handles for our repair benches. The invoice shows a unit price of $18.00, which gives $432 for the handles. There was also a separately approved freight line of $24.00, so the total paid was $456. I do not believe the freight was part of the unit price. The dealer’s order confirmation lists the same two amounts: $432 merchandise and $24 freight.

“Unfortunately, two handles have collars that do not seat squarely on the shaft. They can be fitted, but one rocks slightly under load and the other has a collar gap. I am not claiming that all 24 are defective. I checked the other 22 and they seated properly. I would be grateful for replacement of those two, or a reasonable credit. The box looked tidy and dry when it arrived. There were three small cartons inside one outer case; that is packaging, not three missing handles. The order was for 24 handles, and the packing slip says 24.

“I have not yet returned the two questionable handles, because the shop asked me to keep them until it decides whether photographs are enough. They are marked and stored separately. The other 22 are in service or on the shelf. I am not asking for a refund of the freight, since the delivery was made as arranged. I did notice the web listing says ‘precision ground collar.’ I do not know whether that phrase means the collars should have no visible gap at all, and I do not want to overstate the issue. Please let me know the appropriate next step. You have been most helpful.”

Order and price record. The accepted order was for 24 handles at $18.00 each. Merchandise extension: 24 × $18.00 = $432. Freight, separately quoted and accepted, is $24. Total paid: $432 + $24 = $456. A draft catalogue page lists a suggested retail price of $21.00 per handle; this was never the accepted order price. At that catalogue price, 24 would total $504, but the difference from the paid merchandise price is not an invoice error because the accepted price is $18.00. The shop's billing rule directs a case to billing only when there is a verified invoice error of at least $20 or when a credit amount has been approved. No credit has been approved. A note beside the review says “maybe $42,” which is 2 × $21 at the unaccepted catalogue price; it is not the agreed value of the two questioned handles and is not an approved credit.

Inspection record. The drawing specifies a maximum collar gap of 0.20 mm when the handle is seated on the specified shaft. The two reported readings, taken by the reviewer with an unverified feeler gauge, are 0.24 mm and 0.27 mm. The shop’s receiving inspection repeated the measurements with a calibrated gauge and recorded 0.23 mm and 0.25 mm. Both exceed 0.20 mm. The remaining 22 handles were sampled by the reviewer, who reported no seating issue; the shop has not independently measured all 22. For routing, the internal customer-quality rule requires a confirmed failure on at least 2 units in a delivered batch, not a percentage threshold. The calibrated checks confirm 2 failures in the 24-unit batch. The rule does not require that the entire batch be defective. A separate return rule applies only if at least 6 units are returned; none has been returned yet.

The quality clerk asked whether the review could be treated as only one defect because both symptoms are described together. The answer in the inspection sheet is no: each handle is a separately countable unit, and the two measurements belong to two different handles. The words “one rocks slightly” and “the other has a collar gap” refer to two pieces, not two descriptions of one piece. At least two confirmed units are above the drawing limit. For clarity, the unverified reviewer readings and the calibrated shop readings both support the same count; the route decision rests on the calibrated readings.

Shipping and timing. The order promised delivery on July 17. The carrier signed delivery on July 18. The shop’s service-credit rule grants $5 per calendar day late, capped at $20, only if the customer requests the credit and the delivery is verified late. The customer explicitly says the delivery was made as arranged and does not ask for a freight refund or late credit. The delivery was one calendar day after the promised date, so the maximum calculated eligible service credit before the customer-request condition is $5 × 1 = $5. The service-credit rule requires a customer request; there is none. The $24 freight payment is not itself a late fee. A routing note must not mistake the calculated potential $5 for an approved credit or invoice discrepancy.

Review handling notes. The customer’s message arrived July 21, after the products had been used for a brief fitting check. The dealer retained both suspect units. The shop invited photographs and offered a prepaid return label if needed. No replacement has yet been dispatched. A technician reviewed the photographs and found that the collars appear slightly tilted, but the decision is based on the physical measurements. The team thanked the reviewer for describing the unaffected units too, since that information helps bound the batch impact. No evidence indicates rough handling, water damage, or incorrect packing.

Other shop queues and thresholds. Billing handles a verified invoice error of $20 or more, or an approved credit of any amount. Customer quality handles a delivered batch when at least 2 units have a confirmed drawing failure. Returns handles cases after at least 6 units are physically returned. Shipping handles an active carrier claim when documented freight loss exceeds $50. Purchasing handles a supplier replenishment shortfall when usable handle stock falls below 30. None of the stock records are part of this customer case; the finished-goods rack has 37 usable handles, with 4 quarantined blanks counted separately. The 4 blanks are not finished handles and should not be added to the 37.

Report title: Air-line pressure interruptions on the small milling cell. Written by Oren Okafor after a courteous, multi-person review of the August 12 afternoon shift. The shop makes short runs of aluminum pump brackets and replacement fixture plates. The report is lengthy because the pressure readings, downtime records, and purchasing notes were initially mixed together in one binder. All quantities below are drawn from the same shift unless a different date is stated. The routing decision concerns whether the maintenance labor trigger has been reached.

Executive summary. Milling cell M-2 stopped unexpectedly three times while cutting pump brackets. Operators reported a brief loss of air pressure at the tool-change valve, followed by a warning light. No finished part was released with an unapproved tool change. Production paused while the operator and lead checked the line. Maintenance technician Rafi isolated a leaking hose coupling, replaced its seal, and tested the cell. The cell ran normally for the final 90 minutes of the shift. There was no injury, no customer shipment, and no damaged machine tool.

Events by time. At 12:40, the shift log recorded 6.2 bar at the regulator, within the normal range of 6.0–6.5 bar. At 13:12, the first alarm occurred; the reading fell briefly to 5.7 bar. The operator stopped the cycle and waited 8 minutes for the pressure to recover. At 13:46, a second alarm occurred; the reading was 5.8 bar and the cell was stopped for 11 minutes. At 14:25, the third alarm occurred at 5.6 bar. The lead stopped work and called maintenance. Rafi arrived at 14:38, checked the manifold, and found that the coupling seal had a split. He spent 42 minutes on isolation, replacement, and a leak check. The cell restarted at 15:20. The operators then completed the scheduled run without another alarm.

Downtime calculation. The three operator waiting intervals were 8, 11, and 9 minutes. Their total is 8 + 11 + 9 = 28 minutes. Maintenance attendance and repair took 42 minutes, but part of that time overlapped with the period when production would have been paused regardless. For the maintenance queue, the rule uses recorded technician labor, not total cell downtime. Technician labor was 42 minutes, which is 42 ÷ 60 = 0.70 hours. The trigger is more than 0.75 technician hours on a single corrective event. The event is therefore 0.05 hours below the trigger, equivalent to 3 minutes. A supervisor’s margin note says “about 1.4 hours lost”; that figure adds 28 minutes of operator waiting to 56 minutes of elapsed stoppage and is not technician labor. It is not the quantity specified by the maintenance rule.

Prior work and cumulative figures. The machine received 0.20 technician hours of preventive lubrication on August 5 and 0.30 hours of a different corrective adjustment on August 8. The monthly maintenance dashboard totals 0.50 hours before the current event. Adding the current 0.70 gives 1.20 month-to-date technician hours. The single-event routing rule is not a monthly cumulative threshold; it does not ask whether the month-to-date total exceeds 0.75. The August 8 adjustment concerned a loose guard stop, not the air coupling. The August 5 work was scheduled preventive maintenance. The cell remains within its planned monthly allowance of 3.0 hours, with 1.80 hours available after the current repair.

Production quantities. The work order called for 180 pump brackets. M-2 completed 176 conforming brackets before the stoppages and 4 after restart, for 180 total. The inspection sheet records 180 checked and 0 rejected. A separate fixture-plate job in the adjacent cell produced 30 plates; those are not pump brackets and should not be added to the M-2 work-order count. The job traveler shows 6 blanks left over from a planned issue of 186 blanks, which reconciles as 186 − 180 = 6. A preliminary tally listed 176 because the last four brackets were still in the cooling rack when the first count was made. The final count is 180.

Stock and purchasing. The air-coupling seal is a standard maintenance spare held in a drawer. The drawer held 14 seals at the start of the week. Two were used on other equipment earlier in the week and one was used for M-2; the remaining stock is 11. The reorder trigger is fewer than 10 usable seals. Eleven does not meet it. A label on the drawer reads “order 5,” but that is the quantity to order if the trigger is reached, not the count currently on hand. The purchasing clerk drafted a request for 5 after seeing the label, then held it pending verification. There is no supplier shortage and no purchase order to expedite.

The seal costs $3.25 each. The replacement seal consumed during the incident is valued at $3.25, and the technician labor is recorded separately. A draft expense note says $13.00 because it mistakenly multiplied the $3.25 unit cost by four seals. Four seals were not used in this event; one was used. The nearby $48.75 figure is the value of 15 seals at the standard price and refers to an earlier stock report, not an approved debit or customer charge. No billing transaction arises from these figures.

Safety and quality. The cell interlock remained functional throughout the events. The pressure warning caused the controls to pause the program before the tool change. The quality team verified the first three pieces after restart and then inspected the remaining 177 by the normal plan. All 180 met the drawing. The normal sample of three after restart is not a count of the whole shift's output; the final inspection record covers all 180. No parts were shipped before inspection release. The pressure dips do not create a quality routing trigger unless a nonconforming part is confirmed; the quality log lists zero nonconforming brackets.

Communications. At 15:35, the operator sent a message to the lead: “It felt as if we lost half the shift, but I am grateful the cell is running again.” The phrase “half the shift” is an estimate of experience, not a time entry. The scheduled shift was 480 minutes. Half would be 240 minutes, which is not supported by the time log. The actual recorded operator pauses totaled 28 minutes, and the maintenance technician logged 42 minutes. Another note says “3 alarms × 10 minutes = 30 minutes,” a rounded estimate; the itemized intervals total 28 minutes. The maintenance routing rule specifically uses technician labor rather than an estimate of total disruption.

Applicable queue rules. Maintenance receives a single corrective event if logged technician labor is more than 0.75 hours, or if a machine is declared unsafe to operate. Purchasing receives a request if usable spare seals are fewer than 10. Quality receives a case when any finished item is confirmed outside its drawing tolerance after inspection. Billing receives a case only for an approved customer amount of $50 or more. These triggers are independent. No machine safety declaration was made; the cell passed its operational check. There is no confirmed part failure, no purchasing shortage, and no customer amount. The team asks the reviewer, very politely, to compare 42 minutes with the threshold rather than use the accumulated monthly number or the rounded downtime estimate.

Appendix: arithmetic check. Technician time: 42 minutes ÷ 60 = 0.70 hours. Difference to 0.75 hours: 0.05 hours × 60 = 3 minutes. Monthly maintenance total: 0.20 + 0.30 + 0.70 = 1.20 hours, which is not the tested measure. Spare seals: 14 − 2 − 1 = 11, compared with a trigger of fewer than 10. Brackets: 176 + 4 = 180, with 0 rejected. The $13.00 draft seal expense is incorrect for this event; one seal at $3.25 was consumed. The isolated hose coupling is repaired and the cell has operated normally since restart.

Closing note. The operator, lead, maintenance technician, and quality inspector all supplied their notes promptly and with admirable courtesy. No one is being asked to accept blame for the equipment issue. This report is intended to route the record using the written definitions, rather than the size of the interruption as it felt on the floor. Typed from the notebook of Sven Castillo, who was coordinating a small order of brass adjustment knobs and a separate batch of steel spacers. The original note uses arrows, underlining, and several very polite reminders to “please check the denominator.” It has been expanded into a coherent record because the routing board uses different percentage and dollar thresholds for quality, billing, and shipping. The workshop is small enough that the same people help with packing and inspection, so the notes distinguish the two batches carefully.

“Good morning, everyone. Thank you so much for helping me reconcile Friday’s numbers. The brass adjustment-knob order was for 80 knobs. The job traveler reports 5 rejected knobs during turning, then 3 more rejected during final inspection. These are separate pieces, not repeat inspections of the same pieces; the rejected-parts tray labels show 8 different serial marks. The accepted quantity was 72. The customer shipment contained 72 knobs, exactly as the order required. The final tally is 80 started, 8 rejected, 72 accepted and shipped. Please do not use the first-board figure of 4 rejects; it was written before the final inspection found the additional four.”

“The quality rule on the board sends a batch to quality review when confirmed rejects are 10% or more of the started quantity. Here the calculation is 8 ÷ 80 = 0.10, which is 10%. The threshold includes exactly 10%; it is not ‘more than 10%.’ The eight rejected knobs are confirmed against the drawing and are not recoverable. The other 72 passed. A note on the tray says 9, but that includes one brass sample coupon that was never a finished knob and must not be counted as a ninth rejected unit. The coupon has no serial mark and was used to set the lathe tool.

“Shipment and invoice: 72 knobs at $4.75 each gives $342.00. Freight was $18.00, so the posted total was $360.00. The accepted order confirms those amounts. A packing worksheet temporarily added a $16.00 rush fee, but the customer did not request rush service and the fee was removed before posting. Billing reviews a posted customer discrepancy of at least $15. The posted discrepancy is $0 because the final invoice matches the accepted order. The removed $16.00 line is not a posted overcharge. A draft invoice showing $376.00 was saved before correction and was never sent. Please do not route the account to billing from the draft alone.

“The shipment left on September 5. The promise date was September 6, and the delivery receipt is dated September 6. The shipping desk’s delay rule applies only when the delivery receipt is later than the promise date by at least one calendar day. Difference: September 6 minus September 6 = 0 days. The carrier’s pickup scan says September 5 at 16:40; that is not the delivery date. A handwritten note saying ‘one day from pickup?’ compares two different events and does not create a delivery delay. Freight was accepted in good condition, with no shortage reported.”

“Separate steel spacer batch: work order for 40 pieces; all 40 passed, and all 40 shipped. The spacer drawing uses a 0.8 mm thickness tolerance. Those measurements belong to the spacer job, not the brass knob reject calculation. The steel order invoiced at $2.10 each, total $84.00. A different worksheet lists 80 brass knobs and 40 steel spacers together, with a combined planned value of $510.00. This is a planning total for two orders. It is not a billing discrepancy on the knob invoice.”

The note continues with the packing reconciliation. The brass batch was packed into three cartons: 30 knobs, 24 knobs, and 18 knobs. Thus 30 + 24 + 18 = 72 shipped. Each carton was sealed and weighed. The packing instruction calls for 12 knobs per inner tray. The first carton had two full trays and one tray of 6; the second had two full trays; the third had one full tray and one tray of 6. This gives 6 trays total: 12 + 12 + 6 + 12 + 12 + 12 + 6 is actually 72, with the listed tray breakdown corrected in the margin to 30, 24, and 18. The confusing first transcription said “six trays,” but the correct total is 7 trays, carrying 3 + 2 + 2 trays. Tray count is packaging and does not change the 72-piece shipment quantity.

The first quality checker opened 10 packages and saw no transit damage. The customer inspected 12 of the 72 delivered knobs and reported that all 12 turned smoothly. That sample is not evidence that all eight rejected shop pieces were shipped; the eight were physically retained for scrap before packing. The batch quality trigger uses confirmed shop rejects divided by started units, not customer returns divided by delivered units. The percentage is 8/80 rather than 8/72. Both calculations are visible in the arithmetic margin: 8/80 = 10%; 8/72 is approximately 11.1%. The written rule specifies started quantity as denominator, so 10% is controlling.

Material and purchasing notes. The brass stock rack began with 126 blanks. The knob work order consumed 80, leaving 46 blanks. Purchasing's reorder threshold is fewer than 45 usable blanks. Forty-six is one above the threshold, so no purchasing request is required. The cutter log also records 6 test cuts from a separate offcut; those test cuts were not blanks from the usable rack and must not be subtracted from 46. A chalk note gives “126 − 80 − 6 = 40,” but the 6 represents test cuts from scrap offcut, not usable rack inventory. The steel spacer stock is tracked separately and does not affect the brass threshold.

A supervisor initially asked whether the quality percentage should be treated as 9/80 because the sample coupon had been placed in the rejects tray. The serial-mark check confirms only eight finished knobs were rejected. The shop's written rule counts finished units that fail inspection; the coupon was never a finished unit. Another question was whether the denominator should be 72 because those are the units shipped. The rule explicitly says started quantity, so the 80-piece start is correct. The rejection count is exactly at the 10% trigger; it is neither below threshold nor dependent on rounding.

Applicable routing text copied into the notebook: Quality queue receives a batch at 10% or more confirmed rejects over started units. Billing queue receives a posted customer discrepancy of $15 or more. Shipping queue receives a delivery-delay case if the receipt is at least one calendar day after the promise date. Purchasing receives a request only below 45 usable brass blanks. The rules do not treat an unposted draft or a removed fee as an actual discrepancy. The two product orders remain separate even though they were packed on the same shift and reviewed by the same coordinator.

“Please route each record only where its rule is met. I appreciate the careful arithmetic, particularly the distinction between the eight rejected finished knobs and the sample coupon, and between the promised date and the pickup scan. The packing team was especially thoughtful in retaining the rejected parts and correcting the carton list before closing the job. I have attached the signed delivery receipt and the corrected invoice printout.”

End-of-shift cross-check, signed Sven C.: Brass knobs: 80 started − 8 rejected = 72 shipped. Quality rate: 8/80 = 10%. Accepted invoice: 72 × $4.75 + $18 = $360. Posted billing discrepancy: $0. Delivery lateness: 0 calendar days. Brass stock: 126 − 80 = 46 usable blanks; trigger is below 45.
