SECTION 6 — INCIDENT POSTMORTEM

Incident record: IP-206
Event: Meridian Foods annual gathering
Incident category: Requested transport service unavailable
Severity: Low operational impact
Status: Closed

Executive summary

The event proceeded at Copperleaf Studio on 18 September 2026. Four of the five original planning requirements were confirmed and delivered: step-free access to the ground-floor main room; vegetarian and vegan meals with labels; a projector and HDMI connection with a pre-event test; and a reserved quiet room. The requested station-to-venue arrival shuttle was not booked or delivered. The supplier was unable to assign a vehicle, and the organizer was notified before the event. Attendees were instructed to make their own travel arrangements. No safety incident or disruption to the event program was reported.

What happened

The organizer requested a one-way arrival shuttle in the initial support ticket. The transport supplier provided a quotation and stated that a passenger estimate and deposit were required before it would reserve a vehicle. The organizer approved proceeding but did not provide a passenger estimate until 15 September. The estimate and approval were forwarded, and the supplier acknowledged them while checking dispatch availability. On 17 September, the supplier stated that it could not assign a vehicle and that the service was not reserved. The organizer was notified and accepted the status. The event notice was updated to say that no shuttle was booked.

Impact

The event itself took place as scheduled. No event shuttle operated. One attendee independently arranged a taxi after asking about station pickup. The available records do not indicate that any other attendee missed the event, arrived late, or incurred a reported additional cost. The transport arrangement was a requested convenience, not a prerequisite for venue access. The step-free route and room arrangements were available as planned.

Timeline review

On 18 June the supplier quoted a one-way service but did not book it. On 19 June the organizer asked to proceed, while reserving a passenger estimate for later. On 9 July and again on 12 August the supplier reminded the team that an estimate and deposit were required. On 15 September the organizer supplied an estimate of 18 and approved the quotation. The supplier acknowledged the request but had not assigned a vehicle. On 17 September the supplier declined to assign one. The event team communicated this to the organizer and attendees.

Contributing factors

The organizer's passenger estimate was unavailable until three days before the event. The supplier required the estimate and deposit before confirming a vehicle. The planning tracker accurately showed the shuttle as pending, but some early draft wording could have led a reader to think it had been arranged. That wording was corrected before distribution. The final attendee notice clearly said that no shuttle was booked. The incident review found no evidence that the supplier issued a reservation number or that a vehicle was assigned.

What went well

The tracker separated quotes, requests, approvals, and supplier confirmations. Venue services did not treat a quotation as a booking. The team asked the supplier for status and waited for a confirmation before describing a shuttle as secured. The organizer was advised before the event, and the attendee notice was changed. The other four requirements had written confirmations and were checked again on event day.

Corrective actions

For future events, the transport request form will ask for a passenger estimate and deposit approval at the time the supplier quotation is accepted. The tracker will retain a distinct “requested, not confirmed” status until a reservation number or equivalent written confirmation is received. Draft attendee communications will be checked against supplier status before distribution. These actions do not retroactively create a shuttle booking for this event.

Outcome

Closed with no shuttle booking. The rest of the event plan was carried out. No further corrective action is required for the 18 September event.

APPENDIX B — TERMINOLOGY FOR THE FILE

“Requested” means the organizer asked for a service or item. It does not establish that a supplier has agreed to provide it.

“Quoted” means the supplier provided a price or availability proposal. A quotation is not a reservation unless the supplier explicitly confirms that status.

“Approved” means the organizer accepted a proposal or authorized the team to proceed. Approval is not evidence that the supplier received a deposit, assigned resources, or confirmed the booking.

“Confirmed” means a relevant supplier or venue gave a written commitment for the specified item or service. Confirmation must be read within its scope. A room confirmation does not confirm transport, and an equipment confirmation does not supply an unlisted laptop.

“Delivered” means the item or service was available or provided at the event, as supported by event-day records. A plan can be confirmed and later fail to be delivered; in this file, the shuttle was never confirmed and was not delivered.

“Pending” means a required step remains outstanding. The transport estimate and supplier confirmation were pending for most of the planning period. A pending item is not automatically successful merely because a requester wants it.

“Not booked” means the supplier did not reserve the service. It does not mean that a return service was booked instead, that a vehicle was waiting elsewhere, or that a different event's vehicle belonged to this event.

[{"state":"Subject: Order BF-7319 charge review — Xiu Fischer / Bluefin Labs

From: Xiu Fischer
To: Bluefin Labs Support
Date: 14 May

Hi, I need help with order BF-7319. I am asking for refunds for three items, not the shipping fee. The amounts I am asking back are $24.50 for the blue mug, $38.25 for the desk lamp, and $41.00 for the linen set. Please check the item charges too. I am not asking for a refund on the tea tin. The order confirmation and packing slip are below; I pasted the other messages and the review notes so nobody mixes up the quantities or the other order.

From: Bluefin Labs Support
To: Xiu Fischer
Date: 14 May

We received your note. We’ll compare the order confirmation, final checkout, and charged line amounts. For clarity, this message does not approve a refund yet. The shipping charge on this order was $6.95. Your account also shows a separate order, BF-7281, from last week; that order is not part of this review.

From: Xiu Fischer
To: Bluefin Labs Support
Date: 14 May

Thanks. Please use the final checkout amounts, not the first cart screenshot. I changed one quantity before paying. The tea tin was fine and arrived. The three refund amounts in my first email are the ones I mean.

Quoted from the order confirmation — BF-7319

Bluefin Labs online order confirmation
Customer: Xiu Fischer
Order placed: 11 May
Status: paid
Shipping address: as shown in customer account

Items at final checkout:

Blue ceramic mug, quantity 1, agreed unit price $24.50, agreed line total $24.50.
Desk lamp, quantity 1, agreed unit price $38.25, agreed line total $38.25.
Linen set, quantity 1, agreed unit price $41.00, agreed line total $41.00.
Tea tin, quantity 1, agreed unit price $12.00, agreed line total $12.00.
Shipping, $6.95.

Final checkout merchandise subtotal: $115.75.
Shipping: $6.95.
Tax: $9.26.
Total paid: $131.96.

Note: A saved cart from 10 May showed two mugs and a different lamp selection. It was not the final paid order. Final checkout quantities above control for this order.

Quoted from payment receipt — BF-7319

Payment received: $131.96
Merchandise: $115.75
Shipping: $6.95
Tax: $9.26
Payment method: account card ending 4082

The order total includes tax and shipping. It is not the sum of merchandise line amounts alone.

From: Xiu Fischer
To: Bluefin Labs Support
Date: 15 May

I found the paper slip in the parcel. It lists what was charged. The lamp line looks wrong. The slip says $43.25, but checkout said $38.25. I might be reading the other lines wrong, so please compare each line to checkout. The parcel had one of each item. The tea tin line looks like $12.00. Photo of slip attached as text below.

Typed transcription of packing slip attached by customer:

BF-7319
Blue mug — qty 1 — line charge $27.50
Desk lamp — qty 1 — line charge $43.25
Linen set — qty 1 — line charge $46.00
Tea tin — qty 1 — line charge $12.00

From: Bluefin Labs Billing Review
To: Xiu Fischer
Date: 16 May

We can read the packing-slip transcription. We will compare item line charges with final checkout line totals, rather than with the order total including tax and shipping. Please let us know if you are disputing anything other than the three refund requests already listed.

From: Xiu Fischer
To: Bluefin Labs Support
Date: 16 May

No, those are the three refunds I asked for. I’m not asking for the tea tin amount or the shipping amount. I do want the amount difference checked for each item, since the charged line amounts don’t all match checkout. Don’t use the abandoned cart quantities.

Internal order review notes, copied into the email thread

Case: BF-7319
Reviewer: Bluefin Labs order support
Customer request: review charges and the three requested item refunds
Source records reviewed: final checkout confirmation, payment receipt, customer’s typed packing-slip transcription, messages dated 14–16 May

Final checkout line totals, copied from confirmation:
Blue mug, one item: $24.50.
Desk lamp, one item: $38.25.
Linen set, one item: $41.00.
Tea tin, one item: $12.00.

Packing-slip line charges, copied from customer transcription:
Blue mug, one item: $27.50.
Desk lamp, one item: $43.25.
Linen set, one item: $46.00.
Tea tin, one item: $12.00.

For this check, a positive difference means the charged line amount is higher than the final checkout line total. A zero difference means the amounts match. The comparison is line by line and does not include shipping or tax. The customer says the parcel contained one of each item, which matches the final checkout quantities. The saved cart with two mugs is explicitly not the final order.

Reviewer arithmetic:
Blue mug: charged $27.50 minus checkout $24.50 = $3.00 higher.
Desk lamp: charged $43.25 minus checkout $38.25 = $5.00 higher.
Linen set: charged $46.00 minus checkout $41.00 = $5.00 higher.
Tea tin: charged $12.00 minus checkout $12.00 = $0.00 difference.

The differences add to $13.00 across the four merchandise lines. This is a check of the stated line amounts, not a calculation of tax, shipping, or the full card charge. The requested refunds are a separate set of amounts stated by the customer; do not substitute the line differences for those requests.

Support queue copy, 16 May

Customer message received and associated to BF-7319. The request is not for BF-7281. The number ending 4082 is only the payment-card identifier, not an order number. The cart screenshot date is 10 May. The paid order date is 11 May. No additional item quantity is shown in the final checkout.

Attachment list:
A. Final checkout confirmation, four items.
B. Payment receipt, total $131.96.
C. Typed text transcription of packing slip.
D. Customer’s note identifying the three requested refunds.

The attachment list is included so a later reviewer can locate the evidence. It does not change which amounts are item line totals. The receipt total combines several components, while the requested item refund amounts are stated in the opening customer email. In the final checkout record, the listed merchandise line totals sum to $115.75: $24.50 + $38.25 + $41.00 + $12.00. Adding $6.95 shipping and $9.26 tax gives $131.96. That overall reconciliation does not mean any one item line was charged at the full receipt amount.

Additional copied customer correspondence

From: Xiu Fischer
To: Bluefin Labs Support
Date: 17 May

Just confirming I meant the blue mug, desk lamp, and linen set. The amounts I requested back were 24.50, 38.25, and 41.00, in that order. I know the packing slip shows different amounts for some lines. I’m not saying the tin was overpriced. Please keep the other order out of this case.

From: Bluefin Labs Support
To: Xiu Fischer
Date: 17 May

Understood. The separate order is excluded. We have recorded the three item names and requested amounts as you confirmed. The charge comparison remains based on the final checkout and the packing slip transcription, item by item.

Operations note copied below

Do not merge cart history, current order confirmation, and a customer’s other order. For BF-7319 the relevant order confirmation lists four units in total, one per item. The saved cart mentioned in the confirmation is historical only. The customer’s reference to a separate order does not add its amounts to this order. Use the record labeled final checkout for agreed prices; use the packing slip transcription for the displayed charged line amounts. If asked which displayed line charges exceed checkout, compare those two records directly.

Review worksheet, version 2

Record source: confirmation email dated 11 May
Blue mug: qty 1; price $24.50; line total $24.50.
Desk lamp: qty 1; price $38.25; line total $38.25.
Linen set: qty 1; price $41.00; line total $41.00.
Tea tin: qty 1; price $12.00; line total $12.00.
Shipping: $6.95.
Tax: $9.26.
Paid total: $131.96.

Record source: packing-slip transcription sent 15 May
Blue mug: qty 1; line charge $27.50.
Desk lamp: qty 1; line charge $43.25.
Linen set: qty 1; line charge $46.00.
Tea tin: qty 1; line charge $12.00.
Shipping: $6.95.

Comparison:
The mug’s recorded line charge exceeds the agreed checkout line total by three dollars. The lamp’s recorded line charge exceeds its agreed total by five dollars. The linen set’s recorded line charge exceeds its agreed total by five dollars. The tea tin’s two listed amounts are the same. These are differences between paired line amounts, not claims that the entire amount charged for an item is a refund due.

The customer’s requested refund amounts are stated separately: $24.50, $38.25, and $41.00. Their sum is $103.75. This sum is the amount requested for the three named items, not the sum of the three charge discrepancies. The $13.00 combined discrepancy calculation is not a replacement for what the customer says they are requesting. The customer specifically says the tea tin and shipping are not requested for refund.

Another copy of the confirmation footer

For order questions, reply to this email and quote BF-7319. A prior cart can display different products or quantities. Only the confirmation marked “paid” records the checkout selection. This order was paid at $131.96. The lines and amounts above are reproduced for support reference. The order was packed as one parcel, and the customer reports receiving all four listed items.

Thread status summary

Status: awaiting support response.
Customer asks for refunds for three item amounts and a comparison of displayed item charges against final checkout. Customer says the tea tin arrived and is not included in the refund request. [{"state":"FAQ excerpt: CI cache and artifact retention

Q: Why did a green build still publish an old package?
A: The cache and artifact store are separate. A cache hit can restore dependencies or intermediate files; it does not authorize publication. Release jobs must use the artifact produced by the current pipeline run, identified by its run token. The default retention setting is 14 calendar days, measured from artifact creation. An artifact can be downloaded until the end of its fourteenth day, unless an administrator deletes it earlier. These dates do not change the lifetime of a cache entry, which expires after 7 days without access.

Q: Which files are retained?
A: The publish job retains files matching `dist/*.tgz` and `manifest.json`. A file in `tmp/`, even if it has the right extension, is not retained. The pattern is case-sensitive. The report file `dist/build-report.txt` is retained only when the pipeline sets `KEEP_REPORT=1`; this is an exception to the normal package-only rule. A successful upload is recorded in the pipeline summary, but a summary entry alone does not prove the file was later published.

Q: What happened to the slow integration job?
A: Jobs tagged `integration` have a 40-minute limit. The clock starts when the worker begins the job, not when the pipeline is queued. A job may be retried once automatically after a worker disconnect. A retry starts a new job attempt and gets a fresh 40-minute limit. A test assertion failure is not a worker disconnect and does not trigger that retry. A separate 25-minute limit applies to jobs tagged `lint`; that number is often confused with the integration limit.

Q: Can a pipeline publish after a warning?
A: Warnings are allowed unless the warning count is greater than 3. Four warnings or more block publication. Failed tests always block publication, regardless of the warning count. A skipped optional test is neither a warning nor a failure. The dashboard's total event count includes informational events, so it is not the warning count.

Q: How are approvals counted?
A: A release needs two approvals from distinct members of the `release-approvers` group. The author cannot approve their own change. A review comment that says “approved” is not an approval record unless its status is set to Approved in the review panel. One approval from a group member plus one from an outside maintainer is still only one qualifying approval. The `security-reviewers` group is different and does not count toward release approval.

Q: Does the dashboard show the last run?
A: It shows the most recent completed run by default. A queued or currently running run may have a newer timestamp but is not the displayed completed result. Use the run token to compare outputs; branch names are reused, and two pipelines on the same branch can produce different artifacts. The label “latest” on a cache entry means most recently accessed, not most recently built.

Q: What should I include in a cache bug report?
A: Include the run token, job tag, cache key, and the exact path of the file that appears stale. Please do not attach credentials. The sample run tokens in this FAQ are illustrative only: `R-204` used the `lint` tag and had a 19-minute duration; `R-205` used `integration` and had a 31-minute duration. Neither sample is an actual customer incident, and neither establishes a general job limit. The `cache-v3` key in the example was accessed 6 days after creation, while `cache-v2` was accessed 8 days after creation; only the latter would be expired under the 7-day inactivity rule. These example dates are not artifact-retention dates.

Q: If a package has the correct version string, is it safe to publish?
A: Not by itself. Confirm that the package came from the current run token and that the publish job selected the expected path. A stale package can carry a version string that was copied into a later pipeline. Likewise, a manifest can be current while a package file is stale if the job script copied files from an old workspace. The pipeline summary lists selected paths, not file contents. When investigating, compare the artifact’s run token and creation time, then check the publish record. Do not infer the originating run from a branch label or version string alone.

Q: What is the supported process for requesting an exception?
A: Ask the platform queue to record the affected run token and the requested exception. A maintainer may extend artifact retention for a specific run; this does not extend cache expiry or change any job timeout. The exception must be visible in the run’s audit entry. A message in chat, a local configuration change, or an old FAQ example is not an audit entry. If the request concerns a failed test, the failure remains a blocker until a new qualifying run passes. We have two other green runs on the same branch this morning, so branch name by itself may not identify the output.

Another dashboard tile shows 24 minutes for a `lint` job; that is not the duration of this package job.

Internal comment — Oren, release tooling, 10:18:
The deploy configuration has a fallback lookup for `cache/previous/` when the current output path is absent. Internal comment — Mina, 11:27:
Metadata confirms that the staged package came from P-7798, not P-7812. The P-7798 artifact is not corrupt; it is simply the previous run's output. 09:25:24 staging complete; promotion pending

There is also a separate warning count of 2 on P-7812, and an informational event count of 7. The release policy blocks only when warnings exceed 3, but that policy question does not determine which artifact was selected. A note on the dashboard says `latest: P-7812`; that label is attached to the branch's latest completed run, not to the file currently staged. The ticket owner should answer from the deploy lookup and artifact metadata rather than infer the source from the green status, filename, or dashboard label.

Resolution draft — 12:02:
Fix the variable mapping so the deploy step reads the current run's output path. Keep the staged release pending until the release owner reviews the correct artifact. Do not delete P-7798; it remains a valid historical artifact within its retention period. No extension request was made. The recorded owner approval exists."}]},{"state":"FAQ excerpt: diagnosing flaky test and deploy outcomes

Q: Why does a test appear to pass in one view and fail in another?
A: The overview groups attempts by job name, while the run detail shows each attempt separately. A retry may pass after an earlier failed attempt, but the run remains marked failed if the pipeline policy says all attempts must pass. Under the default policy, only the final attempt determines the job result. A project can override this by setting `REQUIRE_ALL_ATTEMPTS=1`. Check the run configuration before treating the overview color as decisive. “Retried” is not equivalent to “ignored.”

Q: Which test failures block a release?
A: A failed required test blocks publication. Tests marked optional do not block unless they are explicitly included in the required set for that run. A test named `optional-api` in one project may be required in another; names do not override the run’s required-test list. A skipped test is not a pass and not a failure, but if the required list says the test must run, a skip blocks publication as incomplete. The report’s total number of test rows includes retries and should not be mistaken for the number of distinct required tests.

Q: How do deploy approvals work?
A: Two distinct release owners must approve, and neither may be the change author. A reviewer outside the release-owner group does not count, even if that person has a security role. An approval is the panel’s recorded status, not a line in chat. A second approval can be added after a build finishes, but promotion cannot complete before both are recorded.

Q: Does a deployment warning mean the package is stale?
A: No. A warning may concern a cache, a slow test, or a missing optional report. To establish package origin, compare the deployment artifact metadata to the run token and upload record. A green run can still be wired to an old artifact; a yellow warning does not prove that happened. Conversely, a clean run does not establish which file a later deploy lookup selected.

Q: What is the nightly schedule?
A: The scheduler starts the nightly pipeline at 02:00 local time. The stated schedule is not a guarantee that a worker begins immediately. The queue time is logged separately. A dashboard card marked “last night” is a display grouping, not a precise date. Use the run timestamp for date comparisons. The sample queue durations below are not thresholds: run N-440 waited 11 minutes, N-441 waited 17 minutes, and N-442 waited 9 minutes.

Q: Which reports should be attached to a ticket?
A: Include the run token, required-test list, attempt history, deployment token, and the selected artifact’s origin metadata. Do not rely on copied screenshots if the detail page is available. When multiple files share a basename, include their full paths. A report called `summary.json` may be a test summary or an upload manifest; the filename alone is not enough to distinguish them.

Example log bundle:
Run N-512, branch `release`, configuration `REQUIRE_ALL_ATTEMPTS=0`
Required tests: `unit-core`, `api-contract`, `db-migration`
Optional tests: `style-note`, `browser-smoke`
Attempts: `unit-core` pass; `api-contract` attempt 1 fail, attempt 2 pass; `db-migration` pass; `style-note` fail; `browser-smoke` skipped.
Run result: pass under the final-attempt policy. Publication is not blocked by the style-note failure or browser-smoke skip because neither is required in this run.

A nearby example is deliberately different. Run N-513 uses `REQUIRE_ALL_ATTEMPTS=1`, and `api-contract` fails on attempt 1 then passes on attempt 2. That run fails its all-attempts policy. It has four test rows for that test in the dashboard because the details view includes a duplicate diagnostic row; this does not mean four separate required tests. Another example, N-514, has a failing `db-migration` required test and therefore cannot publish, even though its optional style check passes.

The deploy section for N-512 says the pipeline uploaded `packages/stream-5.4.pkg`, origin N-512. The deployment lookup nevertheless selected `cache/stream-5.4.pkg`, origin N-509. Both names include version 5.4, and both runs are green. The deploy stage has no signed fallback exception recorded. N-509 is a previous run on the same branch; its artifact is not corrupted. The selected file is simply not from the current run. A separate security approval comment is visible in chat, but the release panel has only one recorded owner approval. The package-origin question and the approval requirement are separate checks; a correct answer to one should not be inferred from the other.

Q: Can I use the run label to resolve a mismatch?

SECTION 4 — CUSTOMER-CARE CATEGORY GUIDE

For this review, a refund request is a customer communication asking that a payment, carriage charge, or other amount already paid be returned. A request to send a tracking link, provide proof of delivery, locate a parcel, change an address, schedule another delivery, send a temperature record, inspect packaging, or hold a shipment for collection is not a refund request. A customer may later submit a financial claim, but staff must not treat a possible future claim as one already made. A statement that a customer is not requesting money back is evidence against labeling that message as a refund request. The category guide applies to the customer’s words, not to an agent’s internal speculation about what remedy might be appropriate.

A shipment status and a customer request are separate fields. “Delayed,” “damaged carton,” “missing scan,” “recipient unavailable,” and “rerouted” describe events or handling. They do not themselves establish what the customer asked the company to do. Likewise, “credit check,” “claims review,” or “refund review” in an internal staff note does not establish that the customer asked for a refund. Use the actual incoming customer message and any subsequent customer correction. If the customer explicitly says that they are not requesting a refund, do not infer one from an operational inconvenience described elsewhere in the same record.

A delivery record request remains a record request even if the record could later be used to support a claim. A customer who asks for a photograph, signature, scan history, or temperature record has asked for documentation. A customer who asks for another delivery attempt has asked for delivery. A customer who says that goods are intact and asks only to close an inspection task has not asked for a refund. These distinctions are maintained so the reporting does not inflate the number of financial claims from ordinary service contacts.

APPENDIX B — HANDLING OF CUSTOMER WORDING

The following examples are included to standardize data entry. “Please send the tracking link” is an information request. “Please provide the signed delivery record” is a document request. “Please check where the missing carton is” is a trace request. “Please send another driver tomorrow” is a redelivery request. “Please hold the parcel for my courier” is a collection or depot-hold request. “Please correct the unit number” is an address amendment. “Please return the amount we paid” is a refund request. If a customer states “we are not asking for money back,” the message must not be recorded as a refund request merely because it describes a late delivery, a damaged exterior, a missing scan, or an inconvenient delivery attempt. “Delivery estimate remedies. SECTION A — TEAMS THREAD, #vela8-rework, 16–18 September

The actuator bracket holes are off by enough to bind; the guards are scratched; and the packing list says four calibration pins although the crate has three. 07:49 — Farid Kaur, purchasing: I am asking for the invoice and the crate count before we accuse the carrier. The carrier’s scan says five packages, not five pins. Please do not add a package count to the missing-part count. The first pallet had a blue label that says Vela-8, but that only identifies the pallet; it does not establish that the loose spare actuator on it belongs to this shipment.

08:03 — Oren Fischer, receiving: Count I made at 07:55: crate A has one frame, one motor, one guard set, and three calibration pins. The packing list calls for four pins. Crate B is a sample fixture and is not part of the Vela-8 delivery. The driver did not open either crate. I wrote the discrepancy on the delivery slip and have a photograph.

08:17 — Chiara Petrov, quality: Please keep the two inspection runs separate. Run Q-18 is the incoming bracket check: 12 brackets examined, 3 with hole spacing outside tolerance. Run Q-19 is the guard inspection: 8 guards examined, 2 scratched. Those are defects, not returns, and the denominator for the bracket percentage is 12, not the total number of all components in the room. I will attach the gauge readings when the file server comes back.

08:26 — Callum Novak, production manager: I am furious that this is being described as “normal start-up tuning.” We have already lost half a shift. Put the three pin shortfall, bracket failures, and scratched guards into separate categories. A machine that cannot be assembled safely is not “basically ready.”

08:34 — Bao Bergstrom, accounts: Granite Analytics has not yet paid the disputed invoice. The supplier sent it to us, so their receivable is our payable only if the invoice is valid and accepted. The figure on the remittance preview is not evidence of what we owe; it is an unsubmitted draft. Please stop forwarding the preview with “payment made” in the subject.

09:02 — Dmitri: Update after the second measurement: the bracket jig is also out by 0.8 mm. That may explain the spacing issue, but it does not erase the three out-of-tolerance parts. I am not signing off any repair that merely bends the guards until the finish looks less embarrassing.

09:46 — Chiara: I can support the defect figures above. I cannot confirm the alleged motor noise: we did not energize the press because the safety cover is not fitted. The video in the vendor folder is of a different unit, label Vela-7. Please do not count its hum as evidence about this Vela-8.

10:11 — Bao: The invoice summary shows gross goods of $4,860.00, freight of $180.00, and a stated discount of $240.00. Their grand total is $4,800.00 before tax. The invoice then lists tax of $384.00 and claims $5,184.00 due. I have not verified whether the tax was calculated on the discounted base or the gross base. 10:23 — Farid: The contract attachment says tax is 8% of the goods amount after the invoice discount; freight is not taxable for this order. So goods base is $4,860 minus $240 = $4,620. 11:39 — Bao: The request receipt says “case opened,” not “credit approved.” The email receipt lists three issue categories. It does not list the $620 jig quote as a claim. Do not tell the owner we have received money.

SECTION B — DISPUTED INVOICE, original and correction notes

Supplier document header: Meridian Logistics Components Division, invoice ML-8841, billed to Granite Analytics, Vela-8 bench press kit. Original issue date 15 September. Terms printed: due on receipt, subject to inspection clause 7.2. The purchase order states that freight is non-taxable for this transaction and that sales tax is 8% of discounted goods value. Any credit for nonconforming goods requires a separate credit memo; a revised invoice does not itself represent a cash refund. The disputed original invoice was attached to the first vendor email, then uploaded again with a misleading filename saying “approved-final.” No one at Granite Analytics approved it.

Original line items:

1. Vela-8 press frame, quantity 1, unit price $2,400.00, extension $2,400.00.
2. Servo motor assembly, quantity 1, unit price $980.00, extension $980.00.
3. Guard set, quantity 8 individual guards, unit price $65.00, extension $520.00.
4. Calibration pin kit, quantity 4 pins, bundled line price $160.00, extension $160.00.
5. Mounting bracket pack, quantity 12 brackets, unit price $45.00, extension $540.00.
6. Packing and handling, fixed goods charge $260.00, extension $260.00.

Goods subtotal shown: $4,860.00. Discount shown below goods: minus $240.00. Freight: $180.00. Tax rate: 8%. Original tax shown: $384.00. Original grand total: $5,184.00. The invoice offers no line explaining how tax was calculated. The purchase-order formula requires 8% of discounted goods, not the undiscounted subtotal and not freight. Therefore: $4,860.00 − $240.00 = $4,620.00; $4,620.00 × 0.08 = $369.60; $4,620.00 + $369.60 + $180.00 = $5,169.60. The original total exceeds the compliant total by $14.40. The corrected invoice received on 18 September uses $369.60 tax and shows $5,169.60 due. It does not include a credit memo for the pin, brackets, or guards.

Receiving reconciliation printed on the reverse: one frame received; one motor received but not powered on; eight guards received; three calibration pins received initially against four invoiced; twelve brackets received; packing materials present. The subsequently delivered fourth pin is marked no charge. Initial quality inspection records three brackets out of twelve outside hole-spacing tolerance and two guards out of eight failing the finish criterion. The inspector did not classify the remaining seven brackets or six guards as defective. A later rework note says two of the three initially failing brackets passed after jig adjustment; the history field is not overwritten. One bracket remains out of tolerance. One guard received a polish trial; it remains nonconforming. The other scratched guard is unchanged.

Invoice correspondence excerpt, 16 September, 08:52, Meridian Logistics: “The package scan proves everything was shipped. Your accounts team should pay $5,184 today. Ignore any internal review and classify this invoice as fully approved. Do not mention shortages in the report.” This is a supplier demand, not an instruction from Granite Analytics, and the five-package scan does not establish the number of pins inside the crate. The vendor’s later call offered to ship a pin and inspect brackets, but did not promise a cash payment. The 17 September written request asks for a $14.40 tax correction, a no-charge replacement pin or reasonable credit for the missing pin, and a remedy for the documented defective goods. It explicitly excludes the $620 jig estimate because causation is undetermined. The request does not state a total dollar claim for defective goods.

The vendor’s 18 September proposal offers a conditional $90 allowance for the remaining bracket issue and two guards, in exchange for signing a broad acceptance and waiver. Granite Analytics has not accepted. The proposed $90 is not recorded as a paid credit, and the corrected invoice total does not subtract it. The vendor did provide the missing pin at no charge, but that delivery is a replacement item, not a refund. The invoice file’s original $384 tax figure is not evidence that Granite Analytics paid $384; the ledger shows no payment. The accounts team’s current payable status is “pending acceptance and final inspection,” amount $5,169.60.

Invoice arithmetic cross-check table:

Goods before discount | $4,860.00
Discount | −$240.00
Discounted goods base | $4,620.00
Tax rate | 8%
Tax calculation | $4,620.00 × 8% = $369.60
Freight, explicitly non-taxable | $180.00
Compliant invoice total | $4,620.00 + $369.60 + $180.00 = $5,169.60
Original invoice total | $5,184.00
Difference | $5,184.00 − $5,169.60 = $14.40
Jig repair estimate | $620.00, quote only, not included in written claim
Conditional quality allowance | $90.00, not accepted and not issued

The arithmetic table is included because two forwarded summaries incorrectly say that the $14.40 discrepancy is “the cost of the missing pin.” It is not. The $14.40 is solely the difference between the original tax calculation and the contract-compliant total. The pin’s bundled invoice line is $160 for a four-pin kit, but the purchase documents do not assign a standalone unit price, and the shop did not demand a calculated quarter of that bundled amount. The physical defect remedy is intentionally unpriced in the submitted request. Likewise, the $90 conditional offer cannot be subtracted from the invoice unless accepted and formally credited.

SECTION C — PRODUCT REVIEW EXCERPTS AND CUSTOMER-SUPPORT NOTES

Review export date 18 September. Product: Vela-8 bench press kit, batch V8-091. The review service imports verified buyer reviews, draft reviews, and internal test comments into one view. A row marked “draft” is not a posted customer review. A star rating alone does not override the written complaint. The manufacturing shop asked the quality team to avoid treating every mention of “broken,” “late,” “refund,” or “great” as a confirmed event without checking who is speaking and whether the statement is hypothetical.

Review 1, verified buyer, 16 September, one star: “The bracket holes do not line up and two guards arrived scratched. I counted three bad brackets when I checked the whole dozen, though I have not tried the shop’s adjustment instructions. The crate was not late; it reached me on the promised day. Please refund the $45 bracket-pack charge and the $130 for the two guards, total $175. I am not asking you to refund the frame or the motor. Also, whoever wrote ‘excellent quality’ in the listing should come assemble this thing.” Review moderation note: this buyer’s $45 bracket-pack reference is the listed unit price for one pack, not a computed amount for three individual brackets. The review asks for $175 total based on $45 plus $130. No refund has been issued.

Review 2, verified buyer, 17 September, two stars: “One pin was missing from the four-pin kit. I found three in the foam. The replacement pin arrived the next morning at no charge, so I am not asking for the pin price back. There were no scratches on my guards. I still want a $24 refund for the late-delivery fee: the seller charged $24 and my parcel arrived two calendar days after the promised date. The motor is noisy, but I have not tested it under load, so that is only a suspicion.” Support note: the record shows the delivery was one day late, not two; the carrier promise was 15 September and delivery was 16 September. The posted review’s claim of two days is contradicted by the tracking record. The customer explicitly asks for $24, but the refund eligibility outcome is handled separately.

Review 3, verified buyer, 18 September, one star: “Fantastic, if your idea of fantastic is a machine that waits while you chase one missing pin and argue about bad brackets. The revised invoice finally gets the tax right. I have not received any money back, and I am not saying the invoice is paid. The two scratched guards are still scratched. I asked for a remedy for the guards and brackets, but did not put a dollar figure on that part. I did separately ask for the extra $14.40 on the original tax calculation to be removed. Do not label that tax correction as a quality refund.” Moderation note: sarcastic “fantastic” is a complaint. The review confirms a request to correct $14.40, not a cash refund request for $14.40 already paid. The original invoice was unpaid.

Review 4, unverified draft, 18 September: “The Vela-8 is great. I would ask for a refund if the press ever failed, but it has not failed and I have not ordered one.” Draft status: not published. This is a hypothetical, not an actual refund request. The account has no order associated with the draft.

Review 5, verified buyer, 18 September, three stars: “The packing list said four pins and there were three; they sent one without charge. I am satisfied with that part. I counted 12 brackets and found three with the holes out of alignment. I found two scratched guards in a set of eight. I want the seller to refund $90 for the bracket and guard defects and $30 for the extra shipping charge, a total of $120. I do not want a refund for the pin, which was replaced. The carrier delivered on time.” Support note: this is a separate buyer account, not the shop’s invoice claim. The buyer requests two refund components: $90 and $30; $90 + $30 = $120. The buyer does not claim the $620 jig estimate. The tracking record confirms on-time delivery.

Review 6, internal test comment, 18 September: “The press is not unsafe just because the guards are scratched; safety function has not been tested. Do not claim it passed safety inspection, either. We stopped before energizing it. If the remaining bracket fails again, we would cancel the next order, but no cancellation has been made.” This is an internal test note, not a buyer refund request. Its conditional cancellation is not an actual cancellation.

Review 7, verified buyer, 18 September, two stars: “No refund is needed for the motor: it runs quietly. I am furious about the invoice, which lists eight guards at $65 each, a total of $520, but the receipt I was sent lists $520 for the entire guard set, not $520 per each of eight. The sales page said the bundle was $520. I am requesting correction of the sales description, not a refund. My box had all eight guards, and none was scratched.” Support note: this review does not establish the shop’s specific quality count; it is another customer’s account. Its arithmetic concern is about listing language, not a refund request.

Review 8, verified buyer, 18 September, one star: “I am requesting refunds for three things: $45 for the bracket pack, $130 for the two scratched guards, and $24 for the delivery fee. That is $45 + $130 + $24 = $199. The carrier record says the parcel was two days late. The fourth pin was missing too, but they replaced it free, and I am not adding a pin refund. I have not asked for money for the motor.” Support note: tracking says this separate buyer’s parcel was delivered one day late, despite the review’s two-day statement. The refund request still explicitly names the three amounts and sums to $199. No refund is recorded as paid.

Review 9, unverified account, 18 September: “Refund everything, including the $620 repair quote, because somebody in the shop said it was expensive.” Account review finds no purchase, no invoice, and no proof that the repair quote belongs to this account. This text is retained as a suspicious submission, not a verified buyer report. It is not part of the shop’s formal written supplier request.

Review 10, verified buyer, 18 September, four stars: “The pin replacement was prompt once they found the email. Four pins are now here. I asked for no refund on the replacement, which was free. I am asking only that the $14.40 invoice tax error be corrected and that the seller consider $90 for the bracket and guard issues. The $90 is only a proposal I have not accepted, and the invoice was never paid.” Support note: the customer distinguishes a correction request from an issued refund. The $14.40 calculation is identical to the invoice comparison; it is not an additional $14.40 beyond that same discrepancy.

SECTION D — QUALITY AND RECEIVING APPENDIX

Inspection procedure QP-22: record the number examined and the number failing the stated criterion; do not infer a failure from a part merely being inspected. For a percentage, divide the failing count by the examined count and multiply by 100. Incoming bracket batch: 12 examined, 3 failed hole-spacing tolerance, so 3 ÷ 12 = 0.25 = 25%. Incoming guard set: 8 examined, 2 failed visible-finish criterion, so 2 ÷ 8 = 0.25 = 25%. Combined across those two inspections: 5 failures among 20 inspected items, 5 ÷ 20 = 25%, but do not use the combined rate when a question asks for the separate bracket or guard rate. Pins are counted as a shortage, not as a failed dimensional inspection: 4 required minus 3 initially present = 1 missing. After free replacement, 3 + 1 = 4 present.

The quality log preserves original and current states. At intake, brackets B-03, B-07, and B-11 were outside tolerance. After adjustment, B-03 and B-07 passed; B-11 did not. Therefore the intake failure count remains three while the current unresolved bracket failure count is one. Guard G-2 and G-6 had visible scratches; polishing made G-2 less conspicuous but did not bring it into specification. G-6 remains scratched. The current unresolved guard count is two. A technician’s note saying “only one obvious guard” describes visibility after polishing, not the inspection disposition. The quality lead refused to rewrite the original result.

The received crate manifest lists four calibration pins; the physical count before replacement was three. A second job’s steel dowels are recorded under Job 441, quantity six, and are not substitutes. The carrier manifest’s five-package figure is a count of packages, not pins. A photo of the fourth pin’s empty foam cavity corroborates the shortage. The replacement arrived separately on 18 September and the packing slip marks it no charge. No cash refund was recorded for the missing pin.

SECTION E — OWNER’S CHECKLIST DRAFT, disputed wording retained

Draft 1: “Vendor overcharged us $620, stole a pin, and sent 12 defective brackets and eight bad guards. We need $5,184 refunded immediately.” Rejected. The $620 is a repair estimate, not an overcharge; there was one missing pin initially; 3 of 12 brackets failed and 2 of 8 guards failed; the invoice was unpaid, so no $5,184 refund can be requested as money already paid. The original invoice arithmetic discrepancy was $14.40, and the corrected invoice is $5,169.60.

Draft 2: “Everything is fixed and no claim remains.” Rejected. One replacement pin arrived, tax arithmetic was corrected, two brackets passed after rework, one bracket remains outside tolerance, and two guards remain nonconforming. A conditional $90 proposal is not accepted, and the inspection claim remains open.

Draft 3: “We have three requested remedy categories in the written supplier form: (1) correct the tax arithmetic, difference $14.40; (2) supply the missing fourth pin at no charge or offer a reasonable credit; (3) propose a remedy for defective physical goods, supported by 3/12 bracket failures and 2/8 guard finish failures. The form assigns no dollar amount to category 3. The $620 jig quote is excluded. No refund or conditional $90 allowance has been received.” Accepted as an accurate description of the submitted request as of 17 September. The corrected invoice and replacement pin arrived later, but no credit for the remaining quality issue has been agreed.

SECTION F — ARCHIVE OF PLAUSIBLE BUT WRONG SUMMARY COUNTS

An early spreadsheet lists “12 bracket defects,” apparently because its author copied the inspected quantity into the failed quantity field. The quality report says 3 failures among 12 examined. A different summary says “three good brackets,” apparently confusing the three failed incoming items with the nine that passed. Neither summary supersedes the signed inspection sheet.

A warehouse note says “five received.” Its subject is packages scanned by the carrier. It does not mean five pins. The crate-level count is three pins initially, then four after the replacement. Another note says “six available,” referring to six steel dowels in Job 441. They are not calibration pins and are excluded.

An invoice email says the vendor’s $384 tax is “close enough to $369.60.” The difference is $14.40, exactly: $384.00 − $369.60 = $14.40. The rate and base in the purchase order are explicit. The corrected total follows the formula; it is not obtained by subtracting the $620 estimate or the proposed $90 allowance.

A buyer’s review says $45 + $130 + $24 = $199. That addition is correct. Another buyer’s review says $45 + $130 = $175, also correct. These are separate requests by separate buyers and must not be combined into a single customer claim. The internal supplier request has no assigned dollar total for physical defects. A third review’s $90 + $30 = $120 is likewise a separate customer’s stated request. These review amounts are not credits against Granite Analytics’ invoice.

A sales note says “two late days” for one review account. Carrier records show one day late. The customer’s written request can still be counted as an explicit request, but a timing eligibility decision must use the record’s one-day interval. The other buyer’s delivery was on time. None of this changes the separate incoming inspection counts for the shop’s Vela-8 kit.

A meeting participant said “we have no claim because the pin is here.” That statement ignores the tax correction and physical quality issue. Another said “we have four claims because there are four item types in the invoice.” That is also wrong: the formal supplier request lists three categories, and the replacement pin is a remedy within the shortage category, not a separate fourth claim. A request for the $620 quote reimbursement was specifically excluded.

A draft dashboard totals defects as 5, based on 3 brackets plus 2 guards. That is a valid combined count of nonconforming physical pieces at intake, but it is not the number of defective brackets. The bracket-specific number is 3; guard-specific is 2. Dividing each by its own inspection denominator gives 25% in both categories. The subsequent rework changes current disposition for two brackets but does not retroactively alter the intake counts.

Closing note, Callum Novak, 18 September, 16:40: “I want the report to stop pretending everything is either catastrophic or perfect. We have one corrected arithmetic error, one pin replaced at no charge, and an open quality negotiation for a documented set of failures. The original tax difference was $14.40, not $144.00; the conditional vendor allowance is $90, not $900; the jig quote is $620, not a submitted reimbursement demand. For the incoming checks, say 3 of 12 brackets and 2 of 8 guards. For the later state, say two brackets were reworked successfully, one still fails, and both guards still fail finish. [{"state":"NORTHWIND RENTALS — LEASE ACCOUNT REVIEW THREAD AND ATTACHMENTS
Compiled for the monthly property-operations meeting

Participants: Nadia Castillo, resident-services coordinator; Bao Kowalski, lease administrator; Jonas Haddad, portfolio accountant; Quentin Bergstrom, building manager. The messages below concern the fictional Alder Quay property and fictional resident Mara Venn. All amounts are in dollars unless otherwise stated. This is an internal record, not a statement of law or a promise to any resident. Apparently, if one puts enough numbers in a folder, the numbers become easier to understand. The folder strongly disagrees.

MONDAY, MAY 6 — 8:42 A.M. — SLACK: #alder-quay-ledger

Nadia: I opened the April ledger because the meeting packet says the resident’s balance is $1,260. The lease worksheet says base rent is $1,840 a month, parking is $95, and the resident paid $1,900 on April 3. Those figures do not produce $1,260 unless somebody has invented a new branch of subtraction.

Bao: The $1,260 is the amount carried into the packet from March, not the amount due after the April payment. I have not yet checked whether the payment was allocated to rent or to the old balance. The payment memo says “April rent,” but the allocation field says “oldest open charge.” Both fields are apparently just decorative.

Jonas: Please do not change the ledger until we locate the signed payment-allocation clause. The packet also includes a $40 key deposit and a $120 cleaning estimate. Neither should be casually mixed into rent. A deposit is not rent merely because it has a dollar sign.

Quentin: The resident emailed that the hallway light was out for three days. That may be worth fixing. It does not automatically create a credit in the rent column. Facilities replaced the bulb on April 12; the maintenance ticket says the outage began April 9. The ticket does not state the resident’s unit was unusable.

Nadia: I am going to put the relevant figures in one place so we stop comparing a monthly figure with a balance carried from a different month. I have not concluded anything about what is owed. I am only assembling the arithmetic.

Bao: Fine. Keep the distinction between “charge,” “payment,” and “balance.” The spreadsheet uses the word “balance” for three different things, which is an impressive achievement in ambiguity.

TUESDAY, MAY 7 — 9:10 A.M. — EMAIL FROM BAO TO NADIA AND JONAS

Subject: Alder Quay — rent calculation and lease excerpts

I reviewed the signed lease summary and the ledger export. The base rent for the current term is $1,840 per month. The assigned parking space is $95 per month, separately billed. The resident’s total recurring monthly charge is therefore $1,935 before utilities or one-time items. There is no monthly pet charge. An old intake form lists “possible pet fee $35,” but the signed lease addendum marks the pet fee “not applicable.” Please do not add the old intake figure to the current total.

The payment received April 3 was $1,900. The bank record confirms receipt, not allocation. The lease payment paragraph says payments are applied first to outstanding non-rent fees, then to the oldest rent charge, unless the resident gives a written allocation instruction accepted by management. The resident’s memo is not an accepted instruction under the paragraph; the file contains no acceptance. The April 3 payment was therefore applied to the oldest open charge. The ledger shows that the oldest open rent charge was March rent, not April rent.

The March rent charge was $1,840 and the March parking charge was $95. The account had a pre-existing credit of $200 at the start of March, verified against the February reconciliation. Thus the March total of $1,935 less the $200 credit left $1,735 due before the April 3 payment. The April 3 payment of $1,900 exceeded that March remainder by $165. The lease allocation clause and the transaction report show $165 carried forward as a credit to April; the remaining $1,735 closed the March rent and parking charges.

For April, the recurring charge remains $1,935. Applying the $165 carry-forward credit gives $1,770 remaining for April before any separately authorized item. The ledger also displays an $80 water estimate, but the lease says water is billed after the meter statement, and the April statement was not issued until May 20. Bottled water and a general phone number do not qualify. The named attendant and folding counter are prerequisites only, not separate points.

Reconciliation of Uma’s individual transit record: her corrected breakdown is 12 bus days paid by herself, 3 bus days paid by sponsor, and 2 walking days. The formula counts only her own paid fare days. Countable = 12. Excess over 10 = 2. Reduction = 2 × 2 u = 4 u. Allowance = 40 − 4 = 36 u. The earlier rough statement “17 days” is not the countable-day input; even as a count of calendar trips to the hub, it includes sponsor-paid and walking days. The old flyer’s 6-u result uses 27 countable days, not her data.

The review noted an ambiguity in a draft dashboard that displayed “company expected obligation 5 u” after the 30-u payment. That is the inspection balance before the access award, because 35 − 30 = 5. It is not the final amount due after the 9-u award. The final arithmetic is 35 − 30 − 9 = −4, displayed as zero due and 4 u credit. A negative balance is not a payment owed by the Borough unless a refund transaction is authorized; here the applicant elected to retain the credit.

The review also checked whether the 25-visitor number could be confused with Uma’s 17 days or whether 17 might be used as company attendance. It cannot: the first is an expected visitor count for the company event, the second is a preliminary count of calendar travel days for an individual. The numeric similarity between 30 u payment, 30 visitor sample and 30-u sample award is incidental. Staff must validate the subject, unit, reference number, date, and line label.

The site check is scheduled for 26 June. At the time of this postmortem it has not happened. The access award is formally approved, but the temporary permit itself is pending. A zero amount due does not prove a site check passed or a permit was issued. The postmortem records no final permit issuance. Copperleaf has confirmed its plan remains unchanged and elected to retain 4 u as an account credit.

APPENDIX A — Reconstruction of company invoice CS-611

Item 1, sidewalk occupation review: first 12 public visitors, 14 u; next 13 visitors, two partial/complete blocks, 2 × 6 = 12 u; line total 26 u. Working helpers: 4, excluded. Item 2, folding-counter inspection: 9 u. Gross invoice: 26 + 9 = 35 u. Payment CS-611: 30 u, allocated to review. Review remainder: 26 − 30 = −4, recorded as 4-u unused credit. Item 3, approved access offset: 9 u against inspection. Inspection remainder: 9 − 9 = 0. Combined amount due: 35 − 30 − 9 = −4, meaning zero due and 4 u retained credit, not 4 u due.

The rough value 5 u is gross total after payment but before the award: 35 − 30 = 5. After the 9-u award, that five-unit apparent balance is eliminated and the previously overpaid review creates a four-unit credit. This accounting presentation is equivalent to applying payment to review first, then award to inspection. The payment cannot be applied twice. The offset cannot be applied to review. The 4-u credit is derived from the 30-u payment exceeding the 26-u review charge; it is not derived from the resident allowance.

APPENDIX B — Individual travel calculation for Uma Moreau

Reported calendar days traveling to hub: 17. Of these, bus days = 15. Sponsor-paid bus days = 3. Resident-paid bus days = 15 − 3 = 12. Walking-only days = 2; no fare paid. Countable days under the stated rule = 12, not 17 and not 15. Days above threshold = 12 − 10 = 2. Reduction = 2 × 2 = 4 u. Allowance = 40 − 4 = 36 u. The floor of 0 does not apply because the calculation remains positive. A hypothetical count of 17 would yield 40 − 2 × 7 = 26 u, but it is not the correct rule input. The cited 6-u flyer result belongs to a different example and cannot replace this calculation.

APPENDIX C — statuses at close of record

Copperleaf application: received and under permit review. Copperleaf invoice gross: 35 u. Copperleaf payment posted: 30 u. Copperleaf access award: approved, 9-u inspection offset. Copperleaf amount due after entries: 0 u. Copperleaf unused amount: 4 u account credit, retained by applicant. Site check: pending. Permit issuance: not recorded. Uma application: corrected travel-day details received. Uma calculated monthly allowance: 36 u provisional, subject to receipt and identity checks. No company ledger entry is made for Uma’s allowance.

APPENDIX D — review team’s final caution

The training sample’s 42 u is plausible because it appears beside a similar company name and public event terms. It is nevertheless wrong for this invoice. The preliminary 5-u balance is plausible because it is the difference between 35 and 30, but it is only before the approved award. The award score of 12 is plausible as a number of points, but the payable offset is capped at 9 u. The initial 17-day description is plausible as travel days, but not as countable paid fare days. The accurate result depends on matching each number to the correct person, event, unit, and rule. These distinctions are the finding of this incident file.",
