[{"state":"Granite Software card-dispute review packet: Quill Foods account and Bluefin Supply terminal

Compiled for the weekly operations meeting by Jonas Haddad, with review comments from Greta Iyer. The packet includes the meeting record, a product review, and a customer chat transcript. It is intentionally more comprehensive than anyone requested; the archive export evidently charges by the page, not by the useful sentence.

MEETING NOTES — TUESDAY, 14 MAY

Attendees: Jonas Haddad (disputes), Greta Iyer (payments), Nadia Lindqvist (support), Chiara Fischer (reconciliation), and Quentin O'Neill (terminal operations). Zoltan Bergstrom sent written comments afterward. Subject: review of three card transactions reported by Quill Foods and the handling of cardholder communication. No one proposed changing the card network rules. The group did propose making our internal notes less mysterious, which is apparently a quarterly tradition.

Jonas opened by stating that the account holder had supplied a register summary, three receipt images, and a copy of the statement. The customer’s message refers to “the Bluefin counter,” but the merchant records identify the location as Bluefin Supply’s demonstration counter inside the Quill Foods market. The names are similar enough to guarantee at least one person will confuse them, so this packet keeps the distinction explicit. Quill Foods is the cardholder’s business and Bluefin Supply is the merchant. Granite Software provides the case portal; it did not sell the goods and did not process the purchase at its own office.

The cardholder says one visit resulted in three separate debits. The first receipt shows a tasting set for $18.40. The second shows a reusable container for $12.60. The third shows a countertop scale for $41.25. The cardholder’s handwritten note beside the receipt bundle says, “I thought the scale was included in the demonstration, but I see it was rung separately.” The register log and signed receipt both show a purchase, not a duplicate. The statement entries are $18.40, $12.60, and $41.25. The sum of those three entries is $72.25. A nearby transaction at the same merchant, from the prior week, was $27.25. That old amount is not part of the disputed visit, although the customer’s first portal message initially placed it in the same paragraph.

Greta asked the team to distinguish the customer’s requested remedy from the total of every transaction mentioned in the packet. The customer’s current request is limited to the scale, whose individual debit is $41.25. The cardholder is not requesting a refund for the tasting set or container. Jonas noted that the portal summary showed a total of $72.25 because it auto-added all three entries when the customer attached the receipts. The summary is a useful display of the visit total, not a statement that every dollar in that display is disputed. “A grand total that is not the requested amount,” Greta said, “is a small but reliable way to make the next email longer.”

The merchant’s posted return policy says an unused scale can be returned within 14 calendar days of purchase if the original packaging is retained. The customer’s receipt is dated 2 May. The first chat asking about a return arrived 11 May, nine calendar days later. The customer says the package has not been opened. The customer does not say the scale failed, was damaged, or was never delivered. The merchant’s response says staff can inspect it at the counter. These facts matter to the merchant conversation but do not change which amount the customer identified as the item in question. The 14-day policy uses calendar days, not working days; no one needs to derive a new convention from the word “business” because the policy does not use that word.

Nadia read the initial support note aloud: “Customer unhappy with Bluefin; possible duplicate charge; asks about money back.” She said the note is a compressed paraphrase, not a verbatim request and not a finding that the charges were duplicated. The customer used “money back” only when discussing the scale. The receipt sequence, merchant log, and statement show one debit per listed item. The customer did not assert that the $18.40 tasting set appeared twice. There is a separate authorization hold of $15.00 in the statement screenshot, but the bank marked it expired and it is not included in the posted debits. The hold should not be added to the three posted amounts just because it appears in the same screenshot. The actual debit entries are still $72.25 altogether.

Chiara summarized the reconciliation. The till recorded one $18.40 line, one $12.60 line, and one $41.25 line. The card processor settled those lines in a single batch, but the bank statement displays three separate posted transactions. The batch settlement total, $72.25, matches the arithmetic total of the three entries. The merchant’s daily report separately includes $9.50 from another customer and $27.25 from the cardholder’s prior-week purchase. Neither is part of this visit’s three-line total. The daily report’s gross figure is therefore not the figure to use when describing what the customer currently seeks back. Jonas asked whether the case portal could show both the visit total and the selected disputed line more clearly. Greta replied that this had been raised last month, which is probably why the ticket now has a cheerful status label but no actual design change.

The meeting reviewed how the portal handles a customer selecting one or more statement entries. If the customer chooses all entries, the portal carries the sum into its case summary. If the customer selects only one entry, the summary should carry only that entry’s amount, even when the supporting attachment shows a larger purchase total. In this case the customer initially selected all three entries while uploading the receipt bundle, then corrected the selection in the chat. The correct current scope is one entry, the scale debit for $41.25. The earlier selection was an input error, not a final request to reverse the entire visit. The case history retains both selections, and the later customer message is the controlling clarification.

For training purposes, Jonas read out a mock statement: “There are three amounts here, and obviously we should take the largest one because it looks important.” No one treated that sentence as a rule. It was a dry joke about the portal’s tendency to make the most prominent number seem authoritative. The relevant distinction is whether the customer specifically requested return of the amount, not which number happens to be largest, boldest, or located in the heading. The amount on the scale line is $41.25; the visit total is $72.25; the separate prior-week amount is $27.25; and the expired hold is $15.00. They are four different figures serving four different purposes.

The meeting also recorded an example of a neighboring case to prevent accidental blending. Bluefin Dental, a different merchant, submitted a $33.80 transaction in April. That transaction involved a different cardholder and is not associated with Quill Foods. Its amount appears in the reconciliation dashboard because the dashboard is organized by merchant-family tags, a tagging scheme that has never met a human being it could not confuse. It is not part of the case packet and must not be combined with any Quill Foods transaction. No participant suggested otherwise. The team agreed that future exports should suppress unrelated examples when producing a case-specific view, assuming the export feature eventually develops a sense of context.

A second neighboring example concerned a Granite Software test card. During a portal demonstration, an analyst entered $40.00 as a sample amount and then reset the demonstration. The test entry has a reference beginning DEMO and was never posted to a customer account. It appears in the internal training appendix only. It is not an additional purchase and does not increase the disputed amount or visit total. The test card record exists so that the product team can test the arithmetic display. As Greta observed, the demonstration managed to reproduce the exact sort of ambiguity it was meant to prevent, which at least gave the team something to discuss.

The group checked the amount fields in the case record. “Merchant amount” for the scale line: $41.25. “All selected transaction amounts” before correction: $72.25. “All selected transaction amounts” after correction: $41.25. “Customer stated requested return” in the chat summary: $41.25. “Amount eligible for return under merchant’s policy,” pending inspection: not yet determined. These fields are not synonyms. The amount sought is clear even though the merchant has not yet decided whether to approve a return. The bank dispute outcome is also pending. Nothing in the packet says that a refund has already been issued or that the bank has ruled in the cardholder’s favor.

Jonas asked whether a customer’s use of the phrase “I want this sorted” should be recorded as a refund request. Nadia replied that it depends on the surrounding statement. Here, the customer wrote, “Please refund the $41.25 scale purchase; I will bring the unopened box in.” The request is direct. The phrase is not merely a complaint about service, and it is not a hypothetical threat to request money later. The customer also says, “I am not asking you to return the other two lines.” The negation narrows the request; it does not cancel the explicit request about the scale. The support note should preserve the distinction instead of reducing everything to “possible money issue.”

Greta suggested that the decision record should state the arithmetic plainly: $18.40 + $12.60 + $41.25 = $72.25 for the three purchases. The customer asks for the $41.25 scale line, not $72.25. The $27.25 prior-week purchase, $15.00 expired hold, $9.50 other-customer line, $33.80 Bluefin Dental entry, and $40.00 demonstration amount do not belong in that request. That sentence should be enough to prevent the common error of treating every number on the page as a disputed debit. It may not prevent it, but at least the error will then be documented in a more elegant font.

The meeting ended with action items. Nadia will update the case note to quote the customer’s request and identify the single line. Chiara will ask the reporting team to separate posted transactions, expired authorizations, and unrelated merchant-family records. Quentin will check whether the counter can inspect the sealed package during the return period. Greta will review the portal’s selection summary. Jonas will make sure the customer receives a plain-language update. The update should not promise a refund; it should confirm that the request concerns the scale line for $41.25 and explain that the merchant’s inspection and the bank’s review remain separate steps.

PRODUCT REVIEW — CASE PORTAL AMOUNT SUMMARY, INTERNAL REVIEW DRAFT

Reviewer: Greta Iyer. Product: Granite Software case portal, version 4.8.3. Review date: 14 May. Test account: fictional Quill Foods card profile. The product review is included because the support team asked for evidence about how the amounts were displayed. It is not a separate customer communication, and its conclusions should not be mistaken for a bank decision. The prose below retains the usual dry tone because the interface has earned it.

The case page presents a list of posted items, pending items, and archived demonstrations. The posted items table has three rows for the 2 May Bluefin Supply visit: tasting set $18.40; reusable container $12.60; countertop scale $41.25. A small total beneath those rows shows $72.25. The total is correct for all three rows. The trouble is that the screen initially places the word “case amount” beside that total, even if the customer has selected just one row. In this case, the user saw $72.25, selected the three rows during upload, and later clarified in chat that only the scale line was the subject of the return request. The revised selection now shows $41.25. The display should not be treated as the customer’s final scope once a later clarification changes it.

The page also shows a gray row for an expired $15.00 authorization. It is not a posted debit, and the label “expired” is visible, though apparently not visible enough to stop someone from adding it mentally to everything else. A separate archive link contains the $27.25 prior-week purchase. The daily merchant feed includes $9.50 from another customer. A merchant-family dashboard includes a $33.80 Bluefin Dental transaction, and the product demo appendix contains a $40.00 test amount. These figures are all plausible-looking amounts in the same broad interface, but only the three posted lines from 2 May contribute to the $72.25 visit total. Only the $41.25 line is currently being requested back.

In the test script, a reviewer was asked to calculate the total of the three 2 May rows. The answer is $72.25: first $18.40 plus $12.60 gives $31.00, then adding $41.25 gives $72.25. A separate reviewer mistakenly got $87.25 by adding the $15.00 expired authorization. That result is not the posted transaction total, because the authorization did not settle. Another reviewer got $99.50 by adding the $27.25 prior-week charge as well. That is a total across selected historical items, not the total for this visit. A third reviewer got $107.75 after also including the $8.25 shipping estimate shown in the merchant’s draft invoice. The estimate was never charged. There is always another number if one searches long enough; mathematics is not the interface’s only usability problem.

The product review considers whether the customer actually asked for a refund. The chat transcript contains the sentence, “Please refund the $41.25 scale purchase; I will bring the unopened box in.” That is an explicit request for the amount attached to the scale line. The customer’s earlier wording, “Can someone tell me why there are three entries?” is a question about the statement, not on its own a request to return all three entries. The customer later says that the tasting set and container were purchased and are not included in the request. The fact that all three appear on the same receipt bundle does not enlarge the request. The portal’s total is a computed purchase total, not a substitute for the words in the customer’s later message.

The review also checks whether there is evidence of a duplicate charge. The register record has one item scan per product and the bank statement has one posted transaction per product. The merchant’s batch contains a single settled amount of $72.25, which corresponds to those three lines. There is no second $41.25 debit. The customer did not allege that the scale charge appeared twice; they questioned whether the scale was included in a demonstration and then requested a return. A support shorthand saying “possible duplicate” is unsupported and should be removed. A $15.00 authorization appeared temporarily, but it expired and is not a second settled debit. The distinction is simple, which makes it all the more impressive that the shorthand managed to lose it.

The interface includes a reminder about the merchant return policy: unused merchandise may be returned within 14 calendar days if packaging is retained. Receipt date: 2 May. Contact date: 11 May. Counting from the purchase date, 11 May is nine calendar days after 2 May, so the contact occurred inside the stated period. That is not a calculation of the amount requested, and it does not mean the return is automatically approved. The merchant still needs to inspect the packaging. The product review recommends that the portal show the contact date and policy window separately from the transaction amount. A green “eligible” badge would be misleading before inspection, so no one recommends adding one just to make the page feel more decisive.

The amount field should retain cents and should never be rounded to whole dollars in the customer-facing summary. If $41.25 were shown as $41, a customer might reasonably ask what happened to the other 25 cents. If the $72.25 visit total were shown as $72, the same problem would occur. The display currently uses two decimal places. The team tested a locale setting that uses a comma as the decimal separator, but the case account is configured in dollars with a period. No currency conversion is relevant here. There is no exchange rate, foreign-currency debit, tax recomputation, gratuity, or installment balance to apply. The values in the packet are already the posted dollar amounts.

A further concern is that the interface uses the same blue highlight for selected rows and for rows that match a search. During testing, an analyst searched for “scale,” saw the $41.25 line highlighted, and concluded that only the scale was selected. In fact, all three transaction checkboxes remained selected from the earlier upload. The customer corrected the selection through chat, and the final case record now reflects one line. The product team should use different visual treatments for search matches and selected items. The meeting notes mention this because the former selection explains why a $72.25 amount appeared in the initial summary. It does not change the later, explicit scope.

The support workflow has a field called “requested amount,” populated from the customer’s text when an agent saves the conversation. In the current case it reads $41.25. The separate field called “transaction total” reads $72.25. The separate field called “amount already credited” reads $0.00. These numbers are all correct and refer to different things. There is no issued credit in the statement, merchant log, or chat. The customer has asked for a return, but the request has not yet resulted in a refund. A request should not be described as a completed credit merely because the number is present in a field called requested amount.

The test team tried several misleading prompts. One said, “The visit total is $72.25, so the customer asked for $72.25 back.” This is incorrect because the customer expressly limited the request to the $41.25 scale line. Another said, “The purchase is only $41.25 because that is the amount sought.” This is also incorrect if the question concerns the full visit total; the three posted entries add to $72.25. A third said, “The cardholder wants the $27.25 old purchase reversed as well.” The old purchase is listed for comparison, but no such request appears in the transcript. These tests verify that a reviewer must match each figure to its stated role rather than select the nearest amount or the largest one.

The product review’s recommendation is to label the lines “visit total,” “selected amount,” “expired authorization,” and “previous purchase,” rather than to show a single ambiguous grand total. The selected amount should update after the customer changes their selection. It did so after Nadia corrected the case record. The audit trail should retain the earlier $72.25 selection and the later correction, because both events happened. The current state should not silently erase the history, and the history should not override the current clarification. This is a fairly ordinary requirement for software that records events in time, though it has been assigned a surprisingly dramatic ticket number.

The review was not an assessment of whether the customer’s belief about the demonstration was correct. The merchant’s demonstration sign says the scale is sold separately, and the receipt lists it separately at $41.25. The customer acknowledges seeing the separate line after reviewing the receipt. The customer can still ask to return an unopened item under the posted policy. The support team should avoid describing the request as a claim that the item was stolen, never received, or charged twice. None of those claims is in the chat. The review is about the amount and the way the portal represents it.

For audit traceability, Greta checked the math a second time against the receipt image. Line one: $18.40. Line two: $12.60. Together those equal $31.00. Line three: $41.25. Adding it gives $72.25. The scale line alone remains $41.25. The expired authorization is $15.00 and has a zero settled amount. The prior-week line is $27.25. The other-customer sale is $9.50. The unrelated Bluefin Dental transaction is $33.80. The test amount is $40.00. The draft shipping estimate is $8.25. None of those nearby figures alters the arithmetic for the three posted rows or the customer’s explicitly selected item.

CUSTOMER CHAT TRANSCRIPT — 11 MAY

Participants: Quill Foods cardholder (account verified in the support system), Nadia Lindqvist (Granite Software support). The transcript is lightly formatted for readability. Timestamp zone is local to the customer account. Automated notices are included where they help explain the sequence; they are not customer statements. The machine-generated banner that says “case amount $72.25” reflects the original three-row selection, not a separate statement by the customer.

09:02 — Nadia: Hello. I can see the receipt images and the statement excerpt. Before I submit anything, could you tell me which line or lines you want us to review? The upload screen has all three purchases checked, and its displayed total is $72.25.

09:04 — Customer: The display is doing its best impression of a precise answer. I bought the tasting set for $18.40 and the container for $12.60. I am only asking about the scale, listed at $41.25. I thought that came with the demonstration, but the receipt does show it separately. The box is unopened.

09:06 — Nadia: Thank you. To confirm, should I leave the $18.40 and $12.60 entries out of the request and keep the $41.25 scale entry?

09:07 — Customer: Yes. Please refund the $41.25 scale purchase; I will bring the unopened box in. I am not asking you to return the other two lines. Apparently specifying one item is now an advanced accounting feature.

09:09 — Nadia: I have updated the selection to the scale line only. The case screen now shows $41.25 selected. The total for the three purchases on 2 May remains $72.25, because $18.40 + $12.60 + $41.25 = $72.25. Those are different figures: the visit total and the amount you asked to have returned.

09:11 — Customer: Correct. I also see a $15 authorization on the screenshot, but the bank says it expired. I am not including that. There was a $27.25 purchase the week before, which was fine. I do not want that included either. I know the screen likes a crowd.

09:13 — Nadia: Understood. I will record the current request as $41.25 for the scale only. The earlier screen selection included three lines, but your later message clarified the scope. The $15.00 authorization is expired and is not a posted debit. The earlier $27.25 purchase is outside this request.

09:16 — Customer: The merchant says the return period is 14 days and my receipt is dated 2 May. I wrote today, 11 May. That is nine days, so the timing should be okay. I can bring the package to the counter.

09:18 — Nadia: The dates are within the merchant’s stated 14-calendar-day window. Bluefin Supply will need to inspect the packaging before deciding whether to accept the return. We can record your request, but I cannot promise the merchant will issue a credit before that inspection.

09:20 — Customer: Fine. I am requesting the money back for the scale, not claiming it has already been returned. I have not brought it in yet. [{"state":"PUBLIC SERVICE ACCESS AND PERMIT REVIEW
Consolidated administrative record
File reference: PS-46-218
Prepared for internal reconciliation

This record brings together three kinds of material received by the regional service desk: a product review submitted through the online feedback form, a pasted spreadsheet used by an applicant to summarize a small public-benefit claim, and an invoice submitted with a permit-support request. The records are reproduced or transcribed for review. Amounts are stated in dollars unless otherwise noted. The review concerns arithmetic in the documents, not the applicant’s eligibility or the merits of any permit decision. No external schedule or policy is incorporated by reference. Each exhibit contains its own figures and labels.

The service desk’s intake convention is to preserve each contributor’s own description of an amount. A number appearing in a heading is not automatically the total of the entries below it. When a total is requested, the entries explicitly identified as components of that total are added, and unrelated entries are not included. A discount is subtracted only when the record identifies it as applying to the same group of charges. Amounts that are merely quoted as estimates, comparisons, or prior submissions remain separate figures. The three exhibits were assembled in the order received, and the accompanying clerical notes describe where the records came from. The notes do not change the figures in the exhibits.

The first item was submitted using the public feedback form after a demonstration of a web-based permit tracking product. The form asked users to describe one feature they valued and one concern they wanted the agency to record. It did not ask reviewers to calculate a score. The reviewer nevertheless included a short breakdown of the subscription price, a claimed rebate, and the amount the reviewer said remained payable. The arithmetic in that breakdown can be checked from the values printed in the review itself.

The second item is a spreadsheet paste supplied in plain text. The submitter says it is a reconciliation of reimbursable costs for a benefits-navigation workshop. The columns are labelled category, count, unit amount, and extended amount. The paste includes a claimed grand total and a separate reference estimate from an earlier planning sheet. The planning estimate is not a line in the submitted claim. The extended amounts are shown as supplied, but the record provides counts and unit amounts so that each relevant multiplication and addition can be checked independently.

The third item is an invoice-style schedule attached to a request for a temporary public-way permit. It lists services, quantities, unit prices, a subtotal, and a credit. The schedule also includes a separate optional service that the submitter marked as not ordered. That optional figure appears in a nearby explanatory note, but it is not one of the invoiced line items. The invoice’s stated amount due can be compared with the listed charges and credit without relying on any outside fee schedule.

The intake clerk did not certify any submitted calculation. The present record is designed to retain both the original claims and the component figures, including discrepancies, so that reviewers can distinguish a stated amount from an amount supported by arithmetic. Where a calculation is repeated in a later note, the repetition is identified as a quotation rather than a new entry. The following sections reproduce the exhibits and their surrounding administrative context.

EXHIBIT A — ONLINE PRODUCT REVIEW

Submission channel: public service product feedback form
Product described: PermitPath Desk, a demonstration tool used to track permit applications and benefit referrals
Reviewer name entered: Nadia Delgado
Organization field: Foxglove Studio
Review status at intake: received and retained as submitted

Review text:

“I used PermitPath Desk during the public counter demonstration because I wanted to see whether one screen could show both a street-use permit and a related household-support referral. I tested the sample dashboard with the demonstration account and then reviewed the price panel shown to visitors. I am not saying that the system issued a permit or approved a benefit; the account used for the demonstration had sample records only. What follows is my experience of the product information and the arithmetic that appeared on the price panel.

“The main screen was clear enough for a visitor who had not used it before. I could see the application reference, the department handling it, the status label, and a short list of missing documents. The interface did not make me guess whether a record was a permit matter or a referral matter. The two types of record used separate headings. That distinction matters because the counter staff explained that the visitor-facing page is intended to display procedural information, not to make a decision about entitlement. I found the headings useful, and I did not see a sample record presented as a final approval.

“The search box accepted a reference number and returned the sample application. I also tried a search using the sample street name and a search using a partial household reference. The first search was fast. The second did not return a result until I included another word. The third returned two sample records, which the interface kept separate. These tests were informal. They should not be interpreted as a performance study, because I did not run a timed comparison or use a production account. I mention them because the search feature is one of the things a small studio would use when helping a resident find the right notice.

“The product page described a monthly base subscription of $480 for the demonstration package. Under that price, the page listed two optional modules, each priced at $135 per month. The page showed the base and both modules as separate entries, with the modules marked selected in the demonstration cart. I copied those amounts into my notes before the demonstration ended. In my review draft, I wrote that the three selected monthly entries came to $760. That figure was not a quote from the agency; it was my addition of the three prices printed on the demonstration page. The relevant figures are $480, $135, and $135. The calculation is $480 + $135 + $135, or $750. My draft’s $760 total was ten dollars too high. The demonstration screen did not display a separate $10 fee, and I did not see a fourth selected item. I have left the mistaken $760 figure in this review so that it is clear what I originally wrote, rather than silently replacing it.

“The product page then showed a one-time setup charge of $90. The page put that charge in a separate section headed ‘one-time setup,’ not in the monthly subscription list. I did not include it in the monthly amount I calculated above. If someone adds the setup charge to the first month’s selected monthly entries, the first-month combined amount would be $840, using $750 in monthly items plus $90 once. That combined first-month amount is not the recurring monthly subscription. The price panel also included a small-print note that the example was illustrative and that the agency would have to confirm any actual purchasing terms. I am not treating the display as a contract.

“The checkout preview applied a promotional credit of $125 to the first billing period only. It was shown below the selected monthly entries and the setup charge. I read the display as a first-period reduction, not as a permanent reduction to each month. If all selected entries and the one-time setup charge were collected in the first period, and if the credit were applied once as displayed, then the arithmetic would be $750 + $90 − $125 = $715 for that first period. The preview did not say that the first-period amount was the same as a recurring monthly amount. I did not see a credit of $115, despite a figure of $115 appearing in an unrelated sample note elsewhere on the screen. The relevant credit in the checkout preview was $125.

“The summary box displayed a large figure of $825 beside the words ‘estimated first period before credit.’ I initially thought that figure was another subtotal, but the three selected monthly entries plus the setup fee do not add to $825. They add to $840. The box may have been a stale sample or may have used a configuration that was not visible in the demonstration cart. I cannot resolve that from the review screen. The visible line entries remain the figures I copied above. For purposes of my own arithmetic, I would use the selected entries and the separately labelled setup charge rather than the unexplained $825 summary. The $825 value is included here because it appeared on the preview and could be mistaken for a line-item total.

“I tested the help link on the price panel. It opened a page with contact information and an explanation that the support team could clarify feature availability. The support page did not say that every optional module was required. In the cart, the two modules were selected, but a visitor could deselect them. I did not assume that the displayed configuration was the only available configuration. A different cart with neither module would show the base price alone, while one selected module would show the base price and one module price. Those are comparisons only; the three selected entries in the configuration I reviewed remain the base plus two modules.

“The status timeline in the sample dashboard used plain language. One example showed a request received, a document check, and a referral to another unit. The sample did not show a final benefit decision. Another example showed a permit record with a notice that a drawing was missing. The timeline did not tell the visitor that a missing drawing had been accepted. I thought this separation between ‘received’ and ‘approved’ was helpful. The interface could still be improved by making the distinction more prominent on the mobile display, where the status text wrapped onto a second line.

“I found the product’s printed labels generally formal and readable. A few labels were abbreviated, but the surrounding text made them understandable. The demonstration staff did not promise that the product would shorten processing times. The feedback form asked me whether I would recommend the interface for a pilot, not whether I could verify any claim about service outcomes. I would recommend a limited pilot after the price panel is reconciled, because the record display was easier to follow than the paper packet used in the demonstration. I would not use my review as evidence that the tool reduces delays or changes eligibility decisions.

“The price panel’s arithmetic matters because a reviewer comparing packages may rely on the figure that appears as a total. My own draft contained the wrong sum. It is possible that someone might read $760 and assume there is another charge, but I saw no additional selected charge of ten dollars. I also saw the $825 summary figure, which is not explained by the visible component entries. These discrepancies are not a complaint about a charge actually collected. No payment was made during the demonstration, and the account was not connected to a billing method. They are comments about the displayed example and the calculation in my review.

“For clarity, the monthly configuration I tested had one base entry at $480 and two selected module entries at $135 each. The one-time setup entry was $90. The promotional credit was $125 and applied to the first period in the preview. A separate reference in the display showed $115, but that was not the credit applied to the cart. The $760 figure was my mistaken sum of the three recurring entries. The component arithmetic gives $750. Adding the one-time setup gives $840 before the credit, and subtracting the first-period credit gives $715. The $825 summary did not match those component calculations. These are the figures I intended the agency to have when reading my product comments.”

End of review text.

Clerical context for Exhibit A:
The public feedback form automatically added a receipt number but did not verify figures. The amount field accepted free text. The reviewer used the same field to explain the monthly selection, the one-time setup, and the promotional credit. The intake clerk preserved the field verbatim. The words “my mistaken sum” and the arithmetic in the review are part of the submitted text, not a later correction by the agency. The form did not ask for a refund, did not report a completed purchase, and did not provide a payment receipt. No amount was recorded as paid.

The product demonstration materials were retained separately from this record. Their existence does not supply additional prices for the selected cart described in the review. The only relevant component prices in the submitted account are the base subscription, the two selected modules, the one-time setup charge, and the stated first-period credit. The other figures in the review are expressly described as a mistaken sum, an unexplained summary, or a comparison. The review’s qualitative comments about the screen, search, and labels are retained as context, but they do not alter the price arithmetic.

EXHIBIT B — PASTED SPREADSHEET

Source description: applicant’s plain-text reconciliation for a benefits-navigation workshop
Submitter name appearing in sheet heading: Greta Castillo
Program contact named in the cover note: Bluefin Analytics
Spreadsheet title: Workshop access costs, version 3
Currency: dollars

Pasted sheet, as received:

Category | Count | Unit amount | Extended amount | Note
Printed application guides | 24 | 3.25 | 78.00 | standard copies
Large-print guides | 6 | 5.50 | 33.00 | accessible format
Interpreter sessions | 3 | 42.00 | booked blocks
Transit passes | 18 | 4.75 | attendee support
Room use | 1 | 160.00 | community room
Captioning setup | 1 | 65.00 | single setup
Refreshments | 20 | 2.40 | light service

Claimed eligible total: 1,076.00
Planning estimate from earlier worksheet: 1,080.00
Unclaimed reserve shown in planning sheet: 40.00

Cover note copied with the sheet:

“I am sending the plain-text version because the portal preview changes the column spacing. The entries are the quantities and rates we used for the workshop reconciliation. The amount in the final column is intended to be the extension for that row. The claimed eligible total is the sum of the seven row extensions above. The planning estimate was carried forward from an earlier worksheet and is not an additional category or an eighth line. The reserve was not spent and is not included as a claim. I have kept those figures in the paste because they were present on the planning worksheet and help explain why its estimate differs from the submitted total.

“The seven listed categories are application guides, large-print guides, interpreter sessions, transit passes, room use, captioning setup, and refreshments. The counts and unit amounts are shown beside each category. The sheet’s row extensions should be checked against those quantities and rates before anyone relies on the claimed total. In the previous version, a count was copied into the wrong row, and the result was corrected before this version was sent. No outside rate is needed to check the arithmetic in this version.

“The planning worksheet contained a rough estimate of $1,080.00. It was prepared before the final quantities were known and includes a reserve line of $40.00. The reserve is not an amount requested from the program. The submitted claim uses only the seven categories listed in this paste. The total field in the portal is an entry made by me; it is not an agency determination and it is not an amount already reimbursed. I have not received payment on this claim.”

Row-by-row calculation notes preserved below the paste:

Printed application guides: 24 copies multiplied by $3.25 each. The calculation is 24 × 3.25 = $78.00. The extension shown is $78.00.

Large-print guides: 6 copies multiplied by $5.50 each. The calculation is 6 × 5.50 = $33.00. The extension shown is $33.00.

Interpreter sessions: 3 blocks multiplied by $42.00 each. The calculation is 3 × 42.00 = $126.00. The extension field on the pasted row says $126.00. The note field says “booked blocks”; the sheet does not claim a fourth block.

Transit passes: 18 passes multiplied by $4.75 each. The calculation is 18 × 4.75 = $85.50. The extension shown is $85.50. A separate transportation planning note elsewhere in the packet mentions $84.50 as an earlier estimate for passes. That earlier estimate does not replace the count and rate in this submitted row.

Room use: 1 booking multiplied by $160.00. The calculation is 1 × 160.00 = $160.00. The extension shown is $160.00. A draft agenda lists a room estimate of $150.00, but the submitted sheet uses the room-use amount shown in its row.

Captioning setup: 1 setup multiplied by $65.00. The calculation is 1 × 65.00 = $65.00. The extension shown is $65.00. A note in the meeting planning file refers to a possible $60.00 setup option, but the submitted row uses $65.00.

Refreshments: 20 servings multiplied by $2.40. The calculation is 20 × 2.40 = $48.00. The extension shown is $48.00. The number 20 refers to the planned servings on this line, not to the total number of workshop attendees.

The sheet was pasted from an office file, and the original cell formulas are unavailable in the portal. The row calculations are reproduced here from the count and unit amount columns. The extended amounts total $595.50, not $1,076.00. The addition is $78.00 + $33.00 + $126.00 + $85.50 + $160.00 + $65.00 + $48.00 = $595.50. The claimed eligible total field of $1,076.00 is therefore not the arithmetic sum of these seven visible line items. This reconciliation note was made for internal checking and was not sent to the applicant as an adjustment.

The difference between the claimed total and the sum of the listed extensions is $480.50: $1,076.00 − $595.50 = $480.50. The earlier planning estimate is $1,080.00, which is $4.00 higher than the claimed total. The unclaimed reserve of $40.00 is not sufficient to explain the $480.50 difference, and in any case the cover note says the reserve was not spent and is excluded. The sheet does not identify an additional eligible item of $480.50. A reviewer should not invent a line item to make the claimed total fit the visible entries.

The plain-text sheet contains no formula column, and the submitter’s cover note explicitly states that the claimed eligible total is intended to equal the sum of the seven row extensions. The fact that the estimate from the earlier worksheet is close to the claimed figure does not make it the total of the submitted lines. The $1,080.00 planning estimate and the $40.00 reserve appear as separate planning figures. They are not additional amounts to be added to the seven category extensions. The sheet’s line items can be independently checked by multiplying each count by its corresponding unit amount and summing the resulting extensions.

Internal transcription check:
The clerk compared the pasted values against the uploaded spreadsheet preview. The preview displayed the same seven categories and the same counts and unit rates. The preview’s total cell showed 1,076.00, matching the claimed total in the pasted text. It did not expose a formula, and the clerk did not treat the displayed total cell as proof that the arithmetic was correct. The preview had no hidden eighth line visible to the intake clerk. The earlier planning worksheet was mentioned in the cover note but was not uploaded as a separate claim schedule.

The sheet’s figures are not all estimates. The first three columns identify the submitted quantities and rates. The extension column gives the corresponding row amounts. The two larger summary figures are explicitly distinguished by the submitter: one is the claimed eligible total and the other is an older planning estimate. The reserve is explicitly unspent. The planning note’s possible $60.00 setup option and the draft agenda’s $150.00 room estimate are examples from earlier planning material, not alternate rates to substitute into the submitted rows. Likewise, $84.50 is described as an earlier transit-pass estimate, whereas the submitted row provides 18 passes at $4.75 each.

No reimbursement decision is contained in the spreadsheet paste. The submission does not say that the claim has been approved or paid. It is a record of requested costs for a workshop, with a claimed total that can be compared with its underlying rows. The service desk retains the original $1,076.00 entry so the reconciliation issue remains visible. The clerk’s calculation does not determine which costs may ultimately qualify under any program rule; it only checks whether the total field equals the sum of the listed amounts.

A second manual addition was performed to check the result without using the extended-amount column as a starting total. The seven products are: 24 times 3.25 gives 78; 6 times 5.50 gives 33; 3 times 42 gives 126; 18 times 4.75 gives 85.50; 1 times 160 gives 160; 1 times 65 gives 65; and 20 times 2.40 gives 48. Adding 78 and 33 gives 111. Adding 126 gives 237. Adding 85.50 gives 322.50. Adding 160 gives 482.50. Adding 65 gives 547.50. Adding 48 gives 595.50. This independent calculation agrees with the sum of the extensions printed in the spreadsheet.

The $1,076.00 claimed total is more than the verified sum of the listed lines by $480.50. It is not the sum of the seven extensions. The $1,080.00 planning estimate is not the correct sum either; it is merely the earlier estimate described in the cover note. The $40.00 reserve is unclaimed and unspent. The $4.00 difference between the claimed amount and the earlier estimate is not an itemized service cost. These figures are kept distinct in the record to prevent a reader from treating a nearby summary or planning amount as if it were a calculated line-item total.

EXHIBIT C — INVOICE AND PERMIT-SUPPORT REQUEST

Submitter: Quentin Moreau
Service provider named on invoice: Kestrel Logistics
Permit-support file: temporary public-way access request
Invoice reference: KL-8042
Currency: dollars

Invoice header:

Service period: administrative preparation for a temporary public-way request
Bill-to: permit applicant file
Invoice date: entered on provider’s copy
Payment status: no payment recorded in the attached materials

Line-item schedule:

1. Site plan printing and binding — quantity 4 sets — unit price $32.00 — line amount $128.00
2. Route measurement and map preparation — quantity 3 hours — unit price $58.00 — line amount $174.00
3. Public notice packet assembly — quantity 5 packets — unit price $22.00 — line amount $110.00
4. Accessibility review session — quantity 2 sessions — unit price $85.00 — line amount $170.00
5. Delivery of filed copies — quantity 1 trip — unit price $46.00 — line amount $46.00
6. Permit-support administration — quantity 1 service — unit price $210.00 — line amount $210.00

Invoice subtotal printed by provider: $838.00
Courtesy credit printed below subtotal: $64.00
Amount due printed by provider: $764.00
Optional expedited courier, not ordered: $38.00

Provider’s attached explanation:

“The six numbered entries above are the services included in this invoice schedule. The optional expedited courier is displayed for reference only and was not ordered. The customer asked that the arithmetic be reviewed before the papers were forwarded with the permit-support request. The amount due should equal the sum of the six numbered line amounts, less the $64.00 courtesy credit. The credit is a deduction from this invoice, not an additional service charge. The optional courier is not part of the subtotal or amount due.

“The line amounts were calculated from the quantities and rates printed beside them. Four sets at $32.00 are $128.00. Three hours at $58.00 are $174.00. Five packets at $22.00 are $110.00. Two sessions at $85.00 are $170.00. One trip at $46.00 is $46.00. One administrative service at $210.00 is $210.00. The subtotal field on the printed invoice reads $838.00. The credit field reads $64.00. The amount due field reads $764.00. Those are the figures printed on the invoice; the arithmetic should be checked from the numbered entries.

“The optional courier amount of $38.00 was not authorized by the customer and was not included in the numbered schedule. It was shown on a separate line under ‘not ordered’ because the service provider’s template lists possible delivery choices. A previous draft included a standard delivery estimate of $41.00, but that estimate was removed when the six numbered items were finalized. Neither the $38.00 optional service nor the $41.00 draft estimate is an invoiced line in this version.”

Arithmetic review note prepared by intake:
The six line amounts sum to $838.00: $128.00 + $174.00 + $110.00 + $170.00 + $46.00 + $210.00 = $838.00. The printed subtotal is consistent with the listed lines. Subtracting the $64.00 credit from the $838.00 subtotal gives $774.00, not $764.00. The invoice’s printed amount due is ten dollars below the amount supported by its listed charges and credit. The optional $38.00 courier is not included in this calculation because it is expressly marked not ordered. The earlier $41.00 estimate is likewise not part of the final schedule.

The separate arithmetic check for each line is as follows. Four times $32.00 is $128.00. Three times $58.00 is $174.00. Five times $22.00 is $110.00. Two times $85.00 is $170.00. One times $46.00 is $46.00. One times $210.00 is $210.00. The sum of those products is $838.00. The credit is $64.00, so $838.00 minus $64.00 equals $774.00. Adding the unordered $38.00 courier would produce a different amount, but the record says it was not ordered and it is not among the numbered line items. The $41.00 figure belonged to an earlier draft and was removed.

The amount due as printed, $764.00, is not supported by the six line entries and the credit listed on the same invoice. The discrepancy is $10.00 because $774.00 minus $764.00 equals $10.00. No separate $10.00 credit or adjustment is shown. The explanation does not authorize the intake clerk to create one. The invoice remains preserved as received, and the arithmetic note is an internal check, not a revised invoice or a finding about whether any service is allowable for permit purposes.

Context from the permit-support packet:
The attached invoice was submitted as supporting material for an administrative request. It is not itself a permit, an approval, or a determination that any public-way use has been authorized. The packet contains a cover page identifying the requested service and a checklist of supporting papers. The cover page does not add charges to the invoice. It records that the invoice was received for review and that no payment receipt was attached. The provider’s schedule is the only document in the packet that lists these service costs.

The intake clerk noted that the invoice template includes fields for a subtotal, credit, and amount due. The template does not calculate totals automatically in the plain-text copy. The printed numbers were transcribed exactly as they appeared. The clerical note was prepared by summing the numbered lines and applying the credit once. The amount due of $764.00 was not inferred from a payment record. It is simply the figure printed in the provider’s amount-due field. The arithmetic-supported result from the listed values is $774.00.

The courier figures are retained because they are close enough to the other amounts to cause confusion if the invoice is read quickly. The final schedule has a $38.00 optional courier line explicitly identified as not ordered. The $41.00 figure is described as a prior draft estimate that was removed. Neither is part of the six numbered charges. The correct subtotal calculation uses the six numbered charges only. The correct net calculation then subtracts the printed $64.00 courtesy credit from that subtotal.

The provider’s note says that the customer asked for an arithmetic review. That statement explains why the invoice was included with the packet; it does not change the amounts. The record does not say that the customer paid $764.00 or $774.00. It does not say that the provider issued a refund. It does not say that the permit was granted. The only numerical conclusion available from the invoice itself is whether its printed subtotal and amount due are consistent with the listed entries and credit.

Cross-exhibit intake summary:
The product review contains a mistaken draft sum, a one-time fee, and a first-period credit. Its monthly selected entries are distinct from the setup charge and credit. The spreadsheet contains seven submitted rows, a claimed total, an earlier estimate, and an unspent reserve. The invoice contains six numbered charges, a credit, and two excluded delivery figures. Each exhibit identifies which amounts belong to the calculation it describes. The intake record retains inconsistent stated totals rather than silently changing them.

The review’s arithmetic can be checked using the three selected recurring entries: $480.00, $135.00, and $135.00. Their sum is $750.00. The review itself says that the draft figure of $760.00 was a mistaken sum and that there was no fourth selected item or separate $10.00 fee. The one-time $90.00 setup and $125.00 first-period credit belong to a different calculation. The $825.00 summary is unexplained by the visible components and does not replace their arithmetic.

The spreadsheet’s seven products total $595.50. The claimed field reads $1,076.00, while the earlier estimate reads $1,080.00 and the reserve reads $40.00. The submitter says the claimed total is the sum of the seven row extensions and says the reserve is not spent. The pasted values do not include an eighth claimed category. The verified sum is therefore based on the seven printed lines, not the planning estimate or reserve.

The invoice’s six numbered charges total $838.00. The $64.00 courtesy credit reduces that subtotal to $774.00. The printed amount due is $764.00, which is $10.00 lower than the calculation supported by the listed figures. The $38.00 optional courier was not ordered, and the $41.00 estimate was removed from an earlier draft. Neither is included in the subtotal or the amount due calculation.

Record-integrity note:
This consolidated record preserves submitted material, transcribed values, and clerical arithmetic checks. A value described as “claimed,” “printed,” “estimated,” or “optional” retains that status throughout the record. A calculation performed here does not transform a claim into an approved benefit, an invoice into a paid bill, a product review into a procurement commitment, or a permit-support request into an authorization. The arithmetic questions that can be answered from this record concern the figures and relationships explicitly stated in the exhibits.

For the product review, the decisive components are the selected monthly base and two selected modules. A reader who adds those entries obtains $750.00. [{"state":"Larkspur Health — School of Continuing Studies
Course Administration Record: Winter Skills Certificate
Compiled for internal review, 18 February

PART I. EXECUTED COURSE-SERVICES AGREEMENT AND AMENDMENTS

1. Parties, purpose, and record hierarchy

This agreement concerns the administration of the Winter Skills Certificate offered by the School of Continuing Studies at Larkspur Health. The school is the course provider. Harbor Software is the learning-platform vendor and administrative-services contractor. The agreement does not make Harbor Software the provider of instruction, the issuer of certificates, or the owner of student tuition balances. The school retains those functions. Harbor Software supplies roster processing, course-shell configuration, attendance exports, and scheduled notices under the school’s direction.

The signed agreement, its numbered amendments, and the course-specific fee schedule form the governing record. In case of conflict, the most recently signed amendment controls only the provisions it expressly changes. A draft, an internal planning estimate, a message requesting a change, or a statement that a change is expected does not amend the agreement. A staff member’s summary is not controlling where it differs from a signed clause. This hierarchy is repeated here because several planning notes below use tentative figures that were never approved.

The administrative record contains student information solely for course operations. It is not a clinical record. References to Larkspur Health in the course title do not mean that students receive medical services. Harbor Software’s role is limited to the services expressly listed in the agreement.

2. Base services and charges

The base agreement covers one winter term, consisting of four independently scheduled modules: Foundations, Applied Practice, Review Lab, and Capstone. The school may enroll students in individual modules or in the full certificate. The platform fee is assessed per active student-module enrollment, not per student across the entire certificate. An active enrollment is one that remains on the school’s official roster at the applicable census time. A student enrolled in three modules therefore counts as three student-module enrollments for the variable platform charge.

The base platform rate is $42 per active student-module enrollment. A separate fixed configuration charge of $180 applies once per term, regardless of the number of modules. The configuration charge is not repeated for each module and is not included in the per-enrollment rate. The school pays Harbor Software for these platform services. Students’ tuition and school fees are collected by the school, not by Harbor Software.

The initial estimate used 24 active enrollments in Foundations, 20 in Applied Practice, 18 in Review Lab, and 16 in Capstone. That estimate produced 78 student-module enrollments. At the base rate, 78 multiplied by $42 equals $3,276; adding the one-time $180 configuration charge yields an estimated $3,456. The estimate is not an invoice and is not a minimum purchase commitment. Actual billing follows the census roster and any applicable signed amendment.

3. Schedule and census rules

For each module, the census occurs at 5:00 p.m. local time on the second calendar day after that module’s first scheduled class. A withdrawal recorded before the census is excluded from that module’s active enrollment count. A withdrawal recorded at or after the census remains billable for that module, even if the student does not attend later classes. The census is module-specific: withdrawing from one module does not automatically withdraw the student from another module.

The student roster is frozen for billing at the census time. A correction to a misspelled name does not change the count. A duplicate account is removed only if the registrar confirms that it represents the same student-module enrollment. A student who transfers between sections of the same module is counted once. A student who is enrolled in two different modules is counted twice under the base agreement.

The first scheduled class dates in the approved schedule are 6 January for Foundations, 13 January for Applied Practice, 20 January for Review Lab, and 27 January for Capstone. Accordingly, the respective census deadlines are 8 January at 5:00 p.m., 15 January at 5:00 p.m., 22 January at 5:00 p.m., and 29 January at 5:00 p.m. These dates are calendar-day calculations; weekends do not extend them. The schedule was approved in Amendment 1. A subsequently circulated calendar with a different date is not effective unless executed as an amendment.

4. Original reporting package

The base reporting package includes a weekly roster export and one end-of-term attendance summary. It does not include custom analysis, manual reconciliation of student fee accounts, or staff calls to students. The school must provide Harbor Software with the authorized roster and notify it of approved changes. Harbor Software may identify discrepancies, but the school decides whether a student is enrolled, withdrawn, or eligible for a certificate.

A weekly roster export is delivered as a spreadsheet. It contains the student identifier, module, section, roster status, and the date and time the status was last changed. The school is responsible for checking whether the export matches its registrar system. If the school does not report a discrepancy within five business days, the export is treated as accepted for operational purposes; that acceptance does not alter the census rules or authorize a charge inconsistent with the signed rate schedule.

The attendance summary reports the number of sessions recorded as attended, excused, or absent. It does not independently determine eligibility for a certificate. The school’s certificate rule, if any, is administered by the school and must not be inferred from a platform report. Harbor Software does not make academic decisions and may not tell a student that a certificate has been earned.

5. Amendment 1 — signed 22 December

The parties executed Amendment 1 on 22 December. It changes the module schedule and adds an attendance-import service. The schedule dates listed in Section 3 above are the dates approved by Amendment 1. For attendance imports, the vendor charges $65 for each module for which the school requests an import. An import is charged per module, not per student. The school requested imports for all four modules. Thus the attendance-import charge is four multiplied by $65, or $260.

Amendment 1 does not change the $42 base platform rate, the one-time $180 configuration charge, or the census rule. It does not authorize Harbor Software to collect student tuition. It does not set a new maximum enrollment. The amendment’s signature page is complete and signed by authorized representatives of both parties. A note in the school’s planning spreadsheet saying “$60 per module should be enough” predates the signed amendment and has no effect.

For clarity, if all 78 estimated student-module enrollments remain active, the base platform and configuration estimate remains $3,456. Adding the $260 attendance-import service gives $3,716. This is still an estimate because the actual number of active enrollments is determined at the module-specific census times. The estimate excludes student tuition, school assessment fees, and any optional services not listed in an executed document.

6. Amendment 2 — signed 10 January

Amendment 2 was signed by both parties on 10 January. It adds a two-dollar data-reconciliation surcharge for each active student-module enrollment in the Applied Practice and Review Lab modules only. The surcharge is not imposed on Foundations or Capstone. It is added to the $42 base platform rate for the two specified modules; it does not replace the base rate. The surcharge is assessed using the same census roster as the base platform fee.

The signed language states: “For Applied Practice and Review Lab only, the vendor shall invoice an additional $2 per active student-module enrollment. No such surcharge applies to Foundations or Capstone. All other rates and census rules remain unchanged.” The amendment has no retroactive effect on a module whose census occurred before it was signed, except that Applied Practice and Review Lab censuses had not yet occurred on 10 January. It therefore applies to those modules under the listed schedule. The Foundations census had already occurred on 8 January, but the amendment would not impose the surcharge there in any event. Capstone remains excluded.

A billing clerk’s draft calculation assumed that the surcharge applied to all 78 estimated enrollments, producing $156. That calculation is incorrect because only Applied Practice and Review Lab qualify. Using the original estimate of 20 Applied Practice and 18 Review Lab enrollments, the estimated eligible count is 38, and 38 multiplied by $2 equals $76. If actual census counts differ, the invoice uses the actual eligible count. The signed amendment controls over the draft calculation.

7. Amendment 3 — signed 16 January

Amendment 3 was signed 16 January. It adds an optional manual-reconciliation service, available only if the school submits a written request identifying the module and the reconciliation period. The fee is $90 for each requested module-period. A request covering two modules and two separate periods creates four module-period units, not two. The service is not automatically included in the base reporting package or Amendment 1’s attendance imports.

The school’s 16 January request expressly asked Harbor Software to reconcile the Foundations and Applied Practice rosters for the opening period and the subsequent correction period. That request therefore covers two modules multiplied by two periods, or four units. At $90 per unit, the authorized service charge is $360. The request did not ask for reconciliation of Review Lab or Capstone. An email subject line later said “all modules reviewed,” but the email body confirmed that the phrase referred to the complete review of the two named modules, not the addition of two further modules. The signed amendment requires a written request identifying the modules and periods; the 16 January request satisfies that condition only for Foundations and Applied Practice in the two periods specified.

Amendment 3 does not change the per-student base rate, the $2 surcharge, the $65 attendance-import fee, or the fixed configuration charge. It does not make manual reconciliation a per-student service. The relevant unit is one requested module-period. If the school asks only a question about a module without requesting the service, no manual-reconciliation fee is due.

8. Amendment 4 — signed 23 January; exception clause

Amendment 4 establishes a service-credit rule for a vendor-caused delay. If a scheduled export is delivered more than one business day after its stated delivery deadline, and the delay is attributable to Harbor Software, the school receives a $25 credit for that export. The credit is limited to one per affected export. It does not apply to a delay caused by the school’s late roster submission, a school-requested hold, a platform outage outside the vendor’s control, or a corrected export replacing an export that was timely delivered. Credits are applied to the next vendor invoice and cannot be paid directly to students.

The agreement defines a business day as Monday through Friday, excluding the two closure dates expressly listed in the term calendar: 1 January and 20 January. No other holidays are excluded for this contract. The export deadline is the end of the stated date. The one-business-day grace period is calculated by counting the next business day after the deadline as day one. A credit applies only if delivery occurs after the end of that grace day. Delivery by the end of the grace day is not “more than one business day late.”

A planning note says, “Every late file gets $25.” That note omits the causation and exception requirements and is not the contract rule. A separate note says, “20 January is a Monday, so count it as the first business day.” That is also incorrect because the signed calendar expressly makes 20 January a closure date.

9. Service deadlines and actual export events

The schedule states that weekly roster exports are due by 6:00 p.m. on the listed dates. The relevant log records four events. The Foundations opening export was due Friday, 10 January. Harbor Software delivered it Tuesday, 14 January at 10:00 a.m. The school’s roster file had been received on time, and the vendor’s incident record attributes the delay to a queue failure in Harbor Software’s export process. The next business day after 10 January was Monday, 13 January; the export was delivered after that day ended. The event meets the delay and causation conditions, so one $25 credit applies.

The Applied Practice opening export was due Friday, 17 January. The school delivered its roster file on Monday, 20 January, after the stated submission cutoff. The export was delivered Wednesday, 22 January. Although delivery was later than the nominal due date, the incident record attributes the delay to the school’s late roster, a stated exception. No credit applies to that export. In addition, 20 January is a closure date under the defined calendar and is not counted as a business day.

The Review Lab opening export was due Friday, 24 January. Harbor Software delivered it Monday, 27 January at 3:00 p.m. The vendor’s incident record says the file was held at the school’s request while the registrar resolved a duplicate-account question. A school-requested hold is an express exception. No credit applies to that export, even though the elapsed calendar time may look similar to the Foundations delay.

The Capstone opening export was due Friday, 31 January. Harbor Software delivered it Tuesday, 4 February at 9:00 a.m. The export was due on Friday, 31 January; the first business day after the deadline was Monday, 3 February, and the second was Tuesday, 4 February. Because the clause requires delivery after the end of the one-business-day grace day, delivery on Tuesday is more than one business day late. The vendor’s incident record attributes the delay to its own queue failure, and the school had submitted the roster on time. One $25 credit applies.

A separate corrected export was delivered on 5 February to replace the Capstone export. The original Capstone export was delivered late; the corrected export is not an additional scheduled export and does not generate a second credit. The clause limits the credit to one per affected export and excludes a corrected export replacing a timely delivered export. It does not create an additional credit for a correction to an already credited late export. The eligible credits for the four listed scheduled exports therefore total two multiplied by $25, or $50.

10. Registrar roster ledger

The following counts distinguish preliminary planning estimates from census counts. Counts in this ledger are student-module enrollments, not unique people across the term. Each status time is local time. Registrar confirmations are authoritative for whether a withdrawal was recorded before the applicable census.

Foundations census: 8 January at 5:00 p.m. The roster shows 24 enrollments at the deadline. One student withdrew at 4:42 p.m. on 8 January, leaving 23 active enrollments. A separate student changed sections within Foundations at 4:55 p.m.; that transfer does not add or remove an enrollment. Another student’s name was corrected the next morning without changing the student identifier. The billable count is 23.

Applied Practice census: 15 January at 5:00 p.m. The roster initially showed 20 enrollments. One student’s withdrawal was recorded at 5:03 p.m., after the census. That enrollment remains billable. One additional student was entered twice under two usernames, and the registrar confirmed before invoicing that both usernames were the same student’s single Applied Practice enrollment. Removing that confirmed duplicate leaves 19 distinct student-module enrollments, including the post-census withdrawal. The billable count is 19.

Review Lab census: 22 January at 5:00 p.m. The roster shows 18 enrollments. One student withdrew at 4:59 p.m. and is excluded. Another student asked by text to withdraw at 4:58 p.m., but the registrar did not record or confirm the withdrawal until 5:06 p.m. The agreement uses the time the withdrawal is recorded, not the time a student sends an unprocessed request. That enrollment remains active and billable. The billable count is 17.

Capstone census: 29 January at 5:00 p.m. The roster shows 16 enrollments. Two students withdrew at 4:40 p.m. and 4:50 p.m.; both are excluded. A third student stopped attending but did not withdraw and remains on the official roster. A student transferred between Capstone sections at 4:30 p.m., which does not create a second enrollment. The billable count is 14.

The actual total active student-module enrollments are therefore 23 + 19 + 17 + 14 = 73. The initial estimate was 78, a difference of five. At $42 per enrollment, the base variable charge is 73 × $42 = $3,066. Adding the one-time $180 configuration charge gives $3,246 before other services, surcharges, or credits. A draft invoice instead multiplied 78 by $42 and added $180, yielding $3,456. That draft uses the planning estimate rather than the census ledger and is not the final base calculation.

11. Amendment-specific arithmetic based on the confirmed counts

The attendance-import service applies to all four modules under Amendment 1. Four module imports at $65 each equal $260. This is a per-module amount and does not depend on the number of students.

The Amendment 2 surcharge applies only to Applied Practice and Review Lab. Their confirmed counts are 19 and 17, respectively. The eligible total is 19 + 17 = 36 student-module enrollments. At $2 each, the surcharge is 36 × $2 = $72. Foundations’ 23 and Capstone’s 14 are not added to this surcharge calculation. A worksheet that multiplies all 73 active enrollments by $2 reaches $146, but that applies the surcharge to two excluded modules and is inconsistent with the signed clause.

The Amendment 3 manual-reconciliation request covers Foundations and Applied Practice in two periods each. The units are Foundations-opening, Foundations-correction, Applied Practice-opening, and Applied Practice-correction: four module-period units. Four multiplied by $90 equals $360. The 16 January request does not include Review Lab or Capstone. It also does not authorize charging per student or treating every roster export as an additional reconciliation period.

The service-credit clause yields two credits, one for the late vendor-caused Foundations export and one for the late vendor-caused Capstone export. The Applied Practice delay resulted from the school’s late roster; the Review Lab export was held at the school’s request. Neither qualifies. The two eligible credits total $50. The corrected Capstone export does not add a third credit.

Combining the confirmed items gives base platform and configuration charges of $3,246, attendance imports of $260, the applicable surcharge of $72, and manual reconciliation of $360. These charges total $3,938. Subtracting the $50 service credit yields a net vendor invoice of $3,888, before any tax treatment not specified in this record. This total excludes student tuition and school fees because those are not vendor charges under the agreement.

A circulated summary gives $3,966 as the expected net amount.
