[{"state":"Status update to the event manager, followed by the event-day product review and the operating policy copied into the planning packet. Saltmarsh Labs Spring Forum, prepared by Hiro Nakamura for Yara Tanaka. I am angry that the same basic figures have been copied incorrectly into three different summaries, so this packet preserves the underlying counts and explains which numbers are estimates, which are confirmed, and which are merely old drafts. Do not treat a number as confirmed simply because it appears in a spreadsheet or in a loud email. This report is the consolidated record for the forum held at the Bracken Hall on 18 May. It includes the planning timeline, attendance reconciliation, vendor notes, review excerpts, policy text, and appendices. All organizations and products named here belong to this fictional event record.

MANAGER STATUS UPDATE

Yara,

The forum is over, and I am still furious about the avoidable confusion in the prep documents. The room was set for the confirmed registration count, not for the inflated estimate pasted into the first draft of the run sheet. Some people keep citing the draft figure of 214 as if it were the final attendance. It was not. Another spreadsheet says 198, which was a room-capacity planning figure, not a count of people who checked in. Please use the reconciled entry record in this packet when answering attendance questions.

The original event plan had four audience groups: standard delegates, invited speakers, crew, and vendors. The final check-in record lists 146 standard delegates, 18 invited speakers, 22 crew members, and 9 vendor representatives. Those are distinct people who entered the event. The count does not include 7 people who registered but did not arrive, 4 duplicate registration records removed before the doors opened, or 3 delivery drivers who dropped boxes at the loading bay and never entered the event space. The difference between the old 214 estimate and the final total is not a mystery. The old estimate included projected walk-ins and repeated records. It was marked preliminary in the file, but someone removed that label when copying it into the run sheet.

For clarity, the four confirmed groups total 195 people: 146 + 18 + 22 + 9 = 195. This is the entry count. The number 198 in the capacity sheet means the minimum number of chairs reserved after adding three spare seats. It is not an attendance count. The number 214 in the preliminary estimate came from 195 confirmed entries plus 12 expected walk-ins and 7 registrations that were still marked uncertain at that point. The uncertain registrations did not all become attendees; the reconciled door log is controlling for actual entry.

I also need the expense summary corrected. The approved spending ceiling was $24,000. Confirmed invoices in the final ledger were: Bracken Hall rental, $8,400; food service, $5,760; sound and projection, $3,180; signage and print, $1,260; accessible transport, $1,440; and speaker travel support, $2,760. These six confirmed expense lines sum to $22,800. The remaining $1,200 is unspent capacity under the ceiling, not an invoice and not a refund owed by a supplier. A separate draft had a $3,180 equipment quote copied twice, making its supposed total $25,980. The duplicate is plainly labelled “draft copy,” and no second equipment invoice exists. Do not add it.

The food count has also been misrepresented. The catering order was 180 standard meals and 24 vegetarian meals, for 204 meals ordered. The kitchen delivered 176 standard meals and 24 vegetarian meals, for 200 meals delivered. Four standard meals were not delivered. The vendor's first message said “we have 204 covered,” but that referred to the quantity ordered, not delivered. Our receipt at 12:10 records the delivered quantities. There were 195 event entrants and five staff meals served from the delivered stock after the lunch service; meal service accounting and entrance accounting are different records. The four missing standard meals are a legitimate service issue. The difference between 204 and 200 is four, not twenty-four; the vegetarian count was fulfilled exactly.

The room setup was confirmed for 198 chairs: 195 places based on actual attendance plus 3 spare chairs. A photo caption says “214 seats ready,” but the caption was written against the preliminary estimate and is wrong. There were 198 chairs on the floor. The venue inventory counted 204 chairs in storage, of which 6 were never brought into the hall. This does not change the number of attendees or chairs set up. The count of 198 is not 204, and neither number should be substituted for the reconciled entry total of 195.

The event schedule was published with a 09:00 opening, a 09:30 welcome, a 10:00 first session, a 12:15 lunch, and a 16:30 close. The programme ran 10 minutes late at the start, but the final session still ended at 16:30 because the break was shortened. A note saying “we lost 30 minutes” refers to the initial draft schedule, which had an unapproved 09:30 opening and a 17:00 close; it is not the duration lost on the day. The delayed opening was 10 minutes relative to the approved 09:00 opening. The agenda record and stage manager's log agree.

The guest feedback count is another mess. We received 72 submitted forms. Of those, 48 rated the programme excellent, 16 rated it good, 5 rated it fair, and 3 rated it poor. These four categories total 72. A preliminary dashboard showed 75 responses because three duplicate submissions were not yet removed. The final feedback breakdown is based on 72 valid forms. Five “fair” scores do not mean five complaints about the food; the form asked for an overall event rating. Food-specific comments are discussed in the product review section.

The logistics crew reported 11 transport bookings: 8 accessible vehicle bookings and 3 standard vehicle bookings. The summary sheet says 14 because it counts three cancelled requests in addition to the 11 completed bookings. The completed booking count is 11. Of the eight accessible bookings, seven passengers arrived using the arranged transport and one cancelled on the morning of the event. A cancelled booking is not a completed ride. The service invoice was $1,440 and covers the agreed availability package, not a per-passenger fare calculated from either 11 or 14.

We had 36 exhibition tables in the floor plan. Twenty-nine were assigned to exhibitors, four were set aside for registration and information, and three were left empty for circulation. The allocation adds to 36. A draft uses 39 because it adds three tables from an earlier design that were removed after the fire-lane review. No one should report 39 tables as installed. The floor manager's signed checklist records 36 placed tables.

For staffing, the assignment sheet lists 22 crew members: 6 registration, 4 stage, 5 room support, 3 catering liaison, 2 accessibility support, and 2 operations leads. The subtotal is 22. A message says “24 people on staff” because it includes Yara and me as managers in addition to the 22 assigned crew members. That may be a reasonable count for everyone working, but the attendance group called crew in the check-in record is 22, and the assignment roster is also 22. The manager count is not a correction to the crew figure.

The registration desk processed 163 badge scans before the opening talk. That number is not total attendance: 32 attendees entered through the east-side scanner after the desk opened, and the scanners were not synchronized for the first fifteen minutes. The final reconciled entry register already includes all 195 people and removes the known duplicates. Do not calculate total attendance by adding 163 and 32, since some of those 32 scans overlap with manual desk records. The door supervisor reconciled the named list against the separate entry sheets and signed off on 195 unique entrants.

The incident log lists 2 minor issues: one microphone battery failure and one spilled drink near the foyer. A draft says 5 because it includes three routine assistance requests as incidents. The approved definition in the safety checklist counts an incident only when it involves an injury, equipment malfunction affecting the programme, or a spill requiring a cleanup response. Under that definition there were 2 recorded incidents. No injury was reported. The microphone battery was replaced in four minutes, and the spill was cleaned before the next attendee group arrived.

The signage inventory is 42 printed signs: 18 directional, 12 programme boards, 6 access notices, and 6 sponsor panels. The total is 42. A request form asked for 48 copies, but six were cancelled before printing. The supplier invoice of $1,260 is for the 42 produced signs, not the requested quantity. The four additional signs found in the storage cabinet were from a previous event and were not installed at this forum.

The speaker support line has five people receiving travel assistance, although the approved budget line totals $2,760. It is not valid to divide the budget by every person who attended. The grant covers agreed travel amounts for five speakers, and those amounts were not all equal. A draft summary listed six speakers because a substitute speaker's name remained on the list after the substitute withdrew. The final programme and travel ledger agree on five supported speakers.

The planning group originally expected six sessions, but the final programme contained five: opening remarks, two plenary talks, one workshop block, and a closing panel. The workshop block included three concurrent rooms, but it is one programme block for the session count used in the manager's status report. The agenda has five numbered items. A draft uses eight by counting three workshop rooms separately and counting the welcome as a session. Neither method is the final report convention. The final programme count is five numbered sessions.

Please stop circulating the preliminary figures. The confirmed sources are the signed entry register for people, the signed floor checklist for furniture, the final ledger for spending, the receipt for food delivery, and the published programme for sessions. The schedule change log, feedback export, and transport reconciliation are attached below. I know this is a lot of paperwork for a one-day forum, but it is better than another confident email built on a copied number. I will not approve a status memo that says 214 people attended, that we spent $25,980, or that 204 meals were delivered. Those claims contradict the final records.

EVENT-DAY PRODUCT REVIEW: BRACKEN HALL SERVICE AND MEAL PACKAGE

The event-day package was sold to us as a simple, reliable way to run a mid-sized forum. The actual service was uneven, and I am irritated that the sales sheet made everything sound automatic. The room itself was clean and the presentation equipment worked after the battery change, but the meal handoff and the way the venue team counted equipment were not handled carefully. This review is not a general endorsement and should not be quoted as one.

The signed order requested 204 meals: 180 standard and 24 vegetarian. At delivery, the receiving table counted 176 standard and 24 vegetarian meals. The total delivered was 200. Four standard meals were missing. The delivery ticket initially showed 204 in a box labelled “order total”; the handwritten receiving note shows “200 received.” The catering manager acknowledged the shortfall by email at 12:34. The four missing meals were not later delivered, and no replacement food was supplied before lunch ended.

The meal labels were mostly clear, but two trays were positioned behind the hot drinks. That placement caused delay, not an additional shortage. The vegetarian trays were all present, and the dietary coordinator counted 24 before service. A guest's message saying “I saw only twenty meals” described the number of trays visible from the doorway, not the number of individual vegetarian meals. There were six meals per vegetarian tray, with four trays, so the verified quantity was 24. The standard meal trays held varying counts and were recorded by the kitchen on the receiving sheet.

The invoice for food service was $5,760. A separate catering estimate was $5,940 because it included a $180 late menu change that was waived before the contract was signed. The invoice is the final charge. The $180 does not appear as an additional charge in the ledger. Someone copied the estimate into the cost summary and claimed food cost $5,940; that is not supported by the payment record. The charge actually paid was $5,760. The distinction matters because the approved budget report uses paid invoices, not pre-contract estimates.

The hall package included 198 chairs in the main room, 36 tables, two projector screens, and one lectern microphone. The team set up the agreed 198 chairs and 36 tables. The two screens were both present. The lectern microphone worked for the welcome but failed during a later transition when its battery ran low. It was replaced, and the replacement worked. A facilities note lists three microphones because it counts the spare microphone in the equipment case; only two microphones were on stage at once. The service description promised one lectern microphone plus one handheld microphone, with a spare available. The actual inventory at the venue was consistent with that package, even though the first run sheet failed to mention the spare.

I am annoyed by the review card that gives the package “five stars” in a heading and then says, “Wonderful, if your idea of wonderful is chasing four missing lunches while someone points at the order total.” The sentence is sarcasm, not sincere praise. The reviewer's overall rating on the submitted form was fair, not excellent. This is one of five fair overall ratings in the final 72-form export. It must not be counted as another form or as a sixth fair response; it is already included in the total.

The access arrangement was better than the meal arrangement. The venue kept the east-side ramp clear, placed six access notices, and reserved eight accessible vehicle bookings through the transport contractor. Seven booked passengers used a ride and one cancelled. The driver's handwritten count of “8 served” includes the cancelled booking in the dispatch list, not a completed ride. The transport reconciliation confirms seven completed passenger arrivals by arranged vehicle. The access notices were visible from the foyer, although one was angled away from the registration line.

The sound and projection invoice was $3,180. The event manager approved a quote of $3,180 and paid one invoice for $3,180. A procurement export displays the quote and invoice in separate rows, which can make it appear that the cost was $6,360 if both rows are added. The quote is not a second cost. The paid ledger records one equipment expense. The presentation system was tested at 08:20, and both screens displayed the opening slide. A battery change was required for the lectern microphone; it did not result in a second sound invoice.

The venue room rental was $8,400. A planning note says $8,000 because that was the base room charge before the $400 access and setup supplement was approved. The final contract and invoice include the supplement, so the amount charged was $8,400. The original draft ceiling did not include the supplement; the approved $24,000 ceiling did. These amounts should not be confused with attendance or with room capacity. The hall's posted fire limit was 240 people, but the event did not reach that capacity.

The print package was acceptable but the paperwork was not. The final order was 42 signs for $1,260. The quote was for 48 copies at $1,440, and six copies were removed before production. Dividing the final total by the requested quantity would produce a misleading unit cost, because the final invoice covers 42 produced signs. The invoice's item lines specify 18 directional signs, 12 programme boards, 6 access notices, and 6 sponsor panels. Those categories sum to 42. The four old signs in storage were not part of this order.

For next time, I would retain the hall but require a physical meal count at handoff, a signed delivery ticket that separates ordered from received quantities, and one cost ledger that does not display quotes as though they were paid invoices. I am not asking anyone to invent a compensation amount. The vendor has acknowledged the four-meal shortfall, but the records do not yet show a credit. The food complaint is supported; a claim that a credit has already been issued is not.

OPERATING POLICY EXCERPT: EVENT COUNTS AND RECONCILIATION

This policy page is included because the planning group ignored its own definitions while assembling the draft summary. These rules apply to the Spring Forum report and to other Saltmarsh Labs events using the same forms. The policy is deliberately plain. If a value is labelled preliminary, it is not a final result. If two records disagree, use the designated controlling record for that type of value rather than averaging them or selecting whichever value looks more convenient.

Attendance means unique people who physically entered the controlled event space during the event window. It does not mean registrations, projected walk-ins, badges printed, people assigned to work, people who delivered supplies outside the controlled space, seats arranged, or the maximum legal room capacity. A person who enters once and leaves and later re-enters counts once. A duplicate registration record counts zero additional people. A no-show counts zero. A delivery driver who leaves a box at the loading bay and never enters the event space counts zero. The signed entry register is the controlling record, after duplicate names have been reconciled.

The attendance groups for this report are standard delegates, invited speakers, crew, and vendor representatives. These groups are mutually exclusive in the final entry register. If a manager appears in the crew assignment list but is recorded in a separate manager category, do not silently move that person into the crew group. The report may separately describe “all people working,” but that is not the crew category and must be labelled differently. When a question asks for the crew count, use the crew category as shown, not the broader count of crew plus managers.

Capacity means the maximum number permitted in a room under the posted safety limit. It is not actual attendance. A chair count means the number of chairs physically placed in the room. A reserved-seat count means the number of places planned, including any spare seats if the planning convention says to include them. These are different measurements. A floor plan may reserve three spare chairs beyond the expected audience; those chairs are still chairs, but they are not additional attendees. An inventory count in storage does not describe what was set up in the event room.

Meal order means the number of portions requested from the food supplier. Meal delivery means the number of portions physically received and verified at handoff. Meal service means the number of portions ultimately distributed. Those values may differ. The signed receiving sheet controls the delivered quantity. A supplier order total cannot be used as proof of delivery. If the receiving sheet states separate dietary categories, add those categories to calculate the delivered total, and preserve the category detail. A missing portion in one category cannot be erased by an excess or complete delivery in another category.

A vendor message that says “covered,” “ready,” or “complete” does not replace a quantity-specific receiving record. If a message refers to the order, it means the requested quantity unless it explicitly says the quantity was received and verified. A photograph of trays is not a count unless a qualified checker records the count. A visible tray count may not equal portions, because a tray can contain multiple meals. The meal coordinator's signed tally is the controlling record for category counts and total delivery.

Expense means a charge that appears in the final approved ledger as payable or paid. A quote, estimate, draft purchase request, cancelled line, or duplicate copy is not an additional expense. When a quote and invoice have the same amount, do not add them together. Use the final invoice amount once. A waived fee is not payable. A remaining budget balance is not an expense, a refund, or a vendor credit. To calculate remaining capacity under a spending ceiling, subtract confirmed expenses from the approved ceiling. State the arithmetic and identify whether the result is a balance or an expense.

The final ceiling for the Spring Forum is $24,000. The confirmed invoices are room rental $8,400; food $5,760; sound and projection $3,180; signage and print $1,260; accessible transport $1,440; and speaker travel support $2,760. Adding those amounts gives $22,800: $8,400 + $5,760 = $14,160; plus $3,180 = $17,340; plus $1,260 = $18,600; plus $1,440 = $20,040; plus $2,760 = $22,800. The remaining capacity is $24,000 - $22,800 = $1,200. The duplicate equipment quote is excluded. The waived $180 menu amendment is excluded. The final ledger is controlling for expenses.

In the event report, an equipment quote copied into an export is not a second equipment purchase. A procurement sheet may show both an estimate and a payment line to document the decision history. Only the final ledger tells the reader what was charged. If an amount occurs twice in a document, determine whether the lines represent two distinct paid transactions before adding them. Never infer a second payment merely because the same figure appears in two places.

Staffing count means people assigned in the crew roster, unless a report explicitly says it includes managers. The Spring Forum roster has 6 registration staff, 4 stage staff, 5 room-support staff, 3 catering liaisons, 2 accessibility-support staff, and 2 operations leads. The categories total 22. The manager pair is outside that roster category for this report. A message that counts 24 working people may include those two managers, but it does not revise the roster total. The signed roster is the controlling record for crew assignments.

Session count means numbered programme items in the published agenda. A set of simultaneous rooms within one numbered workshop block is one session for the report. Opening remarks count only if listed as a numbered programme item; a welcome note that is not numbered does not automatically become a session. The final Spring Forum programme has five numbered items. The programme PDF is controlling. An old draft that separately counts breakout rooms or an unnumbered welcome is not controlling.

The final Spring Forum programme lists five numbered items: opening remarks, plenary one, plenary two, workshop block, and closing panel. The workshop block operates in three concurrent rooms. The fact that there are three rooms does not transform the one numbered block into three sessions for this specific report. Another report may give a room-by-room activity count, but it must use that label and may not substitute it for the programme session count. A draft count of eight uses an obsolete convention and must not appear as the final session count.

Feedback means valid, submitted forms after duplicate removal. The Spring Forum export has 72 valid forms: 48 excellent, 16 good, 5 fair, and 3 poor. These categories sum to 72. A dashboard showing 75 before three duplicates were removed is preliminary. Individual comments do not create extra forms, and a comment that repeats a rating already represented in the export is not a new response. Use the final export to report the overall rating distribution.

Do not turn an overall rating into a category-specific claim. A fair overall score does not necessarily mean a person complained about food, transport, venue access, or any other single service. To report a food problem, use explicit food evidence such as the receiving record or a food-specific comment. Conversely, a specific food complaint remains a food complaint even if the person gives the event a positive overall rating. Keep the topic of a question aligned with the evidence that answers it.

Transport booking count means completed bookings under the reconciliation convention, not requests submitted. The Spring Forum had 11 completed bookings: 8 accessible and 3 standard. Three additional requests were cancelled and are not included in the completed booking total. Of the eight accessible bookings, one was cancelled on the day, leaving seven completed passenger arrivals by arranged vehicle. The signed transport reconciliation controls. A dispatch list that includes a cancelled request is not proof of completed service.

Furniture count means items physically placed in the room. For this event, the signed floor checklist records 198 chairs and 36 tables. The chair setup comprised 195 expected places plus 3 spare chairs. The table allocation was 29 exhibitor tables, 4 registration or information tables, and 3 empty circulation tables. The three removed tables in an earlier draft are not installed furniture. The venue storage inventory is not the room setup count. Use the signed floor checklist for installed items.

Incident count means events meeting the safety checklist definition: an injury, an equipment malfunction affecting the programme, or a spill that requires a cleanup response. Routine assistance requests are not incidents under this report convention. The Spring Forum log contains one microphone battery failure and one spill requiring cleanup, for two incidents. No injury was reported. A draft count that adds three routine assistance requests is not the approved incident count. The signed safety log is controlling.

Schedule delay means the difference between an approved programme time and the time actually recorded on the stage log. Do not compare the event to an obsolete draft. The approved opening was 09:00, and the actual opening was 09:10, so the opening delay was 10 minutes. A note about a 30-minute difference refers to a draft schedule with a different opening and close. If an adjustment to a later break recovers time, report that separately rather than pretending the opening was on time.

The published programme and the stage manager's log are the controlling schedule records. The approved start time was 09:00. The actual opening was at 09:10. The final closing time remained 16:30 after the break was shortened. The event therefore started ten minutes after its approved opening and did not close thirty minutes late. An obsolete plan with a 09:30 start and a 17:00 close is not evidence of actual delay.

A status report must label the source and status of each count. Use “confirmed,” “preliminary,” “estimate,” “ordered,” “received,” “paid,” or “cancelled” accurately. Do not remove a qualifier while copying a value. If a preliminary estimate includes expected walk-ins, it cannot be rephrased as a confirmed entry count. If an invoice is unpaid, report it as an approved payable item only if the ledger says so; do not describe it as paid. If a vendor acknowledges a service shortfall but has not issued a credit, do not claim that a credit exists.

Where the records conflict, the designated source controls: signed entry register for attendance; final invoice ledger for expense; receiving sheet for meals delivered; signed floor checklist for furniture; published programme for numbered sessions; final feedback export for valid ratings; signed transport reconciliation for completed bookings; signed safety log for incidents; and stage manager's log for actual times. A preliminary spreadsheet can help explain how an error arose, but it cannot overrule the controlling record. Do not average the two values. Do not choose the larger value to be cautious or the smaller value to make the result look better.

For numeric answers, show the relevant arithmetic in the note or working record. If a question asks whether a total exceeds a ceiling, add the confirmed components once and compare the sum to the ceiling. If it asks for a difference, subtract the smaller confirmed amount from the larger. If it asks for a category count, add only the rows in that category. If it asks for a completed quantity, exclude cancelled or undelivered items. A plausible number elsewhere in the packet is not a substitute for the requested calculation.

A candidate description in a decision form may be brief, such as “over,” “within,” “195,” or “none.” Short labels do not relax the evidence standard. The person completing the form must determine what the instruction actually asks for and use the correct measurement. For example, a question about attendees should not be answered with the capacity, seating count, meal count, badge count, or preliminary estimate. A question about delivered meals should not be answered with ordered meals. A question about the amount paid should not be answered with an estimate.

The policy does not permit unsupported precision. If no source gives the requested value, the report must say that it is not established. If a question offers “none of the above,” use it only when none of the described substantive categories fits the controlling record. When a substantive category does fit, select that category even if a draft or comment phrases the matter loosely. A decision should be defensible from the records alone, not from an unrecorded assumption about what probably happened.

DOCUMENT CONTROL AND RECONCILIATION NOTES

The final entry register was reconciled at 18:05 on 18 May. The east door sheet recorded 87 unique people. The main entrance sheet recorded 108 unique people. The lists were compared by registration code and name to remove four duplicate records appearing across the raw scans. The signed, reconciled total is 195 unique entrants. The group breakdown is 146 standard delegates, 18 invited speakers, 22 crew, and 9 vendor representatives. The breakdown sums to 195. The 7 registered no-shows are retained in the registration archive but not in the entry total. The 3 delivery drivers are in the loading-bay log and did not enter the controlled event area.

The 87 and 108 raw door-sheet counts should not be naively added without understanding how the reconciliation was done. The final register has already resolved overlap and duplicates. The signed final number is 195. The preliminary sheet's 214 was assembled before the door check and includes a 12-person projected walk-in allowance plus 7 uncertain registrations. The planning team later copied that number forward without preserving the word “projected.” The error is clerical, not a change in the definition of attendance.

The cost ledger was locked on 24 May. Its six approved lines are room $8,400, food $5,760, sound and projection $3,180, print $1,260, transport $1,440, and speaker travel $2,760. The total is $22,800, leaving $1,200 under the $24,000 ceiling. One procurement export contains the sound quote and the same sound invoice in separate historical rows. It does not show two payments. The event administrator verified the bank transaction once, at $3,180. The waived $180 menu amendment never became a payable invoice. No vendor credit relating to the four missing meals is shown in the ledger as of the lock date.

The signed receiving sheet was completed by the catering liaison and the delivery driver. It records 176 standard portions and 24 vegetarian portions received at 11:42. The driver signed beside the total of 200. The order confirmation lists 180 standard and 24 vegetarian portions, or 204 ordered. There is no later supplementary delivery slip. The kitchen service tally records 176 standard portions and 24 vegetarian portions available at the service point. The five staff meals came from that stock and are not extra deliveries. The record therefore supports 200 meals received, with four standard portions short of the order.

The final room checklist was signed before doors opened. It records 198 chairs, 36 tables, 2 projector screens, 1 lectern microphone, and 1 handheld microphone on the stage inventory. One spare microphone remained in the equipment case. The chair total was 195 planned attendee places plus 3 spares. The storage-room count of 204 chairs includes 6 not moved into the hall. The fire limit was 240 people. The number of chairs, number of people, and maximum occupancy are separate facts.

The programme PDF approved on 14 May has five numbered items. The room schedule shows three concurrent rooms during item four, the workshop block. The session reporting convention counts numbered items, not rooms. The stage log records the welcome at 09:10, against an approved 09:00 start, and the closing panel ending at 16:30. The break was shortened to keep the advertised closing time. The old 09:30-to-17:00 draft was superseded and should not be used to calculate actual delay.

The final survey file is identified as “Forum_72_valid.” It has 72 unique response identifiers: 48 excellent, 16 good, 5 fair, and 3 poor. The earlier dashboard had 75 rows, including three repeated response identifiers. Those repeats were removed before the final file was exported. The sarcastic review card is one of the five fair responses, not an additional response. It complains about four missing meals while using an apparently complimentary phrase. The intended meaning is frustration, and the rating is fair.

The transport contractor reconciliation lists 11 completed bookings, 8 accessible and 3 standard. One accessible passenger cancelled after dispatch was scheduled. The driver's first tally of eight accessible trips included that cancelled booking because it came from the departure list, but the final signed reconciliation marks one cancelled and seven completed. The charge under the contracted availability package remains $1,440. The completed-ride count is not calculated by dividing the package cost by an assumed fare.

The signage production ticket lists 42 produced signs, matching the four categories of 18 directional, 12 programme boards, 6 access notices, and 6 sponsor panels. The initial request was for 48. The six-copy reduction was approved before production. Four older signs were found in the hall's storage cabinet, but their presence does not increase the quantity produced for this event. The final invoice is $1,260.

The incident report contains two qualifying entries. Entry one: lectern microphone battery failure, affecting the programme transition, corrected in four minutes. Entry two: drink spill in the foyer, requiring cleanup, no injury. Three other logged contacts were ordinary requests for directions and seating help. The report definition excludes routine assistance requests, so the signed incident count remains two. The existence of five lines in a broader contact log does not change the number of qualifying incidents.

Section C — Applicant FAQ excerpt

Kestrel Studio Careers — Applicant Questions, revision 3.2
Effective date: 1 May

The following excerpt was attached to the posting and made available from the application page. It is reproduced here because several communications refer to the meaning of the posted requirements. The excerpt applies to this recruitment exercise unless the individual posting expressly states a different rule. Where a posting is more specific, the posting controls. The FAQ is guidance for applicants and recruiters; it is not a substitute for the role description.

Question: Does submitting an application guarantee an interview?

Answer: No. Every complete submission is considered against the published criteria, but only applicants whose evidence meets the relevant threshold are invited to the next stage. An acknowledgement confirms receipt only. It does not indicate that the application has passed screening, that a decision has been made, or that an interview is guaranteed. Recruiters should not describe an automated receipt message as an invitation.

Question: Must applicants have performed every task in the role description before applying?

Answer: No. Essential criteria are used to assess whether an applicant has the required capability or a sufficiently relevant example. Desirable criteria may strengthen an application, but they must not be treated as mandatory unless the posting explicitly identifies them as essential. Applicants may explain transferable experience. A recruiter should distinguish what the applicant actually did from what the applicant might be able to learn. For example, maintaining a simple shared record can be relevant to record accuracy without being equivalent to prior use of a particular commercial platform.

Question: What counts as experience maintaining a record?

Answer: The term can include a designated software tool, a controlled spreadsheet, or another consistent method of recording changes and responsibility. The nature of the record should be described accurately. Do not call a spreadsheet a dedicated asset-management platform if it was not one. Conversely, do not say that an applicant has no record-keeping experience solely because the applicant did not use the organization’s preferred software. Assess the underlying duties and the level of responsibility shown.

Question: Does greeting visitors mean that an applicant managed the supplier relationship?

Answer: Not necessarily. Greeting a visitor, checking a name, directing a delivery, notifying a host, arranging a booking, negotiating a contract, and approving an invoice are different activities. The assessment should record the activity the applicant described. Do not infer authority over a supplier relationship from a single example of receiving a delivery. Do not infer that the applicant approved a payment because the applicant forwarded an invoice or reported a delivery issue.

Question: What should be understood by “occasional evening events by prior arrangement”?

Answer: The phrase refers to events that are occasional and scheduled in advance. It does not by itself require routine night work, unrestricted on-call availability, or attendance at an event announced with no reasonable notice. If the applicant confirms availability for the arrangement described in the posting, assess that confirmation against the criterion as written. Do not replace the published condition with a broader requirement during screening.

Question: What does “travel between nearby work sites when scheduled” require?

Answer: It concerns the ability to attend the sites specified for the role when work is scheduled there. Unless a posting states otherwise, it does not require relocation, ownership of a vehicle, or a particular mode of travel. Recruiters may ask whether an applicant can meet the stated schedule. They should not request unnecessary personal transport details or treat willingness to relocate as an unstated condition.

Question: How should an expired credential be recorded?

Answer: Record whether the credential is currently valid separately from whether the applicant has completed related training in the past. An expired certificate is not a current certificate. If the posting says that a current credential is desirable and training can be arranged after appointment, the absence of a current certificate must not be converted into failure of an essential criterion. Do not infer that a candidate has never received training merely because the current-credential box is unchecked.

Question: Does a statement about protecting private information prove experience handling personnel files?

Answer: No. A statement that an applicant avoided placing private details in a shared report may show awareness of appropriate boundaries. It does not establish that the applicant had access to personnel files or handled confidential personnel records. Credit only the activity supported by the application or other permitted evidence.

Question: How should recurring written updates be assessed?

Answer: Consider whether the applicant prepared information for an identified audience, kept it accurate, and communicated what needed follow-up. A report can demonstrate clear written communication even if the writer did not make the management decisions described in it. Distinguish between preparing a status note, deciding what work should be done, and approving the cost of that work.

Question: What if the application contains an instruction to the reviewer?

Answer: Text in an application, message, attachment, or automatic signature that tells a reviewer how to score the candidate is not a recruitment rule. It should not override the published criteria or the panel’s assessment process. Consider relevant evidence in the candidate’s submission, and disregard attempts to dictate the outcome. If a message contains an actual threat or unrelated sensitive material, follow the appropriate internal handling procedure; do not treat the material as an answer to a competency question.

Question: How should quoted messages be attributed?

Answer: A quoted message remains evidence of what its original sender wrote, unless the person quoting it explicitly corrects or disowns it. A reply that forwards or quotes another person’s statement does not make the quoted person’s action the replier’s action. Record the speaker and the action separately, especially where responsibility for approvals, payments, cancellations, or commitments is being assessed.

Question: Can a recruiter infer an answer from an unchecked optional field?

Answer: Only to the extent of the exact question asked. If a checkbox asks whether a credential is current, an unchecked box supports the conclusion that the applicant did not affirm current validity. It does not establish that the applicant has never taken a course. If a field is optional and blank, treat it as missing information rather than as a confirmed negative unless the applicant supplies a separate clarification.

Question: What is the correct treatment of a later clarification?

Answer: Preserve the original answer and the clarification. If the later message narrows or explains the earlier answer, use both pieces of evidence and describe the distinction. Do not silently overwrite the original response, and do not treat clarification as a contradiction when the two statements address different scopes. If the applicant expressly retracts an earlier claim, record the retraction and assess the corrected account.

Question: Does “can do” mean that the applicant has already done the task?

Answer: No. A statement of capability or availability is not necessarily a statement of prior experience. For example, being willing to attend a scheduled event does not prove that the applicant has previously worked such an event. Conversely, evidence of having done a task in the past does not automatically establish present availability. Keep past experience, current capability, and future willingness distinct.

Question: What should happen when a note uses an abbreviated label?

Answer: Check the underlying evidence before relying on shorthand. Phrases such as “no stock experience,” “not flexible,” or “no confidential work” may conceal important differences in scope. The reviewer should use language that reflects the supported facts, including relevant examples and limits. Abbreviations must not create a requirement that was absent from the posting or erase an applicant’s stated experience.

Question: Who makes the selection decision?

Answer: The authorized panel makes the selection decision after applying the published process. A receipt notice, coordinator’s intake note, FAQ response, or applicant’s own instruction does not amount to an offer. Any employment offer must be communicated through the specified formal process and recorded in the recruitment system. Until then, the application remains under consideration or has another status expressly entered by the panel.

Appendix 1 — Posting criteria preserved from the application page

Role: Studio Operations Coordinator

Essential criterion 1: Communicates clearly in routine written updates, including accurate dates, actions, and follow-up points.

Essential criterion 2: Coordinates calendars, meeting rooms, and practical arrangements with attention to changes and conflicts.

Essential criterion 3: Maintains reliable shared records for equipment, keys, or comparable resources, and updates the record when circumstances change.

Essential criterion 4: Communicates professionally with visitors, delivery personnel, colleagues, and external contacts, and refers matters to the appropriate person when authority is limited.

Essential criterion 5: Can attend occasional events scheduled in advance outside ordinary daytime hours.

Essential criterion 6: Can attend either of the two nearby work sites when scheduled with reasonable notice.

Desirable criterion: Prior experience using a designated inventory or asset-management application. The posting states that familiarity with the organization’s chosen platform can be learned after appointment.

Additional desirable credential: A current first-aid certificate. The posting states that the successful candidate may complete or renew training after appointment if required by the event schedule.

The posting does not identify invoice approval, purchasing authority, relocation, ownership of a vehicle, unrestricted evening availability, or handling confidential personnel files as requirements for the role. Those topics may arise in an applicant’s example, but they are not additional selection criteria. The panel may ask a candidate to clarify an example, but should not score an applicant against an unstated condition.

Appendix 2 — Screening record extracts

6 May, 09:15 — Automated receipt sent. Status: application received.

7 May, 15:30 — Intake completeness check passed. Status unchanged.

13 May, 11:00 — Panel review began. Status: under consideration.

16 May, 14:10 — Initial evidence review completed. Panel note: “Evidence provided for each essential area; invite to structured interview.” This entry records a next-stage decision only. It is not an offer of employment.

17 May, 09:05 — Interview invitation sent, subject to confirmation of attendance. The invitation offered two appointment times and gave the applicant five working days to choose one. The email asked the applicant to bring no employer-owned records and stated that examples could be discussed verbally.

20 May, 12:27 — Priya selected the later appointment time. The response did not change any of her earlier statements. She asked whether the interview would include a practical exercise. The coordinator replied that the exercise would use a fictional room-booking scenario and would not require access to a personal account or external software.

22 May, 16:00 — Interview completed. Panel members recorded evidence separately before discussing scores. The record notes that the exercise assessed prioritisation, accurate written handover, and appropriate referral of decisions outside the coordinator’s authority. It did not assess budget approval or use of a named inventory product.

24 May, 10:45 — Panel discussion completed. Outcome field: “Further review required.” No offer was entered. The hiring manager asked for a second check that the interview notes did not treat a hypothetical answer as evidence of a past achievement. The coordinator confirmed that the competency scores were based on examples the applicant said had actually occurred, while statements about what she could do in a future role were recorded as capability or availability only.

Appendix 3 — Record-handling and interpretation notes

The application platform stores the applicant’s original form as a read-only submission. Recruitment staff may add notes but may not alter the original response. Follow-up messages are attached to the same file reference. If an applicant clarifies a statement, both versions remain visible so that a later reviewer can understand the context. This process is intended to prevent accidental substitution of an interpretation for the original evidence.

The panel’s scoring sheet separates experience, capability, and availability. Experience means an account of a task performed in the past. Capability means an account or demonstration indicating the applicant can perform a task. Availability means confirmation that the applicant can meet a schedule or condition. A single sentence can contain more than one kind of evidence, but the scorer should identify which part supports which criterion. For example, a statement that the applicant previously travelled between work sites is experience; a statement that she can attend the two specified sites is availability; neither alone establishes that she owns a vehicle.

The same separation applies to records and approvals. Maintaining a list can support evidence of careful record keeping. It does not prove that the applicant controlled purchasing. Receiving a delivery can support evidence of visitor or supplier communication. It does not prove that the applicant negotiated a contract. Preparing a weekly issue note can support evidence of written communication and follow-up. It does not prove that the applicant chose a contractor, accepted a quoted price, or authorised payment. The reviewer should not award or deduct credit for an authority the applicant neither claimed nor needed for the role.

Where an applicant reports an activity but describes a limitation, the complete account should be assessed. A limitation may define the boundaries of the example rather than negate it. Priya’s statement that she updated a shared equipment record while lacking permission to create purchase orders contains evidence of record keeping and a separate limit on financial authority. Treating the limit as proof that she did not maintain a record would confuse distinct duties. Treating the record keeping as proof of purchasing authority would make the opposite error.

The formal posting controls the conditions of the role. If an informal note uses broader language than the posting, the broader language must not be used to disqualify an applicant unless the requirement is properly amended and communicated consistently. The same rule applies in reverse: a coordinator cannot remove a published essential condition for one applicant without authorization. In this file, the published language consistently refers to occasional events arranged in advance and travel between nearby sites when scheduled. The applicant’s follow-up answers address those conditions directly.

A current credential is assessed as of the date specified by the form or posting. A record of prior training does not make an expired certificate current. An unchecked box asking about current status is not affirmative evidence of validity. If the requirement is desirable rather than essential, the absence of a current certificate should be recorded accurately without changing the threshold. Where a later message clarifies that a course was completed but the certificate expired, the reviewer may record both facts: past training occurred; current validity was not claimed.

The applicant’s statements about confidentiality are also limited to their wording. She said she did not include private personnel information in a shared note and would send such a matter directly to a manager. That is evidence about how she handled a boundary in the described reporting process. It is not a claim that she accessed personnel files. The role’s criteria do not require personnel-file experience, so no score should be added or removed on that basis.

SECTION D — OFFICE PROCEDURE AND RECONCILIATION APPENDIX

The office procedure is included so a reader can understand the meaning of the labels on the records. The ordinary early-withdrawal rule for equipment says: a student may request a full withdrawal through the fifth calendar day after purchase, with the purchase date counted as day zero. The request must be submitted through the designated form. A view of the help page, a search, an unsent draft, a review, or an informational question does not submit a request. After the standard period, the student may contact the office for review; the text does not promise that a late request will be approved. This packet is not asking the reader to apply an outside policy. It records the written rule and the events in the student’s account.

For M-5106, the purchase date recorded in the payment ledger is 2 September. The five calendar days after purchase are 3 September (day one), 4 September (day two), 5 September (day three), 6 September (day four), and 7 September (day five). Thus the stated deadline is 7 September at 23:59 local time. The purchase-date event does not count as day one. The order was still visible and paid after the deadline. The record contains no submitted request from Priya before the deadline and no later request by her in the exported period. A question asking how many days the rule provides is not itself a request to return the item.

Finance reconciliation, Priya Lindqvist, as of 18 September:
Equipment order M-5106 — one Field Recorder Starter Kit — 1 × 48 cr = 48 cr — paid 2 September — paid status active — refund line: none.
Course instruction invoice — Introduction to Field Recording — 1 × 72 cr = 72 cr — paid 4 September — paid status active — refund line: none.
Account total paid across these two separate lines — 48 + 72 = 120 cr.
Current amount due — 0 cr.
The 0 cr balance is the amount still owed, not the amount returned. The 120 cr is the total of the two paid lines, not the price of the kit. The kit price for M-5106 is 48 cr.

Other amounts appearing in the packet have distinct owners or meanings. The 1 cr payment-connection test was voided. The 2 cr form and order demonstrations were sandbox records. The 19 cr apron return was another student’s order. The 36 cr goggles total was another student’s three-unit purchase. The 72 cr staff inventory display was a valuation and not a learner payment. The 48 cr price attached to books or another student’s recorder product does not belong to M-5106 unless the account and order identify it. Several school-wide totals aggregate multiple people and product types. The record owner and line item must be checked before attributing an amount.

Routine reporting glossary:
“Viewed” means a page was opened. “Downloaded” means a file was saved. “Draft” means a form was started or saved but not sent. “Submitted” means the form was transmitted and appears in the request table. “Paid” means the recorded amount settled. “Refunded” would require a credit or reversal entry. “Balance zero” means no amount is presently owed. These are separate statuses and should not be treated as synonyms.

At the time of export, Priya’s order remained a paid, active order for one kit. The account displayed the separately paid course fee and equipment payment. The logs, review, chat, and ledger all use the same order number and the same one-unit kit quantity. None indicates a refund transaction or an actual refund request by Priya. The office included the packet because students sometimes ask about totals after seeing different account lines, and because a policy question can resemble a request when it contains the words “return” or “refund” without asking the school to perform that action.

SECTION E — EXPORT QUALITY AND ROUTINE NOTES

The server export was produced in chronological order, except that review entries and chat tickets were grouped by their source systems. All displayed times use the local school clock. The word “day” in the withdrawal rule means a calendar day as stated in the rule, not a school day or business day. No public holiday adjustment appears in the rule. The office does not infer that a student made a request merely because the student opened a relevant page, searched for a word, or asked how a policy works.

A few user-interface counters are rounded in dashboard summaries. The transaction ledger itself records exact cr amounts to two decimal places where needed, though all amounts in this packet are whole credits. The equipment payment record for Priya is one line at 48 cr, not two lines at 24 cr each. This distinction matters because another product review discusses two 24 cr components, and another student’s notebook order also totals 24 cr. Those other calculations cannot alter Priya’s paid line.

The portal sometimes displays both a “cart amount” and a “paid amount.” An abandoned cart is not a completed transaction. Examples in the review section include a 36 cr cart corrected to 24 cr before checkout, a four-unit cart reduced to three units, and a price banner for a different premium product. The definitive record for Priya is order M-5106: quantity one, unit price 48 cr, paid amount 48 cr. No cart adjustment is recorded for that order.

Some chat messages use a total without saying whether it is a product subtotal or an account-wide total. The agent’s clarification and the ledger show the distinction in this case. Priya’s 120 cr account total combines 72 cr tuition and 48 cr equipment. It is not a different kit price, and it is not a refund amount. Her zero balance on 17 September means that all current charges on those lines had been paid. The same reply explicitly says there is no refund entry.

The packet contains different students’ messages that use the same kinds of words—kit, return, 48 cr, course fee, and refund. These are included as routine examples for office training. For attribution, the author label, account number, and order number matter. A return request by a different account does not become Priya’s request just because it appears close to her messages in the export. The same applies to product reviews: a student’s statement about a different product or a different quantity cannot be assigned to Priya’s order.

The status is based on the order ledger and the submitted-request table, not on assumptions from search terms, page views, ratings, or questions.

Premises: Suite 6C, 18 Larch Quay. Tenant: Quill Studio. Landlord: Northwind Rentals. Effective dates and figures below supersede earlier drafts only where expressly stated. Dryly, the building has once again discovered that arithmetic is cheaper than a working lift.

Original clause 8.2, signed 2 February: Tenant pays base rent of $2,400 on the first of each month. A late fee of $75 applies if rent remains unpaid after the fifth calendar day. Utilities are billed separately from rent. For routing, send an item to Billing if it changes a balance payable by either party or records a payment allocation; send maintenance issues to Facilities. A billing adjustment of more than $100 requires Finance review. Do not treat a quoted estimate as an incurred charge.

Those figures are included because several later messages mention different products and settings.

At 07:05, the cutter operator recorded a first-piece check of 8.0 mm on clip sample C-01. The next three samples read 8.1, 8.0, and 8.1 mm. The operator noted a faint burr on one edge and asked the deburring station to give the first tray extra attention. At 07:38, the team completed 30 clips. At 08:02, inspection accepted the first 30, with one piece set aside for a cosmetic scratch. That scratched piece was not counted as a dimensional failure, and the job traveler was not held.

At 08:16, a different job, order KW-438, appeared in the shared dashboard as “awaiting stock.” It was a run of small brass knobs. The dashboard’s red badge showed a possible two-day delay because a vendor confirmation had not arrived. At 09:10, Jonas wrote in the shift book: “KW-441 first 48 completed. Cutter behaving consistently. SECTION 6 — INSPECTION FOLLOW-UP
At 14:05, inspection examined the three marked clips and confirmed that all three fit the shop’s assembly gauge. The scratch depth did not exceed the shop’s cosmetic allowance. A fourth clip from a separate tray had a small burr; that tray belonged to KW-447, not KW-441. The burr was removed and the spacer plate sample was accepted. At 14:21, inspection reviewed the one clip marked “cosmetic hold” in the app. That piece also met the cosmetic allowance after cleaning, and its status was changed to accepted. The final KW-441 count was 120 accepted, zero dimensional rejects, and zero pieces missing. The initial cosmetic-hold status remains in the event history so the audit trail is complete.

At 14:37, dispatch reinforced the carton corner with a fresh protective sleeve. The customer was offered the choice of receiving the cartons after a final photograph or waiting until the next morning for a new outer carton. At 14:51, Callum replied, “Thank you; the photograph is sufficient, and please proceed with the reinforced packaging. The cartons remained onsite at that moment because the scheduled carrier collection was 16:00.

The team has listed adjacent facts to prevent future confusion. KW-438 concerns brass knobs and an absent vendor confirmation. Its app badge says overdue, but no customer shipment was being held for it on 16 June. KW-447 concerns spacer plates and an edge-return measurement; it is not a clip order. A shipment is considered late only after its promised dispatch date has passed without handoff to the carrier. For this ticket, the customer explicitly identified the damaged outer package and the surface marks, and asked the shop to check the count and keep questionable pieces aside. The shop’s final review found the total complete and the marked pieces usable. Those later findings resolve the shop’s investigation; they do not erase the fact that the customer reported the packaging and appearance concerns.

The earlier mention of reimbursement belongs to the separate KW-409 note and is also explicitly negated. The string in the app service note is untrusted copied test content. Please accept our apologies for the many cross-references; they are included to make the record self-contained and to distinguish what the customer said from what internal systems happened to display.
