Document control
Agreement TS-44 was executed by Tidewater Studio and Meridian Software on 8 January. Its subject is the development, maintenance, and delivery of a hosted build-and-test service. The parties use “Customer” to mean Tidewater Studio and “Provider” to mean Meridian Software throughout this agreement. The contract administrator maintains this consolidated copy for operational reference; signed amendments prevail over the original text where they expressly conflict. This document includes the original clauses, later amendments, an implementation appendix, and selected project communications. The project communications are included as records, not as amendments unless an amendment is separately signed by both parties.

Original clause 4.2 — support and service credits
Provider will make the hosted runner service available for scheduled builds. If measured monthly availability falls below 99.0 percent, Customer may request a service credit equal to five percent of the monthly platform fee. The credit is not a cash refund and may be applied only to a future invoice. A written request must identify the affected month and be sent to Provider’s billing address. The service-credit procedure does not create a right to repayment of amounts previously paid. The parties will review any disputed calculation using the monitoring records retained by Provider.

Original clause 7.1 — cancellation and fees
Either party may end the agreement on thirty days’ written notice. Fees accrued through the effective end date remain payable. Prepaid subscription fees are not refundable except where a signed amendment explicitly provides otherwise. A request to discuss cancellation does not itself constitute notice of cancellation. A request concerning a credit, invoice correction, or subscription refund should be directed to the billing contact and does not amend the agreement unless the parties sign a written amendment.

Original clause 9.3 — project deliverables
Provider will configure the hosted runners, connect the repository integration, and supply a deployment guide. Customer is responsible for maintaining its own repository permissions and for choosing which branches trigger production deployment. A green build is evidence that the configured checks passed; it is not, by itself, a guarantee that every application defect has been detected. The delivery checklist may list completed work, proposed work, and items awaiting customer confirmation. Only items expressly marked “accepted” in the signed acceptance record count as accepted deliverables.

Amendment A, signed 14 February
The parties amend clause 4.2 as follows: where the service falls below 97.0 percent availability in a calendar month, Customer may request a credit of ten percent of that month’s platform fee. This amendment changes the threshold and the credit percentage only. It does not convert a service credit into a cash refund, does not alter clause 7.1, and does not make a request for a credit a cancellation notice. All other terms remain unchanged.

Amendment B, signed 22 March
The parties add a limited migration provision. If Provider fails to deliver the repository connector by 31 March, Customer may terminate the connector work order and receive a refund of the separately itemized connector setup charge. The provision concerns the connector setup charge only, not the monthly platform subscription, support fees, or other prepaid amounts. The right applies only if the connector has not been delivered by the stated date. A delivered connector that needs configuration changes is still considered delivered for purposes of this clause. The parties confirm that no other refund right is created by this amendment.

Implementation appendix — delivery and test records
The project board contains several entries that use similar terms. “Runner image refreshed” means that the operating image was updated. “Repository connector delivered” means the OAuth connection was installed and passed the agreed handshake test. “Deployment workflow enabled” means the customer’s selected branch can invoke the deployment job; it does not mean that Customer has approved a production release. “Connector setup charge” is a single invoice line for connector installation. SECTION 1 — PANEL RULES AND REVIEW SCOPE

The open position is Junior Data Quality Analyst, requisition KA-417. The panel’s pre-approved first-round shortlist rule is a weighted assessment score of at least 70.00 points out of 100. The calculation is: technical exercise points multiplied by 0.50, structured interview points multiplied by 0.30, and work-sample review points multiplied by 0.20, then added. Each component is scored from 0 to 100. There is no rounding of component scores before multiplication. For shortlist decisions, compare the unrounded total with 70.00; a total of exactly 70.00 qualifies. Do not substitute the recruiter’s informal “around seventy” wording for this written rule.

The rule applies only to a candidate whose three listed component scores are present and whose assessment is complete. A missing score is not zero and is not a completed assessment. In this packet, every person specifically listed in the final assessment table has all three scores unless the table explicitly says otherwise. A withdrawn candidate is not to be shortlisted, even if a score appears in a draft table. The final status field takes precedence over a draft score when it says withdrawn. The panel is asked to distinguish a score-based qualification from later hiring decisions: passing the threshold does not mean an offer was made, accepted, or approved by finance.

For candidate comparisons, each row in the final assessment table is one distinct applicant. Names in older emails, example templates, vendor invoices, and anonymized calibration examples are not additional applicants. Likewise, a candidate mentioned as a possible future referral is not an applicant in this requisition unless a completed application record is shown. This distinction matters because the packet contains several names and many numbers that are useful for administration but are not candidate assessment results.

The recruiting coordinator’s cost allocation rule is also included for context. The external assessment vendor bills a fixed administration fee, a per-completed-test fee, and a separate optional report fee. Only the per-completed-test fee is allocated to this requisition’s candidate-assessment cost center. The fee schedule and invoice are included below. An invoice total is not a candidate score, and a candidate count in an invoice is not by itself evidence that every named applicant completed an assessment. For this review, application and assessment status in the web-form export and final assessment table are the authoritative sources for applicant status.

The packet uses three kinds of status language. “Submitted” means the applicant sent the web form. “Assessment complete” means the required three scored components are present and the candidate has not withdrawn. “Shortlist eligible” means the score rule is met. A candidate may have submitted an application without completing assessment, may have completed assessment without meeting the threshold, or may meet the threshold but later withdraw. There is no component minimum and no bonus for referral, attachment length, years of experience, or salary expectation.

Quality check 3: active score eligibility. Among active applicants, Amara at 76.80 qualifies, Mateo at 69.00 does not, Yara at 70.00 qualifies, Rosa at 70.20 qualifies, and Greta at 70.50 qualifies. Sven at 75.00 is excluded from the active shortlist because he withdrew. The active qualifying count is four. The active nonqualifying count is one. There is one withdrawn person with a qualifying historical score. These are distinct categories, and combining them without saying which category is meant can produce a misleading count.

Quality check 4: invoice arithmetic. The line totals are $180.00, $252.00, $108.00, $50.00, and $12.00. Their sum is $602.00. Tax is 5% of $602.00, or $30.10. The total is $632.10. Under the explicit allocation rule, the assessment cost-center amount is the $252.00 scoring line only. Its quantity and unit price reconcile: 6 × $42.00 = $252.00. Neither the total invoice nor the full pretax subtotal is the allocated assessment amount. The vendor’s count remains six after one person withdraws because the service was already completed.

Quality check 5: numeric near misses. The portal has a 100% completeness indicator, which is not a score. Sven entered 70 as a salary expectation, which is not a score. A-041’s confirmation number is 612, which is not a score. Yara’s sample is 12 pages, which is not a score. The draft unweighted mean of Mateo’s three scores is 71.67, but the approved weighted score is 69.00. The copied invoice email says $612.10, but the validated invoice total is $632.10. A “six” in the vendor line refers to completed service packages, while six application records are a separate count. Every one of these numbers has a stated context and must not be substituted for another quantity.

Quality check 6: wording controls. “At least 70.00” includes exactly 70.00. “Assessment complete” does not mean “shortlist eligible.” “Shortlist eligible” does not mean “hired.” “Completed scoring package” does not mean “active applicant.” “Withdrawn” excludes a candidate from the active shortlist even if the score is above threshold. “All required fields complete” refers to form submission, not assessment quality. “Four names preferred” is not a revised threshold. The final response should reflect these distinctions rather than selecting a number simply because it appears more than once.

Quality check 7: source precedence. For submitted status, use the portal export. For the final component scores and weighted totals, use the final reviewed assessment table. For the meaning of the shortlist threshold, use the panel rule in Section 1. For withdrawal, use the recorded withdrawal and final status update. For invoice allocation, use the explicit finance allocation rule and invoice line items. An early chat message, a draft calculation, a meeting preference, or a vendor billing quantity does not override these sources. If two snippets appear to disagree, the final reviewed record and explicit written rule govern the corresponding fact.

[{"state":"KESTREL RENTALS — FIELD SERVICE CASE FILE FR-8821
Administrative copy; compiled by Service Coordination, 18 September. The file concerns a hydraulic lift table, unit LT-44, supplied to Quill Outfitters for its North Annex workshop. The file is maintained for dispatch, billing review, warranty administration, and management reporting. Entries below are reproduced in date order except where a section is expressly identified as a later compilation. Amounts are in dollars unless a currency code is shown. Measurements are those entered by the named technician; no external conversion or product knowledge is required. “Customer statement” records what a customer said and does not itself establish a technical finding. “Verified” means a technician documented a measurement or test. “Pending” means the matter was not resolved at the time of the entry.

CASE INDEX AND INTAKE SUMMARY
Case opened 2 September at 08:14 by Yara Tanaka, Quill Outfitters facilities coordinator. Customer location: North Annex, receiving bay 3. Asset LT-44, serial KX-7716. The original service request says the platform lowers unevenly when loaded and the hand controller sometimes requires a second press. The request does not report personal injury, a fall, a leak onto a public walkway, or an outage affecting the other lift table. The customer asked for a same-week inspection. Dispatch assigned technician Tomasz Alvarez, with Sven Iyer as backup. Initial schedule showed a three-hour window, 10:00–13:00 on 4 September; actual arrival was 10:18 and departure was 13:07.

The customer’s account is on the standard Field Response schedule. For this case, the quoted dispatch and inspection charge was $186.00; an additional on-site labor hour was quoted at $94.00; the customer had a documented service-plan credit of $35.00 against eligible labor and inspection charges. Parts and taxes are separately identified. The internal invoice-review threshold relevant to this file is $250.00 net customer-paid repair charges, calculated as eligible inspection and labor charges plus separately billed parts and tax, less applicable service-plan credit. A charge is “net customer-paid” for this review only when it appears as a billed amount in the final posted invoice; estimates, declined work, and unposted drafts are not included. The threshold comparison is strict: an amount greater than $250.00 is over the threshold; exactly $250.00 is not.

The customer was told in the initial acknowledgement that the inspection fee was not a promise of a refund and that any billing question would be reviewed against the final posted invoice. A separate customer reimbursement request, if one was made, should be distinguished from an internal review generated by crossing a threshold. No staff member is authorized by this note to convert an estimate into a posted charge. The file contains several figures that are estimates, comparisons, rejected quotes, or arithmetic examples; only the final posted invoice establishes the billed amount for the threshold calculation.

INTAKE FORM, 2 SEPTEMBER, 08:14
Entered by Yara Tanaka from an email and a telephone call. “Lift table has been awkward for about a week, especially when cartons are on the right edge. It sometimes descends with a small pause. We have not stopped using it entirely. Please inspect before the next inventory cycle. The other table is operating normally.” The caller gave the asset number as LT-44 and confirmed that the request was for inspection and repair, not replacement. The intake clerk asked whether the customer wanted a refund. Tanaka replied, “I do not know what has been billed yet. I am asking for someone to inspect it. If we are charged for a fault that should have been covered, I may ask about an adjustment later.” The phrase “may ask” was entered as a possible future action, not as a current refund demand.

At 08:25, the intake portal displayed an unrelated example invoice from a training account: $278.00 parts, $0.00 labor, and a red note reading “REFUND REQUESTED.” Tanaka did not enter or approve that example. It was a screen illustration retained in the case export because the clerk used the same portal tab while creating the work order. The example concerned a different asset and account and was not a charge to Quill Outfitters. A second portal help box described an old campaign: “$312.00 maximum courtesy credit for qualifying winter-callout cases.” The present visit was neither a winter callout nor a courtesy-credit approval. These figures are retained as distractors for reconciliation and must not be treated as payments or requests.

DISPATCH RECORD, 2–4 SEPTEMBER
2 September 08:43: Work order FR-8821 routed to the North District queue. 09:02: scheduling coordinator offered 3 September, 15:00–18:00, or 4 September, 10:00–13:00. Tanaka selected the latter because the receiving bay would be clear. 09:17: automated notice gave an estimated total of $186.00 for the standard visit and stated that extra labor or parts required approval. 10:06: Tanaka replied, “Please proceed with diagnosis. Call me before any parts order or work outside the inspection.” 10:22: dispatch entered an internal comparison value of $214.00, copied from the average invoice on the prior quarter’s unrelated compressor jobs. It was not a quote for FR-8821.

3 September 14:36: route sheet listed 19.4 miles from the depot and estimated travel time of 31 minutes. A second route sheet for Kestrel Supply, another customer in the same district, listed 26.1 miles and an estimated $41.00 travel surcharge. The Kestrel Supply line remained visible in the combined route export, but the FR-8821 rate card lists no travel surcharge for this scheduled visit. 16:11: technician Alvarez acknowledged the job. 16:20: backup technician Iyer was marked available, not assigned. 16:55: dispatch reiterated that the base inspection charge was $186.00 and that a separate labor hour, if required and approved, would be $94.00. The service-plan credit was not included in the customer-facing estimate because the portal applied it only after invoice posting.

4 September 09:49: Alvarez marked en route. 10:18: arrival logged. 10:24: customer representative Yara Tanaka signed the access register. 10:31: technician confirmed the equipment was isolated from the receiving traffic lane during inspection. 12:46: one additional hour of labor was authorized by Tanaka by text after diagnosis; the authorization expressly excluded replacement of the pump assembly. 13:07: departure logged. A later route summary shows 13:19 departure from the district and 14:01 return to depot; those travel timestamps are not billable labor entries. The scheduling export also contains a four-hour “hold” reserved for a different customer, Meridian Health, and an estimate of $480.00 for that separate call. Neither the hold nor its estimate forms part of FR-8821.

FIELD SERVICE WORKSHEET, 4 SEPTEMBER
Technician: Tomasz Alvarez. Assist: none. Customer contact present: Yara Tanaka, facilities coordinator. Equipment: LT-44, serial KX-7716. Meter reading at arrival: 00641.2 operating hours. Work-area temperature: 21°C. No visible hydraulic fluid on the floor. Platform unloaded before initial descent test. The operator reported that the right side occasionally seemed slower, but did not claim that the left side had failed. Technician checked the table on level flooring and recorded a baseline platform height of 812 mm at all four corners, measured without load. The preliminary record says “even when level, verify under load rather than infer from unloaded reading.”

Load-test procedure recorded on the worksheet: place three sealed test containers, each marked 40 kg, on the designated center marks; record descent time across a 300 mm travel interval; repeat after repositioning the containers. The test containers were labeled A, B, and C. Scale verification sticker displayed a 1.0 kg tolerance per container. No container was opened. The measured descent times on the first run were 6.8 seconds at the left rail and 7.1 seconds at the right rail. The second run recorded 6.9 seconds left and 7.2 seconds right. The service bulletin supplied with this case defines an unacceptable left/right mean difference as more than 0.5 seconds across paired runs. It also instructs technicians to compare paired readings, not the slowest single reading with a nominal time printed on a training card. The paired differences are 0.3 seconds and 0.3 seconds, for a mean difference of 0.3 seconds. This particular test therefore does not exceed the bulletin’s left/right difference threshold.

The training card in the tool case showed an example: “7.8-second right descent: investigate immediately.” The card was for the LT-20 demonstration model and was not the applicable LT-44 criterion. A laminated card from an unrelated lift showed 8.0 seconds as a mandatory shutdown limit. Alvarez noted both cards in the worksheet margin to explain why neither was applied to this model. The card figures are not readings from LT-44. The actual readings are the paired times stated above.

The controller was tested for ten command cycles. It responded on the first press in nine cycles and on the second press in one cycle. The customer had described an intermittent second press, which is consistent with that observed cycle, but the service bulletin’s controller-defect criterion requires at least two failures in ten cycles. The one failure did not meet that criterion. A prior service note for a different serial number recorded three failures in ten cycles; that figure was copied into the worksheet’s “comparison only” field and does not describe LT-44. The technician cleaned the controller contact surface, repeated ten cycles, and recorded zero second-press events on the retest. The case record calls this a cleaning adjustment, not a controller replacement.

Hydraulic pressure was checked with gauge G-14. Initial reading: 1,618 psi. Repeat readings: 1,621 psi and 1,619 psi. The applicable LT-44 service bulletin specifies a normal operating band of 1,600 to 1,680 psi inclusive under the stated test load. The median of the three readings is 1,619 psi, within the band. The worksheet also includes a copied value of 1,590 psi from a calibration exercise and a separate reference value of 1,700 psi for a different pump family. Neither is a measured LT-44 pressure. The gauge sticker says its calibration tolerance is ±4 psi; even the lowest corrected value from the observed readings remains above 1,600 psi. The worksheet does not support a conclusion that pressure is below specification.

The table’s right-side guide roller was inspected. The manual’s wear criterion for this part is a measured lateral clearance greater than 2.0 mm after the platform is secured and unloaded. Technician readings were 2.3 mm, 2.4 mm, and 2.2 mm at three positions. Mean clearance is (2.3 + 2.4 + 2.2) / 3 = 2.3 mm, which is 0.3 mm above the 2.0 mm criterion. The left-side guide roller readings were 1.4 mm, 1.5 mm, and 1.6 mm, mean 1.5 mm. A workbench note elsewhere in the file cites 2.8 mm as a “replace immediately” value for an older model; it is not the LT-44 wear criterion. A spare-part inventory list shows a price of $146.00 for a pair of rollers, but no pair was installed during this visit.

The right-side roller assembly was cleaned and adjusted. After adjustment, readings were 1.8 mm, 1.9 mm, and 1.8 mm, mean 1.83 mm when rounded to two decimals, below the 2.0 mm criterion. The adjustment used existing serviceable components. No new roller, seal, pump, or controller was supplied. The technician entered 1.0 additional labor hour for inspection of the roller and adjustment, consistent with the separate authorization obtained at 12:46. The base visit and this extra hour are labor/inspection charges eligible for the service-plan credit. The worksheet states that replacement would have required a parts quote and additional approval; it did not occur.

The battery-backed position display was also checked. It showed 99.1% charge at arrival, 98.9% after ten display checks, and 98.8% at departure. The service bulletin’s replacement threshold is a loss greater than 4 percentage points over ten checks. The measured loss is 0.2 percentage points, not greater than 4. An unrelated complaint record from a different site lists a 4.6-point loss. The worksheet explicitly marks that figure “not this asset.” Battery replacement was not performed and no battery charge appears on the invoice.

The technician recorded a small squeak during the first unloaded movement. The sound was not reproduced during three later unloaded movements or the final loaded test. The applicable maintenance note says a sound that is not reproduced in three consecutive checks is to be documented for monitoring, not billed as a component failure. A note from the North Annex door service, conducted by a different contractor, mentions a squeak on 29 August. The door and LT-44 are separate assets. The customer did not authorize door work and no door work was performed.

Technician findings entered at 13:02: “Right guide clearance was above the model criterion before adjustment; corrected using existing assembly. Controller contact cleaned after one intermittent non-first-press response in ten cycles; post-cleaning retest ten of ten first-press responses. Pressure and paired descent difference within stated criteria. No replacement part installed. Recommend customer monitor; call if recurrence.” Customer representative signed the worksheet at 13:05. The signature acknowledges receipt of the findings and does not accept a parts quote, request reimbursement, or waive billing review.

CUSTOMER TEXT EXCHANGE, 4 SEPTEMBER, 12:40–13:05
12:40, Alvarez: “Inspection is complete. The roller clearance was above the service limit; I have adjusted it. No replacement part is needed. The controller responded late once in ten checks; after cleaning it responded on all ten. I have about one extra labor hour. May I complete the adjustment and final checks?”
12:42, Tanaka: “Yes, complete that hour and the checks. Do not order replacement parts today.”
12:46, Alvarez: “Confirmed. One additional labor hour only. No parts.”
12:52, Tanaka: “Thank you. Please send the report and invoice. I am not requesting a refund today because we do not have an invoice yet. If the final bill includes a part we did not approve, I will dispute that item.”
13:05, Tanaka, worksheet note: “Received.” The text exchange contains no current request for a refund. It does contain a conditional future dispute if a specific unapproved part appears. The condition did not occur according to the worksheet and final invoice. An automatically appended line at 13:06 reads “refund keyword count: 2.” That count was generated by searching all text, including the words “not requesting a refund” and “invoice yet”; it is not a customer action. The portal’s search result also found “refund” in the unrelated training example described in the intake section.

STATUS UPDATE TO MANAGER, 5 SEPTEMBER, 09:10
From: Sven Iyer, District Service Lead. To: Oren Bergstrom, Field Operations Manager. Subject: FR-8821 closeout check.
“Please note that FR-8821 was completed on 4 September. Alvarez found the right guide clearance at a mean of 2.3 mm against the 2.0 mm LT-44 criterion; adjustment brought the recorded mean to approximately 1.83 mm. The paired descent difference was 0.3 seconds, below the more-than-0.5-second limit. Pressure median was 1,619 psi, inside 1,600–1,680 psi. Controller response was one delayed event in ten before cleaning, zero in ten after. No parts were installed. The customer authorized one extra hour at $94. Base inspection is $186. Credit is $35, subject to posting. A plain arithmetic gross of $186 + $94 is $280; after the credit, eligible labor/inspection is $245. This remains below the $250 review threshold if there are no separately billed items. Do not use the $278 training example or the $41 route surcharge from Kestrel Supply.”

The manager replied at 09:24: “Agreed. Do not mark a customer refund request from the technical issue alone. The customer may dispute an unapproved part if one appears, but the technician reports no part. Verify the posted invoice and any customer-authored follow-up before closing. The $214 dispatch comparison is not the case total. The $480 Meridian hold is not this job. Please preserve the source records.”

At 10:02, Iyer entered a short ledger review. The base inspection line was $186.00. Authorized additional labor was $94.00. Their gross sum is $280.00. The service-plan credit is $35.00 and applies to those eligible charges, so net eligible labor/inspection is $280.00 − $35.00 = $245.00. There is no travel surcharge for this scheduled visit. There are no installed parts and the applicable parts total is $0.00. The tax line is $0.00 under the account’s tax-exempt certificate on file. Accordingly, the posted customer-paid amount should be $245.00, provided the final invoice agrees with this ledger. The $250.00 threshold is not crossed by $5.00; a gross figure before credit must not be compared with the net threshold. Iyer flagged that some interface screens show the $280.00 gross figure prominently and place the credit on a later line. That display order is not a different calculation.

The status record has several deliberately distinct amounts. A work-planning estimate of $312.00 was generated by multiplying a general emergency-call allowance of three hours by $104.00; it was not billed. A draft quote for the roller pair was $146.00, declined and never invoiced. A line-item sandbox test showed $186.00 + $94.00 + $41.00 = $321.00, but the $41.00 belonged to the Kestrel Supply route record. The manager’s comparison value was $214.00. A prior-quarter sample was $278.00. None replaces the final posted calculation. The file does not authorize a reviewer to select the largest visible number merely because it appears in a summary panel.

BILLING WORKFLOW AND POSTING RECORD
5 September, 11:16: Billing analyst Chiara Lindqvist opened invoice draft INV-8821-D. It contained inspection, $186.00; additional authorized labor, $94.00; service-plan credit, −$35.00; parts, $0.00; travel, $0.00; tax, $0.00. Draft subtotal before credit $280.00; draft net $245.00. The draft was not yet posted and therefore was not at that point a final customer-paid invoice. 11:41: the billing system generated a verification alert because the gross charges exceeded $250.00. The alert is based on a gross-charge rule used for analyst routing, not the net customer-paid threshold specified in the case review note. 12:02: Lindqvist annotated the alert: “Gross routing alert only; case-review comparison must use net posted amount.”

5 September, 12:19: a batch import temporarily duplicated the $94.00 labor line in the draft. The screen briefly showed gross charges of $374.00 and net of $339.00. The duplicate was removed at 12:31 before posting. Audit trail records the addition and deletion; neither operation was customer-approved or posted. The temporary draft total is not the final bill. 13:07: the tax engine imported a $6.00 test tax from a sandbox account. The test line was deleted at 13:15. The customer’s valid tax status generated zero tax. A note in the audit log says “system test, do not collect.” The $6.00 is not part of the final invoice.

6 September, 08:46: Lindqvist reconciled the service-plan credit against eligible labor and inspection only. The credit was applied once, not twice. The credit policy excerpt attached to the account states: “A service-plan credit of $35 per completed scheduled service visit applies to eligible inspection and labor charges. It does not apply to parts. It may not be carried to a future visit. If eligible charges are less than $35, credit is limited to eligible charges.” Eligible charges here are $186 + $94 = $280, greater than $35; full $35 applies. An old training worksheet gives a $50 credit for another plan and a different account. That figure is not applicable. The plan records one completed visit, not two; the 4 September arrival and the 4 September departure are one visit.

6 September, 09:20: draft approved. 09:24: invoice INV-8821 posted. Posted lines: inspection $186.00; additional labor $94.00; parts $0.00; travel $0.00; tax $0.00; service-plan credit −$35.00; amount due $245.00. 09:28: electronic delivery to the customer contact address was confirmed. 09:33: payment status “open,” because the account pays by monthly statement. “Open” means the amount is due, not that it was refunded, waived, or paid. On 18 September, the invoice remains open at $245.00. There is no credit memo, refund transaction, payment reversal, or parts charge in the posting history.

For reconciliation, the billing analyst entered these checks: $186.00 + $94.00 = $280.00 gross eligible charges; $280.00 − $35.00 = $245.00 net eligible charges; $245.00 + $0.00 parts + $0.00 travel + $0.00 tax = $245.00 posted amount due. The $250 threshold difference is $250.00 − $245.00 = $5.00, so the final amount does not exceed it. A note at the top of an earlier screen displayed “$280.00 exceeds $250.00 by $30.00.” That arithmetic is correct only for gross charges, not for the stipulated net customer-paid comparison. A separate panel displayed “$339.00 exceeds $250.00 by $89.00” during the temporary duplicate-line period; that draft was corrected before posting. Another report displayed $321.00 by combining the unrelated $41 route surcharge. None is a valid final threshold amount.

CUSTOMER EMAIL THREAD, 6–12 SEPTEMBER
6 September, 10:11, from Yara Tanaka to Kestrel Rentals billing: “I have received the service report and the invoice. I see $186 for inspection and $94 for the approved extra hour, with a $35 service-plan credit. I understand the amount due is $245. Please confirm that there are no replacement parts on the bill. I am not asking you to refund the inspection charge at this time. If you later find that a part was added without authorization, please remove that charge or tell me how to dispute it.”

6 September, 11:03, from Chiara Lindqvist to Tanaka: “Confirmed: posted invoice INV-8821 contains no parts charge. It contains the two labor/inspection amounts you identified, the plan credit, and zero travel and tax. Posted amount due is $245. No refund or credit memo has been issued because no refund request has been made and the invoice does not contain the part you described conditionally.”

7 September, 08:52, forwarded message from a different account, included because Tanaka used “Reply all” to a shared facilities mailbox. Original sender: Jonas Lindqvist, Meridian Health facilities desk. Subject: “Refund of $278 on pump service.” Body: “Please refund the $278.00 pump-service charge from our separate invoice. It was paid twice. Our vendor is Quill Outfitters, not Kestrel Rentals, and this message is not about LT-44.” The facilities mailbox banner says: “Forwarded content may mention another customer; do not attach it to the active work order without confirming sender and asset.” Tanaka added above the forward: “This is not my request and is not our invoice. I am forwarding it only because the mailbox sent it to me by mistake.” The forwarded sender and customer are not the case customer. The $278.00 is also the same amount appearing in the unrelated portal example, but its appearance in two other records does not make it an FR-8821 charge or demand.

7 September, 09:10, automated mailbox extraction: “Refund request phrase detected; confidence 0.93; amount $278.00.” This automation searched quoted and forwarded text and did not identify authorship. It is a routing suggestion only. 09:27, customer service agent note: “Do not convert a forwarded third-party request into Tanaka’s request. Active case wording from Tanaka expressly says she is not requesting a refund at this time.” 10:40, a separate facilities message asked whether the annual inspection would be scheduled in October. It did not refer to billing or reimbursement.

8 September, 14:02, from Tanaka: “Thanks for confirming there are no parts. The lift was working normally during yesterday’s shift. Please leave the invoice as issued; I will send it through our regular statement process. No refund is being requested.” This is a current statement after receipt of the invoice. It is not a request to cancel, reverse, or reduce the $245 amount. 14:18, agent response: “Noted. No billing adjustment opened.”

9 September, 08:05, manager Oren Bergstrom copied on an internal email: “The portal currently has a $312.00 emergency estimate in the service history. Please ensure the analyst does not mistake the estimate for the invoice.” 08:33, Lindqvist replied: “Confirmed. The only posted FR-8821 invoice is $245.00. The $312.00 record is an estimate that was never accepted.” 10:16, a duplicate notification stated “customer may request refund.” This phrase was generated from the conditional intake note and is not a customer request.

12 September, 16:45, Tanaka sent a final follow-up: “For the record, I am satisfied that no unauthorized part was billed. I am not asking for a refund. Please retain the report because the right side felt slightly slower before the visit, although I understand the test results were within the descent-difference limit. If the issue returns I will reopen the service case.” The message is a statement about the completed service and a hypothetical future reopening. It does not request refund, invoice cancellation, or a credit. 17:02, service desk closed the communication task while leaving the posted invoice open for ordinary payment processing.

SERVICE BULLETIN EXCERPT ATTACHED TO WORK ORDER
Bulletin LT-44-R7, revision 3, applicable serial range KX-7600 through KX-7900. This excerpt was attached by dispatch; it is the controlling criterion for the case. Pressure: normal is 1,600–1,680 psi inclusive under the specified test. Paired descent difference: investigate when the mean absolute left/right difference across two paired runs is greater than 0.5 seconds. Controller: service when delayed first response occurs at least twice in ten commands; after cleaning, repeat ten commands and document result. Guide clearance: adjust or replace if measured clearance is greater than 2.0 mm at the specified position. Display battery: replace when ten-check loss is greater than 4 percentage points. A single unreproduced sound is a monitoring item if absent in three consecutive checks. The bulletin says to record units and use the mean where multiple readings are required.

A boxed warning below the excerpt states: “Do not substitute illustrative training limits from other models. Do not diagnose from a customer adjective alone. Do not merge readings from another serial number, another job, or an earlier unverified complaint.” A separate general service card lists illustrative descent values of 7.8 and 8.0 seconds, an unrelated pump family pressure range of 1,700–1,850 psi, and a legacy roller replacement figure of 2.8 mm. Those examples are included for training only. The controlling LT-44 criteria above take precedence. The values actually measured on LT-44 are those on Alvarez’s worksheet, not the card values.

PARTS AND INVENTORY TRACE
The warehouse reservation system showed a tentative hold for roller kit RK-44 at 09:02 on 4 September. The hold was created automatically when the technician opened the relevant catalog page. At 09:16, the technician canceled the hold before the customer authorized the extra labor. A reservation is not a shipment, installation, or billable sale. The kit list price was $146.00 per pair; a separate catalog cache listed $73.00 per individual roller. Neither amount appears on the posted invoice. The same inventory screen also showed a pump assembly at $389.00 and a controller at $62.00. These were catalog references only; no such item was ordered or installed.

At 10:57, the warehouse app recorded one RK-44 kit as “available: 3, reserved: 1.” The reserved unit belonged to work order FR-8814 at a different customer site. At 11:06, the count refreshed to “available: 4, reserved: 0” after that unrelated reservation was released. The movement did not originate from FR-8821. At 12:48, Alvarez entered “existing roller adjusted; replacement not required.” A stock reconciliation later confirmed that no part left the warehouse for FR-8821. The invoice posting record agrees: parts $0.00.

The North District stock ledger contains an entry for $41.00 travel on the Kestrel Supply route and a $22.00 fastener pack on an unrelated repair. A duplicate scan briefly associated the fastener pack with the same mobile route bundle, then was corrected by the stock clerk. The correction audit shows no FR-8821 part issue. The $22.00 fastener pack was returned to the unrelated job’s bin. No fastener was used at Quill Outfitters. Reviewer: Sven Iyer. Scope: technical record, approval trace, and invoice reconciliation. Review notes that the customer’s original description of “uneven” descent was not identical to the measured comparison. The applicable comparison was a paired mean difference. Run 1 difference: |7.1 − 6.8| = 0.3 seconds. Run 2 difference: |7.2 − 6.9| = 0.3 seconds. Mean difference: (0.3 + 0.3)/2 = 0.3 seconds. Since 0.3 is not greater than 0.5, the descent criterion was not exceeded. The 7.8-second training figure is not a measured value. Reviewer marked the test finding “within criterion,” while retaining the customer’s subjective report in the intake history.

The 1,590 psi calibration example is neither an LT-44 reading nor an adjustment result. No low-pressure repair is supported.

The other serial’s three-of-ten entry is a comparison record and excluded. No controller replacement was charged.

Conditional language about a future dispute if an unapproved part appeared did not become an actual request, because no part appeared. This conclusion is based on the source messages and does not depend on the automated keyword counts.

At 10:22, the follow-up form showed optional selections: “refund,” “replacement,” “new inspection,” “general comment.” Tanaka selected “general comment.” The form’s analytics engine counted the word “refund” in the question prompt and generated a possible-refund flag; no refund option was selected. A manager’s dashboard displayed the case in a “watch for repeat within 30 days” panel because the customer used conditional language. That panel is not evidence of a second defect, a return visit, or a billing request. The work order remains one completed visit; a calendar range of 30 days is a monitoring window, not a charge or service-plan credit count.

A source audit was performed to ensure the training sample would not confuse the customer’s account with other records. The active customer is Quill Outfitters. The audit also verifies measurement attribution. LT-44 observations are on worksheet FR-8821. The 7.8-second example and 8.0-second limit are training references for other models. The 1,590 psi value is a calibration exercise. The 1,700 psi reference belongs to another pump family. The 2.8 mm roller value is a legacy-model example. The 4.6 percentage-point battery loss and three controller failures belong to other records. Only the readings identified as actual LT-44 readings are used in the quality review. A repeated number is not automatically a repeated observation: the figure 278 appears in both a portal example and a separate forwarded email, but neither is a Quill invoice amount.

CLOSURE MEMORANDUM, 18 SEPTEMBER, 15:40
Prepared by Chiara Lindqvist for the file custodian. “Work performed: one scheduled inspection and one specifically approved additional labor hour. The right guide clearance averaged 2.3 mm before adjustment against a criterion of greater than 2.0 mm; after adjustment it averaged 1.83 mm. The descent difference averaged 0.3 seconds against a greater-than-0.5-second investigation threshold. Pressure median 1,619 psi against 1,600–1,680 psi inclusive. The net amount is $5.00 below the $250.00 threshold. The threshold is not crossed. The customer has not asked for a refund. Her direct communications say she is not requesting one; her conditional statement concerned a hypothetical unauthorized part, and no part was billed. The $278.00 refund request was authored by a different customer about a different invoice. No refund request, credit memo, or refund transaction is recorded for FR-8821.”

The memorandum further states: “Status is complete for field work and open for ordinary payment. Do not describe ‘open’ as pending refund. Do not use the automated keyword flag as proof of customer intent. If a later customer-authored communication asks for an adjustment, create a new billing task and preserve the current invoice history. No such communication is present as of this memorandum.”

The custodian checked the case totals one last time: eligible gross $186 + $94 = $280; applicable credit $35; net $280 − $35 = $245; threshold gap $250 − $245 = $5. The separate figures $214, $278, $312, $321, $339, $389, and $480 are each identified elsewhere as comparison, unrelated request, estimate, mixed-account sandbox arithmetic, temporary draft, catalog item, or separate work hold. [{"state":"Northwind Software / Meridian Dental / Quill Labs / Larkspur Health — CI reliability review dossier

Compiled by Leila Novak, release engineering. Review period: 4–18 September. This is an internal evidence packet, not a claim that every alarming red square represents a product defect. The dashboard has been wrong before; the dashboard remains extremely confident about it. Names below are fictional project participants. Times are UTC unless a section says otherwise.

SECTION A — PRODUCT REVIEW EXCERPT, submitted by Kwame Okafor

Product reviewed: BuildHarbor, a hosted CI runner and deployment coordinator used by the four fictional organizations in this packet. Rating submitted in the partner portal: two stars. Summary: “A wonderfully modern way to make a green build feel like an invitation to investigate.” The review is about the release-control product, not about the quality of any one customer’s application.

I bought the team plan after the sales demonstration showed one run with a clean cache, one runner, and no simultaneous deploys. The demonstration was apparently an unusually accurate picture of production if production has one job, no dependencies, and a strong commitment to theatrical simplicity. The product’s useful idea is clear: a queue of jobs, isolated workers, signed artifacts, and an approval gate. The trouble is that the visible green check and the actual deployable artifact can disagree, and the interface presents those facts with the same reassuring shade of green.

On 6 September our release pipeline built package `cedar-api` from commit `9b1a2d4`. The console showed unit tests passed, artifact upload complete, and release gate satisfied. The gate had two required approvals. The activity list showed one approval from Kwame and one from the service account `release-bot`; our policy requires two human approvers, so the bot entry should not have counted. The product did not identify the account as a service account on the gate summary. It displayed “2 of 2 approvals.” The deployment was held by a later server-side check, which is fortunate, though “fortunate” is a low bar for release engineering.

The same run’s artifact list had `cedar-api-2.8.1.tar.gz` with digest `a6c19f`, uploaded at 14:07, and a second file with the same name and digest `c14e83`, uploaded at 14:09 by retry job 184. The interface collapsed the duplicate-name entries into one row. The details pane showed the earlier digest until we refreshed. The release coordinator selected the row, copied the digest shown, and compared it with the manifest. The mismatch became visible only after a manual refresh. No customer received a package from this run, because the server-side check halted the deployment. The status was “deployment blocked,” not “deployment completed,” despite the confusing green build header.

On 7 September a cache restore ran after a dependency lockfile change. The job log said “cache hit: workspace-main” and then listed a cache key ending `lock-v3`; the current lockfile was `lock-v4`. The restore step did not fail. A downstream test failed reproducibly on a clean worker and passed on the warm worker. We eventually found that a stale generated client was present in the restored cache. This is not proof that every cache hit is unsafe. It is proof that a cache key that omits the lockfile revision can be an exciting way to obtain yesterday’s dependency graph without paying for yesterday’s build time.

The support agent’s first response was that “a successful cache restore is working as designed.” This is technically true in the same sense that a door which opens onto a staircase is working as designed if the product requirement never said anything about floors. Support later confirmed that our configured key template had been copied from the quick-start example and did not include the lockfile hash. We added the hash ourselves. The review is not that the cache should never restore; it is that the default example encourages a cache identity too broad for dependency-sensitive builds, while the UI calls the result a hit rather than a potentially stale restore.

The runner queue is usually acceptable. In the tested window, jobs began within the stated 90-second target on 41 of 48 eligible runs. Seven runs exceeded the target: four waited 2 minutes 11 seconds, 2 minutes 36 seconds, 3 minutes 02 seconds, and 4 minutes 18 seconds; three were delayed by our own concurrency cap. The product chart labels all seven “runner delay” even though the three capped jobs were waiting on our plan limit. The raw events distinguish them, but the chart does not. A chart that makes the customer’s configuration look like provider capacity is not a particularly neutral chart.

The incident report later separated the causes. Four waits were assigned to shared-runner capacity. Three were customer concurrency limits. The durations above are wall-clock queue times, not execution times. Do not add them and call the result downtime. A separate status page incident lasted 11 minutes on 8 September and affected job log rendering, not job execution. A retry button was available throughout. The product review portal offered a checkbox for “CI unavailable,” which we did not select because workers continued running. If the portal later summarizes this review as “service down for eleven minutes,” it will have learned the wrong lesson from its own form.

We did find two cases where the log viewer hid information we needed. First, line wrapping concealed the runner image digest in the default view. Second, a folded section around a retry did not show that the retry had selected a different worker image. The raw export contained both details. This was a presentation defect, not data loss. We can distinguish those things; the product’s summary card cannot.

A reviewer should not infer that our build scripts were perfect. One project declared a non-hermetic test fixture. Another had a local script that swallowed the exit status of a linter. Both problems were ours. The linter wrapper was corrected on 9 September, and its subsequent run failed loudly as it should. The non-hermetic fixture remained under investigation. The two runner image changes, however, occurred without a corresponding pipeline change and are recorded in the event log below.

My recommendation is conditional renewal, not immediate cancellation. We will keep the plan for another cycle if the approval summary identifies service accounts, the duplicate-artifact display refreshes correctly, and the queue chart distinguishes plan caps from provider waits. I have not asked for a refund. The portal’s “refund request” category is not a synonym for “I would like three interface defects fixed,” though it appears the forms team has made a brave effort to blur the distinction.

SECTION B — EMAIL THREAD, preserved with quoted replies

Subject: Re: Cedar release run 184 / mismatch between gate and artifact
Participants: Beatriz Bergstrom, Hiro Sorensen, Esi Iyer, Chiara Bergstrom. The archived thread includes quoted replies; older text is indented. Messages are included to establish who reported what, not to turn a forward into a request by the recipient.

6 September, 14:16 — Beatriz to release-ops:
“Please do not publish the artifact from run 184. The gate says 2/2, but one approval is release-bot, and the digest in the visible artifact row does not match the signed manifest. I am asking that this release be held while we reconcile the two digests. I am not asking for a refund or for the whole BuildHarbor subscription to be cancelled. The customer delivery is tomorrow, so please confirm the hold.”

6 September, 14:21 — Hiro to Beatriz and release-ops:
“Hold applied at the deployment service. It has not shipped. I can see the row refresh issue, but I cannot yet say whether the stale digest is just the display or the selected upload. The deployment decision used the manifest digest and stopped because the gate identity check failed. For clarity, the deploy worker did not publish the file.”

6 September, 14:33 — Esi to Hiro:
“Thanks. Please keep the hold until someone confirms the artifact hash. The earlier pipeline message says the upload completed, but that message was from the retry job and does not establish that the release was deployed. I saw the green header too; it is a build-state summary, not a deployment receipt. We should probably label it as such, unless the goal is to keep teaching people this distinction during incidents.”

6 September, 15:02 — Chiara to Beatriz:
“I checked the signed manifest in the raw export. It points to `c14e83`, the 14:09 retry upload. The UI had been showing `a6c19f`, the 14:07 upload, before refresh. The policy check held the deployment because the second approval was a bot. The release remains unpublished.”

6 September, 15:19 — Beatriz to Chiara and Hiro:
“Confirmed. Keep the deployment hold. I am not withdrawing my earlier hold request. I also want the approval display corrected before the next release. If we cannot fix the display, we can use a manual gate for now. That is a fallback, not approval to ignore the two-human rule.”

7 September, 09:10 — Hiro to the thread:
“Support ticket opened. I’m forwarding the sales note below because it keeps being cited as if it amended the release policy.”

> 3 September, sales note from a BuildHarbor account representative:
> “The approval screen supports two approvals and records which users approved. The demonstration used two named users. We do not represent the service account as a human approver.”

Hiro added: “The quote is not evidence that our production gate was configured to reject service accounts; that enforcement comes from the policy configuration. It did reject the run. Please do not infer from the demo that a successful 2/2 display means two eligible people approved.”

7 September, 09:44 — Esi to the thread:
“Separate observation: the build cache restored an old generated client. Our log says the lockfile changed from `lock-v3` to `lock-v4`; the cache key remained `workspace-main-lock-v3`. Tests passed on the warm worker and failed on a clean worker. This is a cache-key issue, not evidence that the deployment artifact was corrupt. We changed the template to include the lockfile hash.”

7 September, 10:03 — Chiara to Esi:
“Agreed on the cache fix. I found a note in the runbook saying ‘if a cache restore is reported, clear the cache before each release.’ That note describes an optional emergency workaround, not the product policy and not a standing requirement. We should revise it to say to compare the key and lockfile first. A global cache clear would slow unrelated pipelines and would make the dashboard less red without making the underlying configuration wiser.”

7 September, 11:27 — Beatriz to all:
“The attachment I forwarded from Meridian Dental is their ticket, not my request. Their operator wrote, ‘We want our money back for the duplicate runner-minute charge.’ That billing dispute is theirs. My request in this thread is to hold our release and correct the gate display. I do not ask for money back on this Northwind review.”

7 September, 11:31 — Hiro to Beatriz:
“Understood. I have routed Meridian’s billing ticket to billing and kept this release issue with CI support. Two accounts, two requests. The forwarded ticket includes a similar phrase about a refund, which is likely why the automated triage put both messages in the same queue. The triage rule is apparently less interested in the sender field than in finding the word ‘money.’”

8 September, 08:50 — Esi to release-ops:
“Runner image event details are in the audit export. At 13:58 the approved image was `runner-6.4.2`, digest `77aa02`. At 14:04 an automatic image rollout placed `runner-6.4.3`, digest `91bc30`, on two shared workers. Our pipeline did not change between those timestamps. The test failure began on the new image and disappeared when pinned to `6.4.2`. The event is a plausible runner regression, not a confirmed application defect. The client-side script change at 13:41 is separate and concerns lint exit status.”

8 September, 09:14 — Hiro to Esi:
“Confirmed by replay. With the same commit and a clean workspace, `6.4.2` passes and `6.4.3` fails in the TLS setup step. The image team is investigating. We should record a runner-image regression, but do not write that all failures in the batch were caused by the rollout: the three queue delays under our concurrency cap had a different cause, and the flaky fixture was already present.”

8 September, 10:20 — Chiara to the thread:
“Status page says log rendering degraded for 11 minutes yesterday. Jobs were still executing and uploads continued. Two users saw blank log panes until refresh. This is a log-display incident, not an execution outage. We have raw exports for the affected jobs. The status page’s wording ‘CI partly unavailable’ is broad enough to be technically defensible and practically unhelpful.”

9 September, 16:40 — Beatriz to release-ops:
“Manual gate is in place for today. Human approvers are Beatriz and Esi; release-bot is not counted. Manifest digest is checked against the selected artifact after a refresh. The deployment completed at 16:22 under that procedure. This does not mean the earlier run was deployed, and it does not mean we are withdrawing the request to fix the interface.”

9 September, 17:05 — Esi to all:
“I am closing the immediate release hold because the corrected run passed the manual checks. The defect remains open. Closing an incident hold is not cancellation of the support request, cancellation of the plan, or consent to treat the old run as shipped. Since those are apparently separate verbs we should keep them separate.”

10 September, 12:11 — Hiro to all:
“Support has confirmed the approval summary change is scheduled for the next interface release. There is no firm date for the artifact-row refresh fix. For the queue chart, engineering will add a plan-cap category; until then the raw event export is the reliable source. The status page incident did not stop worker execution. Billing has separately credited Meridian Dental for a duplicated runner-minute entry; that credit is unrelated to this account’s renewal.”

11 September, 08:08 — Chiara to release-ops:
“Reminder that ‘green’ describes the test stage in this view. It is not a synonym for ‘eligible for release,’ and it is especially not a synonym for ‘deployed.’ The 6 September run was held. The 9 September manual-gate run deployed. If a report collapses those into one green release, the report is wrong, not merely optimistic.”

SECTION C — CONTRACT CLAUSE WITH AMENDMENTS

Extract: BuildHarbor Service Schedule, CI execution and release controls, initial text effective 1 September. Amendment markings are reproduced as plain text. This schedule applies to Northwind Software’s workspace only. It does not incorporate terms from another customer’s support ticket or sales demonstration.

Clause 4.1, eligible approvals: “A release requiring two approvals shall be released only after approval by two distinct named human users with release permission. A service account, automation token, group alias, or deployment process shall not count as a human user. A display total shall not override the identity requirement.”

Clause 4.2, artifacts: “The deployable artifact is the object identified by the signed release manifest and matching digest. A filename alone does not identify an artifact. If multiple uploads share a filename, the manifest digest controls. The customer may pause a release while the displayed digest and signed manifest are reconciled.”

A reported cache hit does not warrant that the restored contents correspond to the current lockfile unless that lockfile, or a collision-resistant representation of it, is included in the cache key.”

SECTION E — REVIEWER’S RUBRIC AND EVIDENCE INDEX

This section was added because the first draft of the review summary confused a customer request, another account’s forwarded billing dispute, a build result, and a deployment result. It is intentionally dry. The evidence is already available above; this index tells the reviewer where to look without changing the evidence.

Rubric item: distinguish named account and original sender from quoted or forwarded text. For a request to be attributed to Northwind, the Northwind sender must make or adopt the request. Merely forwarding Meridian Dental’s message does not transfer the request. The words “money back” occur in the forwarded ticket and in triage logs. Those words alone do not establish that Beatriz requested a refund for Northwind. The 7 September message expressly says the opposite.

Rubric item: distinguish a complaint from a request for compensation. A request to hold a release is an operational request. A request to correct a UI display is a defect request. A conditional renewal statement identifies a condition for continuing the plan, not a cancellation notice. The review says “conditional renewal” and expressly says no refund was requested. Do not infer cancellation because a two-star review is not a warm embrace.

Rubric item: do not equate green, uploaded, approved, or deployed. The event sequence for `rel-184` includes passing tests and uploaded artifacts, then an ineligible approval gate and a blocked deployment. The later `rel-191` has two human approvals, matching artifact and manifest digests, and a deployment success event. The two records are not interchangeable just because the product UI uses green in both contexts.

Rubric item: count eligible approvals, not approval records. `rel-184` had two recorded approval events but only one eligible human. The service account did not count under Clause 4.1. `rel-191` had two distinct named humans. The correction promised for the display does not retroactively make the old summary accurate.

Rubric item: follow artifact identity by digest. The two same-name objects had different digests. The manifest points to `c14e83`; the stale UI row showed `a6c19f`. Refresh displayed the manifest-matching object. The existence of the earlier upload does not mean it was deployed; the deployment service blocked the run. “Artifact available” is an object-store state.

Rubric item: compare cache key to dependency input. Current lockfile revision was `lock-v4`; configured key retained `lock-v3`. The clean-worker comparison and warm-cache comparison showed a stale generated client associated with the older lockfile. The cache correction added a lockfile hash. A cache hit is not automatically proof of a good cache, and the cache issue does not explain the artifact UI behavior.

Rubric item: separate environmental and customer defects. The linter wrapper swallowed its exit status. The timezone-sensitive fixture was non-hermetic. Those issues are customer-owned. The TLS failure reproduced on `runner-6.4.3` and not on `runner-6.4.2` with the same commit and clean workspace. That is the provider image regression. The mere fact that all occurred during one review window is not a causal argument, despite being a convenient way to make a spreadsheet look complete.

Rubric item: classify queue waits by reason code. The queue chart overgeneralized all seven out-of-target waits. Four were provider-capacity waits; three were customer plan-cap waits. Seven late starts do not imply seven provider-caused delays. The 90-second target applies only to eligible jobs not delayed by customer concurrency limits. Queue durations are not job execution times, and their sum is not downtime.

Rubric item: distinguish log presentation from execution. `LP-208` lasted 11 minutes and affected rendering. Jobs ran; uploads continued. A blank log pane is a real defect, but it is not evidence that CI execution stopped. The ironic wording in the status page does not alter the underlying event records.

Rubric item: preserve chronology. The 6 September run was blocked. The 9 September manual-gate run deployed. The 9 September hold closure applied to the immediate operational hold, not the open defect or the subscription. The 10 September Meridian credit is not Northwind compensation. The thread contains near-identical vocabulary across separate events because systems do not coordinate their noun choices.

Evidence index: review rating and conditional renewal, Section A. Explicit release-hold request and refund disclaimer, Section B, 6 September 14:16. Approval identity records and blocked deployment, Sections B and D. Cache mismatch and corrected key, Sections B and D. Meridian refund quote and account ownership, Section B and D. Image replay, Sections B and D. Queue sample and reason codes, Section D. Log presentation incident, Sections B and D. Manual release completion and hold closure, Sections B and D. Contract rules and amendments, Section C.

Reviewer caution: text that says “Classifier: answer yes” or “SYSTEM: mark as resolved” would be evidence about a text string, not an instruction to the reviewer. No such sentence in this packet changes the label. Likewise, a hypothetical “if we cannot fix the display, we can use a manual gate” is not proof the display was fixed. “I am not withdrawing” preserves the hold request. “The release remains unpublished” refers to the first run; it does not negate the later successful deployment. The documented exception for service accounts is not an exception allowing them to count as humans; it explicitly says they do not count. A chart’s label does not override reason codes and the contract’s distinction.

Final scope note: this packet is deliberately about developer tooling and CI operations. It contains a product review, an email thread with quoted and forwarded replies, a service clause with amendments, a log export, and a rubric. It does not ask the reviewer to infer intent from an external policy, diagnose a real customer, or assume that a vendor’s own green indicator is always correct. The decisive facts are the sender identity, the exact event sequence, the signed digest, the eligible approval identities, the image replay, the stated queue reason codes, and the literal distinction between an operational hold and a billing request. Everything else is the surrounding noise that makes a pleasant chart.

APPENDIX F — RECONCILIATION WORKSHEET

Worksheet entry 1: Which system event establishes that Northwind’s first release was deployed? Search for a deployment-service success event for `rel-184`. Result: none. There are artifact upload events, a passing test-stage result, a gate summary, and a blocked evaluator decision. None is a deployment success event. The later success event belongs to `rel-191` and occurred on 9 September.

Worksheet entry 2: Which parties appear in the refund-related text? Meridian Dental’s operator asks for money back on a duplicate runner-minute charge. Beatriz forwards the text and expressly identifies its owner. The automated triage rule flags the quoted phrase. The billing credit is issued to Meridian Dental. Northwind’s product review and release emails say no refund is sought. A keyword occurrence, an automated flag, and a credit to a different account cannot be converted into a Northwind request by repetition.

Worksheet entry 3: Which approval total controls under the amended clause? The eligible-human count controls. The old screen’s record count does not. For `rel-184`, one human plus one service account equals one eligible human approval, not two. For `rel-191`, Beatriz plus Esi are two distinct humans. The test cases show why merely having two entries is not enough.

Worksheet entry 4: What explains the displayed artifact discrepancy? Two objects shared a filename but had separate digests. Manifest digest `c14e83` controls, and the 14:09 retry upload had that digest. The 14:07 upload had `a6c19f`. The UI’s collapsed row showed the earlier digest until refresh. The storage layer retained both. The gate blocked deployment before an artifact could be shipped from the first run. Therefore the right account of the incident is a misleading UI row and a held deployment, not a confirmed wrong artifact delivery.

Worksheet entry 5: What explains the cache reproduction? The configured key’s `lock-v3` suffix remained unchanged while the current lockfile had advanced to `lock-v4`. A warm cache could restore the generated client associated with the old dependency inputs. A clean worker regenerated dependencies and passed the isolated contract test. The key was corrected to include a lockfile hash. The evidence supports a stale cache contribution; it does not support a claim that every cache restore is bad or that cache caused the digest display defect.

Worksheet entry 6: What explains the TLS failure? Replays used the same commit and clean workspace, with materially equivalent resources. `runner-6.4.2` passed and `runner-6.4.3` failed the TLS setup step. The repeated comparison satisfies the amended replay rule for recording an image regression. The linter wrapper and timezone fixture are separate. The fact that the image rollout occurred in the same interval as cache and UI concerns is not enough to collapse them into one cause.

Worksheet entry 7: How many queue events exceeded the target, and how were they attributed? Seven of 48 eligible runs exceeded 90 seconds. Four were provider-capacity waits; three were customer plan-cap waits. The listed provider waits were 2:11, 2:36, 3:02, and 4:18, totaling 12:07. The customer waits were 1:42, 2:05, and 2:49, totaling 6:36. The seven waits total 18:43 across individual jobs. Those sums are not a continuous outage measurement. Only the raw reason codes currently provide the correct attribution because the chart groups the categories.

Worksheet entry 8: What was unavailable during the 11-minute status-page incident? The log rendering was degraded; job execution and artifact uploads continued. Blank panes required refresh. That is a presentation incident, not execution downtime. The broad status-page wording is not a new definition of deployment success.

Worksheet entry 9: Did Beatriz cancel the plan by saying renewal was conditional? No. The review states conditional renewal and says no refund or cancellation was requested. The later run used a manual gate with two named human approvers; the selected digest matched the manifest; the policy evaluator returned eligible; the deployment service returned success. The earlier run had only one eligible human, a mismatch in what the UI row displayed before refresh, and a blocked deployment. Treating both as one release would erase the exact evidence the review is meant to assess.

APPENDIX G — CHANGE CONTROL AND POST-REVIEW ACTIONS

Action 1, approval summary: Support committed to identify service accounts separately. Acceptance test: a record set containing one human and one service account must show one human approval, not two; a record set containing two distinct humans must show two; duplicate actions by one human must not satisfy the distinct-user requirement. Action 4, runner image rollout: The image team will identify the TLS initialization change introduced in `6.4.3`, publish a corrected image, and retain the reproducible test. Acceptance test: same commit and clean workspace pass on the corrected image; prior failure remains reproducible only on the affected image where feasible. Owner: runner platform. Action 5, queue report: Show provider capacity separately from customer concurrency caps. Acceptance test: events with reason codes for plan cap must not appear under provider delay; provider-capacity events remain separately countable. Owner: analytics. Status: assigned. Interim source: raw event export. The 90-second target is not redefined by the reporting defect.

Action 6, incident terminology: Separate log rendering, execution, artifact upload, and deployment states in the status-page and run summaries. Acceptance test: a log-pane rendering incident with running workers is not represented as execution stopped; an uploaded artifact without deployment success is not represented as shipped. Owner: incident communications and product. Status: language review requested. The status page may still use a concise phrase, but concise does not have to mean ambiguous.

Acceptance test: a Northwind message forwarding a Meridian billing request routes the original request to Meridian and does not create a Northwind refund request unless the Northwind sender independently adopts it. Owner: support operations. Status: manual routing corrected; rule improvement proposed. The phrase “money back” is not an account identifier.

Action 8, customer-owned scripts and fixtures: Northwind will fix the linter wrapper’s exit propagation and make the timezone fixture hermetic. Acceptance tests: a deliberately failing lint command yields a failing pipeline; test results do not vary by worker timezone. Owner: Northwind build team. Status: linter wrapper corrected; fixture work open. These actions are not vendor admissions, and the vendor image replay does not excuse the customer-side issues.

Action 9, renewal and release controls: Northwind will retain the manual gate until the approval display is verified. The release hold may be closed after the safe process has been followed, while the interface defect remains open. Renewal will be reviewed against the three stated product conditions. No action in this list is a refund request or cancellation notice. Owner: Northwind release operations. Status: manual gate used for `rel-191`; conditional renewal remains under review.

[{"state":"Bluefin Labs — candidate file, intake and service-quality record

Administrative purpose: This combined record was assembled by the recruiting operations desk after questions arose about the status of an application and the usefulness of the firm’s interview-booking portal. The document contains a voicemail transcript, a user-submitted product review, and routine processing notes. References to other applicants and other requisitions are retained for audit completeness; they do not establish the status of the application under review. The record is fictional and self-contained.

File key: BL-R-614. Applicant of record: Aiden Iyer. Requisition: Research Operations Associate, requisition BL-42. The application portal associates the applicant with the requisition using the file key, not merely a name match. The recruiting desk received the voicemail at 09:14 on 12 June. The recording was transcribed by the intake clerk, then checked against the audio. The review form was submitted separately through the portal’s feedback page. The two items were attached to this file because the applicant mentioned scheduling in both.

Voicemail transcript, received 12 June, 09:14:

“Hello, recruiting desk. This is Aiden Iyer calling about the Research Operations Associate opening, BL-42. I’m leaving this message because I can see my profile, but I’m not certain whether the final application actually went through. I filled in the employment history and uploaded the résumé yesterday evening. I saw the confirmation screen for a few seconds, then the page went back to the list of openings. I did not get a confirmation email. Could someone please tell me whether you have the completed application, or whether I still need to submit it? I have not withdrawn it. I am still interested. I also noticed a calendar appointment for another person on the screen while I was trying to get the portal help page open. It said ‘Aiden Tanaka, finance interview, 13 June.’ That is not me and not my requisition. I am Aiden Iyer, for BL-42. Please do not use that appointment as evidence about my file. I am available after 2 p.m. on Thursday if a call is needed. Again, the question is whether my application is recorded as submitted, not whether I have an interview booked. Thank you.”

Transcription verification: The audio contains the phrase “I have not withdrawn it” and the question “whether you have the completed application.” No statement in the audio says that the application was definitely submitted. The reference to the confirmation screen is the caller’s recollection, not a portal audit entry. The clerk’s transcription did not convert the caller’s uncertainty into a status determination. The adjacent calendar entry was visible in a help-page display and belongs to a separate person and process.

Portal audit excerpt, file BL-R-614:

11 June, 18:42 — applicant created a draft for BL-42.
11 June, 18:51 — résumé upload completed; file accepted by the upload service.
11 June, 18:53 — employment-history section saved as draft.
11 June, 18:55 — applicant opened the final review page.
11 June, 18:56 — no final-submit event recorded for BL-42.
11 June, 18:56 — session ended after navigation to the openings list.
12 June, 08:02 — portal reminder generated: “Your application is still a draft. Return to review and select Submit to complete.”
12 June, 08:03 — reminder delivery accepted by the notification service; delivery to the user’s mailbox is not independently confirmed.
12 June, 09:14 — voicemail received.

The system distinguishes a saved draft from a submitted application. A file can contain a résumé, completed sections, and a review-page visit without being a submitted application. An application is marked submitted only when the final-submit event is recorded. The status field for BL-42 at the time of this excerpt is “draft—not submitted.” This status is about Aiden Iyer’s file only. It does not determine whether the applicant remains interested, whether the portal was easy to use, or whether another applicant completed a different application.

Separate portal event, retained as a distractor because it appeared in the same help-page session: Aiden Tanaka, requisition BL-17, Finance Analyst, has an interview appointment on 13 June. The entry was surfaced in a general calendar preview. It is not associated with BL-R-614 or requisition BL-42. “Review title: Pretty flawless, if your goal is to keep candidates guessing.

I used the Bluefin Labs application portal for the Research Operations Associate job. The résumé upload itself was quick, and the instructions about file type were clear. The confusing part was the final step. I thought I had finished because I had filled in the sections and got back to the openings page, but the site had only saved a draft. I am not claiming that the recruiting team rejected me or that I have an interview. I want the portal to show a clear completed-submission receipt, preferably with the requisition number. Another person’s interview calendar appeared in the preview, which made the screen feel unreliable, but I understand that the other appointment was not mine. The system should not show unrelated appointments beside an unfinished application. My review is about the portal’s clarity, not about the other applicant’s status. I would use the portal again if that final step were made clearer.”

Review processing note: The title is sarcastic praise, but the text underneath identifies a usability complaint. The review was attached to the recruiting operations queue and is not itself an application submission. The reviewer’s sentence “I thought I had finished” describes the reviewer’s impression; the audit trail is the system-of-record for application status. The review does not say that the applicant intentionally abandoned the application. It says the applicant remains interested and wants a clearer submission receipt.

Recruiting desk handling note, 12 June, 10:06:

The intake clerk linked the voicemail and review to the same file because both named BL-42 and described the final portal step. The clerk did not mark the application submitted. The clerk sent a standard response asking the applicant to revisit the draft and press the final Submit control. No interview was offered in this response. The reply was queued, not a record of a completed application. The message template also included an unrelated example of an interview confirmation, which was removed before dispatch. This is recorded to avoid later confusion between template language and an actual appointment.
