BL-42, Research Operations Associate — owner: recruiting operations; status: draft—not submitted; next action: applicant to submit; no interview appointment recorded.
BL-17, Finance Analyst — owner: finance recruiting; status: interview scheduled for Aiden Tanaka; date: 13 June; unrelated to BL-42.
BL-39, Data Quality Coordinator — owner: recruiting operations; status: submitted application received from Leila Castillo; review pending; unrelated to BL-42.
BL-51, Lab Logistics Assistant — owner: campus recruiting; status: application submitted by Hiro Mensah; screening call proposed; unrelated to BL-42.

The existence of submitted applications elsewhere in the queue does not change the draft status of BL-42. Likewise, the existence of an interview booking for BL-17 does not establish a booking for BL-42.

Portal behavior summary prepared for service review:

The portal has three principal application states: started, draft, and submitted. “Started” means the applicant opened a requisition but did not save any application content. “Draft” means one or more sections or uploaded documents have been saved, but the final submission control has not generated a successful event. “Submitted” means a successful final-submit event has been written to the audit log and a receipt has been generated. A receipt may be delayed in email delivery, but the audit event remains authoritative. A user’s recollection of seeing a confirmation screen is not substituted for an event record when the event record is available.

The calendar preview is supplied by a separate scheduling component. It may display appointments for other applicants if the user opens a generic help or availability panel. The preview does not grant access to another applicant’s file, and it does not transfer an appointment between records. An appointment is linked to a candidate and requisition identifier. Similar names do not create a match. For that reason, the clerk documented the Aiden Tanaka event as a nearby but unrelated item rather than using it to complete Aiden Iyer’s record.

Service review observation: Several applicants have described the transition from the review page to the openings list as misleading. The review page allows the user to save a draft, and the openings list displays both drafts and submitted files. The badge for a draft is displayed in grey; the badge for submitted is green. In a small-screen view, the badge may be below the visible portion of the page. The portal team is considering a more prominent receipt. The service review has not authorized staff to infer submission from a user’s confidence, from a saved résumé, or from a visit to the final review page.

No decision about candidate suitability is contained in this record. The file does not state whether Aiden Iyer meets the job requirements, whether a recruiter has evaluated the résumé, or whether the applicant would be selected. It documents a procedural status and a portal feedback issue. The distinction matters because an application can be incomplete while the candidate remains interested, and a portal can receive a negative review even when the applicant has not been rejected.

Applicant identity checked against the requisition-specific file key: yes.
Name on BL-42: Aiden Iyer.
Résumé present in draft: yes.
Employment history saved: yes.
Final-submit event: no.
Submitted receipt generated: no.
Interview appointment on BL-42: no.
Applicant withdrawal request: no.
Portal usability review: received.
Review sentiment: negative about final-step clarity despite sarcastic title.

The checklist is a summary of events already described, not a substitute for them. “Résumé present” must not be read as “application submitted.” “No withdrawal request” must not be read as “application complete.” A complaint about the portal does not alter the workflow state. An unrelated appointment elsewhere in the calendar does not supply missing evidence about this file.

Appendix A, notification template audit:

The standard notification begins, “Thank you for completing your application.” That line is used in one template after submission and is not included in the draft reminder. In the response to this voicemail, the clerk selected the draft-help template, whose actual first sentence was, “Your record currently appears as a draft.” The template preview briefly showed the submission template because the agent had searched for “application.” No submission message was sent. The template preview is preserved as a procedural artifact and does not show that BL-42 entered the submitted state.

Appendix B, reviewer comments:

A service analyst wrote: “The applicant says the screen looked finished, and a nearby interview was visible. We should be careful not to mistake either item for a successful submission.” A second analyst noted that the voicemail’s wording is a request for verification rather than an assertion of completed submission. A third analyst recommended that the portal display the requisition code on every status page. These comments are internal observations. They do not create or modify any portal event.

Appendix C, contact chronology:

11 June, 18:42 — draft created.
11 June, 18:51 — résumé uploaded.
11 June, 18:53 — employment history saved.
11 June, 18:55 — review page opened.
11 June, 18:56 — session ended; submit event absent.

All times are local to the Bluefin Labs recruiting operations office. The chronology contains no later submission event. If a later event is recorded, the file should be updated from the audit system rather than inferred from this record. At the time represented here, the decisive status remains draft—not submitted.

A “candidate” is a person associated with a recruiting record. An “application” is the candidate’s submitted response to a particular requisition. A “profile” may exist before an application is submitted. A “draft” is saved content that has not completed the final submission action. An “appointment” is a scheduled meeting associated with a candidate and requisition. “Portal feedback” is a comment about the service and does not itself constitute an application event. These terms are used consistently in this file.

Closing disposition: File BL-R-614 remains open for applicant action. The system shows a saved draft for BL-42 and no final submission. [{"state":"STATUS UPDATE TO PROPERTY OPERATIONS DIRECTOR
Prepared by Esi Haddad, 18 September 2026
Subject: Northwind Studio, suite 4B, lease reconciliation and close-out review

Purpose and scope

This report consolidates the lease file, payment ledger, maintenance correspondence, meter records, and the move-out reconciliation for Northwind Studio’s tenancy at the fictional Alder Quay building. The unit is suite 4B. The tenant’s authorized signatory was Oren O'Neill; building operations handled the account through the property office. The report is intentionally limited to what is in the attached file. It does not assume a local legal rule that is not quoted in the lease. Dates in this report use day-month-year format. Amounts are in dollars. A credit is shown as a negative amount; a charge is shown as positive. “Posted” means entered in the ledger, not necessarily properly due. “Paid” means the bank record shows cleared funds, not that the underlying charge was agreed.

The records came from several systems. The tenant portal export ends on 31 August. The bank settlement report ends on 5 September. The facilities work-order export includes two later corrections entered on 8 September. I have kept those corrections visible rather than silently overwriting the original entries. A reviewer should distinguish the event date from the date on which a staff member typed the note. For example, a technician can complete work on 4 August and the administrator can enter that fact on 8 August. The latter date is not the repair date.

The lease cover sheet identifies an initial term from 1 January through 31 December 2026. The signed amendment changes the monthly base rent effective 1 April. The rent schedule in the signed amendment is the controlling schedule for this reconciliation. The portal had a manually loaded schedule, and the portal’s data-entry history is included later because it explains why the posted totals differ from the signed schedule. The amendment does not alter the utility allocation, parking price, deposit, or the late-charge provision.

Document hierarchy in the file

The executed lease, signed amendment, signed building rules, and signed move-in condition form are treated as operative documents. Drafts, unsigned proposals, template clauses, internal notes, and tenant comments are retained as evidence of communications but are not treated as changes to the lease. No countersigned document changing the April rent schedule was found. The tenant submitted a request to waive a charge; a request is not itself a waiver. The property manager’s email saying “I will review this” is not approval. The formal approval log contains no approval for the disputed entries.

The lease says monthly base rent is $2,400 for January, February, and March, and $2,520 for April through December. Rent is due on the first calendar day of each month. The signed amendment was executed on 15 March and expressly says the new monthly figure begins 1 April; it does not say that March is prorated or retrospectively adjusted. The lease separately lists an optional reserved parking stall at $120 per month if selected. Northwind Studio selected one stall, P-17, in the signed parking addendum. The addendum remains active through 31 August, the stated tenancy end date. A separate loading-bay pass is not included in the addendum.

For water and common-area electricity, the lease schedule assigns suite 4B a fixed 12 percent share of the building’s monthly allocable cost. The schedule defines allocable cost as the building’s recorded monthly water and common-area electricity invoices, excluding the owner’s office and excluding suite-specific electricity. It does not define a different percentage by season. The building statement lists the relevant invoice totals and the shares billed to the other suites. No evidence in the file establishes that the 12 percent figure changed. Individual-suite electricity is separately metered and billed at the meter’s recorded kilowatt-hours multiplied by the stated rate of $0.20 per kilowatt-hour. The lease contains no minimum-use charge for that meter.

The lease’s late-charge paragraph states: “A late charge of $40 may be assessed only where rent remains unpaid after 5:00 p.m. on the fifth calendar day of the month. No late charge shall be assessed where the tenant’s bank has transmitted cleared funds by that deadline, even if the portal posts the payment later.” This wording is quoted because staff notes sometimes describe the rule as “five days after due date,” which is an incomplete paraphrase. The payment file includes bank transmission and clearance timestamps. A separate sentence says a late charge is not rent and cannot be included in the base-rent calculation. No late charge is compounded.

Security deposit is $2,400, held under the receipt dated 2 January. The move-in form lists the tenant’s original deposit as $2,400 and does not record any additional deposit payment. The move-out clause permits deductions for documented physical damage beyond ordinary wear and for unpaid sums that are actually due under the lease. It does not permit a deduction for ordinary cleaning, routine maintenance, or an estimate that is not supported by an invoice. The clause requires the owner to provide an itemized statement and supporting documents. Whether any particular deduction qualifies is outside this report unless the file contains the necessary evidence.

Overview of the issue being reviewed

At the end of August, Northwind Studio asked the property office to reconcile its account before the final deposit statement. Oren’s message said that several line items appeared inconsistent with the executed documents. The request did not claim that every entry was wrong. It specifically asked the office to verify monthly rent, shared utilities, and late charges, while also asking that any agreed parking charge be left alone. A forwarding note from a facilities clerk later summarized the request as “tenant disputes all charges”; that summary is not an exact quotation and conflicts with Oren’s message. The original message is reproduced in the correspondence section.

The review below separates three questions that were mixed together in the portal discussion. First, which amount categories have a calculated discrepancy between the operative document or source record and the ledger? Second, which maintenance matters are supported by the date and cost records? Third, which move-out line items are supported by the required combination of evidence and contractual rule? The fact that a charge appears in the ledger does not resolve any of these questions. Likewise, an entry’s numerical difference alone does not establish a contractual entitlement; the text of the relevant document is included so that the calculation can be checked.

Ledger snapshot and rent calculation

The signed rent schedule yields three months at $2,400 and five months at $2,520 through the end of August. The expected base rent for January through March is 3 × $2,400 = $7,200. The expected base rent for April through August is 5 × $2,520 = $12,600. Therefore the expected base-rent total for the eight-month period is $7,200 + $12,600 = $19,800. The portal ledger instead contains base-rent entries of $2,400 for January, February, and March, followed by $2,580 for each of April, May, June, July, and August. Its posted total is $7,200 + (5 × $2,580) = $20,100. The difference is $20,100 − $19,800 = $300, or $60 for each of the five months from April through August.

The portal’s original schedule upload, dated 16 March, says “April annual uplift: 7.5% rounded to next ten dollars.” The lease amendment has no 7.5 percent formula and states the actual replacement monthly amount as $2,520. The upload note was entered by a temporary administrator, and the history says it was copied from a draft worksheet. The worksheet is not signed. There is no additional amendment raising the agreed $2,520 to $2,580. In a later email, the property office acknowledged that the portal schedule may have been populated from the draft. The acknowledgement does not itself calculate the credit, so this report shows the arithmetic explicitly.

A separate rent invoice of $120, dated 1 June, is labelled “annual common room access.” The lease schedule and amendment contain no annual common-room access charge. The building’s signed rules say that the small common room is available to all tenants without an access fee. A draft 2025 budget refers to a proposed $120 access fee, but the draft was not signed and the fee was not added to the lease. The invoice was paid with the June transfer, which does not make it part of the agreed base rent. The account export placed this item in a miscellaneous column, not in the monthly base-rent column.

The portal also shows an $85 charge described as “rent interest correction” on 1 July. There is no calculation sheet attached. It is not a stated rent installment and does not match the lease’s fixed late charge. The note says it was entered to clear a warning generated by an older portal migration. The payment log does not show any separate $85 transfer. This item should not be confused with the $40 late-charge entries reviewed below. The report does not treat the unexplained $85 label as evidence of interest due, nor does it combine it into the calculation of scheduled base rent.

The signed parking addendum produces an expected total of eight months × $120 = $960 for January through August. The ledger has eight monthly entries of $120, totaling $960. The bank records show those amounts included in the respective monthly transfers. Parking is not one of the line items Oren challenged. The loading-bay pass appears on the building’s security log on three dates, but there is no charge in the ledger for that pass and no signed document that sets a price. It is therefore not part of the parking total. These details are included to prevent a reader from treating every reference to parking or access as the same type of charge.

Shared utility records

For the utility share, the building invoice summary lists allocable monthly water and common-area electricity costs as follows: January $1,000; February $1,200; March $900; April $1,500; May $1,100; June $1,300; July $800; August $1,400. The 12 percent share under the signed schedule is, respectively, $120, $144, $108, $180, $132, $156, $96, and $168. These entries add to $1,104. The calculation is the sum of the eight monthly shares: $120 + $144 + $108 + $180 + $132 + $156 + $96 + $168 = $1,104. The source invoices are attached in the building archive, and the listed totals match the monthly invoice summaries in the statement export.

The portal billed Northwind Studio $150, $180, $135, $225, $165, $195, $120, and $210 for those same months. Each is 15 percent of the listed allocable cost, not 12 percent. The portal total is $1,380. The difference is $1,380 − $1,104 = $276. The erroneous 15 percent figure appears in a migration note dated 3 January that says “use suite allocation default pending review.” A later signed schedule in the lease file supplies the actual 12 percent allocation. The file does not show a signed modification after that schedule. The total share for the other suites in the statement export is not needed to determine the 4B percentage, but it provides a cross-check: the amounts assigned to 4B were generated from the 15 percent default rather than the 12 percent schedule.

The individual-suite electric meter is a separate calculation and should not be folded into the shared utility percentage. The monthly meter readings show 410, 380, 460, 430, 500, 450, 390, and 470 kilowatt-hours from January to August. At $0.20 per kilowatt-hour, expected individual electric charges are $82, $76, $92, $86, $100, $90, $78, and $94, totaling $698. The ledger lists exactly those eight amounts, totaling $698. The electricity statement uses the correct rate, and the meter readings reconcile to the technician’s meter log. The property office’s draft email once called all utilities “overstated,” but the individual meter figures do not support that generalization. Only the shared allocation has the percentage discrepancy described above.

An early draft of the utility worksheet used a rounded “about $1,400” total and then applied 12 percent to that single approximate number. That would not reproduce the invoice-by-invoice result. The proper method is to apply the contract percentage to each listed month, or equivalently to the exact sum of the monthly invoice totals. The building’s exact allocable costs total $9,200: $1,000 + $1,200 + $900 + $1,500 + $1,100 + $1,300 + $800 + $1,400 = $9,200. Twelve percent of $9,200 is $1,104. Fifteen percent is $1,380. The amount difference remains $276. The approximate worksheet was never posted and is not the source of the ledger charges.

The statement includes a separate $54 “utility administration fee” in February. The signed lease schedule does not list an administration fee, and the building rules describe the monthly allocation as the tenant’s share of the defined invoices, without a fixed surcharge. The February invoice note says “small-office admin, 4B,” but no supporting formula or signed authorization accompanies it. It is outside the monthly shared-cost calculation above. A different building, Tidewater Annex, has a $54 fee in a sample form stored in the shared template folder. That form is neither addressed to Northwind Studio nor signed by this tenant. It appears in the file only because the accounting clerk used the shared folder while looking for an invoice template.

Payments and late-charge audit

The payment history records the date and time the bank transmitted each monthly payment and the separate portal posting time. For January, the bank record shows cleared funds on 1 January at 14:12. February cleared on 1 February at 10:04. March cleared on 5 March at 16:48. April cleared on 5 April at 16:51. May cleared on 6 May at 09:17. June cleared on 5 June at 15:03. July cleared on 5 July at 16:59. August cleared on 4 August at 11:20. The ledger’s late-charge entries are $40 for March, $40 for April, $40 for May, $40 for June, and $40 for July, for a posted total of 5 × $40 = $200. January, February, and August have no late-charge entry.

The lease’s deadline is 5:00 p.m. on the fifth calendar day, and it expressly uses cleared funds rather than portal posting time. March cleared 12 minutes before the deadline, so the March charge does not meet the stated condition. April cleared at 16:51, which is nine minutes before 17:00, so April also falls before the deadline. May cleared on the sixth calendar day, after the deadline, so that month meets the stated timing condition. June cleared at 15:03 on the fifth and therefore is before the deadline. July cleared at 16:59, one minute before the deadline, and is also before it. On the file’s dates and the quoted clause, only May’s $40 entry meets the late-charge timing condition. The other four entries total $160 and do not meet that timing condition. This is not an assumption that the portal timestamp controls; it does not.

The portal activity export reports posting dates that differ from the bank record. March posted 6 March, April posted 6 April, June posted 6 June, and July posted 6 July. The automatic charge routine appears to have used the posting date and treated any posting after the fifth as late. That explains why the entries were generated but does not override the signed clause. May posted 6 May as well, but in that month the bank clearance itself was after the deadline. The payment record contains both timestamp fields, and the clause identifies which field governs.

The ledger’s monthly transfers include base rent, parking, utility allocation, and individual meter electricity. Their totals do not change the deadline test because the late-charge paragraph says “rent remains unpaid,” and the bank confirmation records the entire scheduled monthly transfer. A note from the accounting clerk says that the March transfer was “short by utility adjustment”; however, the bank remittance breakdown shows the full amount requested by the portal was transmitted, including the then-billed utility amount. The lease excerpt does not say that a disputed shared-utility calculation turns an otherwise on-time rent transfer into late rent. No written notice states that the tenant’s rent installment remained partly unpaid on March 5.

The report includes an unrelated account for Foxglove Software, suite 3C, in the same building export. That account has a $40 late charge from April and a note reading “funds received 7 Apr.” It is not Northwind Studio’s account, and its payment date is not evidence about suite 4B. In one merged spreadsheet, the Foxglove row sits between Northwind’s April and May rows. The suite identifier is in the last column, not the first. The row has been retained in the raw export but excluded from every calculation in this report.

The maintenance record says no water ingress was observed during the visit.

On 22 June, the tenant reported a slow kitchenette drain. The plumber’s invoice records a $96 visit, including $24 for a removable hair-and-paper blockage in the tenant-side trap and $72 for inspection of the building branch. The lease’s maintenance schedule assigns the tenant the cost of clearing a blockage confined to the tenant-side trap when caused by material found there. The schedule assigns shared branch inspection to the owner. The plumber states the $24 cleaning portion concerned material in the tenant-side trap; the $72 inspection did not find a defect in the branch. The invoice was paid by the property office, and no separate tenant charge is shown in the ledger. The point is recorded here because a later move-out draft incorrectly describes the entire $96 as a tenant damage charge.

A work order on 4 August concerns a stain at the lower wall in the kitchenette. The first technician wrote “possible spill, no moisture reading,” and uploaded a photograph showing a pale mark, without a scale reference. The tenant replied that the mark was present on move-in. The signed move-in form does not mention a stain, but its photographs do not show that particular wall at close range. A second inspection on 8 August found a dry wall and no active leak. No repair was completed. The work-order system has an estimated repaint amount of $180, entered as a planning placeholder, with no painter’s invoice, no authorization, and no indication that work was performed. The estimate is not a paid cost.

On 10 August, a maintenance request reported that the south window latch remained stiff. The technician returned on 12 August, lubricated the latch, and noted normal operation. The parts line is $0; the labor line is $36, assigned to the building’s routine maintenance account. The tenant did not request compensation. A draft move-out checklist subsequently referred to a “$36 broken latch deduction,” but the technician’s actual note says the latch operated after routine adjustment, and the financial entry is a building expense rather than a tenant charge.

On 16 August, Oren reported a loose threshold strip at the suite entry. A technician logged the report and repaired the strip on 18 August. The invoice is $48: $30 for replacement screws and $18 labor. The technician notes that two old screw holes had enlarged through ordinary repeated use; there was no impact damage. The lease’s move-out clause excludes routine maintenance and ordinary wear. The tenant’s email says, “Thanks, this is fixed now; I did not hit it with anything.” The repair was made before move-out and appears in the building maintenance account, not the tenant ledger.

A building corridor cleaning receipt for $64 dated 31 August relates to a spill outside suite 4B. The cleaner’s job sheet identifies the source as a delivery trolley used by the owner’s moving contractor, not Northwind Studio. A concierge note says the tenant had earlier carried boxes through the corridor, but the note does not state that the tenant caused the spill. The $64 receipt was included in an early draft of the suite close-out worksheet, then removed in the 8 September revision. It is not charged to the tenant in the current ledger.

Several maintenance items from other locations appear in the shared work-order export. Suite 3C had a $180 paint job; the boiler room had a $96 inspection; and suite 7A had a $48 threshold repair. Their dates overlap the 4B records, and the export sorts by completion date rather than suite. The four-digit work-order numbers are more reliable than the display order: 4B latch work orders are 4B-0513 and 4B-0812, drain is 4B-0622, wall inspection is 4B-0808, and threshold is 4B-0818. The other records are not evidence that those expenses belong to Northwind Studio.

Move-out condition and draft deductions

Northwind’s lease end date is 31 August. The final inspection took place on 1 September with Oren present. The signed checklist records three items: two small removable adhesive hooks, ordinary dust on the window sill, and a 4-centimetre scratch on the entry tile. The inspection notes say the hooks were removed at the inspection, the sill was wiped by the building cleaner as part of routine turnover, and the scratch is visible in the close-up photograph but not in the move-in image. The tenant wrote “I do not know when this scratch happened” beside the tile entry and signed the form. That statement neither admits nor denies responsibility.

The signed move-out clause permits a deduction for documented physical damage beyond ordinary wear. It requires a paid invoice or a specific itemized cost record, and it excludes ordinary cleaning and routine turnover. The close-up tile photograph is labelled 1 September and includes a ruler. A floor contractor’s invoice dated 6 September records replacement of one tile, materials $72 and labor $48, for a total of $120. The invoice says the damaged tile was in suite 4B’s entry and that the contractor replaced it. It does not identify who caused the scratch. The inspection form and invoice together document the physical condition and the actual cost; the file contains no evidence assigning the cause to a particular person.

The first draft deduction sheet listed $120 for the tile, $64 corridor cleaning, $96 drain work, $180 wall repainting, $36 latch, and $85 “rent interest correction.” The 8 September revision removed the corridor cleaning, the full drain invoice, the latch amount, and the repaint estimate. It retains the $120 tile invoice and a $24 line labelled “tenant trap clearing,” referring to the June plumber invoice. The revision also retains the $85 “rent interest correction” because an automatic migration report flagged it as outstanding. No supporting interest schedule has been found. A note on the revision says, “If the tenant object, explain the ledger was system calculated.” That note is not an itemized contractual basis.

The maintenance schedule assigns the former only where the blockage is confined to the tenant-side trap and caused by material found there; the plumber’s invoice documents that material and location. It assigns the latter to the owner. The $24 is included as one proposed tenant charge on the revision. It was not previously posted to the rent ledger and is not part of the shared utility calculation. The $72 branch inspection was not proposed as a tenant deduction in the revision. The earlier draft’s $96 line would have included both components and would not match the stated maintenance allocation.

The wall repaint figure is only an estimate. The system entry says “$180 allowance; do not pay until inspection.” The second inspection found no moisture and no completed repair, and no invoice exists. The tenant’s statement that the mark was present at move-in is not confirmed by the available image, but lack of confirmation alone does not create an actual $180 expense. The original move-in photograph is too wide to determine whether a faint mark existed. The file has no signed condition note specifically describing that wall stain. The report therefore does not treat the placeholder as a completed repair cost. The separate contractor invoice for the tile is specific to a different surface and should not be conflated with the wall estimate.

The cleaning deduction has similar limits. The only suite-specific cleaning record is routine turnover of the sill and removal of adhesive hooks during the inspection. No invoice allocates an extra cleaning charge to the tenant. The $64 receipt is for the corridor and identifies the owner’s moving contractor’s trolley. The signed clause excludes ordinary cleaning. The $64 was removed from the revised sheet. A draft note stating “corridor near tenant door, $64” omits the job-sheet attribution and is not the final record.

The security deposit receipt is $2,400, as described above. The draft arithmetic on the 8 September close-out sheet starts with $2,400 and subtracts $120 for tile, $24 for the trap, and $85 for the migration item. That draft total is $2,171: $2,400 − $120 − $24 − $85 = $2,171. If only the two documented physical or maintenance items retained on the revision are counted, the arithmetic is $2,400 − $120 − $24 = $2,256. The difference between those totals is $85. This calculation describes the sheet’s arithmetic, not a final determination that either item is deductible. The migration item’s presence on the sheet does not supply the missing interest basis.

The account’s closing worksheet also displays an alleged deposit balance of $2,300 in one tab. That figure was copied from a prior tenant’s example file. The deposit receipt, tenant ledger, and bank trust-account record each show $2,400 for Northwind Studio. The example tab belongs to a suite in a different building and is marked “training sample.” It is not a second payment, partial refund, or amendment to the 4B deposit. The file contains no bank transfer returning $100 to Northwind during the tenancy.

Document and data quality notes

The source bundle has several known defects. The accounting portal changed vendors in January. During the migration, one property-wide default set the shared utility share to 15 percent. A temporary employee loaded a draft rent escalation worksheet after reading a nonbinding budget note. Some activity times reflect posting, while the bank report reflects clearance. The combined export includes rows for other suites, and the move-out workbook contains a sample tab. These are reasons to use the signed lease, its amendment, source invoices, and suite-specific bank records rather than relying on a spreadsheet’s display total.

The workbook has three versions: “closeout_4B_draft.xlsx,” saved 3 September; “closeout_4B_review.xlsx,” saved 6 September; and “closeout_4B_final_for_review.xlsx,” saved 8 September. “Final for review” is the filename, not evidence of approval. The approval field is blank. The property manager has not signed the close-out statement. The version history shows the $64 corridor receipt was removed on 6 September, the $36 latch amount was removed on 8 September, and the $85 migration item remained. The $180 wall repaint amount appears only in the first draft, where it is marked “estimate.”

A scanned amendment copy has a faint mark over the final two digits of the rent amount. The property office verified it against the signed original retained in the paper file and the tenant’s counterpart, both of which clearly state $2,520. The portal displayed $2,580 because that amount came from the unsigned worksheet. A red annotation on the scan says “maybe 2,580?” and was added by a clerk after scanning. It is not part of the signed document. The arithmetic in the rent section uses the verified signed amount and not the annotation.

The building’s combined utility spreadsheet has both “percentage” and “fraction” columns. In one export, the 12 percent value appears as 0.12; in another, it is displayed as 12. The portal default appears as 0.15 or 15 depending on the export. There is no evidence that one month used a different denominator. The monthly invoices are all listed as allocable building costs under the definition in the lease. Suite 4B’s applicable amount is the percentage multiplied by the entire monthly allocable total, not the total divided by the number of occupied suites. Occupancy changed twice during the eight-month period, but the fixed 12 percent schedule did not change.

The repair-cost spreadsheet has a “requested,” “estimated,” “invoiced,” and “paid” column, but an older export displays only the number and description. For the wall, $180 is estimated, not invoiced or paid. For the tile, $120 is invoiced and the payment reference records settlement on 7 September. For the drain, $96 was invoiced and paid by the building, with the invoice divided into $24 and $72 components. For the latch, $36 is a building maintenance labor cost. These distinctions matter because the move-out clause asks for a documented cost, and the file’s categories are not interchangeable.

A printed status slip from the maintenance desk says “all tenant items billed.” The slip was generated before the 8 September revision, when the first draft still had multiple items. It is a general workflow status, not an itemized decision. The revised workbook, which is also unsigned, contains fewer items. An internal message says “we already billed everything,” but the ledger itself shows no tenant debit for the $24 trap clearing, the $120 tile, or the $180 estimate as of 8 September. The word “billed” in those notes may mean included on a proposed worksheet rather than posted to the tenant account.

Current reconciliation summary

On the evidence reviewed, the scheduled base rent for January through August is $19,800; the ledger’s base-rent column totals $20,100, so the difference is $300. The shared utility allocation under the 12 percent schedule is $1,104; the ledger charged $1,380, so the difference is $276. Individual metered electricity matches at $698. Parking matches at $960. The late-charge ledger totals $200, while the quoted timing rule and clearance data support the timing condition for only one $40 May entry; the other four entries total $160 and fall before the stated cutoff. These are separate calculations and should not be combined into a single generic “rent error” figure.

The common-room $120 line and the $54 administration fee have no signed authorization in the available lease file. The $85 migration item lacks a supporting interest calculation or signed fee term. They are posted or proposed account items but do not arise from the stated rent, parking, utility, meter, or late-charge schedules. The report has not silently included those items in the $300 rent difference, $276 utility difference, or $160 late-charge timing difference. The records state that the common-room line was paid with June’s transfer; the $54 and $85 entries do not have a separately identified bank transfer in the records provided.

For move-out, the file contains a $120 tile invoice and an itemized $24 tenant-side trap-clearing component under the stated maintenance schedule. It also contains an unsupported $180 repaint estimate, a $64 corridor receipt attributed to the owner’s contractor, a $36 building latch maintenance charge, and an $85 migration entry without a supporting basis. The tenant’s deposit receipt is $2,400, not the $2,300 copied from a sample tab. The revised worksheet’s subtraction of $120, $24, and $85 yields $2,171; excluding the $85 migration item yields $2,256. No final approved statement has been issued.

The records are sufficient to reproduce the central calculations, but they do not justify treating every item in a draft, note, or system export as a final obligation. The original tenant request is narrower than the forwarded summary, the bank clearance times are distinct from portal posting dates, and the signed documents take precedence over the unsigned schedule and templates. [{"state":"FAQ excerpt and support desk working file — Bluefin Dental / storefront “MorrowTray”

This is a typed-up packet assembled for the evening support desk. It combines the public FAQ, internal routing reminders, snippets from customer contacts, and an order-status export. The FAQ is the current version unless a dated correction is printed beside it. Spelling and punctuation in the customer snippets are preserved where practical. Queue names are Billing, Delivery, Product Help, and Returns. Agents should route by the customer’s actual issue, not by whichever product or department word happens to appear in a pasted note.

PUBLIC FAQ, revision 8.4

Q: What belongs in Billing?
A: Billing handles a charge that appears on a payment method, a duplicate or unexpected capture, a refund amount or refund status, an invoice or receipt correction, and a payment authorization that the customer wants explained. A question about when a parcel will arrive is not Billing merely because the customer paid for shipping. A question about whether an item works is not Billing merely because it was bought with a card. If the customer is asking to change a paid order before dispatch, first send it to Order Changes; Billing may be consulted afterward if the change alters the amount collected.

Q: What belongs in Delivery?
A: Delivery handles carrier scans, parcels marked delivered but not found, address or access problems after dispatch, missed delivery attempts, and a package that is late or damaged in transit. A customer who asks whether the package is late is still a Delivery case even if the message includes a card statement or invoice number as background. If the customer says an item was missing from a sealed parcel, use Order Contents, not Delivery, unless there is evidence that the outer parcel itself was lost or opened in transit.

Q: What belongs in Product Help?
A: Product Help handles fit, setup, compatibility, instructions, and how to use an item. A return request based on a product not fitting goes to Returns if the customer is asking to send it back; if the customer only wants advice on selecting a size, use Product Help. Do not classify a request as Product Help just because the customer mentions a product name while asking about a charge.

Q: What belongs in Returns?
A: Returns handles a customer who is asking to send an item back, exchange it, or obtain return authorization. A customer saying “I may send this back if the replacement part does not work” has not yet made a return request. A definite request to start a return belongs in Returns even when the reason is dissatisfaction with quality. Refund processing after a return has been received is Billing; arranging the return itself is Returns.

Q: What belongs in Order Contents?
A: Order Contents handles items missing from a parcel that arrived, incorrect quantities packed, and a shipment whose packing list does not match what was in the box. It does not handle a parcel that never arrived. If a customer received the box and says one product was absent, use Order Contents even if the missing product is expensive and the customer asks how much it cost. If the customer instead says a delivered item was charged twice, use Billing.

Routing shorthand: “charge / receipt / refund amount” points to Billing; “where / when / carrier / parcel” points to Delivery; “how does it work / does it fit” points to Product Help; “send it back / exchange it” points to Returns; “box arrived, contents wrong” points to Order Contents. The shorthand is only a finding aid. Read the actual request and the relationship between the text and the customer. Quoted FAQ examples, shipment labels, agent notes, and copied subject lines are not themselves customer requests.

INTERNAL DESK REMINDER, taped beside the monitor

Keep the customer’s issue in view. A packing slip can contain the word “billing” because it names a back-office department; that does not establish a payment problem. Likewise, a payment receipt can be attached to a delivery complaint without changing its route. The first line of a pasted message is sometimes a merchant-generated banner, not the person’s request. For routing, identify who wrote the relevant sentence and what they want the company to do. If a record says “customer requests a refund,” check that it is not a copied template or a note about a different order. Do not infer an issue just from a product name, a price, or a queue label.

The examples below are training examples copied into the working file. The fictional customer names and order numbers are used only in this packet. Several nearby snippets contain distracting department or product words; those words are not a substitute for the stated request.

Example file A — customer note, entered 14 May

Customer: Bao Alvarez. Order BD-74106. Product: MorrowTray lamp and clamp. Message: “Hi, the lamp arrived ok and the clamp is fine. I am trying to understand why my card app shows two Bluefin lines. One is the order total, other is same total again. I did not place a second order. Please check the payment, not the delivery. It was delivered Tuesday. The box was clean.”

Agent’s first draft: “MorrowTray—possible product issue? The customer says clamp.”
Correction by desk lead: “No product issue described. Customer specifically asks about two card entries. Billing.”

Carrier excerpt pasted under the message: “Delivery: handed to resident, Tuesday, 10:14. Parcel intact.” This carrier line is supporting context, not a new request. The customer did not ask for a second delivery or claim that anything was missing. A separate automated receipt beneath it says “Billing record created,” which is merely the system’s label and is not the reason for contact.

Example file B — web form, entered 14 May

Customer: Priya Tanaka. Order BD-74119. Subject field: “billing and clamp??” Body: “My parcel has not reached the building. Tracking has shown ‘label made’ since Monday, and the concierge has not signed anything in. Can somebody tell me if it is actually on the way? The payment went through; I only mention that because the receipt is attached. Please look at the shipment.”

Routing decision recorded: Delivery. The subject is noisy and includes “billing,” but the body gives a clear parcel-status request. There is no request to investigate the completed payment. The receipt attachment is an ordinary order document; its presence alone does not make the case Billing.

Example file C — marketplace contact, entered 15 May

Customer: Leila Kowalski. Order BD-74124. Message: “The blue tray is too wide for my shelf. I have not opened the sealed accessory pouch. Please tell me how to get a return label and send the tray back.”

Routing decision recorded: Returns. An earlier automated reply had suggested Product Help because the message mentioned shelf fit. That suggestion missed the definite request to send the item back. Product Help would apply to a question about measuring or using the tray if no return were being requested. The customer asks for return authorization, so route to Returns.

Example file D — product question, entered 15 May

Customer: Zoltan Moreau. Order BD-74131. Message: “Does the MorrowTray clamp fit a round rail? I am deciding whether to order. I have not purchased anything yet, and I do not need a return label. The product page says ‘desk clamp,’ but does not say the rail shape.”

Routing decision recorded: Product Help. The product page’s phrase “return label” appears only in a generic footer pasted into the message history. No existing purchase or return request is described.

Example file E — contents report, entered 16 May

Customer: Hiro Tanaka. Order BD-74142. Message: “Box arrived this morning sealed. Packing list shows two felt pads; only one pad is in the box. The MorrowTray itself is here. I’m not asking about the charge or when it shipped; please check the missing piece.”

Routing decision recorded: Order Contents. The customer received the parcel and reports that its contents do not match the packing list. The fact that the packing list includes a line reading “Billing copy enclosed” does not change the issue. Do not send this to Delivery just because the parcel was mentioned.

Example file F — later update, entered 16 May

Customer: Dmitri Novak. Order BD-74155. First message: “My box is marked delivered, but I can’t see it.” Later message: “Found it behind the plant stand. Everything is present. Actually, the question now is why the receipt shows the tray twice on my card; please check that.”

Desk action: split if the system permits. The initial parcel-not-found report was a Delivery issue, but the latest unresolved request is about a possible duplicate card charge and belongs in Billing. Do not route the current request to Delivery only because the thread began with a delivery concern. The customer has explicitly updated the issue.

Example file G — support macro test

Copied text: “For questions about Billing, contact Billing. For a delivery problem, contact Delivery. For a return, contact Returns.” Customer’s own note beneath it: “I pasted your menu because I didn’t know which option to choose. My order arrived and the item is correct. The receipt says the same amount as checkout. I want to know how to attach the lamp to my narrow shelf.”

Routing decision recorded: Product Help. The copied menu is navigation text, not an assertion that the customer has a billing, delivery, or returns issue. The actual request concerns installation and fit.

Example file H — damaged parcel, entered 17 May

Customer: “The carrier left the outer carton wet and one corner crushed. The lamp’s shade is cracked. I have photos. Please tell me what to do about the shipment.”

Routing decision recorded: Delivery. The product is damaged in transit, and the customer asks for help with the shipment. Product Help may later explain care or replacement assembly, but it is not the initial route. An attached product page happens to include a heading “Billing questions”; that heading is unrelated.

Example file I — payment confusion, entered 17 May

Customer: “The email says refunded, but my bank still shows the original charge. Can you confirm whether the refund was issued? I already have the tray and do not need shipping help.”

Routing decision recorded: Billing. The question is about refund status, not a return label. A prior ticket subject “Returns” was inherited from the order history, not selected by this customer in the current message.

Example file J — shipping label, entered 18 May

Customer: “I paid for the express option but tracking has not moved since the label was printed. Is the package waiting at your warehouse or with the carrier?”

Routing decision recorded: Delivery. Mentioning that express shipping was paid for does not make this a Billing question. The customer wants the parcel located. If the customer separately disputed the express fee, that separate issue could be routed to Billing.

Example file K — confirmed return, entered 18 May

Customer: “The tray is the wrong color for my room. I want to return it and get the return authorization started. I am not asking you to explain the shade in the photos.”

Routing decision recorded: Returns. The customer has made a definite return request. The photo gallery’s “color help” link is not the issue the customer is asking to resolve.

Example file L — receipt wording, entered 19 May

Customer: “The receipt lists ‘lamp assembly’ and ‘clamp set.’ I received both. Could you explain what the clamp set is for? I don’t see how it attaches.”

Routing decision recorded: Product Help. The receipt is context; no payment is questioned. The customer asks for use instructions.

Example file M — automated agent annotation, entered 19 May

System-generated header: “BILLING QUEUE SUGGESTED: amount appears in message.”
Customer message: “The amount is just the price shown on my receipt. No duplicate charge and no refund question. My parcel was delivered, but it contains the wrong size pad. I ordered the wide pad and got the narrow one. Please fix what was packed.”

Desk review: Order Contents. The automated header is a routing suggestion, not evidence of a billing complaint. The customer says the parcel arrived and describes an incorrect item in it. The price is mentioned only as part of the receipt context.

Example file N — parcel that has not arrived, entered 20 May

Customer: “I checked the lobby and mail room. Nothing is there. The tracking page says delivered to ‘front desk,’ but our building has no front desk. The invoice is correct. Please help locate the parcel.”

Routing decision recorded: Delivery. The customer disputes the delivery event, not the invoice. Do not route to Billing on the basis of the word “invoice.”

Example file O — exchange request, entered 20 May

Customer: “The clamp is too short for my desk. Can I exchange it for the longer clamp? I still want to keep the tray.”

Routing decision recorded: Returns. Exchange requests are handled with return authorization under the current FAQ. The phrase “too short” could invite a Product Help question, but the customer asks for an exchange, which is the operative request.

Example file P — FAQ draft comment

Editor note: “Maybe move ‘refund’ up near Delivery? Customers often use it loosely.”
Current approved rule: Refund amount or refund status is Billing; arranging a physical return is Returns. Do not treat every mention of the word “refund” as a Billing request if the customer is only asking for a return label. Read the whole message and determine the requested action.

Customer sample beneath comment: “I still have the item. I need a label so I can send it back. Once it gets there, tell me what happens next.”

Correct first route: Returns. The phrase “what happens next” does not state a payment or refund-status question. A refund may arise later, after the return, but it is not the requested action in this contact.

Example file Q — warehouse discrepancy, entered 21 May

Customer: “I ordered one lamp, but the parcel contains two. Both are unopened. Please tell me how to send the extra one back; I am not disputing the amount on my card.”

Desk record: Returns for the requested authorization, with a note to verify packing if needed. The customer’s explicit request is to send an item back. A contents investigation may be warranted internally, but do not substitute that possibility for the customer’s requested routing. The card statement is expressly background.

Example file R — attachment-only confusion, entered 21 May

Customer message: “Hello, order not here yet. I’m attaching the receipt because the form required a file. Tracking says it left the depot yesterday. Please tell me where it is now.”

Desk record: Delivery. The attachment requirement explains why the receipt is included. A scanner that sees “receipt” and “order total” could suggest Billing, but the customer’s actual question is parcel location.

Example file S — correct goods, wrong charge, entered 22 May

Customer: “The tray came and is exactly what I ordered. My card statement has one line for the order and another line labelled ‘Bluefin Dental web.’ Is that second line yours? I am asking about the statement, not the parcel.”

Desk record: Billing. A line on a card statement is the issue. Product and delivery details are included to rule out confusion about the shipment, not to request help with it.

Example file T — customer asks about order contents, entered 22 May

Customer: “Parcel received. The instruction booklet is missing, but the lamp and all the hardware are present. Can you send the booklet or tell me where it is?”

Desk record: Order Contents. The customer reports an item missing from a received parcel. A generic footer says “For product questions, contact Product Help,” but this is a missing-in-box request, not a use question.

Example file U — routing review card

Reviewers should identify the core request, not the most prominent noun. In the two messages below, “refund” appears in both, but only one is a payment-status contact.

U1: “I want to return the lamp. Please send the label. I understand any refund comes after inspection.” Route: Returns.

U2: “The return was completed last week, but I cannot see the refund on my card. Please confirm the payment status.” Route: Billing.

The separate outcomes illustrate that routing depends on the customer’s present request. They do not create a blanket rule that every return mention is Returns or every refund mention is Billing. The desk should preserve the customer’s own wording and route the unresolved question.

Example file V — chat handoff, entered 23 May

Customer: “I’m not sure if this is the right menu. I need to know whether my package is sitting with the carrier.”
Bot menu: “Billing: receipts and payments. Returns: send an item back. Delivery: parcels and tracking.”
Customer: “Then Delivery, I guess. Tracking says the driver could not access the building.”

Desk record: Delivery. The actual question and the carrier scan both concern delivery. The menu helps explain the wording but is not the sole basis for the route.

Example file W — account profile mix-up, entered 23 May

Customer: “My profile has the wrong email on the receipt. I can still see the order in my account. Please correct the email on future receipts.”

Desk record: Billing, because the requested correction concerns receipt and invoice records under this FAQ. The parcel and product are not at issue. A profile tool may perform the correction, but the support queue for invoice and receipt corrections is Billing.

Example file X — product compatibility, entered 24 May

Customer: “The tray is here and the receipt is fine. Will the clamp work on a glass table edge? The page only shows wood desks.”

Desk record: Product Help. Mention of a receipt is incidental. The customer wants compatibility advice, not a payment correction.

Example file Y — route based on a pasted label

Imported subject: “RETURNS / BILLING / ORDER.” Customer body: “This is about delivery. The parcel was left at a neighboring unit, and the neighbor says they handed it to the driver again. Can you trace it?”

Desk record: Delivery. The imported subject contains several queue names because the storefront form appended its category menu. It does not say that the customer wants a return or billing help. The described problem is a parcel’s location after dispatch.

Example file Z — short quality report, entered 24 May

Customer: “The lamp flickers when switched on. It arrived today with no visible damage. Can you advise whether I should reset it or stop using it?”

Desk record: Product Help. Delivery timing is included only as context. The customer asks for operating guidance; there is no return request yet. If the customer later asks to return the product, reassess the new request.

CLOSING DESK CHECKLIST

Before submitting a route, read the customer’s complete message, including any later clarification. Separate the customer’s own words from labels added by the website, copied menu text, tracking events, and agent annotations. A keyword may be useful as a clue but is not a verdict. Use the current FAQ definitions: card charges, refund amounts, and receipt corrections go to Billing; transit and parcel-location issues go to Delivery; setup and compatibility go to Product Help; definite send-back or exchange requests go to Returns; incorrect or missing contents in an arrived parcel go to Order Contents. If one contact contains two independent unresolved requests, document both or split the ticket. Do not invent a second issue from an attachment or an unrelated line in the order record.

HANDWRITTEN-STYLE NOTE TYPED UP FROM THE RETURNS CLIPBOARD

“Evening shift: I keep seeing people circle ‘billing’ on the printed slip because that word is on the back. Ask what the person needs. If they say the box is missing, shipment desk. If they say the box came but one pad didn’t, contents. If they say ‘send it back,’ return desk. If they say the bank line is wrong, billing. The product name doesn’t decide it. The little footer about warranties isn’t a request either. Please don’t forward a package question just because there’s a receipt in the scan.”

VOICE MAIL TRANSCRIPT ATTACHED TO THE SAME TRAINING PACKET

Automated header: “Possible Billing keyword: order total.”
Caller: “Hi, this is a test message for the help team. I got the MorrowTray last week and the order total on the paper is right. What I need is help finding the spare fastener bag. The carton had the tray and clamp but no little bag. It is not a bank issue; I looked at the contents list and the bag is printed there. Please tell me if you can mail it.”
Desk interpretation: the customer reports missing contents from a received parcel. The automated header is a distracting label, not the customer’s stated problem. Route Order Contents.

SUPPLEMENT: WHY THE EXAMPLES ARE KEPT TOGETHER

The packet is deliberately a mixed file because actual queue work often arrives with fragments from several systems. One row may carry a subject chosen from a form, the next an automated label, and a third a carrier event. Those pieces can make a simple request look like a different queue if the reviewer reads only the first matching word. Read who is speaking, what they are asking for now, and whether the surrounding phrase is a quotation, a system note, an attachment label, or an actual complaint. The FAQ’s queue definitions remain the authority for these examples.

A receipt can be included to establish which order a customer means without becoming a dispute about the receipt. A shipping fee can be mentioned while asking where a box is, without turning the matter into a dispute about the fee. A product can be named in a return request without making the question a request for usage advice. Conversely, the appearance of a queue name in an automated header does not prove that the customer wants that queue. When another department may eventually be involved, route the stated initial request and leave a clear handoff note rather than guessing at the later issue.

For example, a customer who says “I paid for delivery and it is still not here” has asked for a parcel-status investigation. A customer who says “the parcel arrived, but I was charged twice for delivery” has asked about a payment. The similar words do not erase the difference between their requests. A customer who says “the lamp does not fit and I want to exchange it” has asked to exchange; a customer who says “will the lamp fit this shelf?” has asked for advice. Likewise, a customer who says “my box arrived with one piece missing” is not reporting that the carrier lost the box. Small contextual details determine which queue owns the next action.

Do not use the examples as rigid templates. Apply the definitions to the current message, including any correction or follow-up. A customer may begin with one concern and later clarify a different one, or may have two separate concerns. If two independent requests are present, note the split. If an old order subject conflicts with a clear current message, the current message controls the routing of the current unresolved request. The queue choice should be explainable from the actual words of the customer without relying on a system guess.

This file was assembled from a shift notebook, a voicemail transcription, and a short FAQ excerpt used by the Harbor Logistics storefront team. The storefront sells home storage items from Larkspur Studio and a limited set of Bluefin Labs accessories. The names in this packet are fictional and the order codes are training references. Notes were typed from a hurried page; fragments, repeated words, and shorthand have been retained. Route requests by the work the customer is asking the support team to do. Nearby labels, other customers’ problems, and form metadata can be distracting.

CURRENT QUEUE DEFINITIONS, copied from the FAQ card

Billing handles a disputed payment, duplicate charge, refund status or amount, and a correction to a receipt or invoice. Delivery handles carrier status, a parcel that has not arrived, a parcel delivered to the wrong place, and transit damage. Returns handles a definite request to send an item back or exchange it. Product Help handles advice about assembly, dimensions, fit, or use. Order Contents handles a parcel that arrived with an item, part, or quantity missing or incorrect. A queue label printed by the storefront is not enough by itself; the customer’s own request is what matters. When a message has two independent requests, record both or split it rather than allowing an unrelated detail to hide one.

The FAQ card’s examples are short on purpose. “Receipt attached; where is my box?” is Delivery. “Box arrived; card shows a duplicate charge” is Billing. “Item arrived; please exchange it” is Returns. “What size bracket fits?” is Product Help. “Parcel arrived without the bracket listed inside” is Order Contents. These examples are aids, not substitutes for reading a complete thread. A customer can mention a receipt without disputing it, mention a product without asking how to use it, or mention shipping while making a payment complaint.

TYPED-UP HANDWRITTEN SHIFT NOTE, page 1

“Morning desk—please stop routing by the giant bold tag at top of copied form. It comes from old checkout menu. Read the lines under it. If person says the courier put parcel at wrong unit, that’s delivery, even if line says invoice attached. If parcel in hand and contents not right, contents. If wants to send back, returns. Payment query is billing. Ask what they want us to do, not what words the website stamped onto page.”

Below that, written in the margin: “Larkspur Studio names printed on box aren’t an issue category. A customer can say ‘Larkspur’ about an order and be talking about any of the five queues. Same with Bluefin Labs on a receipt.”

NOTE 1 — contact from Leila Kowalski, ticket HL-93018

Imported tag: “PAYMENT / BILLING”. Form attachment: order confirmation. Customer text: “My box is still at the carrier depot, according to the last scan. It has not come to our address, and the hallway camera shows no delivery today. The confirmation is attached because the web form asked me to upload something. Can you find out when it is moving?”

Customer text: “The storage rail arrived and looks fine. My receipt has the correct amount. I need to know whether the short bracket will fit a 38 mm shelf lip; the measurement chart shows only 32 mm. Please advise before I install it.”

I’m not calling about the card charge; it looks fine.”

Subject auto-filled: “Billing—receipt”

VOICE MAIL TRANSCRIPT, page 2 of the typed notebook

Automated greeting: “For billing, say payment. For delivery, say parcel. For returns, say return.”

Caller: “I keep getting the billing menu, but this is about the box. It says delivered to a loading bay that our building doesn’t have. The receipt is fine; I only have it in front of me because the model number is printed there. I need someone to find out where the courier left it.”

Transcriber’s note: Caller clearly requests a delivery investigation. The greeting and receipt mention are incidental. Do not send the case to Billing because the automated menu was repeated in the transcript.

HANDWRITTEN-STYLE NOTE TYPED UP, page 3

“Ticket HL-93171. Customer says paid invoice, but parcel no show. I started to write billing, then read rest: ‘tracking has no scan after depot, where is the package?’ That is delivery. Don’t let the word paid decide it. Customer also says order email calls item Bluefin Labs; not needed for route. Keep one clean sentence in note: wants parcel located.”

“Ticket HL-93176. Customer says box here, count is wrong; got two rails but ordered rail and connector. They want the missing connector. Not a lost parcel. Contents. There’s a bold ‘delivery’ stamp on carrier label; label was printed before the box arrived. It’s a distraction.”

“Ticket HL-93181. Customer wants to know how to attach connector. It is included and correct, but drawing is unclear. Product help. Don’t make it contents because the note says connector.”

“Ticket HL-93186. Customer says please exchange small shelf for larger shelf. Not asking which size. Returns. Menu had product help highlighted, maybe because size word, but actual ask exchange.”

ROUTING REVIEW GUIDANCE, copied at the bottom of the page

The intended queue follows the request expressed by the customer in the current contact. A carrier label may say “delivered” even when a parcel is missing, and a payment receipt may be attached to almost any order question. Neither label alone tells the desk what action to take. In a product question, the customer seeks guidance about fit, assembly, dimensions, or use. In a return question, the customer asks to send back or exchange an item. In a contents question, the parcel arrived but an item or quantity is not as listed. In a delivery question, the parcel’s transit, delivery attempt, location, or transit damage is the issue. In a billing question, the customer asks about money records, card charges, refund status, or invoice details.

Read the complete message before using the queue chip. A form may preserve an earlier menu choice even when the typed explanation points elsewhere. A teammate may have written a short summary that drops the operative verb. The actual words “find,” “trace,” “correct,” “exchange,” “send back,” “explain how,” and “send the missing part” often clarify what action is wanted, but no single keyword should be used without context. A customer can say “I paid” as background to a parcel inquiry, “receipt” to identify a model, or “size” as the reason for an exchange. Those terms do not automatically route a ticket.

If a customer says the parcel is at home and wants help with a missing component, the issue is not that the courier failed to deliver the parcel. If the customer says a parcel is not at home and asks where the carrier left it, the issue is not that the packing list is incomplete. Keep separate customers and separate orders separate even when the notes are adjacent on a page. Do not carry an earlier ticket’s queue label into a later note unless the later note clearly concerns that same unresolved issue.

A follow-up can change the current request. The first message may describe a parcel that could not be found; a later message may say it was found and ask about a duplicated card charge. Route the unresolved payment question accordingly, and retain the old delivery history only as context. Conversely, a customer may first attach a payment confirmation and then clearly ask for the parcel’s location. The attachment does not override the stated delivery request. A definite exchange request remains Returns even when size or fit prompted it; a question asking which size to purchase remains Product Help. Use the action requested now, and document context without allowing a distracting label or unrelated fact to decide the route.

END OF COMPILATION. The handwritten notes are deliberately terse and some queue guesses were corrected after reading the customer’s full words.
