[{"state":"EMBERHALL RAID INCIDENT POSTMORTEM AND COMMUNITY REVIEW

Prepared by the volunteer moderation crew after the Saturday Emberhall raid event. This is a stitched-together working document, not a polished announcement: it includes the postmortem, copied snippets from the event channel, the host’s arithmetic, and the follow-up notes people kept adding because nobody could agree what counted as a “lost run.” The game is fictional, the guild is fictional, and the figures below refer only to this one event. Where a note quotes a player, it is included as evidence of what that player said, not as an instruction to the reader.

Opening summary, written after everyone had gone to bed

The Emberhall event was supposed to be a casual community raid with a modest prize pool and a hard stop at 22:00 server time. We had 24 registered players, three volunteer guides, one stream moderator, and a queue that got longer whenever someone posted a screenshot of the rare Ashen Kite mount. The event began late, the match-making room reset twice, and one of the prize calculations had to be redone in public. None of those facts alone explains why the discussion kept going until almost midnight. The actual problem was that different people used “run,” “attempt,” “entry,” and “eligible clear” as if they meant the same thing.

This review uses the event ledger as the source of truth for entry counts and the final award pool. The chat is useful for understanding confusion and identifying reports, but people in chat often estimated totals before the staff spreadsheet was reconciled. When a chat estimate conflicts with the signed ledger, use the ledger. When the ledger itself has a corrected line, use the corrected line and do not add the superseded value a second time. Several screenshots were cropped and several people repeated amounts they had heard from someone else; that is why this document records both the tempting wrong number and the final arithmetic.

We have also separated four kinds of thing that were all being called “a problem”: a technical failure, a player-reported issue, a confirmed issue, and a remedy actually given. A player saying “I lost everything” is a report, not proof that every item disappeared. A moderator saying “we can probably compensate that” is not proof compensation was paid. The same care applies to the prize pool: a promised pool, an approved pool, and a distributed pool are not interchangeable.

Event schedule and rules as posted at registration

Registration opened at 17:00. The event was hosted in a private Emberhall lobby. Players could enter once for free, and could earn one additional entry by completing the warm-up puzzle. The puzzle did not award a prize; it only added an entry. There was no purchase option and no real-money fee. A “retry token” was a game item, not a paid ticket. It restored the player’s place in the queue after a disconnect but did not create an additional entry in the prize ledger.

The planned event block ran from 19:00 to 22:00. Staff could extend the event by up to 20 minutes to finish a match already in progress, but that extension did not permit starting a fresh match. The first announcement mistakenly said “we can keep going until 22:30”; it was corrected in the pinned message at 18:42. The correct rule was 22:20 for finishing, with no new match after 22:00. The distinction matters because people later counted a 22:08 start as a valid event match. It was not.

Prize rules were posted in the same registration panel. The event had a fixed community pool of 480 ember shards. The pool was divided among eligible clear teams in proportion to qualifying points, subject to a per-player cap of 90 shards. A team’s points were the total of its members’ verified objective scores, not its damage total. If a team had a disconnect before the final checkpoint, it could receive a partial score only when the replay showed the objective was completed before the disconnect. A lobby crash before checkpoint completion earned no objective points. Individual consolation awards could be granted from a separate volunteer reserve, but those did not come from the 480-shard pool and were not automatic.

The staff reserve was 60 shards, held separately from the pool. It could be used only for a logged, approved consolation award. The reserve was not a hidden extension of the main pool. Someone in chat later added 480 and 60 and announced a 540-shard award total, which was not what the approved distribution showed. The reserve stayed untouched for this event. The ledger has a zero in the reserve-issued column.

For purposes of this review, a “technical issue” means an observed failure in the event system, including a lobby reset, match-making fault, invalid checkpoint state, or delayed result sync. A “player report” means a player explicitly said they experienced a problem. A “confirmed loss” means staff could verify the loss from the replay or event record. These categories can overlap, but are not synonyms. One player may report a problem that turns out not to be a technical issue, while a technical issue may affect several players who never file a report.

Crew and communication setup

The volunteer crew had one event host, one lobby operator, two guides, and one moderator. The host maintained the spreadsheet and announced the prize calculations. The lobby operator could restart the event room but could not edit player scores. Guides helped players find the puzzle and explained which checkpoint was active. The moderator watched chat, removed spam, and forwarded complaints to the host. No one had a dedicated support ticket queue, which meant that a player could tell a guide, then repeat the same thing in general chat, and later tell the moderator. Those are multiple messages but not necessarily multiple independent incidents.

We planned a single public status message for any interruption longer than five minutes. In practice, there were three different message streams: the event channel, the general guild channel, and the stream chat. The status message in the event channel was the authoritative one. The stream overlay lagged behind it. People who were watching the stream sometimes saw the old countdown and assumed the event was still running. We should have put a visible “schedule corrected” marker on the overlay rather than merely editing the pinned post.

The staff agreed before the event that numerical statements should include their source. That agreement was followed inconsistently. A message saying “six people were dropped” might mean six entries, six unique players, or six disconnects. A message saying “we’re short 120” might mean the pool was short of the original estimate, not that 120 shards were missing from the ledger. This review keeps the raw figures close to the relevant explanation so that a later reader does not have to infer which meaning was intended.

Pre-event checks

At 16:40 the lobby operator created a test room with four volunteer accounts. The first test confirmed that the warm-up puzzle awarded one extra entry. A second test showed that leaving and rejoining did not award another entry. The third test showed that a reset lobby could preserve the room’s player list while losing the active checkpoint. This was recorded as a known risk, but the crew thought the room reset had been fixed in the previous patch. That assumption was too optimistic.

At 17:12 the host imported the registration list. It contained 24 unique player names and 27 total entry rows because three players had completed the puzzle. The first draft spreadsheet mistakenly showed 28 rows because one player’s puzzle completion had been copied twice. The duplicate was removed before the event started. The final registration count was therefore 24 people and 27 entries, not 28 people and not 28 valid entries. A screenshot of the draft count remained in the planning channel and was later mistaken for the final count.

At 18:10 the team reviewed the prize formula. The initial estimate was 480 shards. A volunteer asked whether the 60-shard reserve should be added to the advertised pool. The host replied that it should not: the reserve was for separately approved consolation awards only. The public panel continued to display 480. A line in the planning notes saying “480 + 60 possible” was a discussion of the reserve, not authorization to distribute 540 shards.

At 18:42 the event host corrected the end-time post. The original draft had said that matches could continue until 22:30. The correction stated: “No new match after 22:00. We can let a match already underway finish until 22:20.” Two people reacted to the old post before it was edited, and one quoted the old wording later. The corrected post was pinned. A reaction to a superseded draft does not change the rule.

Event timeline, as reconstructed from server logs and chat

18:55 — The host opened the event room. The room showed 27 entry slots, corresponding to the 27 valid entry rows. Three players had two entries each; all other registered players had one. This did not mean there were 27 people in the room. There were 24 unique registered players. The waiting room showed 22 connected accounts at the instant of opening because two had not yet joined.

19:03 — The first match began. The warm-up puzzle had been explained twice, but several players were still asking whether a retry token was an entry. A guide answered that it was only a queue-preservation item. No one bought anything, and no money changed hands.

19:14 — The lobby operator saw a brief increase in latency. The status indicator turned yellow for 38 seconds. Players reported a short freeze, but the replay shows no checkpoint failure during that interval. The team did not count this as a lost run. It is a technical performance warning, not a verified loss.

19:21 — The first full room reset. The lobby reset log recorded 12 connected accounts. Those 12 accounts were returned to the waiting room. Five players immediately wrote that they had been “kicked out,” but three of them were able to rejoin without losing a checkpoint or an entry. The remaining two were in the active match and had their checkpoint state cleared. The log shows one reset event affecting 12 connected accounts, not 12 confirmed losses.

19:24 — The lobby operator reopened the room. The event channel message said, “We are back; please check your entry count before queueing.” One player’s entry display was one lower than expected because the interface temporarily hid the puzzle bonus. The spreadsheet still showed the correct entry. The display refreshed four minutes later.

19:38 — A second room reset occurred, this time after the operator attempted to remove a stuck spectator. The reset log again showed 12 connected accounts, but the population was not the same as at 19:21. Staff initially added 12 and 12 and announced that 24 players had been affected. That was wrong: there was overlap, and the unit in the log was connected accounts, not unique players. After matching account IDs, 17 unique players had experienced at least one reset, while five were reset both times. Of the 17, only four had a verified interrupted objective, and two of those recovered the objective from replay evidence.

19:42 — The event host posted the first apology. It said the crew was “looking at four possible checkpoint losses.” That was a provisional count, not a promise of four awards. A player quoted the message as “four guaranteed compensation awards.” The host corrected this in the next message: the replay review was not finished, and any compensation would have to be approved against the separate reserve.

19:51 — The match-making room returned a stale team list. Two players were assigned to a team they had left. One of them was moved successfully before the match began; the other entered the wrong room and waited for six minutes. The second player reported the problem to a guide and later repeated it in general chat. The duplicate report was linked to the same event record.

20:02 — The first eligible clear was recorded. The team’s combined verified objective score was 72. A stream overlay displayed 78 because it included six points of damage that did not count under the posted formula. The host corrected the overlay. The main prize calculation used 72.

20:17 — The event room suffered a result-sync delay. The match had completed, but the results panel showed “pending” for 11 minutes. Three players reported that their scores had vanished. The database log shows that the scores were present and later synced. This was a technical issue and three player reports; it was not a confirmed score loss.

20:28 — The result panel refreshed. One player’s score appeared under the wrong display name due to a cosmetic alias mismatch. The underlying account ID and score were correct. The player said, “I thought my run was gone,” then confirmed that the points were visible. We retained the report as a report of apparent loss, not a confirmed loss.

20:41 — A third interruption occurred when a moderator changed the lobby description while the room was active. The room did not reset, but the queue froze for 94 seconds. Four players reported being unable to press “join.” No entries were lost, and no checkpoint was cleared. This was a technical issue affecting access, not a lost match.

20:58 — The host posted the next score summary. It listed 186 qualifying points across three eligible clears. A player replied, “That’s 196, you forgot the ten from the practice dummy.” The practice dummy score was not an objective score. The ledger remained at 186.

21:06 — A player asked whether an incomplete match could be started because there was “lots of time.” The host reminded everyone that no fresh match could begin after 22:00 and that the allowed extension applied only to a match already underway. This was a question, not a new match authorization.

21:19 — The fourth technical interruption occurred when a checkpoint marker failed to render for one team. The team continued based on the guide’s verbal callout. Replay review later showed that the checkpoint had registered correctly. Two players filed reports, but neither had lost points. The incident was classified as a visual fault, with no award adjustment.

21:33 — One match ended in a valid clear. Another team was still active. The host reminded the crew not to open an additional match after 22:00 even if the active team finished early. A planning note from the previous day, “we might squeeze in five,” referred to five additional warm-up attempts if the room was stable; it was not the final rule and was never approved.

21:47 — The event host estimated 302 qualifying points. The spreadsheet at that moment showed 298. Four points were in a pending replay review and were not included until verified. The difference was not a missing four-point award; it was a provisional score. The host’s public estimate was labeled “rough, not final.”

21:59 — The final fresh match began one minute before the cutoff. The event log records its start at 21:59:42. It was valid under the rule. No fresh match began after 22:00.

22:00 — The room stopped accepting new matches. A separate team was still in an already-started match. The 20-minute completion allowance applied. A spectator posted, “They’re still playing after the end time, so the event rule is being ignored.” That was an understandable but incorrect reading of the rule.

22:08 — A player who had disconnected earlier rejoined the lobby and saw an old “queue open” banner. They clicked it, but the request was rejected. The banner was stale; the log confirms no new match started. The player later said they had been “entered after close.” They had not been entered into a new match.

22:14 — The last active match completed. Its replay showed the final checkpoint was reached before the deadline. The team’s points counted. The host did not extend the event further.

22:19 — The prize spreadsheet exported 480 shards in the pool column and zero in reserve issued. The first export had a formatting error: one row displayed 90 as 9 because the final zero was clipped in a narrow column. The underlying value was 90. A corrected export was posted at 22:31.

22:27 — A player suggested paying everyone affected by a reset 10 shards each. The idea was not approved. The host replied that the reserve rules required an individual verified loss and an explicit approval. No reserve awards were recorded.

22:43 — Staff completed the first replay reconciliation. The qualifying score total was 314, including the four points that had been pending at 21:47. The temporary public estimate had been 302; the spreadsheet had shown 298 before the pending review. Neither was the final total.

23:02 — The host posted the final score and prize breakdown. The event channel was locked to new submissions at 23:30, but players could still add comments to the review document. Several later comments repeat earlier claims and are not additional incidents.

Issue register, reconciled after the event

Issue A: two lobby resets. These were separate technical events, affecting 12 connected accounts each time, with five accounts present in both logs. The count of unique accounts affected was 12 + 12 − 5 = 19 according to the raw connection logs. After excluding two staff test accounts that were not registered players, 17 registered players experienced at least one reset. This is the final unique-player count. It does not mean 17 players lost progress. Four had an objective state requiring review; two recovered their score from replay evidence, and two did not have a verified completed checkpoint.

Issue B: stale team assignment. Two players were displayed on an old team list. One was corrected before entering; one waited six minutes in the wrong room. The wrong-room wait was a genuine access problem, but it did not erase an entry or score. The player filed two messages about the same event. We counted one affected player, not two incidents.

Issue C: delayed result sync. Three players reported missing scores, but the records were present and appeared after the sync recovered. The reports were real; the asserted permanent loss was not confirmed. We cannot call these zero issues simply because the eventual result was correct: the delay did happen and caused confusion. We also cannot call them three confirmed score losses.

Issue D: queue freeze after a description edit. The queue was unavailable for 94 seconds. Four players reported the problem. No one lost an entry, score, or checkpoint. The moderator’s log includes two duplicate reports from people who posted once in the event channel and once in general chat. The final count is four unique reporters.

Issue E: checkpoint marker display. One team saw no marker, but the replay and server state show that the checkpoint registered. Two reports were filed. The visual problem is confirmed; a lost checkpoint is not.

Issue F: stale queue banner after close. One player clicked the old banner at 22:08. The request was rejected, and the match log shows no start after the cutoff. This was misleading interface text, but not an unauthorized match.

The team initially circulated an “affected” total of 17 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 29. That addition is not a count of unique people, because categories overlap and some lines count reports while others count players. The final review does not publish a single total called “affected.” Instead, it reports the specific units above. The figure 29 is retained here only because it appeared in chat and looked precise enough to be repeated. It is not an approved event statistic.

Replay reconciliation and award arithmetic

The final ledger contains four eligible clears. Their verified objective scores were 72, 84, 76, and 82. The total is 72 + 84 + 76 + 82 = 314. The 78 shown on the stream for the first clear included six non-qualifying damage points, so it is not substituted for 72. The 10-point practice dummy suggestion is not an objective score. The four pending points from the 21:47 review were added to the relevant verified team score, which is why the final 314 differs from the earlier 298 spreadsheet and the rough 302 public estimate.

The distribution formula allocated the 480-shard pool according to each eligible clear’s share of the 314 total, then applied the 90-shard per-player cap. The team awards, after rounding according to the posted rule, were 110, 128, 116, and 126 before the cap calculation among individual members. Those team-level figures sum to 480. The per-player cap changed how the team totals were split among members, not the total pool. The first draft of the breakdown showed 480 + 60 = 540 as if the reserve were paid. That was a spreadsheet formula error caused by selecting the reserve column. The corrected distribution is 480 from the pool and 0 from reserve.

The award table has a row for each eligible player. The count is not the same as the number of entry rows: an extra puzzle entry affected eligibility weighting but did not create a second person. There were 24 registered players, 27 valid entries, four eligible clears, and 480 pool shards distributed. Those are four different quantities. Do not add them together or describe them all as “participants.”

The reserve review resulted in no approved consolation awards. The host reviewed the two unresolved checkpoint cases. Neither replay showed completion of the final objective before disconnect. The posted rule required a verified objective completion for partial credit. Because that evidence was absent, neither case qualified for an award. This decision does not mean the players lied about disconnecting. The disconnects occurred; the specific score condition for compensation was not met.

Copied chat excerpts, arranged by subject rather than exact time

Event channel, 19:23 — “I’m back, but my second entry is gone.”
Guide — “The display is hiding puzzle entries right now. Ledger says two; please refresh after the room comes back.”
Player — “Okay, it refreshed. It’s there.”
Moderator note — Same player later posted “lost entry” in general chat. Linked as one temporary display issue, not a permanent entry loss.

General channel, 19:40 — “Twelve people got reset, then twelve more, so twenty-four people are down.”
Host — “The second log can include people from the first one. We’re matching accounts before we publish a unique count.”
Another player — “I was there twice; count me twice if you want the interruption count.”
Host — “We will list reset events and unique accounts separately.”

Stream chat, 20:05 — “The score says 78. Why is the spreadsheet 72?”
Guide — “Six damage points are visible on the overlay but do not count toward objective score.”
Viewer — “So the team got robbed of six?”
Host — “No. The event formula never included damage. The 72 is the qualifying score.”

Event channel, 20:19 — “My score disappeared, did the game eat it?”
Moderator — “The panel is pending. We can see your record server-side.”
Player — “I see it now. False alarm, but that wait was awful.”
Moderator note — The player’s report of a missing score is retained; “permanent deletion” is not confirmed.

General channel, 20:44 — “Can’t click join. This is a disaster, amazing service.”
Guide — “Queue is frozen after the description change. We’re fixing it.”
Player — “I meant the amazing part sarcastically, obviously. I missed the queue window.”
Moderator note — Four distinct accounts reported the freeze. One used sarcasm; the intended meaning was dissatisfaction, not praise.

Event channel, 21:00 — “I calculate 196, not 186. Dummy gives ten.”
Host — “The dummy is for practice. The posted score formula counts objectives only. Current verified total remains 186.”
Player — “Got it; I mixed the counters.”

Event channel, 21:48 — “We’re short four points, so somebody’s score vanished.”
Host — “Not established. Four points are pending replay verification; the visible sheet is 298 and the rough estimate is 302. Neither is final.”
Later correction — The pending four points were verified and included; final total 314 across all eligible clears.

General channel, 22:04 — “They’re playing past ten. New match after close!”
Moderator — “That match began at 21:59:42. It was already in progress. No new match is accepted after 22:00; active matches may finish by 22:20.”
Player — “Ah, I saw the end time and assumed stop means stop immediately.”

Event channel, 22:29 — “Where did the extra 60 go? It said 540 earlier.”
Host — “The 60 is a separate reserve and was not approved for this event. Main pool is 480; reserve issued is zero.”
Another player — “But the spreadsheet has 90, 9, and maybe 60 in different places.”
Host — “The 9 is a clipped display of 90. The reserve column is not a payment. Corrected export is coming.”

Staff room, 23:05 — “Do we count the person who said they lost everything?”
Host — “Count what the logs support. They lost the active checkpoint, not their inventory or every entry. Their phrasing is understandable, but we should not reproduce it as a literal inventory loss.”
Guide — “And the two checkpoint cases?”
Host — “Disconnect confirmed; completed objective before disconnect not confirmed. No partial award under the exact rule.”

Follow-up recommendations

First, keep the event clock, entry count, and prize ledger in separate dashboard panels. The old overlay conflated entry rows and unique players, and the score overlay mixed damage with objectives. A dashboard that shows all the numbers without labels is not transparent; it is a recipe for confidently wrong arithmetic. Each display should say what is being counted, when it was last updated, and whether the value is final, pending, or a draft.

Second, make room resets idempotent where possible. If a reset happens, players should receive one clear status message stating whether their entry, checkpoint, and score are preserved. “You are back” is not enough when the display temporarily hides a bonus entry. The message should avoid implying that every connected account lost progress merely because the room reset affected the whole lobby.

Third, create a single reporting form with a field for the player’s account name, approximate time, match identifier, and what they believe happened. The form should warn that posting the same event in several channels does not create several separate losses. That is not intended to discourage reporting; it makes reconciliation faster and prevents the public count from multiplying duplicates.

Fourth, the prize formula should be explained with a small worked example. We can say: “If the pool is 480 and the verified objective total is 314, team weighting uses the team’s objective score divided by 314; damage and practice points do not count.” The real distribution also involves rounding and a per-player cap, so an example should explicitly say that team weighting and the final individual split are separate steps. Do not show the reserve beside the pool without labeling it “not included.”

Fifth, if staff approve consolation awards, the approval should be entered in the ledger at the same time as the award. A chat promise, a suggestion, or a “probably” should never appear in a total as if the item has been paid. The reserve line should show starting reserve, approved awards, and remaining reserve. For this event those values were 60, 0, and 60. That is more informative than an isolated “60 available” that someone may add to the main pool.

Sixth, the schedule should be written as an action rule, not just an end time. The revised wording should state: “No new match starts at or after 22:00. A match whose server-recorded start is before 22:00 may finish, but not later than 22:20.” This will reduce disagreements based on the ambiguous phrase “event ends at ten.” The event log’s 21:59:42 start is before 22:00, so that match was valid. The 22:08 click was rejected and did not create a match.

Seventh, the stream overlay needs a visible revision time. Editing a pinned post does not update screenshots, cached panels, or a viewer’s recollection. If the rule changes before registration closes, the overlay should say “updated 18:42” and provide the exact corrected wording. A stale banner should disappear automatically when the queue closes, rather than remaining clickable and producing a rejection message.

Eighth, reports of sarcasm should be interpreted in context. “Amazing service” accompanied by a missed queue and an explanation that the praise was sarcastic is a complaint. A moderation summary that labels it praise because it contains the word “amazing” would misrepresent the player. Likewise, “lost everything” should not be copied as a verified fact when the logs establish only a lost checkpoint. The player’s frustration is real even when the literal scope of the phrase is broader than the evidence.

Ninth, distinguish the existence of a technical issue from whether the remedy condition was met. The checkpoint marker failure was a technical issue even though the server registered the checkpoint. The two disconnects were real, but the policy’s partial-credit condition required completed objective evidence, which the replay did not provide. We should explain both parts rather than saying simply “no issue” or “no compensation.”

Tenth, preserve the raw event identifiers in internal notes while keeping public summaries privacy-conscious. The review currently uses account IDs only in the moderator’s private reconciliation file. Publicly, it reports counts and categories. It does not need to publish every player’s name or reproduce every frustrated message. The names in the internal export are not necessary to understand the arithmetic and should not be copied into the public version.

Appendix A: count definitions used in the final review

Unique registered player: one account on the approved registration list, counted once regardless of additional puzzle entries. Final count: 24.

Valid entry: an approved registration entry or one earned puzzle bonus, counted as an entry row. Final count: 27. A player with a bonus can therefore be one unique player and two valid entries.

Connected account in a reset log: an account connected at the instant that one particular reset occurred. The same account may appear in more than one reset log. The two logs showed 12 and 12 connected accounts, with five overlapping accounts; after excluding two staff test accounts, 17 registered players had at least one reset exposure.

Reported problem: a player explicitly reported an issue. Repeated posts about the same event by one player are linked when the record allows it. A report remains a report even if the feared loss is not confirmed.

Confirmed technical issue: a fault shown in a server or moderator record. It may or may not produce a confirmed loss. The queue freeze and visual marker failure count as technical issues; a permanent score deletion does not appear in the records.

Eligible clear: a completed event match with the required objective evidence and a valid start time. A match continuing after 22:00 is not automatically invalid if it started before 22:00 and finished by 22:20.

Qualifying points: verified objective score. Damage points, practice dummy points, and unverified estimates do not count.

Main pool: the 480 shards approved for distribution under the posted formula. It excludes the 60-shard reserve.

Reserve: the separate 60-shard amount that can fund individually approved consolation awards. For this event, approved reserve awards were zero.

Appendix B: arithmetic checks and tempting mistakes

Registration: 24 unique players, plus three puzzle bonus entries, gives 27 valid entry rows. It does not give 27 players. The draft 28 was caused by a duplicated puzzle row and was corrected before the start.

Reset exposure: 12 accounts in the first reset log plus 12 in the second log equals 24 log appearances. Five accounts appeared in both logs, so 24 minus 5 equals 19 unique accounts across those raw logs. Two were staff test accounts, so 19 minus 2 equals 17 registered players. The number 24 is not the unique-player answer; it is the unadjusted sum of appearances.

Final qualifying score: 72 + 84 + 76 + 82 = 314. Replacing 72 with the overlay’s 78 would add six non-qualifying damage points and produce 320, which is not the event total. Adding the practice dummy’s 10 would likewise be wrong. The early 298 spreadsheet and rough 302 estimate are not final; the pending four points were verified, and the complete set of clears totals 314.

Pool: team-level awards of 110 + 128 + 116 + 126 = 480. The separate 60 reserve was not issued, so the event’s distributed total is 480, not 540. The per-player cap affects splits inside team awards and does not add to or subtract from the total pool.

Queue freeze: 94 seconds is 1 minute and 34 seconds. The problem affected access, but no entry or checkpoint was lost. Four unique reporters are recorded, not six messages.

Schedule: 21:59:42 is 18 seconds before 22:00, so that match began before the cutoff. The active match finished at 22:14, six minutes before the 22:20 latest completion time. The 22:08 attempted click was rejected; it was not a match start.

Appendix C: loose notes preserved for context

“Maybe we should just call everybody affected twenty-nine and move on.” Rejected. The arithmetic mixes overlapping people, repeated reports, and distinct categories. A precise-looking sum is not meaningful if the addends have different units.

“Could we award ten to each of the twelve people in the first reset?” Not approved. The twelve are connected accounts, not all confirmed losses, and the policy requires individual verified loss plus approval. No reserve payment was made.

“Perhaps the 60 reserve was supposed to be part of the advertised pool because both numbers were in the panel.” No. The posted description says the 60 is separate and requires individual approval. The main pool remains 480.

“Would it help if we call the score 320 so the six damage points are recognized?” No. Recognition is not the same as qualifying points. The formula explicitly uses objectives, and the overlay was corrected for that reason.

“Could we count the old queue click as a new entry because the player pressed the button?” No. The server rejected the request and recorded no match start. A click is not an accepted entry.

“Do we have to count the player’s second post as another report?” The public log can mention that the player posted twice, but the unique-reporter count is one. Message count and reporter count answer different questions.

“Maybe the last team should be disqualified because they finished after 22:00.” The rule allows an already-started match to finish until 22:20. It began at 21:59:42 and finished at 22:14; it qualified.

“Could a disconnect itself satisfy the partial-credit rule?” No. The text requires replay evidence that the objective was completed before the disconnect. The disconnect is evidence of a connection problem, not evidence of objective completion.

“Maybe that one missing display entry proves the registration total was 26.” No. The ledger had 27 valid entries, and the display later refreshed. A temporary display omission does not change the registered count.

“Could we describe the visual marker failure as a lost checkpoint because the players could not see it?” No. The server state and replay show the checkpoint registered. The visual failure is still a real technical issue, but it is not a confirmed lost checkpoint.

Appendix D: next event checklist, still chatty because we are volunteers

Before opening: verify that the registration import has the same number of unique account IDs as the approved list; separately verify entry rows. Check that puzzle bonuses cannot duplicate on refresh. Test the retry token and confirm that it does not create an extra entry. Confirm that the main pool and reserve appear in separate labeled fields. Capture the final schedule wording and publish it to the event channel and the stream overlay together.

[{"state":"Tidewater Analytics / Meridian Freight — quarterly exception review packet
Prepared with the greatest respect for everyone’s time, and with sincere thanks to the dispatch, warehouse, customer-care, billing, and compliance colleagues who supplied notes. This packet consolidates one shipment review and its surrounding operational records. The sections preserve the distinction between a plan, a scan, a customer statement, a carrier statement, and a confirmed event. References to amounts are in U.S. dollars unless explicitly stated otherwise. Dates use month-day-year. The purpose is to help the operations manager determine which service failures are supported, whether the service-credit calculation is correct, and what the customer actually requested. No entry in this packet changes the stated contractual rules.

Contents
A. Manager status update
B. Shipment profile and booked services
C. Customer chat transcript
D. Warehouse and dispatch notes
E. Meridian Freight event feed
F. Service-credit policy excerpt
G. Rate and charge reconciliation
H. Internal coordination thread
I. Exception taxonomy and definitions
J. Evidence review worksheet
K. Appendix: nearby shipments and lookalike references
L. Appendix: route, facility, and scan glossary
M. Appendix: audit trail and closeout checklist

A. Manager status update
To: Operations manager, Tidewater Analytics
From: Yara Mensah, shipment exception coordinator
Subject: Respectfully submitted: Granite Outfitters order GO-48172, review of the delayed cartons and related service adjustment

Good afternoon. I am grateful for the opportunity to provide a careful update on Granite Outfitters order GO-48172, tendered to Meridian Freight under waybill MF-730184. The shipment consisted of eight cartons of display hardware and six cartons of replacement fittings, for fourteen cartons in total. The merchandise was collected from Granite Outfitters’ North Quay warehouse and was addressed to its Alder Point retail receiving location. The booked service was Priority Road, with a scheduled delivery date of 06-14-2026. The accepted appointment window was 09:00–12:00 local time on that date. The applicable service-credit rule is stated in section F below.

The shipment was not delivered in the booked appointment window. The carrier’s proof-of-delivery event records arrival at the recipient’s gate at 15:26 on 06-15-2026, and the receiving clerk’s signed note records completion of unloading at 15:41. The carrier’s initial customer-facing notice, which said “arriving today,” was sent on 06-14, but a notice is not a delivery scan. The dispatch plan also displayed “on route” at 10:03 on 06-14; that status is likewise not proof of arrival. The confirmed gate arrival was the following day.

The recipient additionally reports that two cartons were wet and one carton had a crushed corner. The photographs and receiving form support the wet-carton report for carton labels 6 and 11. The crushed-corner report concerns carton 9. The delivery receipt says the contents of carton 9 were inspected and found intact; the packaging damage is still recorded as a damage exception, but the customer did not state that the product itself was unusable. The three affected carton numbers are separate identifiers; they do not mean that three cartons were wet. The customer describes two wet cartons and one carton with crushed outer packaging.

For billing review, the booked transportation line is $486.00, the fuel line is $54.00, and the appointment line is $30.00. Those booked service lines total $570.00. The invoice additionally shows an accessorial charge of $18.00 for a second delivery attempt. The dispatch record does not support a second attempt: it shows one unsuccessful arrival attempt on 06-14 and the successful attempt on 06-15, but the booked arrangement and policy classify the first date’s carrier-caused missed appointment as one service failure, not a customer-requested redelivery. A separate $12.00 residential surcharge belongs to another reference and should not be included in GO-48172’s invoice base. The adjusted eligible base is therefore the three booked service lines, $570.00, excluding the unsupported $18.00 and the unrelated $12.00.

The policy provides a credit of 20% of eligible booked service charges when confirmed delivery is more than one calendar day after the scheduled date, provided the delay was carrier-controlled and no listed exclusion applies. One calendar day after the scheduled date is 06-15; a delivery on 06-15 is not “more than one calendar day after” 06-14. However, section F also states that a confirmed missed appointment window qualifies for a 10% credit regardless of whether the late-delivery threshold is met, unless the recipient requested a change or the shipment was held for a documented safety closure. Neither exception is documented here. The appropriate credit is therefore 10% of $570.00, or $57.00, for the missed appointment window. The 20% threshold is not met on the date arithmetic. The invoice adjustment should not be $114.00, which would be 20% of the eligible base.

Please note the distinction between “delivery one day after schedule” and “more than one calendar day after schedule.” The former describes 06-15 relative to 06-14; the latter would require a delivery date of 06-16 or later under the policy wording. No weekend or business-day conversion is specified in this section. The eligible-base calculation is also distinct from the carrier’s broader billed amount of $600.00, which includes the two disputed or unrelated items described above. The recommended adjustment is $57.00, not 10% of $600.00 ($60.00), and not 20% of $570.00 ($114.00).

Current disposition, with thanks to the teams involved: lateness outside the appointment window is confirmed; two wet cartons are supported; one carton has reported outer-package damage; product failure is not established; a 10% appointment credit is supported; a 20% late-delivery credit is not supported; the second-attempt fee is disputed; and the $12.00 residential surcharge is not attributable to this shipment. The customer asked for reimbursement of the delivery charge and replacement of the wet display sleeves, but did not ask for a refund of the merchandise order. Customer-care should kindly respond to those specific requests rather than infer a broader demand.

B. Shipment profile and booked services
Order reference: GO-48172
Customer: Granite Outfitters
Origin: North Quay warehouse, Tidewater Analytics consolidation point
Destination: Alder Point receiving dock, Granite Outfitters
Carrier: Meridian Freight
Waybill: MF-730184
Booked service: Priority Road, appointment delivery
Scheduled service date: 06-14-2026
Appointment window: 09:00–12:00 local time
Carton count at tender: 14
Declared goods value: $8,400.00
Booked transportation charge: $486.00
Fuel charge: $54.00
Appointment charge: $30.00
Booked service subtotal: $570.00
Invoice total as issued: $600.00, before any credit
Items additionally appearing on invoice: $18.00 second-attempt accessorial; $12.00 residential surcharge

The declared value is retained for shipment identification only. It is not the basis for the service credit. The contract excerpt in section F bases service credits on eligible booked service charges. Likewise, the $8,400.00 merchandise value does not establish the amount of a merchandise refund. The warehouse manifest lists eight cartons of display hardware and six cartons of replacement fittings. The labels are sequential, 1 through 14. The recipient’s report identifies wet cartons 6 and 11 and outer-package damage on carton 9. The dispatch record does not show missing cartons. The signed receipt lists all fourteen carton labels as received.

The appointment was requested by Granite Outfitters when the booking was made on 06-08-2026. On 06-12, a carrier planning note proposed a possible 06-15 delivery because of route balancing. Tidewater Analytics did not approve that proposal, and Granite Outfitters did not accept it. The booking remained 06-14, 09:00–12:00. On the morning of 06-14, Meridian Freight sent a generic “arriving today” notice. The notice did not identify a new appointment window and did not ask the recipient to choose another date. Granite Outfitters’ receiving desk was staffed during the full booked window.

A carrier route note at 08:52 on 06-14 says, “Truck held while liftgate inspection cleared; driver to resume once release received.” A later note at 09:17 says the inspection was completed. The event feed records the vehicle in the destination service area at 10:03 but records no gate attempt that day. The supervisor’s note says the driver was directed to complete other stops first. No safety closure, access restriction, recipient-requested change, or weather emergency is recorded for Alder Point. The “possible 06-15” planning note is not a mutually accepted change and does not supersede the booked date.

The next day’s dispatch record has one arrival event, followed by successful delivery. It has no separate unsuccessful stop, no request to retry after a recipient absence, and no additional handling instruction. The fee description “second delivery attempt” therefore appears inconsistent with the operational record. Billing is asked to verify whether the $18.00 line was imported from a different shipment or created from a generic exception code. Please do not treat it as an eligible booked charge in the credit base unless an approved billing record establishes otherwise.

C. Customer chat transcript
Chat reference: CC-99251, opened 06-15-2026 at 16:18 local time
Participants: Nadia Novak, Granite Outfitters receiving coordinator; Callum Nakamura, Tidewater Analytics customer-care associate

16:18: Nadia: Good afternoon, and thank you for taking the time to look into this. We received the fourteen cartons today. The appointment was for yesterday morning, so our team waited at the dock yesterday and did not receive the truck in the window.

16:20: Callum: I am very sorry for the inconvenience, and I appreciate the detailed information. Could you kindly confirm whether all cartons arrived and whether you are reporting damage to the cartons or their contents?

16:22: Nadia: All fourteen arrived. Cartons 6 and 11 were wet on the outside and the display sleeves inside those two cartons are damp. Carton 9 has one crushed corner, but our clerk checked the fittings inside and they appear intact. We are not reporting missing pieces.

16:24: Callum: Thank you. I will record two wet cartons and one carton with outer packaging damage, with no confirmed missing pieces. May I also confirm what resolution you are requesting?

16:26: Nadia: Please reimburse the delivery charge and send replacement sleeves for the wet ones. I am not asking you to refund the $8,400 goods order. The damp sleeves cannot go on display, but the other merchandise is usable.

16:28: Callum: I understand, and I am grateful for the clarification. Our screen currently shows a $600 invoice total. The underlying booking appears to list $486 transportation, $54 fuel, and $30 appointment service, with an $18 second-attempt fee and a $12 residential surcharge. I will ask billing to check those lines before I quote an adjustment.

16:30: Nadia: That would be appreciated. There was no second attempt that we know of. We waited yesterday, then the truck came today. We are a commercial retail dock, not a residence. The schedule email still said the 14th.

16:32: Callum: Thank you for confirming. I see a planning note suggesting the 15th, but it was not accepted as a changed appointment. I will retain the original appointment date for review. For transparency, the policy may provide a 10% appointment credit or a 20% delay credit, depending on the applicable condition.

16:35: Nadia: I am grateful that you are checking. The 20% figure would be welcome, but I understand that the rule may not allow it. We are asking for the delivery charge back, not for the goods order to be refunded. Also, please do not assume our sentence about the 20% means we have proved that threshold.

16:37: Callum: That is very helpful. I will separate your requested remedy from the policy calculation. I will also make sure the replacement-sleeve request is recorded independently from the transport credit. Thank you for your patience.

16:40: Nadia: One more small clarification: the wet report is for exactly two cartons, labels 6 and 11. The third carton, number 9, has crushed outer packaging only. Please do not call all three wet, and please do not say the contents of carton 9 were damaged.

16:42: Callum: Understood. I have written “two wet cartons; one carton with crushed outer packaging; contents of carton 9 appear intact.” I am sorry again for the missed window and grateful for the careful correction.

Transcript handling note: Chat statements are attributed to their speakers. The customer’s mention that 20% “would be welcome” is not evidence that the policy’s threshold is satisfied. The associate’s description of possible policy outcomes is not a customer request. Nadia’s express statement that she is not asking for a refund of the goods order controls the scope of her monetary request. Her request to reimburse the delivery charge and replace damp sleeves is affirmative. No request to refund the full merchandise order appears in the transcript.

D. Warehouse and dispatch notes

06-08-2026, 13:22 — Rate confirmation generated. Transportation $486.00; fuel $54.00; appointment $30.00. The confirmed amount is $570.00. The commodity declared value field shows $8,400.00 and is marked “insurance/reference only; excluded from service-credit base.”

06-13-2026, 09:14 — Carrier system generated route plan for 06-14. Planned service area arrival 09:45. This is a forecast, not an arrival scan.

06-14-2026, 08:52 — Driver message: “Liftgate inspection hold at yard; release pending.”

06-14-2026, 09:17 — Yard controller: inspection cleared; unit released. The record does not show a fault requiring a safety shutdown at the destination.

06-14-2026, 10:03 — Vehicle geofence event, Alder Point service area. No gate scan, proof of attempt, recipient call, or refusal is attached. The supervisor later noted that the driver was assigned to complete two earlier stops before returning to the route. The route did not return to Alder Point that day.

06-14-2026, 10:14 — Automated notification: “Your delivery is arriving today.” This text was sent by a broad route-status rule. It is not a delivery completion notice and does not amend the appointment window.

E. Meridian Freight event feed

F. Service-credit policy excerpt, revision 4.2, effective 01-01-2026
The following language was copied from the policy register and checked against the version attached to the booking. It applies to Priority Road appointment shipments tendered in the service area shown on the waybill.

F.1 Eligible booked service charges. A service credit is calculated only on the transportation, fuel, and appointment charges confirmed at booking. Taxes, declared goods value, insurance premiums, storage, special handling, accessorial charges, and charges not confirmed at booking are excluded. Charges linked to another waybill are never included. A disputed charge remains outside the eligible base unless billing substantiates that it was both correctly assessed and part of the original confirmed booking. For this shipment, the confirmation lists $486.00 transportation, $54.00 fuel, and $30.00 appointment charge.

F.2 Appointment-window credit. If a carrier-controlled failure causes the shipment not to arrive at the consignee gate during the booked appointment window, a credit of 10% of eligible booked service charges may be approved. The proof-of-delivery time is not substituted for the gate-arrival requirement. The window begins and ends at the times accepted at booking. A generic “arriving today” message, route plan, geofence entry, or dispatch intention does not itself constitute gate arrival.

F.3 Delay credit. If confirmed delivery occurs more than one calendar day after the scheduled delivery date, a credit of 20% of eligible booked service charges may be approved instead of, and not in addition to, the appointment-window credit. “More than one calendar day after” means the delivery date must be at least two calendar dates later than the scheduled date. For example, a scheduled date of 06-14 followed by delivery on 06-15 is one calendar day later and does not meet this threshold; delivery on 06-16 is two calendar days later and does. The calculation uses calendar dates, not elapsed business days. A shipment that qualifies for the 20% delay credit receives only that one credit, not both credits.

F.4 Exceptions. Neither credit is available if the consignee requested or expressly accepted a new delivery date before the original window, if a documented safety closure prevented service, or if an accurate address was not supplied. A carrier’s unaccepted proposal to change a date is not consignee acceptance. A general route-balancing note is not a safety closure. The exception must be documented in the shipment record and tied to the applicable waybill. A customer’s later willingness to discuss another date does not retroactively amend the original appointment.

F.5 Damage and missing goods. Service credits under F.2 and F.3 concern service performance only. They do not establish a merchandise refund. Damage claims are reviewed separately. A wet outer carton may support a contents inspection, but the number of wet cartons must be based on recorded carton-level evidence. Packaging damage does not, without further evidence, establish damage to contents. Missing goods require a documented count discrepancy or other affirmative evidence; a late delivery is not evidence of missing goods.

F.6 Customer requests and remedy scope. The agent must record the remedy the customer actually requests. A request for a delivery-charge reimbursement is not a request for refund of the merchandise value. A request for replacement goods is separate from a service credit. A customer’s reference to a possible percentage or policy result does not establish eligibility for that result. Where a customer explicitly excludes a remedy, the agent must not record it as requested.

F.7 Arithmetic and rounding. Apply the selected percentage to the eligible booked service-charge subtotal. Round the final credit to the nearest cent. Do not apply the percentage to declared value, invoice total containing noneligible lines, or a subtotal that includes another waybill. For the confirmed subtotal of $570.00, a 10% credit is $57.00 and a 20% credit is $114.00.

F.8 Documentation. The review record should list the scheduled date, confirmed gate-arrival date and time, booked appointment window, eligible charge lines, applicable exception check, and customer’s requested remedy. If the source materials conflict, prefer an accepted booking and signed operational events over a projected route plan or generic automated notice. A dispatch record may explain cause but cannot create consignee acceptance that is not recorded.

G. Rate and charge reconciliation
Booking confirmation, record BC-48172-06, dated 06-08-2026:
Transportation: $486.00
Fuel: $54.00
Appointment: $30.00
Confirmed service subtotal: $486.00 + $54.00 + $30.00 = $570.00
Declared goods value: $8,400.00, excluded from service-credit calculation

Invoice export, record INV-226-48172:
Transportation: $486.00
Fuel: $54.00
Appointment: $30.00
Second-attempt accessorial: $18.00
Residential surcharge: $12.00
Displayed export total: $486.00 + $54.00 + $30.00 + $18.00 + $12.00 = $600.00

Invoice-line provenance check:
The $18.00 “second-attempt” item was added after delivery in a batch coded EX-2. The batch has no attached driver scan, recipient request, or signed redelivery instruction. Meridian’s event search lists no second failed gate attempt. The charge was not in the confirmed booking. Under F.1, it is excluded from the eligible base unless substantiated as correctly assessed and part of the original confirmed booking; neither condition is documented.

The $12.00 residential line is associated with MF-730196. That waybill is not GO-48172 and does not share the destination. The $12.00 line must be removed from the reconciliation for this shipment. Even if it had appeared on the same invoice export, it would remain excluded because it is tied to another waybill and was not confirmed at booking.

Potential calculations, shown so that reviewers can identify common errors:
10% × $570.00 = $57.00 — appointment-window credit on the eligible base.
20% × $570.00 = $114.00 — arithmetic is correct, but the policy trigger is not met on a 06-15 delivery after a 06-14 scheduled date.
10% × $600.00 = $60.00 — incorrect base because it includes $18.00 and $12.00 ineligible lines.
20% × $600.00 = $120.00 — both the base and the trigger are incorrect.
10% × $8,400.00 = $840.00 — incorrect because declared goods value is not the credit base.
$486.00 + $54.00 = $540.00 — incomplete because it omits the $30.00 booked appointment charge.
$486.00 + $54.00 + $30.00 + $18.00 = $588.00 — not eligible because the extra $18.00 was neither booked nor substantiated.

The arithmetic verification is deliberately explicit: 486 + 54 = 540; 540 + 30 = 570; 10% of 570 = 57. The elapsed date distinction is likewise explicit: 06-15 minus 06-14 by calendar date is one day, not two. Therefore F.3’s “at least two calendar dates later” condition would first be met on 06-16. The fact that delivery occurred after the 09:00–12:00 window on the 14th and on the next calendar date supports the separate F.2 condition; it does not transform the date gap into two days.

I. Exception taxonomy and definitions
For this packet, a service failure means a confirmed failure to perform an accepted service commitment. A proposed appointment change is not an accepted change unless the consignee or authorized booking party confirms it in a recorded communication. A route forecast is not a contractual commitment by itself, but the booking record remains controlling when no approved amendment is present.

A geofence means that a vehicle entered a geographic area around a destination. It does not show that the vehicle reached the gate, that a recipient was available, or that a delivery attempt was made. A gate-arrival scan records arrival at the consignee’s gate. A proof of delivery records transfer and acknowledgement of goods. In this case, the geofence on 06-14 and the gate arrival on 06-15 are separate events.

A wet-carton exception describes moisture affecting an identified carton. The carton count is determined by distinct carton labels with evidence, not by the number of photographs or the number of damage categories. Here, the supported wet-carton count is two: cartons 6 and 11. Carton 9 is a separate packaging-compression report. A carton can be counted once in more than one category only if evidence supports each category; the facts here do not support calling carton 9 wet or its contents damaged.

A missing-goods exception requires a discrepancy between the tendered or expected quantity and the received quantity, supported by records. All fourteen cartons were signed for, so the record does not establish missing cartons. A request for replacement sleeves is a requested remedy for the damp sleeve contents, not a report that the shipment had fewer than fourteen cartons.

A service-credit base is not necessarily the same as an invoice total. The policy definition controls. Items added after booking, items from another waybill, declared value, and unsubstantiated accessorials are excluded. Arithmetic must be performed only after identifying the eligible lines. Applying the right percentage to the wrong subtotal is still an incorrect calculation.

A policy trigger and a percentage are separate questions. The 20% percentage is not selected merely because the delivery was late or because the customer mentioned it. The threshold is delivery at least two calendar dates later than the scheduled date. A 06-14 scheduled date and a 06-15 delivery date differ by one calendar day. The confirmed missed appointment window independently satisfies the 10% rule, absent an exception.

J. Evidence review worksheet
Question 1 review prompts — service failures and physical exceptions
Accepted appointment: 06-14-2026, 09:00–12:00.
Recipient acceptance of change: none; proposed 06-15 date was expressly declined.
Confirmed gate arrival: 06-15-2026 at 15:26.
Delivery completed: 06-15-2026 at 15:41.
Missed appointment window: yes; no gate arrival by 12:00 on 06-14.
Wet cartons supported: labels 6 and 11, two cartons.
Packaging compression: label 9, one carton.
Contents damaged in carton 9: not established; receiving note says fittings intact.
Missing cartons: none established; fourteen tendered and fourteen received.

The supporting evidence is distributed among the booking, event feed, signed receipt, photographs, and chat. A reviewer should not use “arriving today” as proof of timely arrival. Nor should a reviewer count all three cited carton labels as wet. The customer carefully distinguishes the two moisture cases from the compression case. The warehouse record confirms no origin moisture report, while the destination image set and signed note support the later wet-carton report. The causal source of the moisture is not finally determined by this service review, but the existence of the customer-reported and documented condition is supported.

Question 2 review prompts — credit category and amount
Booked service-charge lines: $486 + $54 + $30 = $570.
Excluded invoice lines: $18 unsupported second-attempt line; $12 other-waybill residential line.
Schedule-to-delivery date gap: 06-14 to 06-15 = one calendar day.
Appointment threshold: failed arrival within accepted 09:00–12:00 window.
Delay threshold: more than one calendar day, meaning at least two dates later; not met.
Applicable service credit: 10% × $570 = $57.
No double credit: policy says delay and appointment credits do not stack.

One reviewer initially wrote that a next-day delivery was “two days late” because the appointment was on the previous morning and delivery happened in the afternoon the next day. That statement confuses hours elapsed with calendar-date difference and with the policy’s defined threshold. The policy says a scheduled 06-14 shipment delivered 06-15 is one date later. The shipment did miss the exact booked time window, so the 10% rule applies even though the 20% rule does not. A date of 06-16 would be needed for the latter trigger, absent another policy change.

Question 3 review prompts — customer intent and remedy scope
Affirmative monetary request: reimbursement of the delivery charge.
Affirmative non-monetary request: replacement sleeves for the wet cartons.
Expressly excluded request: refund of the $8,400 goods order.
Mention of 20%: customer says it would be welcome but acknowledges eligibility is not proved.
No request for: refund of all merchandise, compensation equal to declared value, or a refund of every invoice line.

The customer’s exact scope matters. An associate may choose to explain a $57 service credit, but that does not alter what Nadia asked for. “Delivery charge” is not interchangeable with “goods order.” The customer expressly says she is not asking for the latter. The replacement-sleeve request is distinct from the monetary request. An accurate response should address both and should not turn an expressed exclusion into an affirmative refund request.

K. Appendix: nearby shipments and lookalike references

MF-730176 — recipient at Juniper Vale warehouse; one pallet; scheduled 06-13; delivered 06-13; no appointment failure. Invoice includes a $9.00 liftgate line. The destination is not Alder Point and no carton labels overlap.

MF-730196 — commercial reference used for a residential-address delivery elsewhere in the Tidewater Analytics network. Its invoice includes the $12.00 residential surcharge. The destination and consignee are different from GO-48172. The reference appears adjacent in a spreadsheet export because the files were sorted by invoice batch rather than by waybill.

MF-730204 — projected arrival on 06-15, later revised to 06-16. This is a different shipment. Its status is not evidence about the actual gate scan on MF-730184. A route-plan timestamp copied into an operations dashboard can appear beside the wrong waybill when a user filters only by destination region.

GO-48127 — a separate Granite Outfitters order number with a transposed final digits pattern. It contained four cartons and was delivered on 06-12. It is not a predecessor or continuation of GO-48172. Its carton count must not be added to or subtracted from this case.

A draft rate worksheet mentions $588.00 as “service plus attempt.” That figure is $570 + $18. The worksheet was prepared before the event search and is not a confirmed rate. Another calculator tab shows $582.00 as “service plus residence,” which is $570 + $12. Neither figure is an eligible base. The invoice total of $600.00 combines both additions, even though one is unsupported and one belongs to a different waybill.

Several dashboard tiles show “14” in the same row: fourteen cartons, a 14:00 local sorting cutoff, and the number 14 in the scheduled date 06-14. These are unrelated uses of the same digits. The shipment arrived on the 15th, not the 14th. The tender manifest count is fourteen cartons, not fourteen pallets or fourteen wet packages. These details are retained to discourage accidental cross-field substitution.

There is also a generic service guide in the shared folder describing a 15% seasonal courtesy adjustment for a different lane. The GO-48172 booking was Priority Road under revision 4.2, and the relevant excerpt is section F. The general guide is not an amendment to the booked policy. It is not appropriate to average 10%, 15%, and 20%, or to select the most generous number simply because it appears nearby.

L. Appendix: route, facility, and scan glossary
North Quay is the shipper’s consolidation point. It accepted the fourteen cartons on 06-10 and loaded them for linehaul. East Lantern and Blue Heron are intermediate cross-dock facilities. Their scans establish movement through the network but do not establish destination arrival. Alder Point is the receiving dock named in the booking. The local appointment times in this packet refer to Alder Point local time, and all relevant systems were configured to that time zone.

ORIGIN_LOAD means a carrier has accepted the handling units from the shipper. HUB_ARRIVE and HUB_DEPART mean arrival at and departure from a sorting facility. ROUTE_PLAN is a forecast. VEHICLE_HOLD and RELEASE describe vehicle availability. GEOFENCE indicates presence in a configured geographic radius. ROUTE_NOTICE is a notification generated from an operational status rule. APPOINTMENT_END records the booked window ending without a qualifying arrival. GATE_ARRIVE is the relevant arrival evidence for F.2. POD is proof of delivery. DAMAGE_IMAGE indicates that an image was uploaded; the image itself must still be interpreted alongside the receiving record.

A status can be accurate in its own limited sense and still fail to answer the question being asked. The vehicle was in the service area at 10:03 on 06-14, so the geofence entry is not fabricated. It still does not establish gate arrival during the appointment. The notification accurately said that the system expected delivery that day, but expectations do not amend the schedule or prove completion. The next day’s gate scan and signed receipt are the strongest evidence of actual delivery.

M. Appendix: audit trail and closeout checklist
Before closeout, the reviewer should preserve the original booking confirmation, dated 06-08; the unaccepted proposed shift; the recipient’s refusal of that shift; the accepted appointment window; the carrier’s event export; the proof of delivery; the carton images; the billing exception record; and the customer chat. These materials answer different questions and should not be substituted for one another. The booking determines the scheduled service. The route record explains the carrier’s conduct. The signed receipt establishes the received count and written condition. The chat establishes the customer’s requested remedies.

For the billing adjustment, verify the arithmetic once more using the booking lines: $486.00 plus $54.00 equals $540.00; adding $30.00 gives $570.00. Ten percent of $570.00 is $57.00. Twenty percent would be $114.00, but the threshold is not met. The invoice’s $600.00 is not the eligible base: subtracting the unsubstantiated $18.00 and unrelated $12.00 returns $570.00. Do not subtract either disputed line twice, and do not add the $8,400.00 declared value to any service subtotal.

For the date decision, record scheduled date 06-14-2026 and actual gate-arrival date 06-15-2026. One calendar date separates them. The window was 09:00–12:00 on 06-14 and no qualifying gate arrival occurred during it. The 06-15 delivery satisfies neither “more than one calendar day after” nor “at least two calendar dates later.” The latter would begin on 06-16. The 10% window credit does not require that later threshold.

For condition reporting, record two wet cartons, labels 6 and 11; one carton with crushed outer packaging, label 9; no confirmed contents damage in carton 9; and no missing cartons. The signed count is fourteen delivered out of fourteen tendered. The wet sleeves may warrant replacement review, but this does not turn the complete shipment into a shortage claim.

For customer intent, record a request for delivery-charge reimbursement and replacement sleeves for the wet cartons. Record the explicit exclusion of a refund for the goods order. The customer’s conditional or appreciative comments about a possible 20% result should not be converted into either policy eligibility or a request for merchandise refund. If an agent sends a response, it should explain the $57.00 service credit and separately advise on the replacement-sleeve process.

For exceptions, check whether the recipient accepted a new date, whether a documented safety closure prevented service, and whether the address was inaccurate. The file shows no accepted date change, no safety closure, and an accurate commercial address. The route-balancing note is not a safety closure. The vehicle inspection hold at the yard cleared at 09:17; the record does not connect it to an authorized destination closure or establish an exception under F.4. The appointment failure remains carrier-controlled on the evidence provided.

For invoice cleanup, remove or contest the $18.00 “second attempt” fee pending supporting documentation. Remove the $12.00 residential surcharge from this shipment because it belongs to MF-730196. Maintain a note that the initial $600 export mixed eligible and ineligible lines. Ensure the credit calculation is based on the $570 confirmed subtotal and not on a convenience total from the invoice export.

For quality review, retain enough context for a later auditor to reproduce every conclusion without relying on the coordinator’s summary. The decisive records are the booking and recipient’s response for the unchanged date; the event feed and signed receipt for the actual arrival; the policy’s definitions for the credit threshold; the confirmed charges for the base; and the chat for the requested remedies. The surrounding planning notes, dashboard projections, and adjacent invoices are retained because they explain how the confusion arose, not because they override the decisive records.
