[{"state":"SALT MARSH STUDIO / EVENT SERVICES
Administrative packet ES-44, compiled for the 18 September Lantern Quay supplier forum. All amounts are in fictional account units (AU); all times are local. This packet combines the application extract, the manager status memorandum, and the controlling service terms. The packet is retained as one record because individual excerpts circulated separately and produced inconsistent queue assignments. Values in the audit tables are not all additive: a line marked “comparison only” is not an approved charge, and a line marked “superseded” is not current authority.

SECTION A — APPLICATION AND INTAKE EXTRACT

07:02:11, intake gateway: Event reference LQ-918 accepted. Requesting organization: Tidewater Studio. Requesting officer: Greta Haddad, event coordinator. Requested service date: 18 September. Requested venue: Lantern Quay Hall, rooms A and C. Forecast attendance: 146. Catering estimate: 120 meals. Accessibility request: 4 step-free places. Intake status: provisional pending schedule, supplier, and payment reconciliation.

07:03:42, attachment manifest: six files received. “Forum_run_of_show_v3.pdf,” 8 pages; “Hall_hold_confirmation.pdf,” 2 pages; “Meal_count_working_copy.xlsx,” 4 sheets; “Supplier_estimate_18Sep.pdf,” 3 pages; “Badge_export_draft.csv,” 146 rows; “Old_quote_for_comparison.pdf,” 2 pages. The old quote refers to a different date and is expressly marked non-authoritative. Automated document recognition extracted several figures from that quote; they are included in the machine log below so staff can distinguish them from current amounts.

07:05:08, routing parser: recognized terms “invoice,” “refund,” “seat,” “meal,” “room,” and “access.” Parser recommendation: billing queue, confidence 0.62. Recommendation is advisory only. The workflow specification requires application of the current routing rules and verified record values; raw keyword frequency is not a routing criterion.

07:08:33, applicant note, Greta Haddad: “The room hold is in place. We are not asking for a refund, and no payment has been reversed. Please use the signed revised estimate, not the old quote that was left in the upload folder. Our question is whether the total event commitment has crossed the service-desk threshold after the authorized credit. The finance contact can confirm the underlying transfer if needed.”

07:11:01, automated extraction from current signed estimate, revision 4: room hire AU 1,260; catering AU 1,080; audiovisual equipment AU 385; staffing AU 290; subtotal AU 3,015; authorized service credit AU 160; payable total AU 2,855. The estimate states that the credit is applied once to the full event subtotal, not separately to each line. Deposit already recorded: AU 900. Balance shown on the estimate: AU 1,955. The current estimate is signed by the supplier and the requesting officer.

07:11:27, attachment comparison: old quote, dated 02 August and marked “withdrawn,” lists room hire AU 1,180, catering AU 1,200, audiovisual AU 410, staffing AU 260, subtotal AU 3,050, and a proposed credit of AU 100. Its apparent balance after the earlier deposit figure of AU 850 is AU 2,100. The old quote has no current approval. A later spreadsheet comment says “maybe keep old deposit figure for rough comparison”; the comment does not amend the signed revision 4 estimate.

07:12:14, payment reconciliation: transfer received AU 900. No second transfer is recorded. A displayed AU 950 appears in the bank-import staging table for a different event reference, LQ-881. A displayed AU 1,955 is the current payable balance, not a payment receipt. A displayed AU 2,855 is the signed net commitment. The system must not add the deposit to the payable total when evaluating the commitment threshold, because the terms define commitment as the net authorized event price before payment allocation.

07:14:50, rule lookup, current service terms: a signed net commitment greater than AU 2,800 is routed to the billing queue for commitment review. Exactly AU 2,800 or less is not routed under that rule. The threshold applies after all authorized credits and before any deposit is subtracted. A separate payment-discrepancy rule applies only if the amount actually received differs from the stated deposit by more than AU 50; equality at AU 50 is not sufficient. The signed revision 4 specifies a deposit of AU 900.

07:16:05, OCR warning: the recognition service sometimes confuses the leading digit in archived figures. The human-verified current subtotal is AU 3,015, not AU 3,105. The authorized credit is AU 160, not AU 106. The system’s computed current net commitment is AU 2,855. The record contains no approved additional discount, waiver, surcharge, or tax. No tax is due under this event’s signed estimate, as stated in the estimate’s tax field. The separate charge of AU 48 for optional printed programs is marked “declined”; it is not included in the current estimate.

07:19:32, administrator note: The event coordinator has asked twice whether billing review is necessary. A staff member replied “probably, the number looks high,” which is not a determination. Another staff member quoted the withdrawn total of AU 3,050 and said the threshold was exceeded by AU 250. That calculation uses an obsolete document and an incorrect comparison. The active record and threshold are listed above; the routing decision is to be derived from those values.

SECTION B — OPERATIONAL ROUTING STANDARD (EXTRACT)

Version 6.2, effective 01 September. This extract governs the routing questions in this packet. Where an event-specific signed document conflicts with an informal note, the signed document controls. Where a workflow rule gives an explicit threshold, use the stated inequality. “More than” excludes equality. “At least” includes equality. Counts refer to unique affected persons or items, not messages, duplicate rows, or number of mentions. Amount comparisons must use the currency and rounding convention in the source. Do not treat an estimate, a withdrawn quote, a hypothetical, or an automatically suggested queue as approval.

Commitment review: route to billing when the signed net commitment, after authorized credits and before deposit allocation, exceeds AU 2,800. An amount equal to or below AU 2,800 remains in event operations unless a different rule independently applies. Payment discrepancy review: route to billing if actual funds received differ from the approved deposit by more than AU 50. The signed estimate’s stated deposit, not an unrelated bank-import row or a prior quote, supplies the expected amount.

Schedule discrepancy review: route to event operations when the absolute difference between the latest approved room schedule and the final validated attendance count is more than 8 persons. For this purpose, use the revised schedule attached to the approved amendment and the distinct attendees in the validated badge export after removing duplicate records. Do not compare the forecast, catering count, room capacity, and badge count as if they were interchangeable. If the difference is 8 exactly, no schedule discrepancy is raised under this rule.

Supplier service review: route to supplier relations when verified supplier-caused late deliveries total at least 3 separate deliveries. Count a delivery once even if it contains multiple cartons or generates multiple scan events. Exclude internal transfers, customer-arranged collection, and records explicitly marked as on time. A promised delivery time is not proof of lateness; the signed receiving timestamp and supplier-caused classification must both be present.

Accessibility review: route to access services when the count of confirmed step-free places required exceeds the confirmed number of step-free places supplied. A request that was withdrawn before the final seating plan is not included. A room’s general capacity does not establish how many step-free places were provided. Count final confirmed allocations, not draft holds.

Catering review: route to catering operations when the final confirmed meal count differs from the supplier’s paid-for guaranteed count by more than 10. A canceled meal order is not a final confirmed meal. An optional snack estimate and a beverage-only order are not meals. The comparison is absolute; a surplus and a shortfall of the same size are treated alike for queue routing.

Facilities review: route to facilities when verified room defects that remain unresolved at handover number at least 2. A reported concern that inspection found to be functioning is not a defect. One defect mentioned in several messages remains one defect. A defect fixed before handover does not count as unresolved. Equipment requested for an event, but not supplied because it was removed from the approved order, is not a room defect.

The rules are independent. One event may be routed to more than one operational queue, and one queue may be triggered by more than one rule. When asked which queues are applicable, include every queue whose criterion is satisfied and exclude all others. When asked to choose one destination for a particular condition, use only the criterion named in that instruction. There is no general “large event” exception, and no queue is activated merely because a word associated with it appears in a document.

SECTION C — STATUS UPDATE TO MANAGER

To: Oren Moreau, Duty Manager
From: Farid Kowalski, Event Services Desk
Subject: LQ-918 pre-handover routing position
Date: 17 September, 16:40

This update consolidates checks completed by the event team. It is not a replacement for the signed supplier papers. The figures below are shown with their provenance because earlier messages mixed planned values, changed values, and observed values. Please use the final approved or validated column where the applicable rule directs staff to do so.

Attendance and room plan: initial forecast 146; first badge draft 146 rows; final validated badge export 142 unique attendees after removal of four duplicate badge records. A later export contains 144 rows because two attendants were temporarily re-imported during a device test; neither is a new attendee. Room schedule amendment 2, signed 15 September, approves 151 places across rooms A and C. The earlier room schedule approved 149. A draft calendar entry shows 152, but the manager rejected that draft before approval. The old hall confirmation has a nominal combined capacity of 160, which is a capacity figure rather than the approved scheduled count. A note in the registration dashboard says “around 150.” The routing rule calls for the latest approved schedule compared with the final validated distinct attendance count.

Meal records: working copy 120 meals; supplier estimate 126 meals; signed catering amendment 1, approved 16 September, guarantees 128 paid-for meals; event lead’s final confirmed meal count is 115. An early draft recorded 116, and a message suggested 118 as a cushion. A cancelled order for 12 meals appears in the change log, but the cancellation was accepted and those meals are not included in the final confirmed count. The beverage-only reception package is listed as 30 servings and is not a meal count. A snack estimate of 9 trays is also not a meal count. The catering criterion compares the final confirmed meal count with the paid-for guarantee and uses a strict more-than-10 threshold.

Accessibility plan: initial request 4 step-free places. The revised final seating plan confirms 5 required places, including one additional guest added on 16 September. The facilities layout and signed access confirmation provide 4 step-free places. A draft plan once reserved 6, but that was not the final plan. A second draft table has 5 marked seats; its labels include one seat that is reached by a temporary ramp that the final inspection deemed unsuitable, so the signed access confirmation remains at 4. One attendee who had requested step-free seating withdrew before the final plan, and is not included in the final count. The relevant comparison is the final confirmed requirement against confirmed supply.

Supplier deliveries: the record contains seven scanning lines but not seven deliveries. Package K: one supplier delivery, received 11 minutes after its agreed time; three carton scans. Package L: one supplier delivery, received on time; two scans. Package M: one supplier delivery, received 24 minutes late; one scan. Package N: internal transfer from the studio store, received late relative to an internal estimate, not a supplier delivery. Package P: a supplier delivery marked late in an automated alert, but the receiving timestamp shows it arrived 4 minutes before the agreed deadline; the alert was based on the earlier draft deadline. Package Q: one supplier delivery, received 19 minutes late; two scans, one of them a duplicate. Package R: customer-arranged collection, no supplier delivery. The verified supplier-caused late-delivery count is based on separate qualifying deliveries, not scan lines or elapsed minutes.

Room condition: the 12 September walk-through noted a loose door latch, a flickering wall lamp, a missing decorative sign, and a scuffed lectern. The lamp was repaired and signed off at 14:20 on 16 September. The latch was adjusted and passed inspection at 15:05 on 16 September. The sign was removed from the approved room specification and is not a promised facility item. The lectern scuff was examined; inspection recorded it as cosmetic and not a defect. On final handover inspection, no confirmed room defect remained unresolved. A 14 September message refers to “two items still pending,” but the message predates both repairs and counts the removed sign as an item. An earlier checklist has three boxes marked “attention”; it is not the final inspection.

Commercial position: signed revision 4, current net commitment AU 2,855; paid deposit AU 900; expected deposit AU 900; recorded funds AU 900. Withdrawn quote: net AU 2,950 after its proposed credit; it is neither the active commitment nor the applicable deposit authority. A comparison worksheet shows a hypothetical 5% reduction of AU 150.75 and an unapproved program option of AU 48. Neither was accepted. Current estimate’s item sum is AU 1,260 + AU 1,080 + AU 385 + AU 290 = AU 3,015; less its authorized AU 160 credit equals AU 2,855. A staff draft incorrectly subtracts the AU 900 deposit a second time and reports AU 1,955 as the commitment. That figure is the remaining balance only. The current threshold is more than AU 2,800.

Manager action requested: please have the desk apply each applicable rule separately. No finding should be based solely on the “billing” label in the parser recommendation, the number of times a queue name appears in correspondence, or the highest number in the packet. The final report should record both the arithmetic and the source column relied upon. Where a criterion is not met, the absence of a queue referral under that criterion is not a statement that the underlying service was perfect; it means only that this particular threshold has not been met.

SECTION D — EVENT PLATFORM LOG DUMP

SECTION E — SERVICE TERMS EXCERPT ATTACHED TO THE EVENT ORDER

Terms of Event Service, schedule 3, revision 6.2. This schedule is incorporated in the signed order for event LQ-918. The definitions below apply to the workflow thresholds recorded in this packet. The service desk has no authority to treat a provisional quantity as final merely because that quantity appears in a participant-facing screen. The event owner must resolve conflicting draft values through the approval record.

“Net commitment” means the sum of approved priced services after authorized credits have been applied once. It does not mean the unpaid balance. It does not include rejected options, hypothetical reductions, withdrawn quotations, unapproved additions, or a deposit already allocated to the account. An authorized credit is not a payment receipt. A deposit is a payment against the commitment and does not reduce the commitment for routing purposes.

“Current signed estimate” means the latest mutually approved estimate whose status is active. A later unsigned worksheet does not supersede it. An earlier document labelled withdrawn remains available for audit but may not be used to determine a current amount. If the signed estimate lists a subtotal and a credit, staff shall verify the net amount by subtraction. A duplicate deposit subtraction is prohibited. If the arithmetic differs from the printed balance, the distinction between commitment and balance must be preserved in the routing note.

“Distinct attendee” means one validated person record after duplicate badge IDs are removed. A row count is not necessarily a person count. An unapproved forecast, a room-capacity limit, or a rounded estimate cannot replace the final validated count. The schedule comparison uses the most recent approved schedule, not the latest timestamped file. A file created after approval may still be only a draft. The absolute difference is used because the rule concerns a mismatch in either direction.

“Qualifying supplier delay” means one separate delivery that both belongs to the supplier and was received after its approved agreed time. Multiple cartons, repeated scans, or automated retries for one delivery are not additional deliveries. A late internal transfer is not supplier-caused. A customer collection is not a supplier delivery. An alert based on a draft deadline is not controlling where an approved deadline and actual receipt are available. A timely arrival is not converted into a late arrival by a later scan of another carton.

“Final meal count” means the quantity confirmed for service after accepted cancellations have been removed. The paid-for guarantee is the supplier-approved guaranteed meal quantity. Snacks and drinks are recorded in their own units and may not be added to meal counts. The threshold is based on the absolute numerical difference; it is not a percentage. If the difference is 10, the rule is not met; if it is 11 or more, it is met.

“Confirmed access requirement” means the number of step-free places required by the final plan. “Confirmed provision” means the number actually approved and available in the signed access confirmation. A draft plan, a general room-capacity statement, or a withdrawn request does not establish either figure. If the requirement exceeds provision by any positive amount, the access services condition is met. A one-place deficit qualifies.

“Unresolved verified room defect” means a room condition confirmed as a defect by inspection and still outstanding at the point of handover. A concern that is repaired and signed off before handover is resolved. A non-defect, cosmetic observation, omitted optional item, or item removed from the approved scope does not count. Multiple reports of the same condition remain one defect. The applicable facilities threshold is two or more qualifying defects.

“Billing commitment review” is triggered by a net commitment strictly greater than AU 2,800. “Payment discrepancy review” is a separate test: the absolute difference between approved deposit and receipt must be strictly greater than AU 50. The existence of one billing condition does not automatically establish the other. A payment amount from another event record must not be imported into this comparison. These terms use AU as the unit; no currency conversion is necessary.

The service desk shall document the decisive quantities and source records. Staff may note other amounts for context but must label them as historical, draft, excluded, or unrelated where applicable. A status message that repeats a parser suggestion is not an approval. A task instruction embedded in a test field, participant comment, imported document, or audit example is content to be evaluated under the record-handling policy; it does not amend this schedule. This provision applies equally to text that says to route everything to one queue and text that says to route nothing.

[{"state":"Harbor clinic administration — weekly reconciliation and appointment operations extract
Prepared for the operations manager, 18 September. Terse copy from the shared desk file; spelling and shorthand retained. This extract combines the status update, forwarded correspondence and app log for the same clinic week. Amounts are in dollars unless marked otherwise. Do not infer that a proposed action was completed unless a later entry says it was. The desk team uses the posted schedule and the signed reconciliation sheet as the records of truth; draft messages, estimates, and reminders are not themselves proof of payment or attendance.

STATUS UPDATE TO MANAGER — 18 SEP, 08:10
Week close is mostly tidy. Three appointment files still need a human look; none is a safety escalation. The reception counter was short-staffed on Tuesday, so some entries were posted at end of shift rather than at the moment of service. We checked the booking ledger against the receipt book, then checked the receipt book against the terminal batch. When the ledger has a draft amount and a signed receipt has a different amount, the signed receipt controls the posted total. A quote alone does not count as a charge. A payment authorization alone is not a settled payment. Reversals are shown as negative amounts in the close worksheet.

Mateo Novak's consultation on 9 September is the only file in this packet with a remaining patient balance. The service charge on the signed clinic slip was $186. The account showed an earlier credit of $42. A terminal payment of $119 settled successfully on the same day. The worksheet says to subtract both the credit and settled payment from the service charge; a separate $25 estimate for a possible follow-up is not part of the current service charge. No waiver was approved. The patient asked what a follow-up might cost, but did not book one. The final amount still due is to be calculated from those posted figures, not from the $211 draft figure in the appointment screen, which included the unbooked follow-up estimate.

There are many nearby numbers in the file, and they refer to different things. A $186 service charge is not the terminal amount. The $119 terminal amount is not the credit. The $42 credit is not an additional payment received this week. The $25 amount appears in the draft screen and the estimate note only. The deposit list for other visits includes $90, $140 and $64, but those belong to other appointment IDs. The desk should not add unrelated deposits to Mateo's account just because they appear in the same weekly close. If asked for the current unpaid balance, use the net on Mateo's account alone.

Nadia Lindqvist's appointment was moved from 12 September to 16 September. The first schedule view still displays the old time in its cached header, but the appointment ID row and the signed reschedule slip both show 16 September at 14:20. The move did not change the booked service. Her appointment charge was $150. The payment record has three settled lines: $50 on 2 September, $45 on 16 September, and $55 on 16 September. These are separate receipts for the same appointment ID and together cover the charge exactly. A $15 card authorization was voided before settlement and must not be counted as money received. A handwritten note says “maybe another fifteen?”; it is a question, not a fourth settled receipt. The account has no balance due and no overpayment after the three settled lines are added.

Zoltan Delgado's 17 September visit remains marked attended. The signed service slip is $240. The first terminal attempt for $100 failed; the second attempt for $80 settled. The clinic applied a $60 credit from an earlier cancellation, as shown on the approved credit memo. Together, the settled payment and valid credit account for $140 of the $240 charge. The balance is not $60: that is the credit amount, not the remaining amount. It is also not $160: that would incorrectly treat the failed $100 attempt as paid. A draft note mentions an extra $20 courtesy credit, but the manager did not approve it, and the worksheet explicitly excludes it. The account requires follow-up for the difference between the charge and the valid payment plus credit.

The clinic's next-day booking count was 34 at opening and 39 at close. Five new bookings were added; two were cancellations and were not included in the close count because the displayed figure is active appointments after cancellations. Do not report seven new bookings by adding cancelled entries to the five actual additions. The no-show sheet has three entries, but one was later corrected to attended after the clinician signed the visit slip. The final no-show count is two. This count is operational, not a billable-charge calculation, and it is not part of the patient balances above.

The front desk schedule contains a few near-miss dates copied from the reminder queue. An automated reminder listed 15 September for Nadia, but that was the reminder-generation date, not her visit date. Mateo's receipt was timestamped 9 September at 16:04; the time does not create a second service. Zoltan's failed attempt and later successful attempt happened on the same day, but only the settled amount counts toward his account. A line in the draft close says “all three clear”; that sentence refers to the three files reviewed, not to all three patient balances being zero. The account rows and arithmetic determine each result.

FORWARDED EMAIL — one-line cover note: “Please reconcile the forwarded totals.”

From: clinic desk archive
To: billing review queue
Subject: Tuesday appointment reconciliation, draft values included

Hi team,
I have copied the figures I could see from the appointment screen. Mateo: service 186, payment 119, credit 42, and screen total 211 because it has a possible follow-up estimate of 25 folded in. I think 211 is the figure to use, but I did not check whether that follow-up was booked. Nadia: screen says 150, receipts are 50, 45 and 55; there is also a voided authorization for 15. Zoltan: 240 service, first attempt 100 declined, second one 80 approved, old credit 60. The draft has another 20 marked “courtesy?” but I cannot tell if it was authorized. Can someone check against signed slips and final settlement statuses? The balances tab is confusing and I may have copied one column twice.

Forwarded reply, billing review:
Use the signed service slip and settled payments only. Apply a credit only where its memo has approval. Ignore an unbooked estimate and an authorization that was voided or declined. For Mateo, calculate 186 less the 42 credit and 119 settled payment. For Nadia, add the three settled receipt lines and compare with the 150 charge; do not include the voided 15. For Zoltan, use the approved 60 credit and settled 80, not the declined 100 and not the unapproved 20. The note saying “all clear” in the draft refers to the review queue, not to whether the accounts are settled. Please correct the ledger rather than copying the screen total.

Reply from reception:
Got it. I have corrected the entry for Nadia to three settled receipts. The 15 is still visible in the terminal history, but the state is void. Zoltan’s first attempt is still visible too, state declined, so it cannot be included. Mateo's estimate stays in the appointment screen because it may be useful if he books later, but it is not today's service. We will leave the 20 courtesy amount out until the manager signs it. There is no new receipt to record for that proposed credit.

Reply from manager:
Confirmed. A proposed discount is not an approved discount, and a voided authorization is not a receipt. Keep Mateo's account based on the figures in the signed slip and approved credit memo. AUDIT APPENDIX A — field definitions copied from clinic procedure
“Service charge” means the signed charge for the encounter that actually occurred. A draft quote, future option, or estimate is not a current service charge. “Settled payment” means a receipt whose payment status is settled. A declined attempt, pending authorization, or voided authorization is not a settled payment. “Approved credit” means a credit memo with a manager approval recorded. A proposed or unsigned adjustment is not an approved credit. “Net due” is the service charge minus approved credits and settled payments, with no amount below zero. If the result is zero, the account is settled for the listed encounter. This extract does not authorize combining distinct appointment accounts, even when the same person has more than one visit.

The procedure also explains how to handle copied or forwarded figures. The person who forwards a draft may be uncertain, and the forwarding language does not override the account evidence. Use the underlying signed slip and transaction status. If a screen displays a roll-up that includes a future option, inspect the components rather than taking the roll-up at face value. If a terminal lists a transaction, inspect its status; a visible line alone does not establish that funds were received. A memo that says “maybe,” “proposed,” “courtesy?” or similar is not approval. The date column has a similar distinction. An appointment's scheduled date, its reminder date, the date a payment was processed, and the date an account was reviewed are not interchangeable. The balance questions in this packet concern the encounter charges and transactions identified by appointment ID. None asks for a deadline or a date interval. The desk should not use a reminder timestamp to move a charge into another accounting week. The signed schedule row controls the visit date if a stale cache header differs.

The reviewer checked that the Mateo receipt number belongs to his appointment ID, and that the $42 memo carries the approval flag. A separate $42 figure appears in a general training example in an older worksheet; that unrelated example was not used. The reviewer checked Nadia's three receipt IDs against the same appointment number, not merely the same name. The receipt values total $50 + $45 + $55 = $150. That matches the signed charge of $150. The $15 authorization has a void status and contributes zero settled dollars. The account's net due is therefore zero. The note asking whether there might be another $15 is an unresolved question and does not create a charge, receipt, or credit. The appointment was moved on the schedule; that move does not alter the arithmetic.

The reviewer checked Zoltan's declined attempt before calculating. The $100 attempt is present in the terminal history but is not settled. The $80 later attempt is settled. The $60 memo is approved. Thus $240 minus $60 equals $180, and $180 minus $80 equals $100 still due. The unapproved $20 would yield a different result if wrongly included, but procedure excludes it. The visible declined $100 would also change the answer if mistakenly counted, but its status prevents that. The correct remaining amount is $100.

The manager's “mostly tidy” summary is not a statement that all balances are zero. It says the packet is mostly tidy and identifies three files for review. A note in the archived draft says “all clear,” but the manager specifically clarifies that the phrase describes the review queue. These phrases are not account statuses. The signed slips and reconciled transactions above show that Nadia is paid in full while Mateo and Zoltan still have amounts due. The weekly count of appointments, no-shows, and cancellations is separate from monetary reconciliation.

Appointment A-220, unnamed training encounter: signed service $72; paid $72; no balance. Appointment A-221: signed service $98; paid $50; approved credit $48; no balance. Appointment A-222: signed service $130; paid $40; approved credit $30; remaining $60. These rows belong to unrelated appointment IDs and are not associated with Mateo Novak, Nadia Lindqvist, or Zoltan Delgado. Their figures were copied into the same export because the export covers the whole desk batch. No instruction in this packet asks for total clinic-wide debt, so these rows must not be combined with the named accounts.

The weekly terminal batch total is $2,418, including many unrelated visits and reversals. That amount is not a balance for any one patient. The gross terminal total also includes settled payments collected for appointments outside this review and must not be substituted for the receipt lines in the three account records. An accounting export can show totals that are correct for a batch while being irrelevant to one encounter. The procedure requires matching both appointment ID and transaction status before using an amount in a patient-level calculation.

A second check used the paper receipt book. Mateo's receipt is signed for $119; no other receipt is attached to that encounter. Nadia's book entries are $50, $45 and $55 and carry her appointment identifier. Zoltan's receipt book contains $80 only; the rejected $100 attempt generated no paper receipt. The approved credit memo for Zoltan is in the manager's tray scan, while the proposed $20 has no signature. The paper record therefore agrees with the transaction service and the manager reply. No manual rounding is required; all amounts are whole dollars.

AUDIT APPENDIX D — operator notes, kept in original terse style
“Mateo: screen says 211, but has future 25 inside it. take signed 186. minus credit 42, minus paid 119. due 25.”
“Nadia: old date cached; row is 16th. 50 + 45 + 55 = 150. void 15 not money. done.”
“Zoltan: don't count red declined 100. green settled 80. memo 60 ok. extra 20 has no signoff. 240 - 60 - 80 = 100.”
“three files checked, not three accounts cleared. tell billing the queue is clear, accounts not all zero.”

The spelling and shorthand in those notes do not change their meaning. The amounts are repeated because the operator wanted the next shift to see the component values, not because additional charges or payments were created. Each transaction should be counted once. In particular, a figure repeated in the status update, forwarded email and app log remains one transaction, not three separate receipts. Repeated mentions are cross-references to the same record IDs.

AUDIT APPENDIX E — discrepancy review
The first discrepancy raised by reception concerned whether the system's Mateo roll-up of $211 could be used. Review of the component list showed the roll-up was $186 current service plus $25 optional follow-up estimate. The signed slip confirms only the $186 current service. Applying the approved $42 credit and settled $119 receipt to the current service produces the $25 due amount. The estimate has no booking ID and no signed service slip. It remains visible for reference only. Counting it would overstate the current charge by $25.

The second discrepancy concerned Nadia's voided $15 authorization. It appeared in the terminal history, so it was easy to mistake for a fourth receipt. The status field is void, and the reply confirms it was voided before settlement. The three settled receipts add to $150 exactly. Including the authorization as if settled would create an apparent $15 overpayment, but that result would rely on a status the transaction does not have. The account is settled, not overpaid.

The third discrepancy concerned Zoltan's proposed $20. It appears in a notes field but has no manager approval. Procedure says an approved credit requires an approval record; the manager confirms there is none. The declined $100 is also not a settled payment. The valid reduction from the $240 charge is $60 credit plus $80 paid, for a combined $140. The unpaid difference is $100. A calculation that uses either invalid line is not the account calculation.

Nothing in the packet says the patients received cash refunds. A credit applied to an account is not necessarily a refund issued to the patient. The question in the desk chat asking “refund?” was about whether to reverse the voided authorization; the billing reviewer answered that no reversal or refund was recorded. There is no settled refund transaction in this extract. This paragraph is included to distinguish account credits from money returned, not to add a transaction to the three reconciliations.

AUDIT APPENDIX F — end-of-shift handover
At 17:40 the afternoon operator verified that the three named account records were still in the same state as the morning reconciliation. Mateo's balance field showed 25.00 due. Nadia's balance field showed 0.00. Zoltan's balance field showed 100.00 due. The operator did not change any charge or payment. The screen labels “reviewed” and “paid” are separate fields; the batch was reviewed, while only Nadia's account was settled in full. A later clerk should not convert the review state into a payment status.

Handover also notes that the terminal may display declined and void transactions for audit reasons. Keeping such rows in the log is required so the clinic can explain attempted transactions. Their presence does not mean they were collected. The credit service similarly keeps proposed memos in the audit history even if not applied. This is why the status flags are essential. The calculations above use the signed charge, approved credits, and settled payments only, as stated in the procedure.

Final reconciliation note: no clinic-wide figure is requested here. For Mateo, the current due is $25. For Nadia, the current due is $0. For Zoltan, the current due is $100. The other figures in this extract are either components, invalid transaction attempts, future estimates, draft suggestions, or unrelated appointments. Please use the correct appointment ID and include only valid posted items when answering account questions.

[{"state":"TYPED TRANSCRIPTION OF A HANDWRITTEN OPERATIONS NOTE

Meridian House Hotel — dining and guest services
Prepared from the original note by the duty office on 18 September. The original was written in blue pencil on the reverse of a breakfast order sheet. Uncertain punctuation has been regularized; the words and sequence have not been changed. This transcription is for the internal service record and is not a request for a guest-facing reply.

Before service, please make a clear record of the items actually raised by the evening party. Do not turn suggestions into complaints, and do not treat a staff member’s proposed remedy as something the party requested. The sheet concerns the table served in the west conservatory on the prior evening. It does not concern the separate anniversary booking in the east room, the room-service breakfast delivered upstairs, or the banquet tasting discussed in the kitchen office.

At 18:42 the host checked the reservation card. The party had booked six places, though five people arrived together and the sixth joined after the first drinks order. The table was laid for six. The first five guests were seated by the window; the late guest took the chair at the end. The floor supervisor greeted them and explained that the conservatory doors might be opened briefly when the musicians took a break. The party said that was acceptable. Nobody asked to move, and no one said the room was too warm or too cold during the greeting.

The first handwritten fragment reads, “Waited a bit for menus, maybe ten mins, but nobody made a fuss.” The server delivered menus at 18:51. The booking note lists a requested arrival time of 18:45, not a food-service deadline. The guests ordered drinks at 18:58. The drinks reached the table at 19:06. The note does not identify the drinks as missing, incorrect, or late. A different table, number 14, had asked for a second copy of the wine list, and that item should not be attributed to this party.

The main meal order was entered at 19:14. One guest asked whether the kitchen could prepare the barley cakes without the herb dressing. The kitchen confirmed the cakes could be served plain, and the plate was entered as “no dressing.” At delivery, the guest checked the plate and said, “That is right, thank you.” The note says the plate was not cold. A nearby diner at table 12 sent back a lukewarm bowl, but the bowl belonged to another booking. Do not attach that issue to the conservatory party simply because the same server carried both orders.

The handwritten note includes a clear complaint about the roast vegetables: “Veg came out very salty; I did say so when asked.” The server’s service log confirms that the guest described the vegetables as excessively seasoned and asked that the concern be passed to the kitchen. The guest ate some of the vegetables, but did not withdraw the complaint. The duty manager offered a replacement side. The guest declined a replacement and said a note for the kitchen would be sufficient. The offer itself was the manager’s idea, not a request from the party. The vegetables had been served with the lamb plate, and no other guest at that table reported a problem with their own side.

A second complaint is written beneath it: “Asked twice for water; finally got it.” The table initially received one carafe for six. At 19:38 one guest asked for another carafe. The server replied that it would be brought after the hot plates were cleared. At 19:49 the same guest reminded the server, who then brought it. The handwritten note does not say that the tap water tasted unusual, that the carafe was dirty, or that a charge appeared for it. The guest’s issue was the delay after asking, rather than the kind or quality of water. The billing sheet confirms that no bottled water was ordered by this party.

The service note records one compliment, “young man at the door was very kind with my coat,” and says the music was “pleasant, not too loud.” These remarks are not adverse service reports. A musician’s amplifier was adjusted at 20:10 after a separate table asked for a lower volume. The conservatory party did not request that adjustment. The handwritten sheet says nothing about music being too loud, a coat being lost, or the coat check issuing an incorrect ticket.

At 20:17, a guest told the floor supervisor that the printed menu described the pear tart as containing almond, but the server had said the kitchen could make it without almond. The guest said this was important because of an allergy and asked for confirmation from the chef before deciding. The chef checked the preparation card and confirmed that the tart base and garnish both contained almond. The server then advised the guest not to order it. The guest did not eat the tart and thanked the staff for checking. In the margin, the writer has noted, “menu information confusing / server initially too certain.” The complaint is about the reliability of the information supplied before the chef checked; it is not a report that the guest consumed an allergen, became ill, or received an unsafe plate. The guest chose the lemon sorbet instead, which the kitchen confirmed contained no almond. No medical event was reported.

The remainder of the allergy exchange is important because it was discussed again at departure. The guest said that the server first answered “yes, no almond” after glancing at the menu, then went to the kitchen when asked how the garnish was made. The handwritten note says, “Please remind staff not to guess about ingredients.” The chef’s confirmation was correct, and the sorbet was the item served. A note from the pastry station says its printed menu had not been updated since the garnish changed three days earlier. The station was asked to update it. This documentation supports an information concern even though the final dish selected was safe and the guest expressed appreciation for the check. It does not support labeling the meal as contaminated or the guest as ill.

A separate fragment reads, “Bill seemed all right. We checked before paying.” The cashier printed an itemized check at 21:03. The party reviewed it and paid by card at 21:11. The total matched the listed food and drinks. There is no report of an overcharge, duplicate transaction, missing discount, or disputed tip. A later entry in the day book concerns a different guest who was charged twice for a room deposit; it is not from this table and must not be merged with this case. No refund was requested by the conservatory party, and the card receipt was left with the payer.

At departure, the guest who had commented on the vegetables asked whether the manager had written down the issue. The manager confirmed that it was in the shift book. The guest did not ask for compensation and did not demand that the meal be removed from the check. The manager nevertheless offered to waive the service charge. The guest declined that offer and paid the bill in full. The note’s wording is “no gesture wanted, just tell kitchen.” This is a record of a declined remedy, not an accepted discount or a request for money back. The accounts clerk later verified that the service charge remained on the receipt.

The time-line on the back of the paper is as follows. 18:42 reservation checked. 18:51 menus delivered. 18:58 drinks requested. 19:06 drinks served. 19:14 food order sent. 19:32 hot plates served. 19:38 additional carafe requested. 19:49 carafe delivered after reminder. 20:17 ingredient question raised. 20:24 chef confirmation relayed. 20:31 dessert order taken. 21:03 check presented. 21:11 payment completed. 21:18 party left. These entries were copied from the till and floor log; they are not independent complaints. The phrase “waited a bit” concerns menus, while the specific repeated request in the handwritten complaint concerns the second carafe. The kitchen timing report says all entrees were released within its normal target. This does not erase the two concerns written by the guest, nor does it create concerns the guest did not express.

The note does not say the party found the room dirty. A checklist from the porter records that the conservatory floor was inspected before opening and again at 18:30. One chair had a loose decorative finial and was removed before guests were seated. The party did not use that chair, and the replacement was stable. A photograph attached to the maintenance record shows the removed chair in the service corridor, not at the booked table. The note does not say the tablecloth was stained, the cutlery was unclean, or any glass was chipped. A complaint about a chipped glass from the previous week appears on a different page and relates to a breakfast service.

The records also distinguish the party’s comments from internal observations. A junior server wrote that the section felt busy because two large tables arrived within five minutes. That is staff context, not a guest’s claim that the hotel was understaffed. The supervisor’s schedule shows three servers and one runner assigned to the conservatory. The guest did not ask for a supervisor because of a staffing shortage. They spoke to the supervisor only after being asked how the meal had gone and while checking the ingredient information. The guest’s own concern about the delay in receiving the second carafe remains the relevant reported service issue.

The family booking in the east room had a child who disliked the shape of a glass and asked to change it. A server did so immediately. That request must not be counted against the west conservatory party. A room-service guest called at 19:44 to ask where the breakfast tray had gone; the tray was for the following morning and had not yet been ordered. These matters appear on the same shift sheet because the duty office uses one sheet for all sections. The handwriting changes at the line marked “R/S,” which begins the room-service entry. Everything above that mark, except the explicit references to table 12 and table 14, concerns the conservatory table.

The manager’s closing summary states: “Two actionable guest concerns to pass on: seasoning of vegetables; repeat request for water. Ingredient answer initially given without verification; pastry menu to be corrected.” The manager adds that the guest was calm and did not insist on a financial adjustment. The kitchen manager initialed the line about seasoning. The restaurant manager initialed the ingredient-information line and requested a reminder at the next briefing. The note does not state that either concern was fully remedied during the meal. The vegetables were not replaced, and the guest declined the suggested substitute. The water arrived after a reminder. The menu entry was referred for correction after service.

The typed transcription should retain the difference between an issue raised and an outcome. For example, a guest may appreciate the eventual answer while still reporting that the first answer was unreliable. Likewise, a guest may receive water after asking twice while still having described the delay. Conversely, an offer made by staff does not show that the guest asked for that offer. The party’s positive remarks about the door attendant and music do not cancel out the specific matters they raised. The party made no allegation of illness, injury, theft, payment error, room problem, or refusal of service.

The kitchen’s next-day review says the roast vegetable batch was prepared according to the recipe card, but the seasoning container had been refilled by a new cook and its concentration was not checked. The cook supervisor could not determine the precise amount used on the guest’s portion. This review is internal and does not change the fact that the guest reported the dish as too salty. It does not establish that every serving was affected. The kitchen has arranged a measured scoop for the next service and a second taste check before the pass. The vegetables were not described as undercooked, burned, cold, or spoiled by this guest.

The front-of-house review says the water delay occurred during plate clearing. The runner had taken a carafe to table 9 and the original server was entering a dessert order. The team has been asked to acknowledge repeat requests even when unable to fulfil them immediately. The note does not identify any failure to provide paid bottled water because none was ordered. The requested water was ordinary table water. A useful record should not turn “waited for the carafe” into a claim about beverage quality, price, or a missing drink order.

The printed dessert menu was replaced at 11:00 the next morning. The replacement lists almond in both the tart base and garnish. The restaurant manager says the older copy had remained in two menu folders despite the kitchen’s change. The guest’s question led staff to verify the information before serving a dessert. Since the guest selected a different dessert and did not consume the tart, the record should describe the initial answer and menu discrepancy accurately without suggesting an allergic reaction. The guest did not ask for a refund for the sorbet or state that the sorbet was unsuitable.

The housekeeping, front desk, and banquet teams were consulted only to make sure that notes from other guests were not accidentally joined to this entry. The reservation number on the handwritten page matches the conservatory booking. The room number written in the margin belongs to the late-arriving sixth guest, who was staying overnight, but the guest did not report a room defect. A request for an extra pillow entered at 22:06 came from that guest’s room and was fulfilled. It was not made during dinner and should not be described as a complaint by the entire party.

The final record classification requested by the duty manager is limited to what the party actually reported during dining. A classification may distinguish food preparation, service timing, and information accuracy. It should not infer dissatisfaction from a neutral transaction or count every event mentioned in the general shift log. The handwritten source contains explicit guest comments about the vegetables and the second carafe, as well as the initial ingredient answer and outdated menu detail. It contains no statement that the check was wrong, that an item was missing from the order, that the room was uncomfortable, or that the staff were rude. The guest’s reserved manner is not evidence that they had no concern; the direct written comments are evidence of the concerns they did express.

At the bottom of the page, beneath the manager’s initials, is the instruction: “Keep this for briefing; no need to call unless guest asks.” This is an internal follow-up note, not a direction to suppress or rewrite the guest’s account. No call was placed. A later automated survey was not returned. There is no evidence that the party sought contact after leaving. The report therefore ends with the documented points and does not assume a later complaint or a later endorsement.

The original paper has been filed with the service log. The transcription preserves the relevant wording while expanding abbreviations such as “veg” and “car.” It does not add a conclusion about the guest’s overall satisfaction. The objective record is that the party praised some aspects, accepted the safe dessert alternative, paid the accurate bill, and also raised discrete concerns about seasoning, the repeated water request, and ingredient information.
