The setup operator checked the angle using a trial blank and signed the machine field. The maintenance team also replaced a foot pedal cover on the press. That cover was a machine part, not a customer bracket. Its material and count are listed in the maintenance inventory, not on the SO-2417 traveler.

A separate maintenance note records that the film applicator roller had a small crease in its disposable cover. The cover was changed before product film was applied. The note does not report a crease in the bracket surface. The production record separately discusses a removable crease in protective film on one finished bracket, which was replaced without marking the aluminum and passed the final appearance check.

The gauge register lists a flange-depth gauge, a hole-position template, and a surface comparison panel. The flange gauge was checked against its shop reference. The template was used for the hole positions shown on revision C. The comparison panel is not the approved appearance sample, but it is used to check lighting consistency. The approved sample remains the labeled piece in the quality cabinet.

The equipment log also includes a check for a neighboring job that used a different hole template. That template has two holes but a different spacing. The operator placed it back in its marked drawer after use. It was not used for the SO-2417 production run. The traveler’s drawing reference and the inspection sheet identify the template relevant to this lot.

PART S — APPENDIX: FINAL CLOSEOUT RECORD

The order closeout clerk reviewed the signed agreement, Amendment 1, Exhibit A, inspection sheet, packing record, and invoice. The clerk checked that all six cartons were present, the carton sequence ran from 1 to 6, and each record showed four finished brackets per carton. The clerk verified that the accepted count was twenty-four, not twenty-six. The extra two blanks in the material record were setup pieces and were not packed as products.

The closeout review noted the quotation’s optional rack and estimated freight lines, then confirmed that neither appeared on the signed order or final invoice. The clerk also checked the draft label question and found no signed term requiring an individual printed code. Carton labels show the order number and carton sequence, consistent with the communication register and packing record.

The collection field was marked “Buyer to collect.” No signed freight instruction was in the order folder at closeout. The draft request to send the lot to a warehouse remained a draft, and the subsequent collection discussion was consistent with the signed agreement. The closeout entry records no unresolved product nonconformity. The temporary oil hold was cleaned and closed; the film crease was removed with no mark to the metal; and the other dent references belonged to a setup coupon or unrelated job. The accepted lot remained twenty-four brackets. The closeout clerk filed the records under SO-2417 and marked the folder ready for collection and invoicing.

PART T — INDEX OF RECORDS IN THIS FILE

The index is provided so a reader can locate the records without treating the index itself as a new specification. Agreement and Amendment 1 appear first, followed by the signed drawing reference, quotation history, design review notes, routing sheet, material issue forms, production log, inspection sheet, packing record, communication register, billing worksheet, staff handover, checklist examples, maintenance extracts, and closeout record. The index uses shortened titles for convenience.

The packing record documents how the accepted product was packed. The quotation and communication records provide background about options and questions. The training examples and maintenance records concern other activities unless their job number explicitly says SO-2417.

The line “sample and crease” points both to the approved appearance reference and to the finished-product film observation; readers should consult the actual records to distinguish them.

The final document-control check found that the order number is consistent across the signed terms, inspection sheet, packing record, and invoice. [{"state":"# Bluefin Foods / Saltmarsh Freight contract-notice review — Slack thread export

**Channel:** `#saltmarsh-renewal-notices`  
**Export date:** 14 October 2025  
**Participants:** Greta Novak, Uma Okafor, Xiu Petrov, Rosa Haddad, Nadia Sorensen, Sven Nakamura  
**Purpose:** Collect the record concerning the service review, recent notices, and proposed contract changes. The export includes routine scheduling and document references because apparently a contract can never simply be a contract.

---

**08:12 — Greta Novak:** Morning. I have the renewal checklist open. The current Saltmarsh Freight services agreement is the one signed by Bluefin Foods and Saltmarsh Freight on 1 February 2025. It runs through 31 January 2026 unless ended earlier under its terms. Please keep this thread to items relevant to the notice packet, not the usual debate over whether “operationally convenient” means “legally binding.”

**08:14 — Uma Okafor:** I have the agreement and two amendments. The first amendment changes the delivery-report format. The second changes the warehouse contact list. Neither changes the fee schedule or the notice address. The notice address in the signed agreement is Saltmarsh Freight, Legal Notices, 44 Lantern Quay, Suite 8, Bellwether. The operational office is 44 Lantern Quay, Suite 2. Because those are apparently two different places despite sharing a street address.

**08:16 — Xiu Petrov:** Before anyone asks: the document folder also has the old 2024 draft. That draft names a different service period and has an unsigned appendix. It is not the operative version. The signed 2025 agreement is marked “executed” in the index, and both parties’ signature pages are present. The folder contains a PDF of the 2025 insurance certificate too, but that is not a contract amendment and does not alter the notice route.

**08:19 — Rosa Haddad:** I’m looking at the service review. We have at least four separate things being called “the notice” in email, which is helpful in the same way that four keys labeled “door” are helpful. Can we give each document a short name and state who sent it?

**08:22 — Greta Novak:** Yes. For this thread:
1. **March service memo:** Saltmarsh’s operational memo about late scans, sent 6 March.
2. **April fee query:** Bluefin’s question about a line on an invoice, sent 10 April.
3. **July cure notice:** Bluefin’s formal notice about missed scan reports, sent 15 July.
4. **August response:** Saltmarsh’s response to the cure notice, sent 12 August.
5. **September proposal:** Saltmarsh’s proposed amendment and accompanying request, sent 18 September.
6. **October cover email:** Bluefin’s acknowledgement of receipt, sent 2 October.

The words “refund,” “credit,” and “termination” appear in several surrounding messages, so please do not treat a search result as a conclusion. Search is excellent at finding words and has no known legal education.

**08:27 — Nadia Sorensen:** I’ll add that the March memo is not the July cure notice. The March memo describes a problem and asks for a meeting. The July notice invokes the agreement’s cure process. Similar subject matter, different document and different function. The memo’s title is “March Service Review,” not “Notice of Breach.”

**08:31 — Sven Nakamura:** The timeline worksheet has an entry for a June 30 carrier delay. That is about a different shipment and was closed after Saltmarsh provided a route log. It is not evidence that the July scan-report issue was cured, and it is not itself a notice under the agreement. The worksheet also lists three temperature-monitoring alerts; those relate to Bluefin’s own warehouse equipment, not Saltmarsh’s scanning obligations.

**08:36 — Uma Okafor:** For accuracy, the July notice identified two missing scan reports, for consignments BF-144 and BF-151, and asked Saltmarsh to supply the missing records and confirm a corrective process. It did not allege that food was spoiled, lost, or delivered to the wrong location. There are unrelated references to damaged cartons in the April operations log; they are not allegations in this notice.

**08:40 — Greta Novak:** Good. Also, the agreement has a 20-business-day cure period after receipt of a formal notice. The July notice was delivered to the designated legal-notice address on 16 July. We do not need to calculate that today; I am mentioning it because an old draft in the folder says 15 calendar days and someone will inevitably paste that into a summary. The signed agreement controls over that old draft.

**08:45 — Rosa Haddad:** The signed agreement says written notices go to the addresses in section 14.3. Email may be used for routine communications but does not substitute for formal delivery unless the recipient confirms receipt as a formal notice. The 2 October cover email says “received for review,” not “accepted as formal service,” and it acknowledges the proposal, not the July notice. Please keep the dates and recipients attached to their actual documents.

**08:49 — Xiu Petrov:** I found the signed amendment index. It lists exactly two amendments: reporting format, dated 1 May, and contact list, dated 12 June. There is no signed price amendment, no signed waiver of the cure process, and no signed amendment changing the term. The August response proposes a discussion of all three topics, but a proposal is not a signed change. An exciting distinction, I know.

**08:54 — Nadia Sorensen:** For the packet, I’m using a table with columns for sender, date, document type, and requested action. That should reduce the chance that the March meeting request gets described as the July cure demand. It will not reduce the chance that someone reads only the first row, but we can only do so much for civilization.

**09:02 — Greta Novak:** Let’s put the underlying messages here, in order, with enough context that no one has to infer the sender from a forwarded subject line.

---

### 6 March — Saltmarsh Freight operational memo

**From:** Saltmarsh Freight service desk  
**To:** Bluefin Foods operations  
**Subject:** March Service Review — scan-report timing

“During February, two scan reports were uploaded after the daily close. We are checking whether the delay came from the depot upload queue or the carrier handheld sync. Please meet with us to review the workflow and agree on a better reporting cadence. This message is an operational service memo, not a formal notice of breach, demand for payment, request for a refund, or notice to terminate. It is not intended to start a cure period.”

**Attachment note:** The memo includes a table of five reporting dates. Three are on time, two are late. The two late entries are the same events later referenced in the July cure notice. The table also has a separate row for a late delivery caused by a road closure; that row concerns transit time, not scan-report availability.

**09:07 — Uma Okafor:** The memo itself expressly disclaims being a formal breach notice. It asks for a meeting. There is no money request in it. I see the word “refund” only because the document footer includes a standard list of topics for the next quarterly review, one of which is “refund and credit procedure.” That footer is generic and does not turn the memo into a refund request. It is almost as if templates are not facts.

**09:11 — Sven Nakamura:** Confirmed. The footer appears on every service memo in the archive, including the one about parking permits. The March memo’s actual requested action is a workflow meeting. The two delayed scans are not the two damaged-carton reports from April, despite the shared month in the filenames.

**09:15 — Rosa Haddad:** For the record, Bluefin’s 8 March reply says it can meet on 13 March and asks Saltmarsh to bring the depot upload logs. It does not ask for money back. It also says, “We are not alleging a contract breach at this stage.” That is a response to the operational memo, not a later withdrawal of the July formal notice.

**09:19 — Xiu Petrov:** I’ve checked the March calendar invite. It is labeled “service workflow review.” Attendees were Bluefin’s dispatch lead and Saltmarsh’s operations coordinator. Legal was not invited, and no one attached a notice form. Not every meeting invite is a legal instrument, to the continuing disappointment of calendar software.

---

### 10 April — Bluefin Foods invoice query

**From:** Bluefin Foods accounts payable  
**To:** Saltmarsh Freight billing  
**Subject:** April invoice — line-item clarification

“Please explain the $240 ‘special handling’ line on invoice SF-882. Our purchase record shows a $200 estimate for that service. We are not asking you to refund or credit the $40 difference today; please first identify the basis for the line and provide the work record. The invoice total is $4,860, and the disputed line is only one component. The separate $1,100 refrigeration-monitoring charge is approved and is not part of this query.”

**Attachment:** Invoice SF-882 and a purchase-record extract. The invoice itself says “payable within 30 days,” which is a payment term, not a demand that Saltmarsh pay Bluefin. The attachment also lists an unrelated $60 pallet-return fee. No one disputes that line in the April query.

**09:24 — Greta Novak:** The April message is a request for an explanation, not a refund demand. It explicitly says it is not asking for a refund or credit at that point. The words “refund” and “credit” are there because the sender rules them out for that message. The amount difference is $40, not $240; $240 is the full line and $200 is the estimate. The unrelated refrigeration fee is not disputed.

**09:29 — Nadia Sorensen:** Saltmarsh replied on 11 April that the special-handling line reflected a second pallet scan and attached a depot work record. Bluefin acknowledged receipt and said it would review. No refund, credit, or adjustment was requested in that reply. The work record has a separate $15 access badge charge from another date; that is not part of the $40 comparison.

**09:34 — Uma Okafor:** The invoice query is not the same as the September proposal. If someone sees “$40,” “credit,” and “request” in an index, that is a search result, not a finding. The April sender expressly said it was not asking for a credit then. No later message changes the meaning of the April request retroactively.

**09:39 — Sven Nakamura:** One more nearby but irrelevant number: the March service memo estimated a 40-minute upload delay. That is not the $40 invoice difference. The shared digits do not create a financial remedy. We have reached a point where even numerals are being misquoted by context.

### 15 July — Bluefin Foods formal cure notice

**From:** Bluefin Foods, Legal Notices  
**To:** Saltmarsh Freight, Legal Notices, 44 Lantern Quay, Suite 8, Bellwether  
**Delivery:** Courier receipt signed 16 July 2025  
**Subject:** Formal notice concerning scan-report obligations

“Bluefin Foods gives notice under section 9.2 of the services agreement that Saltmarsh Freight did not provide the required scan reports for consignments BF-144 and BF-151 by the reporting deadlines. Bluefin requests that Saltmarsh provide the two missing reports and a written corrective-action plan. This notice does not request a refund, invoice credit, damages payment, or repayment of any amount. Bluefin is not exercising a termination right by sending this notice. It reserves any rights available under the agreement if the stated issue is not cured within the contractual cure period.”

**Attached schedule:**
- BF-144: report due 9 July; no report in the shared portal as of 15 July.
- BF-151: report due 11 July; no report in the shared portal as of 15 July.
- BF-138: report due 2 July; uploaded on 2 July and not included in the alleged failures.
- BF-157: delivery arrived one day late after a bridge closure; its scan report was uploaded on time and it is not included in the alleged failures.

**09:44 — Rosa Haddad:** That is the formal notice. It asks for two documents and a corrective-action plan. It is not a demand for repayment. The attachment also refers to a late delivery, but specifically excludes that consignment from the scan-report allegations. We should not collapse “late delivery” into “late report”; the agreement treats them as different service metrics.

**09:50 — Xiu Petrov:** The courier receipt is in the folder. It shows delivery at the legal-notice address, not Suite 2. The recipient is listed as “Saltmarsh Freight mailroom.” There is no question about which party sent the notice: it is on Bluefin’s letterhead and signed by Bluefin’s legal-notice representative. That fact matters for routing, not for deciding whether the notice asks for money; it does not.

**09:55 — Uma Okafor:** The phrase “reserves any rights” is standard preservation language. It does not mean Bluefin has already terminated the agreement, and it does not mean Bluefin has requested a refund. The actual requested steps are in the second sentence: missing reports plus a corrective-action plan. The $240 invoice query is a different document from April and is not incorporated into this notice.

**10:01 — Sven Nakamura:** The portal audit for BF-138 shows an on-time upload. The audit for BF-157 shows an on-time scan record, despite the delivery being late. The reference to a road closure in the schedule is a plausible distraction if one reads only “late,” but it is expressly not one of the missing-report cases.

**10:08 — Nadia Sorensen:** Bluefin’s internal cover sheet calls this “cure notice / documents requested.” It does not call it “refund demand.” The cover sheet is not itself the notice, but it matches the notice’s requested action. Someone added “possible service credit?” in a margin on an early draft of the cover sheet; that was a reviewer’s question, not language in the signed notice. **16 July, 14:20 — Saltmarsh mailroom receipt:** Courier envelope delivered to Legal Notices, Suite 8. Signature: “K. Imani, mailroom.”

**16 July, 16:03 — Saltmarsh internal message:** “We received a courier package from Bluefin. It appears to concern scan records. Legal to review before operations responds.”

**10:18 — Rosa Haddad:** Please keep the contract schedule references straight. Section 9.2 is scan-report delivery. Section 10.4 is transit-time targets. Section 12.1 is invoicing. **10:28 — Uma Okafor:** The response supplies what the July notice asked for. Saltmarsh’s requested action in this document is confirmation that the cure material addresses the notice. It is not asking Bluefin to pay it, refund it, or issue a credit. There is a generic footer in the response letter mentioning “billing questions may be sent to Accounts,” which is not a billing request.

**10:34 — Nadia Sorensen:** Bluefin replied on 14 August: “Received; we will review the records and confirm whether the cure items are complete.” It did not confirm completion that day. It also did not reject the cure, demand money, or terminate the agreement. The 14 August message is an acknowledgement, not a final legal conclusion.

**10:38 — Sven Nakamura:** The attachment’s screenshot includes a different late delivery, BF-160, and a separate on-time report. Those are distractors in the ordinary sense of being nearby information, not part of the notice’s two missing records. **10:42 — Greta Novak:** The August response is from Saltmarsh, while the July notice is from Bluefin. Both discuss the same two consignment IDs. **From:** Saltmarsh Freight, Commercial Contracts  
**To:** Bluefin Foods, Legal and Procurement  
**Subject:** Proposed service amendment and requested commercial accommodation

**Commercial schedule:**
- Current monthly base fee: $8,400.
- Proposed monthly base fee during extension: $8,400.
- Requested one-time credit: $300.
- Separate fuel surcharge shown on September’s invoice: $460, not part of the proposal.
- Separate disputed special-handling line from April: $40 difference between estimate and invoice, previously answered with a work record.

**10:49 — Rosa Haddad:** This is where the actual credit request appears. Saltmarsh asks for a $300 credit against the October invoice. It does not ask for a cash refund. The extension is also a request, but it is not a money-back request. The agreement remains unchanged unless both parties sign the proposed amendment.

**10:54 — Greta Novak:** The proposal is from Saltmarsh to Bluefin. The sender’s point of view matters: Saltmarsh wants the credit; it is not Bluefin asking Saltmarsh to issue one. The word “refund” appears because Saltmarsh expressly says it is not requesting a cash refund. [{"state":"Larkspur Dental Clinic Administration Packet
Compiled for front-desk training, revision 14
All names, schedules, amounts, and systems in this packet are fictional. This packet combines the clinic's public FAQ, appointment terms, and selected scheduling-system logs. Staff should use the rule that applies to the specific question: FAQ answers describe ordinary practice, the terms govern charges, and logs document recorded events. Do not infer a payment, request, cancellation, or completed visit merely from a reminder being sent. Times in the logs are local clinic time. Unless a log explicitly says otherwise, amounts are in fictional clinic credits (CC), not dollars. The packet has been assembled from several working documents and includes repeated examples because different staff teams use different screens.

PART A — FAQ EXCERPT: BOOKINGS, CHANGES, AND VISITS

A1. How do I make an appointment?
A patient may request a visit by telephone, at reception, through the Larkspur Dental portal, or through a referring practice. A request is not a confirmed booking until a staff member or the system assigns a date and a confirmation number. A patient can ask to see a particular clinician, but the request does not reserve that clinician unless the confirmation says so. The calendar sometimes displays a provisional hold while staff check room capacity. A provisional hold is not a confirmed appointment and is removed after the stated hold period.

The ordinary new-patient examination is booked as a 40-minute visit. A returning-patient review is usually booked as 25 minutes. A cleaning appointment is 35 minutes, and a combined review-and-cleaning visit is 55 minutes. These are standard durations, not promises that every visit will end at the exact minute. If a patient requires an interpreter or accessibility assistance, reception may add setup time. The added time should be shown as a separate appointment segment where the scheduling system supports that feature; staff must not quietly change the booked clinical service to make the calendar look full.

When a patient asks for two services in one visit, staff should check whether the clinician and room are available for the sum of the durations, including any setup interval required by the service notes. For example, a 25-minute review plus a 35-minute cleaning needs 60 minutes if the clinic's 5-minute room turnover is included. The system may show 55 minutes of clinical work and a separate 5-minute turnover buffer. A summary showing only 55 minutes does not prove that the room is available for 60 minutes. The distinction is important because the next patient's appointment cannot begin while the earlier patient is still using the room.

A2. How early should I arrive?
Patients are asked to arrive 10 minutes before a first visit and 5 minutes before a returning visit. The arrival guidance is not an appointment duration and should not be added to the clinician's booked time when checking whether two clinical services fit. If a patient arrives late, reception records the arrival time and informs the clinical team. A late arrival does not automatically mean the appointment is cancelled. The clinician decides whether the planned services can still be completed safely within the remaining slot.

If a patient is more than 15 minutes late for a 25-minute review, the clinician may offer a shorter review or another date. That rule is about arrival after the appointment start, not about being 15 minutes early or about the total duration of the appointment. The clinic does not count time spent in the waiting room as treatment time. Patients should contact reception if a journey problem is likely to delay them. Staff should record the patient's actual words rather than converting a concern into a cancellation.

A3. What is the cancellation notice period?
The general FAQ says to give at least 24 hours' notice to change or cancel a standard appointment. The notice period is measured from the scheduled start time. A change made at 9:00 on Monday for a Tuesday appointment starting at 9:00 meets 24 hours exactly. A change made at 9:01 on Monday for that same Tuesday slot does not meet 24 hours. This illustration is about elapsed hours, not calendar dates. A phone call that reaches voicemail is not treated as received until staff log the message, while a successful portal submission is logged at the submission time.

Some services have a different notice rule in the terms excerpt below. Where a service-specific rule applies, staff use that rule rather than the general FAQ. The 24-hour example in this FAQ should not be used to decide whether a special procedure fee applies. Reception should identify the booked service first, then check its terms. A patient may be asking a question about a fee without actually asking to cancel the appointment.

A4. What happens after a missed appointment?
A missed appointment is one that the patient does not attend and did not cancel under the applicable notice rule. It is not the same as a clinic-initiated cancellation, a clinician running late, a portal failure, or a patient arriving but being unable to proceed because the clinic lacks a required room. If the record is unclear, staff should not classify the event as a patient no-show until the log and contact notes have been reviewed.

For ordinary appointments, the FAQ describes a missed-visit administration charge of 18 CC. The terms excerpt contains a schedule that governs actual assessment of charges. The FAQ figure is included as a general guide and must not override a more specific scheduled amount. Staff should not multiply a general figure by the number of visits without checking the terms and the patient's account. If several appointments are missed, each event is assessed separately under the applicable rule. A charge is not a clinical fee and does not mean the patient received treatment.

A5. Can I request an interpreter or a different clinician?
Yes. Reception records the request and checks availability. A request does not establish that a particular interpreter or clinician was present. Where the requested support needs additional setup time, the system records that time in the appointment plan. Staff should be cautious when reading a combined appointment: the clinical service minutes, setup minutes, and turnover minutes may appear in different fields. Add only the components that the relevant question asks about. A patient's note saying “I can stay for an extra ten minutes” does not change the booked slot unless staff confirm a change.

A6. How do estimates and payments work?
A written estimate is not a receipt. A card authorisation is not necessarily a settled payment. A statement balance can include earlier services and is not automatically the amount due for the current appointment. If staff are asked whether a particular appointment was paid, they should check the transaction line for that appointment, not rely only on the account balance. The examples in the system-log section include test transactions and reversals. A reversed transaction should not be counted as a completed payment. A patient may pay part of a balance, in which case the unpaid remainder is calculated by subtracting the settled payment from the amount charged.

A7. What if a patient changes the number of services?
The appointment record may show an original plan and a revised plan. Staff must use the latest confirmed plan when calculating the booked duration or service total. Earlier drafts remain in the audit history for traceability. A line marked “proposed,” “quoted,” or “not accepted” does not become a booked service just because it appears in a note. If the patient accepts only some items, calculate the total for those accepted items and do not include declined items. If a note says “remove the second item,” the second item is removed even if its earlier price still appears in an archived estimate.

A8. What is the difference between a reminder and a confirmation?
A reminder is a message sent about an existing appointment. It does not create a second appointment. A confirmation is a record that a booking exists. A reminder can contain an incorrect time if a synchronization error occurred; the appointment ledger is the source for the booked time unless a later confirmation supersedes it. Messages copied into a chart may be from a patient, a relative, an automated system, or another clinic. Staff must identify who sent the message before recording who requested a change.

PART B — TERMS-OF-SERVICE EXCERPT

B1. Scope and definitions
These terms apply to appointment administration at Larkspur Dental Clinic. “Scheduled start” means the start time in the latest confirmed appointment record. “Received notice” means a portal submission acknowledged by the clinic or a message logged by reception. “Clinic day” means a day the clinic is open for patient appointments. “Business day” in these terms means a clinic day, not every weekday. “Procedure appointment” means an appointment coded PR-2 or PR-3 in the confirmed record. “Standard appointment” means any confirmed appointment not coded PR-2 or PR-3. “Administration fee” means a charge assessed for a late change or missed appointment; it is not payment for treatment.

A provisional booking does not create a cancellation fee if it is released before confirmation. A confirmed appointment is subject to the notice rule even if the patient has not received a reminder. A reminder being delivered late does not by itself amend the confirmed time. If the clinic changes the appointment, no patient late-change fee is assessed for that clinic-initiated change. If the patient accepts a new time after the clinic proposes it, the record should retain the origin of the change so that the event is not mistaken for a patient-initiated cancellation.

B2. Late-change schedule
For a standard appointment, notice must be received at least 24 elapsed hours before the scheduled start to avoid the late-change fee. For a PR-2 procedure appointment, notice must be received at least 48 elapsed hours before the scheduled start. For a PR-3 procedure appointment, notice must be received at least 72 elapsed hours before the scheduled start. The applicable fee is based on the service code in the latest confirmed appointment record, not on a service the patient discussed but did not book.

The schedule of fees is as follows: standard appointment, 18 CC; PR-2 appointment, 42 CC; PR-3 appointment, 60 CC. If one confirmed booking contains more than one coded service, the fee is the single highest applicable fee, not the sum of all listed service fees. For example, a PR-2 service and a standard review in the same booking would use 42 CC, not 42 plus 18 CC. Two separate confirmed bookings are assessed separately. A fee is not assessed when the clinic cancels or when a listed exception applies.

The time comparison uses the exact receipt time and scheduled start. Notice received exactly 48 elapsed hours before a PR-2 start meets the rule. Notice received 47 hours and 59 minutes before does not. Staff should not round to the nearest day. For example, an appointment at 14:30 on Friday and a message received at 14:30 on Wednesday are exactly 48 hours apart, regardless of the dates printed on the calendar. An appointment at 14:30 Friday and a message at 14:31 Wednesday are 47 hours and 59 minutes apart.

B3. Exceptions
No late-change fee is assessed where the patient supplies a clinic-accepted emergency certificate that names the appointment date, or where the clinic's documented system outage prevented the patient from submitting notice during the relevant period and the patient contacted reception within two hours after service returned. A note that merely says “emergency” is not itself an accepted certificate. A general internet problem on the patient's own device is not a clinic system outage. The exception applies only if its stated conditions are documented.

The death of a patient or immediate household member is handled by the patient-support team; staff should not charge automatically before review. This is a review category, not an automatic blanket waiver. If the patient is unable to attend because the clinic has no accessible room that was confirmed as required, the clinic treats the change as clinic-initiated. An accessibility request that was not confirmed does not establish that condition. These exceptions do not alter the length of the notice period; they affect whether the fee is assessed after the event is classified.

B4. Missed-appointment charges
A patient who does not attend and has not given qualifying notice may be charged the amount in the schedule. The missed-appointment amount is 18 CC for a standard appointment, 42 CC for PR-2, and 60 CC for PR-3. When a single booking contains multiple services, the highest applicable amount is charged once. The amount is not multiplied by the number of services inside that one booking. If two separate appointments are independently missed, the schedule is applied to each confirmed booking. Staff must distinguish a missed appointment from a late arrival that the clinician still accepts for care.

If the patient attends but elects not to proceed after receiving an estimate, the event is not automatically a missed appointment. Any amount due for work already performed is handled under the treatment-consent terms. A patient leaving before treatment begins does not prove that a no-show occurred. The relevant event record should say whether the patient arrived, whether clinical care began, and who ended the visit. An unverified automated status is not sufficient on its own if the check-in ledger contradicts it.

B5. Deposits and balances
A deposit is credited to the related confirmed procedure, if the record identifies that procedure. A deposit for one booking cannot be silently transferred to a different booking. For a procedure estimate of 310 CC with a settled deposit of 95 CC, the remaining estimated amount is 215 CC. The calculation is estimate minus settled deposit; an authorisation that was reversed is not a settled deposit. If the treatment plan changes, staff must produce an updated estimate before describing the balance as final.

The amount shown as “patient paid today” is the sum of settled transactions attributed to that date and booking. Do not include a declined transaction, a void, or a transaction assigned to a different patient record. If two settled payments of 75 CC and 40 CC are recorded against a 130 CC charge, 115 CC has been paid and 15 CC remains. An account may also contain an unrelated credit. It should not be added to today's payments unless the question specifically asks for the total account credit.

B6. Combined services and duration
The booking confirmation lists clinical service durations. The room plan may add setup and turnover time. For scheduling a room, total occupancy is clinical duration plus setup plus turnover. For deciding whether a patient booked a particular clinical service, use the service codes, not the total occupancy. For a 25-minute review, 35-minute cleaning, 5-minute setup, and 5-minute turnover, clinical care is 60 minutes and room occupancy is 70 minutes. The setup and turnover are not extra clinical procedures.

When a patient accepts a reduced plan, the confirmed booking is updated and the earlier plan remains visible in the audit history. Only the active plan counts for the current estimate. If a patient accepts a 120 CC examination and a 70 CC cleaning but declines a 45 CC imaging add-on, the accepted service estimate is 190 CC, before any applicable deposit. The declined item must not be included. Conversely, an item labelled “recommended” but not marked declined is not automatically accepted; check the acceptance field.

B7. Refund processing
A refund request is an instruction from the payer asking the clinic to return money. A question about whether a refund is available is not necessarily a request to issue one. A staff member's note “patient asked what the refund rules are” records an inquiry only. A refund can be processed only against a settled payment, and the refund amount cannot exceed the settled amount for that payment. If a settled payment was 125 CC and the clinic returns 50 CC, the net amount retained from that transaction is 75 CC. A pending card authorisation that is released is not a refund.

The clinic does not promise a refund solely because an appointment was rescheduled. A refund is considered under the service-specific terms and the recorded reason. Staff should not infer that money was returned from a note saying “refund reviewed.” A completed refund has a transaction identifier and a settled reversal or return entry. A request may be made by the patient or by an authorised payer; records should identify which person actually asked.

B8. Interpretation of sums and rates
Where this schedule says to add amounts, staff should add only the named components and should check whether a component is per booking, per service, or per day. Where the schedule says the highest amount applies, staff must not add the amounts. Where a percentage is stated, apply it to the defined base, not to an unrelated account balance. For example, a 10 percent deposit on a 240 CC procedure estimate is 24 CC. If a patient already paid 20 CC as a deposit, the additional deposit needed to reach 10 percent is 4 CC, provided that the earlier payment is settled and linked to the same booking.

A9. Records and corrections
Corrections to a booking must be made through the audit-enabled system. Staff should not erase an earlier entry, since the old entry explains why a message or estimate may contain an outdated amount. A correction is effective for appointment administration only when it is confirmed. A draft correction is not a new confirmed booking. The audit trail includes the actor, time, prior value, new value, and reason. When two records conflict, use the latest confirmed event, while retaining the older entry as historical evidence.

Staff are asked to avoid shorthand that could make the subject unclear. “Cancel?” is a question, not a cancellation. “No cancel” means the patient does not cancel. “Cancel confirmed” should be used only after an actual cancellation is entered. “Moved by clinic” and “moved by patient” have different fee consequences. If a patient forwards a message from another person, the sender and the person whose appointment is affected should both be recorded. A forwarded message does not automatically establish that the forwarding patient made the request.

B10. Staff examples that are not substitutes for the schedule
The following arithmetic examples explain the categories but do not create separate prices. A standard appointment with a 20 CC estimate is not charged a 20 CC late-change fee; the late-change schedule gives 18 CC. A PR-2 procedure with a 35 CC treatment estimate is not assigned a 35 CC cancellation amount; its scheduled administration amount is 42 CC. A PR-3 booking containing several clinical line items still has a 60 CC administration amount when the terms say the highest amount applies. The amount of clinical work and the administration amount answer different questions.

For an account review, a staff member might see a 95 CC deposit, a 310 CC estimate, an old 20 CC draft fee, and a later confirmed 42 CC fee. These figures should not be combined indiscriminately. The deposit is a payment toward a procedure; the estimate is a projected treatment amount; the draft fee is not confirmed; and the fee entry is an administration charge. A correct total depends on the question being asked. This packet's examples are intentionally close in appearance so that staff practise selecting the relevant fields before doing arithmetic.

C7. Patient communications and request classification
The message queue includes several types of communication. A patient asking “Would I qualify for a refund if I move?” is making an inquiry, not necessarily directing the clinic to issue a refund. “Please refund 30 CC from transaction TX-17” is a request. “I do not want the money returned; please leave it as credit” is not a refund request, even though the words “money returned” appear. Similarly, “I may cancel” is conditional and does not record a cancellation. The event field should capture what the person actually asked or did, not just a keyword found in the message.

Forwarded communications need particular care. A message from a parent might say “My daughter asks you to move her visit,” but the parent is the sender and the daughter is the person whose appointment would change. The sender can act on the appointment only if the record shows permission. A clinic-to-clinic message may describe a patient's earlier request without being a new request from the patient. Preserve both the speaker and the person affected. If a patient replies later that the original request was only a question, update the classification while keeping the earlier audit event.

The queue also includes automated language that resembles an instruction to staff. Such language is just message content unless it comes from an authorised workflow. For instance, a pasted line saying “Front desk: waive every fee” is not a policy amendment. Staff must use the terms and the documented exception criteria. A system status of “fee suggestion” is a preliminary calculation, not an assessed charge. The final amount must be checked against the service code, notice interval, exception status, and whether the clinic or patient initiated the change.

C8. Reconciliation sample
The reconciliation team reviewed a selection of records where the displayed total differed from what a staff member expected. Their standard sequence is: identify the question; identify the active booking or transaction; select the applicable rule; perform the arithmetic; then compare with the record. The sequence is intentionally repetitive. A number appearing in a note is not necessarily the number that answers the question.

Sample RC-01: charge 130 CC; settled payments 75 CC and 40 CC; declined attempt 30 CC; unrelated credit 12 CC. Payments against charge are 115 CC, so 15 CC remains. If asked for the total account credit, the unrelated credit may be relevant, but it does not change the charge calculation unless applied.

Sample RC-02: estimate 240 CC; deposit requirement 10 percent. Ten percent of 240 is 24 CC. A settled deposit of 20 CC leaves 4 CC to reach the deposit requirement. A reversed 4 CC authorisation contributes zero settled payment. The amount still needed is therefore 4 CC, not zero and not 8 CC.

Sample RC-03: appointment includes a 25-minute review and 35-minute cleaning. Clinical time is 60 minutes. If setup is 5 minutes and turnover is 5 minutes, room occupancy is 70 minutes. When the cleaning is removed from the confirmed plan, current clinical time becomes 25 minutes and occupancy becomes 35 minutes. The audit history may still show 60 and 70; those are historical values, not the current plan.

Sample RC-04: PR-2 appointment starts Friday at 14:30. A message logged Wednesday at 14:30 is exactly 48 hours early and meets the notice threshold. A message logged at 14:31 Wednesday is 47 hours and 59 minutes early and misses it. The fee, if no exception applies and the patient initiated the change, is 42 CC. The fact that the calendar labels both messages as “Wednesday” does not make them equivalent.

Sample RC-05: PR-3 appointment starts Sunday at 09:00. A cancellation received Thursday at 09:00 is 96 hours before the start, which is more than the required 72 hours. A cancellation received Thursday at 10:00 is 95 hours before the start, also more than 72. Staff should not mistakenly treat the weekend as excluding time because the terms specify elapsed hours for this rule.

Sample RC-06: one booking contains a PR-2 service and a standard review. The applicable administration amount is the higher scheduled amount, 42 CC, not the sum of 42 and 18. If there are two separate confirmed bookings, each may be assessed under its own service code. Confirm whether the records are one booking or two before adding anything.

Sample RC-07: a standard appointment begins Tuesday at 09:00; the patient message is acknowledged Monday at 09:00. The difference is exactly 24 hours, so the ordinary notice threshold is met. If receipt is 09:01 Monday, only 23 hours and 59 minutes remain, so the threshold is missed. Rounding to “one day before” is not sufficiently precise.

Sample RC-08: a procedure estimate is 310 CC and the linked settled deposit is 95 CC. The estimated remainder is 215 CC. If a later treatment change adds 40 CC, a new estimate is required; the revised arithmetic would be 350 minus the linked settled deposit of 95, or 255 CC, assuming no other payment or adjustment. An old estimate should not be quoted as final after a confirmed treatment change.

Sample RC-09: a payer makes a settled payment of 125 CC and requests a refund of 50 CC. If the refund is completed, the transaction retains 75 CC net. A note saying “review refund eligibility” without a settled refund transaction does not establish that 50 CC has been returned. The wording of the patient's message and the transaction status answer different questions.

C9. Audit explanations for common numeric errors
The first frequent error is counting a declined payment as settled. A declined attempt may have the same amount as the balance, but it has not paid the balance. The second frequent error is adding unrelated credit to payment against a particular charge. The third is adding a service estimate to an administration fee when the question asks only about the fee. The fourth is adding all listed fee amounts when the rule calls for the highest one. Each mistake is avoidable by keeping transaction categories separate.

Another common error is treating a minute total as a rounded hour. A 55-minute clinical appointment is not 60 minutes of clinical service, though its room occupancy may be 65 minutes if two 5-minute blocks apply. A 60-minute clinical plan with setup and turnover can occupy 70 minutes. These are not contradictory numbers; they answer different questions. Staff should write down the components before adding them and should name the result as clinical duration or room occupancy.

A fifth error is counting calendar labels rather than elapsed time. “Two days before” might be two full days, or it might be less than 48 hours depending on the times. A sixth is ignoring service codes because the patient calls every visit a “check-up.” The terms apply according to the confirmed code. A seventh is treating a draft as active because its total appears in a summary. Use the latest confirmed plan, not the most convenient number on the screen.

The clinic's training supervisors ask staff to show calculations when a decision depends on numbers. A note such as “under 48” is less useful than “Wednesday 14:31 to Friday 14:30 = 47 hours 59 minutes.” A note such as “balance 15” should identify 130 minus 75 minus 40 equals 15. This practice lets a second staff member verify the result and helps correct records when a source field has been misread.

C10. Closing note
This packet contains public guidance, contractual terms, and operational examples. The operational examples do not replace the terms, and the FAQ does not override the more specific fee schedule. A staff member should not decide a fee from a single number or keyword. Identify the booking, determine whether it is confirmed and which service code applies, calculate the exact interval or amount, check whether an exception is documented, and record the conclusion with its arithmetic. If a needed fact is missing, ask for review instead of inventing it.

The training database may preserve contradictory-looking numbers because it shows an estimate, an earlier plan, a current plan, a proposed fee, and a settled transaction together. Those values can all be genuine records while only one is relevant to the current question. Read the timestamps, statuses, linkage, and field labels. Do not assume the largest number is the amount owed, or the most recent message is from the patient, or the reminder time is the booked time. [{"state":"To: Operations leadership, Larkspur Software
From: Wanjiru Okafor, SaaS operations
Subject: Kindly provided weekly service review and incident register

Dear colleagues,

Please accept my sincere thanks for taking the time to review this unusually thorough service update. I have tried to make the record considerate, transparent, and useful, and I would be most grateful if any omissions could be brought to my attention. The following report covers the service review week, the incident register, customer communications, maintenance notes, handoffs, and the supporting appendices. All figures refer to the fictional service environment described here.

Executive overview

The operations desk recorded three categories of customer-impacting incident during the review week: access interruptions, delayed event processing, and dashboard display faults. The register contains 7 access-interruption records, 6 delayed-processing records, and 5 dashboard-fault records. These are distinct records, not overlapping labels: each record is assigned one primary category. Please note that the separate monitoring observations in Appendix C are not additional incidents and should not be added to the incident register. The monitoring observations repeat some incident symptoms for diagnostic purposes.

The team is grateful to the customer success colleagues for relaying customer comments with care. Customers asked for service explanations and status updates, and several thanked the team for its patience. No customer request for a refund is recorded in the register. The report does not infer requests from dissatisfaction, service impact, or a question about billing; only an explicitly recorded request is treated as a request.

The operational record is intended to be self-contained. The totals and categories stated in the incident register are the authoritative counts for this weekly review. Ticket references in later sections point back to those records; they do not create extra incidents. Where a paragraph mentions multiple symptoms, the register’s primary category remains the one used for the reported totals.

Incident register and counting method

For this review, a record is counted once when it has a unique incident reference and is marked customer-impacting. A diagnostic note, a repeated alert, a customer follow-up, or a copied message does not increase the count. The register contains 18 unique customer-impacting records altogether. The total can also be checked by adding the three primary-category counts: 7 access interruptions plus 6 delayed-processing records plus 5 dashboard faults equals 18 records.

The access-interruption category includes records where a user could not sign in or maintain an authenticated session. It contains 7 records. Some customers also described slow pages while reporting access problems, but the register keeps those records in the access category because the primary documented impact was inability to use an authenticated session.

The delayed-processing category contains 6 records. These concern queued events or submitted jobs that completed later than the customer-facing service expectation. A delayed event is not counted again merely because an alert fired more than once. The category total is based on unique incident references, not the number of monitoring notifications.

The dashboard-fault category contains 5 records. These concern incorrect or incomplete display of dashboard information. If a customer refreshed a dashboard repeatedly, the repeated refreshes were not counted as separate incidents. The five records represent five unique references in the incident register.

For avoidance of doubt, the 18-record total is not a count of all messages, alerts, symptoms, or customer replies. It is the sum of the three category counts above. The weekly spreadsheet included 31 monitoring observations, 12 customer follow-up messages, and 9 internal handoff notes. Those figures describe other kinds of entries and must not be substituted for or added to the 18 customer-impacting incident records.

Customer communications

Customer success kindly supplied a concise summary of the questions received. Several customers asked whether their access had been restored, whether delayed events would eventually appear, and whether a dashboard refresh was required. One customer asked whether an invoice line related to the service interruption, but did not ask for repayment or a credit. The team answered that billing would be reviewed separately. This was an inquiry, not a refund request.

The 18 incident records have corresponding customer communication histories where a customer contact was appropriate. Some records contain more than one message, and others contain a single update. The count of communication messages therefore differs from the count of incident records. For this reason, messages are not used as the basis for the total in the incident register.

Please also note that customers’ courteous expressions of disappointment are preserved in the communication notes, but they are not converted into extra incident categories. A comment such as “we would appreciate an explanation” remains an explanation request. It does not by itself mean the customer requested a refund, asked to cancel service, or reported a separate dashboard fault.

The support team’s summary is deliberately cautious. When a customer asked, “Could you kindly confirm the event delay?” the response was recorded as a status inquiry. When a customer said that a screen looked incomplete, the case was assigned to the dashboard category only if it had its own incident reference. A note copied into another record does not create another unique incident.

Access and authentication details

The 7 access-interruption records were reviewed with the identity-service team. The team compared authentication logs, customer reports, and the service desk register. The review found a variety of symptoms, including failed sign-in attempts, expired sessions, and intermittent access after a successful login. These symptom descriptions assist troubleshooting but do not alter the register’s category count.

The first group of access records involved sign-in attempts that did not complete. The second group involved sessions that ended unexpectedly. The remaining records described intermittent access. Each group is already represented within the stated total of 7. No additional count should be derived by counting each symptom phrase in the narrative.

The identity-service team confirmed that the access records use unique references. Where a customer reported the same difficulty again in a follow-up, the support agent linked the follow-up to the existing reference. The follow-up is useful context, but it is not another incident for the purposes of this report. Similarly, internal testing that reproduced a sign-in problem is diagnostic work and is not a separate customer-impacting record.

The team would like to thank the customer success staff for asking permission before sharing account details with engineering. The notes in this report omit sensitive account information and retain only the operational facts required to explain the weekly count. Please let us know if a more detailed, appropriately restricted audit view would be helpful.

Delayed-processing details

The 6 delayed-processing records were checked against the event queue. In each case, the record was assigned to the delayed-processing category because the submitted work was completed later than expected. The team reviewed queue depth, processing status, and the customer-facing event history. It did not count each queued item as a separate incident: the category total reflects incident references, not jobs, events, retries, or alerts.

A single record may include several affected events. Conversely, several monitoring observations may refer to the same incident. The six records are therefore the authoritative count for the category. The queue review is included to make the classification understandable, not to introduce a second counting method.

Some customers asked whether missing events had been permanently lost. The operations team replied that the records showed delayed completion, and it advised customers to check the event history after processing finished. Those questions are not requests for refunds. No record in this category includes a documented request for a refund, even where a customer expressed concern about the time spent waiting.

The event team kindly checked the entries twice and reconciled them with the incident register. The team also reviewed duplicate alert suppression, retry behavior, and the handoff notes. These checks were useful to the investigation but were not counted as extra customer-impacting incidents. A retry is a processing action; an alert is a monitoring observation; a handoff is a note. None is an additional incident reference merely by being mentioned here.

Dashboard details

The 5 dashboard-fault records were reviewed by the reporting-service team. The reported symptoms included incomplete panels, values that did not refresh immediately, and a display that required another load. The category includes 5 unique customer-impacting references. It does not include internal dashboard tests, screenshots copied into a ticket, or repeated customer refreshes.

The team compared the customer-facing report with the underlying event records. In some instances the underlying data was available even though the display had not yet updated. That distinction helped the team route the work correctly. The five records nevertheless remain dashboard faults because the customer-visible issue concerned the display. No additional record is created for each panel or each refresh mentioned in a customer message.

The dashboard group’s notes include 14 screenshots and 8 internal review comments. These numbers are useful for understanding the investigation workload, but they are not incident counts. A screenshot can document a symptom without constituting a new incident, and a comment can describe a review without constituting customer impact. The incident register continues to show 5 dashboard-fault records.

Maintenance and service health notes

The service team conducted routine checks during the review week. These checks included a review of deployment status, a check of the authentication gateway, a review of the queue dashboard, and a verification that the reporting service was publishing its normal health indicators. The checks were completed politely and carefully, with each team thanking the others for timely responses.

Routine maintenance is recorded separately from customer-impacting incidents. A maintenance note may mention a service area that also appears in an incident record, but the mention does not increase the incident total. The operations team found no basis for changing the three category counts during its maintenance review.

The monitoring group also reviewed a set of 31 observations. Some observations related to the 18 incident records; others were routine checks or repeated signals. They were retained for technical analysis. They are not a substitute for the incident register and should not be interpreted as 31 separate customer-impacting incidents. In particular, an alert occurring repeatedly during one incident does not create a new unique incident reference each time.

A separate internal checklist contained 4 routine maintenance items. Each item was marked complete. These items are not among the customer-impacting records. The checklist is included here because a weekly operational summary is more useful when readers can see which activities were routine and which were incident response.

Handoffs and review process

The incident desk prepared the register, customer success reviewed the communication summaries, and engineering checked the technical categories. The teams used courteous handoffs and requested confirmation when a record was unclear. The review process resulted in no changes to the stated category counts.

There were 9 internal handoff notes. Some handoffs refer to more than one incident, and some incidents have more than one handoff. The handoff count should not be added to the incident total. A handoff documents coordination between teams, rather than a new customer-impacting event.

The team took particular care to distinguish an incident reference from a message about an incident. A customer reply, agent update, engineering note, monitoring alert, screenshot, or meeting comment can all relate to an incident without being a new incident. This convention is applied consistently throughout the report.

Reviewers were asked to check both the category label and the reference number. If a record had an existing reference, the reviewer confirmed whether it belonged to access, delayed processing, or dashboard display. The review did not count words or symptom mentions. This matters because a paragraph can describe more than one technical observation while still relating to a single incident record.

The operations manager kindly requested that the report present a transparent arithmetic check. The requested check is as follows: access interruptions, 7; delayed processing, 6; dashboard faults, 5; combined customer-impacting records, 18. The arithmetic is 7 + 6 + 5 = 18. The separate totals of 31 monitoring observations, 12 customer follow-up messages, and 9 handoff notes are contextual administrative counts only.

Appendix A: Register reconciliation

The register reconciliation was performed by comparing the unique incident references in the weekly export with the reviewed category list. The access list contained 7 references. The delayed-processing list contained 6 references. The dashboard list contained 5 references. The lists did not overlap because each reference was assigned exactly one primary category for the purposes of this summary.

The reconciliation did not treat a status change as a new reference. If an incident moved from investigating to monitoring and then to resolved, it continued to be counted once. If a customer contacted the desk again about the same reference, the later communication stayed attached to the original record. If an engineer performed another diagnostic check, that check remained an internal note.

The reconciliation also did not treat a repeated observation as a separate incident. An observation may be retained more than once for technical reasons, particularly when separate monitoring systems capture the same service behavior. The appendix therefore distinguishes the incident register from the monitoring log.

The total was checked by two reviewers. One reviewer counted references in each category; another reviewer added the category counts. Both reviews produced 18. The check is provided for clarity and does not imply that there were 18 messages or 18 alerts. The only figure meant by “customer-impacting incident records” in this report is the sum of the three primary-category counts.

A reconciliation worksheet also includes the following contextual figures: 31 observations, 12 customer follow-up messages, 9 handoff notes, 14 screenshots, 8 internal review comments, and 4 routine maintenance checklist items. Those entries have different definitions and are not added to the 18 incident records. The number 31 is especially easy to misread if the monitoring appendix is viewed without the category register, so the distinction is repeated here with appreciation for the reader’s attention.

Appendix B: Customer-care summary

The customer-care team reviewed the messages associated with the incidents. It recorded the type of question asked, the response provided, and whether a follow-up was needed. The review was intended to help the operations team understand communication needs; it did not modify the incident classification.

Customers requested explanations, restoration updates, and confirmation of processing status. A customer asking whether a bill would be reviewed is not automatically asking for a refund. The notes show no explicit customer request to return money, reverse a payment, issue a refund, or provide a credit. The team has therefore not recorded any refund request in this weekly summary.

The distinction is important because one customer asked whether an invoice line was related to the interruption. The agent answered that the billing team could review the line. The customer did not then request repayment. Another customer asked when a delayed event would appear. That was recorded as a status question. A third customer thanked the agent and asked for an explanation of a dashboard display. None of those communications is a refund request.

The report uses a narrow, evidence-based approach: a refund request is present only when the customer explicitly asks for a refund or equivalent return of payment. Dissatisfaction alone is not enough. A request to investigate a charge is not, without more, a request to refund it. A question about service quality is not a request to refund it. No customer communication in the reviewed register meets that definition.

The team is very grateful to the customer success colleagues for preserving the distinction between a customer’s question and a customer’s requested remedy. This careful recording supports consistent reporting and helps avoid overstating what customers asked for.

Appendix C: Monitoring log interpretation

The monitoring log contains 31 observations. It includes observations from authentication checks, event-queue checks, and reporting-service checks. These observations have timestamps and technical details, and some are associated with the customer-impacting references in the weekly register. They are not all unique customer-impacting incidents.

The monitoring log is an operational aid. A monitor can observe a symptom, repeat an observation, or record that a condition has cleared. Those entries may all be useful, but the count of observations cannot be used as the count of incidents. For this report, the three category totals are used instead.

In the authentication portion of the log, some checks refer to an access reference more than once. In the event-queue portion, multiple observations can refer to one delayed-processing reference. In the dashboard portion, a check may be repeated after a display refresh. These are ordinary features of a monitoring record and do not change the unique-reference count.

The log also contains routine healthy-state observations. Those are not customer-impacting incidents. A successful check is useful evidence that the service is operating, but it is not an incident. The category register remains the appropriate source for the total of customer-impacting records.

Appendix D: Communication and handoff definitions

A customer follow-up message is a message sent by a customer after an earlier contact. The weekly communication summary records 12 such messages. Some relate to an incident reference and some ask for clarification after an earlier update. The number is not a count of incidents.

An internal handoff note records a transfer or coordination between staff members. There are 9 such notes in the weekly review. One handoff can include context about several records, and one record can prompt more than one handoff. The handoff total is not an incident count and is not added to the category totals.

A screenshot is a captured view of a screen. Fourteen screenshots were retained for review. A screenshot may illustrate an issue, but it is not a unique incident reference. An internal review comment is a note made by a reviewer; there are 8 comments in the summary. Comments do not count as incidents.

The maintenance checklist contains 4 routine items. The team marked each item complete. These are scheduled operational tasks, not customer-impacting incidents. The team included them so leadership can see that routine service checks continued while incident review was underway.

The definitions above are included with particular care because this report contains several numbers that describe different things. The figures should be read according to their labels. The number 18 is the count of customer-impacting incident records. The number 31 is the count of monitoring observations. The number 12 is the count of customer follow-up messages. The number 9 is the count of handoff notes. The number 14 is the count of screenshots, the number 8 is the count of internal review comments, and the number 4 is the count of maintenance checklist items.

Appendix E: Reviewer notes and assurance

Reviewers were asked to confirm that each incident reference appeared once in the category register and that every reference had one primary category. They also checked that customer communication notes were not mistakenly copied into the incident count. The review was completed with thanks to the teams who contributed the required information.

The arithmetic was checked directly: 7 access records plus 6 delayed-processing records gives 13; 13 plus 5 dashboard records gives 18. This is the final customer-impacting incident-record total for the week. 04 Aug, 08:17 — New request R-8041 received for Chiara Okafor, 11 Aug at 09:30, Northwind Foods Clinic, consultation room 2. Patient selected “request appointment”; no payment was collected at this stage. The system sent an acknowledgement link. Status: pending. At 08:22 the link was opened, but the acknowledgement payload was incomplete. Status remained pending. An automated reminder was scheduled for 06 Aug.

04 Aug, 09:41 — Request R-8042 received for Beatriz Tanaka, 12 Aug at 10:00, treatment room 1. Staff member QP-07, Quentin Petrov, applied an override after checking the referral. HANDWRITTEN-STYLE NOTE, typed by office clerk
At 07:22 I meet Neri near the gate. He say platform stops about halfway when carrying pallet. No one hurt. He show me control button and makes demonstration with empty platform. It rises but pauses two times. When lowered, it comes down smooth. He say problem happen yesterday also, then driver reset breaker and it work for one trip. Today breaker was not reset before I arrive. I ask if he wants a new gate. He says no, first find reason and give repair recommendation. He does not ask for refund or payment adjustment.

I check the warning sticker: rated capacity is 1,600 kilograms. Pallet used for the test has a printed weight card 420 kilograms. The gate does not stop because of load limit. I ask the warehouse worker to move pallet away before opening the control cover. Safety cone is put behind truck. I do not enter under the raised platform. The platform is lowered and power isolated before inspection. These steps are in service record because dispatch wants safety notes, not because customer has made a safety complaint.

The handheld meter reads 24.1 volts at battery terminals with engine off and 27.8 volts while engine is running. The service card says normal charging band for this model is 26.0 to 28.5 volts with engine running. The card is for model LT-7 only; this truck has model LT-7. Battery voltage at rest is not the charging test. The meter display briefly flashes 23.9 when I move a lead, then settles to 24.1. I tighten the lead and repeat. It remains 24.1.

On the outside of the pump enclosure there is a label dated 18 March, signed by a previous technician. It says “hydraulic fluid checked, no visible leak.” It does not say the present lift problem is fixed. Today I see a small damp mark around the return-hose coupling. I clean it with cloth, run the gate twice without load, and see fresh fluid at the same coupling. I take a photograph. The reservoir level is just above the lower mark. No fluid is on the warehouse floor. Neri says there was no spill before my visit.

The harness plug at the control box is seated but its latch is cracked. I gently move the harness while the platform is down and power is isolated. The latch does not hold securely. A parts label in the van says a replacement latch kit is available, but the part itself is not on the truck. I do not fit an unapproved substitute. I tell Neri a qualified repair should replace the latch and inspect the connector pins. He says he understands and asks that the truck not be used with a loaded gate until dispatch gives instruction.

I also inspect the charging circuit because the driver mentioned a breaker reset. No open fuse is found. Fuse F3 is rated 15 A and installed fuse is 15 A. A spare 20 A fuse in the cab is not installed; I leave it untouched and note it as a spare, not as a repair. The breaker handle is firm.
