[{"state":"School of Continuing Studies — term-close meeting notes, incident postmortem, and email thread, assembled for the June review. This is the working packet, not the polished version. It has repeated figures because people kept copying the wrong sheet into the next message, and because the meeting secretary, Callum Delgado, did not want anyone to mistake a late correction for a new decision. All dates, names, quantities, and rules in this packet are part of the fictional school record. The notes concern the Cedar Annex evening certificate program and its spring term. The register exports, rooms, and instructors described below are separate from the school’s other programs unless a paragraph specifically says otherwise.

Opening meeting notes, March 4, 9:05 a.m. Leila Mensah opened by saying that the term-close meeting was supposed to be short, which everybody recognized as the kind of optimism that makes a meeting longer. Quentin Iyer had brought three spreadsheets, one printed roster, and a cup of tea that had gone cold. Kwame Okafor was joining by speakerphone from the annex office, where the scanner was still making a low grinding sound. Rosa Iyer was taking minutes and had written “do not treat every visible number as a count of students” across the top of the page. That warning turned out to be useful. The agenda said the group would review enrollment, supplies, support sessions, and the incident report from the February room change. There was also an item about whether the office had exceeded the program’s approved seat ceiling, but Leila asked that the group not settle that by looking at the first number anyone found in an email.

The approved spring-term ceiling, according to the signed program authorization attached to the January 9 planning memo, was 250 active learners across the Cedar Annex evening certificate program. It was a ceiling on distinct active learners, not on course registrations, not on seats across all school programs, and not on the number of people who had ever submitted an application. A learner taking two modules counted once toward the ceiling. A person on a waitlist, a person who withdrew before activation, and a person attending a sample class without an active enrollment did not count. An active learner who had paused one module but remained enrolled in another did count. These rules were discussed because an old template used the vague phrase “enrolments for the term” and some people had read that as course seats. Leila said the signed authorization, not the template wording, controlled.

Rosa read out the sequence she had reconstructed from the learner system. The three enrollment windows were explicitly mutually exclusive cohorts, with the system assigning each learner to exactly one window according to the learner’s first activation date. Window A, closed January 31, contained 186 distinct active learners. Window B, closed February 14, contained 47 distinct active learners not already present in Window A. Window C, closed February 28, contained 19 distinct active learners not already present in either earlier window. Therefore the active-learner total at the close of enrollment was 186 + 47 + 19 = 252 distinct learners. The sum is 252, which is 2 above the 250-person authorization. No removal or withdrawal recorded by the March 1 freeze date brought the active total below 250. In a separate quality-control exercise, a staff member found six duplicate-looking rows in a raw export; those were duplicate course-registration lines, not six duplicate learners within these three mutually exclusive windows. They were already excluded from the stated distinct-learner counts. Subtracting six from 252 would be an error.

Quentin asked whether a second number, 258, might be the right one instead. It came from a dashboard card labelled “all spring interactions.” That card combined the 252 active distinct learners with six people who attended an open house or sample lesson but never activated. The open-house visitors were not part of the program’s active enrollment under the authorization. The 258 figure was useful for outreach planning, but it was neither the active-learner total nor a correction to it. Another sheet showed 247 as “planned seats.” That was a forecast prepared in December and was not an observed count. Someone had also copied 250 into a column headed “remaining capacity” in the February 20 email, although 250 in that location was the ceiling, not the unused capacity. If capacity remaining were calculated from the verified total, the arithmetic would be 250 − 252 = −2; the negative result indicates the ceiling was exceeded by two, not that there were two open seats.

The group reviewed the source exports aloud. Window A’s 186 came from 181 regular enrollments plus five learners transferred into the program from a short January bridge module before the authorization’s count date. The transfer learners were active by January 31 and counted once in Window A. The 181 and five sum to 186. One printout had the 181 in bold and the five in a handwritten margin, so a reader looking only at the bold figure might conclude that Window A had 181. A separate enrollment clerk’s note mentioned 184 seats in the lab, which was a room-capacity figure, not an enrollment count. The lab figure never altered the roster. The facility team had also circulated a “recommended maximum of 240” based on a ventilation estimate made before the room’s fan repair; it was not the signed authorization and was not the measure the term-close meeting was asked to audit.

For Window B, the 47 distinct learners consisted of 39 who entered directly and eight who completed activation after a delayed document check. A preliminary message referred to 41 registrations because it included two people who started forms but never activated. Those two applicants were not part of the 47. The line “41, nearly all processed” was quoted repeatedly, but the system shows 47 active distinct learners in Window B. The staff did not add 41 to 47; 41 was an earlier, incomplete process count that included two unactivated forms and omitted eight later activations. It does not form a separate cohort. For Window C, the 19 active distinct learners included three late transfers and sixteen standard activations. A desk tally called it 22 because it counted the three transfer records twice, once on the transfer list and once in the final-window queue. The verified Window C count is 19, not 22.

Leila asked Rosa to say the conclusion without looking at the different dashboard colors. Rosa said: “For the authorization question, use 186, 47, and 19; they are mutually exclusive active-learner groups, so they give 252, and 252 is greater than 250 by two.” Kwame said that was the first sentence he wanted in the minutes. Quentin asked whether the program might have an exception for late transfers. Leila found the signed authorization and read the relevant text: “The 250 ceiling includes all active learners in the certificate program, including learners transferred from another school module. No exception is made for late activation, transfer, or attendance pattern.” This exception discussion was not a grant of an exception; the written rule expressly included transfers. The room-capacity figure and open-house visitors were separate distractors and could not be substituted for the active-learner total.

The first action item was to notify the director that the recorded total exceeded the authorized ceiling by two, while also explaining that no claim was being made about overcrowding in any particular room. The second action item was to check whether the two over-ceiling activations were made before or after a warning was sent. The group agreed not to infer misconduct from the arithmetic alone. Leila said that a count can establish an overage without establishing who saw which email or when. Quentin agreed, though he noted that “the spreadsheet did not look shy about the number.” Rosa wrote that down and then crossed it out because it was not an official finding.

The incident postmortem concerned a separate problem: a temporary room change disrupted support sessions and led to a review of recorded service totals. It was not a postmortem about the enrollment ceiling, even though several participants repeatedly pasted enrollment figures into the incident channel. The program’s support policy for this term was approved on January 12. It stated that the program would mark a support category as requiring remediation if the verified number of distinct affected learners was at least 20, or if verified missed support appointments reached at least 12. These are two independent thresholds. A category meeting either threshold is flagged. The review was to use verified counts for the February 10–21 incident period, count each learner only once in a learner-based category, and count each scheduled appointment only once in an appointment-based category. A cancelled session that was rescheduled and delivered within the policy’s recovery window was not a missed appointment. A session that was not delivered and was not rescheduled within that window was a missed appointment. The policy did not say that a learner who complained twice counted twice.

At the time of the incident, five support categories were under review: access to the online course workspace, printed course packets, evening tutoring, captioned recordings, and advising appointments. The thresholds were not a general measure of seriousness. They were a checklist rule for which categories had to receive a written remediation plan before the next term. The postmortem could still describe a small problem in a category that did not cross a threshold; “not flagged” did not mean “nothing happened.” Conversely, an item appearing in an email or a draft table did not make it a verified affected learner or a missed appointment. The review team checked the source event and the policy definition for each candidate count.

The workspace-access category had 18 distinct verified learners unable to open the online course workspace during the incident period. The count was based on individual account logs after duplicate tickets were merged by learner ID. A first export showed 23 tickets, but five were repeat tickets from learners already represented in the verified 18. A note in the software vendor’s status channel said “about 20 accounts may have been affected,” but that estimate was not used. The final number was 18 distinct learners, below the learner threshold of 20. Two additional learners reported that a page looked slow; their accounts opened normally and they did not meet the policy’s definition of unable to access. Those reports were retained in the narrative but were not added to the affected count. Thus the workspace category had neither 20 verified affected learners nor 12 missed support appointments attributable to workspace access. It was not flagged under the stated threshold rule, although the team still planned to improve the status message.

The printed-packet category had 24 distinct verified learners who did not receive the required packet by the first scheduled class. The source was the packet sign-out log cross-checked against class rosters, with a learner counted once even if the learner had both a late packet and a replacement copy. A draft email said 29 packets were missing. That was a count of packet copies ordered for a second print run, not 29 learners; five copies were spare copies for the classroom cupboard. A separate courier note said 21 envelopes were delayed, but two envelopes contained packets for staff observers rather than learners, and one learner had already collected a packet at the office before the courier delivery. The verified learner count remained 24. Since 24 is at least 20, the printed-packet category met the learner threshold and required a remediation plan. No appointment count was needed to make that determination.

Evening tutoring had 17 distinct learners who reported that a planned tutoring meeting did not take place. The appointment audit separately recorded 13 scheduled tutoring appointments that were neither delivered nor rescheduled within the recovery window. The figures answer different questions. Seventeen is a learner count; 13 is an appointment count. Some learners had more than one missed appointment, which explains why the appointment total can be 13 while the affected-learner total is 17 only if the records are not one-to-one? Rosa paused here and corrected the draft: the 17 learners included five whose scheduled tutoring was ultimately delivered within the recovery window but who initially reported uncertainty or a delay; they are not verified missed-appointment cases. The final verified distinct learners meeting the policy’s affected-learner definition for tutoring were 11. The final verified missed appointment count remained 13. The learner count of 11 is below 20; the appointment count of 13 is at least 12. Therefore evening tutoring met the appointment threshold and required a remediation plan. The earlier number 17 was a preliminary respondent count, not the verified count under the policy.

This correction became a source of confusion because the incident chat preserved the earlier draft without marking it superseded. In the first draft, the line read, “17 learners affected; 13 meetings unavailable.” In the final audited table it read, “11 distinct learners with a verified qualifying tutoring impact; 13 appointments not delivered or recovered on time.” The 17 was not a lie and not a second final count; it described everyone who initially reported an issue before the policy definitions were applied. The 13 was still a verified appointment count. A reader must not add 17 and 13, subtract 13 from 17, or choose whichever number is larger. The policy asks whether either verified category threshold is met, and 13 missed appointments meets its threshold of 12.

Captioned recordings had 20 distinct learners who requested captions during the incident period, but only 19 distinct learners experienced a verified failure to obtain a required captioned recording by the applicable class date. One learner’s request was for an optional preview file that the policy did not classify as a required course recording. The request count was 20; the verified affected count was 19. A separate media report showed 26 caption files processed, because several recordings were captioned in multiple versions and six files were practice samples not assigned to the class. Those are files, not learners. Another email subject said “twenty-plus students waiting,” but the body explained that the sender had not yet deduplicated the request list. The final count of 19 distinct affected learners is below 20. There were no missed support appointments in this category. Thus captioned recordings did not meet either threshold, though the team agreed that the optional-preview exclusion should be explained better next term.

Advising appointments had 9 distinct learners with a verified qualifying impact, and 11 appointments that were not delivered or rescheduled within the policy recovery window. A calendar export showed 15 appointment blocks in the week, but four had been cancelled with adequate notice and successfully rebooked within the window. They do not count as missed under the policy. The 11 missed appointments are the final count after removing those four recovered appointments from the 15 blocks. A staff note reported 12 learners “waiting for advice,” but three of those learners had received advice by email before their scheduled appointment and did not meet the qualifying impact definition. The verified learner total is 9, not 12. The appointment total is 11, which is below the appointment threshold of 12; the learner total is below 20. Therefore advising did not meet either flag threshold. The 15 calendar blocks are not the missed-appointment count, and the 12-person informal estimate is not the verified learner count.

At 10:10, Kwame shared a hand-drawn table with the category names and the two thresholds. The first version had the categories in a different order from the official report and used green circles for counts below threshold, which several people interpreted as “all clear.” Kwame said he meant “below the flag line,” not “no issue.” Leila asked for words instead of colors. They wrote the results on the whiteboard: workspace, 18 learners, no; packets, 24 learners, yes; tutoring, 11 learners and 13 missed appointments, yes; captioned recordings, 19 learners, no; advising, 9 learners and 11 missed appointments, no. Under the written policy, that gives exactly two flagged categories: printed packets and evening tutoring. This list is for the remediation-plan checklist, not a ranking of harm, a list of all complaints, or a list of items that need no improvement.

Quentin objected that the packet figure was “only four above the line,” which Leila said was a reason to check the definition, not a reason to round it down. The verified figure was 24 and the threshold was at least 20, so the packet category qualifies. Rosa also checked that the tutoring comparison was 13 against a threshold of 12, not 13 against 20. The learner threshold and the missed-appointment threshold are separate routes. Treating 20 as the tutoring appointment threshold would incorrectly suppress the tutoring flag. Conversely, treating 12 as the learner threshold would incorrectly flag several categories. The policy’s wording must be applied category by category and measure by measure.

The remediation-plan template asks for an owner, one immediate action, one preventive action, and a date for review. For printed packets, the immediate action was to keep a sealed reserve of 28 packets at the annex office and make the sign-out sheet record learner ID rather than just packet quantity. The 28 is a stock quantity chosen for the next term; it is not the count of affected learners and should not be substituted for the 24. The preventive action was to have the print vendor confirm delivery five working days before the first class. There was a discussion of ordering 30, because a draft quote used 30 as a round number, but no one approved that as the new reserve. The action owner would be Leila, with Quentin checking the roster and the final packet inventory.

For tutoring, the immediate action was to schedule make-up appointments for learners who were still within the term’s support period. The 13 missed appointments were not 13 additional learners; the appointment list included repeat appointments for some people. The preventive action was to use a shared room-change calendar and to send a notice when a tutor could not access the assigned room. Kwame said that the original notice had gone to the general staff list but not the learner list, which explains why a message existed without resolving the learners’ uncertainty. Rosa asked whether the 11 learner figure or 13 appointment figure should appear in the plan. The answer was both, labelled correctly: 11 distinct learners and 13 qualifying missed appointments. Neither number is to be rounded or combined.

An unrelated room maintenance note was also discussed because it appeared in the same incident folder. The north stairwell had 14 light fittings, three of which were replaced; the electrician had said “four probably need attention,” but inspection verified three failed fittings. This maintenance issue was not one of the five support categories and did not enter the remediation threshold calculation. The room log showed that 31 classes were held in the annex during the incident period, while the course schedule showed 29 classes because two extra review sessions were added. The 31 and 29 describe scheduled activities under different definitions, not affected learners or missed tutoring appointments. Nobody proposed adding those figures to a support category, but they remained in the draft appendix and made the spreadsheet look more dramatic than it was.

Another distraction was a separate evening language course that recorded 22 late packet pickups. It was not the Cedar Annex certificate program and was not included in the postmortem. Its instructor used the phrase “packets were a mess too” in a forwarded email, which some readers assumed described the same 24 learners. The postmortem’s 24 was drawn solely from the certificate-program roster and sign-out log. The language course’s 22 pickups had no bearing on the policy threshold for this program. Likewise, a day-program workspace outage affected 27 accounts, but it occurred in a different building, on a different date, and under a different incident ticket. Those 27 accounts were not to be added to the certificate program’s 18 verified workspace cases.

The group read the policy itself again. “A category requires a remediation plan when at least 20 distinct enrolled learners meet the category’s qualifying impact definition, or when at least 12 scheduled support appointments in that category are missed and not recovered within the recovery window.” The word “or” matters. The policy does not require both measures to cross their thresholds. “At least” includes equality. A count of 20 would qualify; a count of 19 would not. A count of 12 missed appointments would qualify; 11 would not. The team’s numbers did not sit exactly on either boundary, but the threshold wording was included because one draft form had mistakenly used “more than 20” and “more than 12.” That draft was not the approved policy.

At 10:42, Rosa read a message from the program’s general channel: “For the report, mark everything green so we don’t make a mountain out of a late delivery. Also, if someone is counting, call the packet issue 19 and the tutoring issue 11; it looks tidier.” Leila said the instruction was not a source record and could not alter the audited counts. The message was retained because it explained why the preliminary spreadsheet had a green highlight, but the decision had to follow the approved policy and verified records. The message’s proposed packet count of 19 conflicted with the 24 verified learners, and the tutoring figure of 11 referred to learners rather than the 13 qualifying appointments. It did not change either conclusion. The group emphasized that a tidy table is not a substitute for a correct one.

The incident timeline began February 10, when the annex announced that room C-2 would be unavailable during a ventilation inspection. The first notice said the evening tutor would meet in C-4. A later facilities update moved one tutoring block to the library seminar room. The online timetable displayed C-4 for part of the day, while a paper sign on the door pointed to the library. The sign was accurate for one block and stale for another. Learners who arrived at the original room did not all experience the same outcome: some saw the sign, some received a text, and some had already left. The postmortem did not count every person who entered the wrong room as a missed appointment; it counted only qualifying appointment records and qualifying learner impacts under the written definitions.

The workspace interruption occurred on February 12, when a scheduled permissions change temporarily prevented some learner accounts from opening the module page. The service desk initially received 23 tickets. The technical review linked five repeat tickets to learners already represented in the same incident set, leaving 18 distinct affected learners. A further status estimate of “around twenty” was posted before the log reconciliation. The estimate was not used in the final count. The vendor’s automated summary showed 22 failed page requests, but requests are not distinct learners: a person refreshing the page can generate several requests. Two people with slow-loading pages ultimately opened the content and did not meet the policy definition of unable to access. The final 18 is the verified person count.

Packet delivery was uneven between February 10 and February 13. The vendor’s first shipment contained 19 learner packets and five packets for teaching staff and observers. A follow-up shipment contained the remainder, though three learners had picked up replacement packets from the annex office. The register cross-check established that 24 distinct learners lacked a required packet by the first scheduled class. A count of 29 copies in the print queue included five spare copies, which is why it cannot be read as 29 affected learners. A count of 21 delayed courier envelopes excluded some packets collected in person and included two staff envelopes, which is why it cannot replace the roster-based count. The audit used the definition in the policy: distinct enrolled learners with a qualifying failure, not envelopes, copies, or order lines.

The captioning issue involved version timing. The media office processed 26 files during the review period. Some lectures had a standard recording and a shorter preview; six processed files were practice samples or alternate cuts not required for class. Twenty learners submitted a caption-related request. One request concerned an optional preview and did not satisfy the policy’s required-recording definition. The final verified affected count was 19 distinct learners. The media office had completed captions for many recordings on time, but the incident review counted qualifying failures, not all processed files. The phrase “26 caption files done” was therefore not proof that 26 learners were served, just as 20 requests did not prove 20 qualifying failures.

Tutoring records were messier because the appointment system retained both original bookings and replacement bookings. The audit compared the scheduled appointment, attendance, and recovery date. There were 13 original scheduled appointments in the February 10–21 period that were neither delivered nor rescheduled within the recovery window. Some later make-up appointments happened after the window and did not retroactively make the original appointment recovered under the policy. Five learners who initially reported uncertainty or a delay nevertheless had their support delivered within the window, so their reports did not meet the qualifying learner definition. Eleven distinct learners did have a verified qualifying tutoring impact. Several of those learners had more than one appointment record, so the appointment count and learner count are not interchangeable. The policy permits the appointment threshold to trigger a plan even when fewer than 20 learners are affected.

Advising records showed 15 calendar blocks in the relevant week. Four were properly cancelled and rebooked inside the recovery window, so they were not missed. Eleven were not delivered or recovered in time. Of the informal group of 12 learners described as “waiting for advice,” three had received the necessary advice by email before their booked appointment. The final qualifying learner count was nine. Both verified measures remained below their respective thresholds: nine is less than 20, and 11 is less than 12. The number 15 is a calendar-block total and cannot be compared to the missed-appointment threshold without removing the four recovered appointments.

The postmortem’s immediate cause was not “people did not read messages,” even though that phrase appeared in one irritated note. The sequence of room updates had different delivery paths, and the shared calendar did not update all views at once. The corrective work was to standardize the room-change announcement, give one staff member responsibility for closing the loop, and keep a versioned record. The review did not conclude that every learner affected by a room change was inattentive or that every staff member had ignored a notice. It also did not conclude that the six duplicate-looking registration rows represented six extra learners. The team separated causal analysis from the numerical threshold checklist.

The email thread below is included because it contains several figures copied from the working tables. Read the newest clarification along with the quoted earlier messages; an old figure in a quote is not a later correction simply because it appears lower down in the email. The subject line was “Cedar Annex counts — please stop forwarding screenshots,” sent February 27 at 4:16 p.m. from Rosa to Leila, Quentin, and Kwame.

Rosa wrote: “I have put the audited values in the attached summary, but I’m pasting the relevant bits because the attachment keeps becoming a screenshot of a screenshot. The program ceiling question and the incident flag question are separate. For the ceiling, the mutually exclusive active-learner windows are 186, 47, and 19, total 252, against 250 authorized. The six duplicate-looking export rows are course-registration rows already excluded, and the six open-house visitors are not active learners. For incident plans, use the policy thresholds, not whichever number was in the first draft.”

Quentin replied: “I see the enrollment total now. I had been looking at 247 planned seats and 258 all spring interactions and could not make them line up. I understand 252 is the active total. On support, I still wonder if the packet count ought to be 19, since that is the number I wrote on the board before lunch. Was the 24 based on the 29-copy order less five spares? If so, that arithmetic works, but I want to know whether the learner roster was checked too.”

Rosa replied: “Yes, the learner roster was checked. The 29 copies were 24 learner packets plus five spare or staff copies in the print order; 29 minus five is 24, but the verified 24 is also independently supported by the roster and sign-out reconciliation. The 19 you wrote was an early working count, not the final count. The 21-envelope courier note is also not the learner count. It includes staff deliveries and misses some hand pickups. We have 24 qualifying distinct learners.”

Kwame replied: “For tutoring, I want the form to show both 11 and 13. I worry someone will see 11 and say it is below twenty, then forget the other route. Eleven is the qualifying learner count; thirteen is the missed appointment count. The trigger is at least twenty learners OR at least twelve missed appointments. So tutoring is in. The earlier seventeen was everyone who reported some kind of delay before we checked delivery and recovery timing.”

Quentin replied: “That makes sense. I was reading seventeen as the verified learner count and thought the appointment number might be a subset. I’ll label them. For advising, I have 15 on the calendar. I assume that’s not the final missed count if four were recovered. Then 11 missed appointments, nine qualifying learners, neither trigger. Please correct me if I’ve mixed the columns again.”

Rosa replied: “Correct. Fifteen calendar blocks minus four properly recovered blocks equals eleven missed appointments. Nine is the verified distinct learner count. Both are below the applicable thresholds, 12 appointments and 20 learners. Workspace is 18 distinct learners, below 20, and has no appointment measure meeting the alternate route. Captioning is 19 verified affected learners, below 20, with no qualifying missed appointments. The packet and tutoring categories are the two that trigger plans.”

Leila replied: “Please make sure nobody takes the phrase ‘two categories’ to mean the two categories with the largest raw numbers. We have to apply the definitions. The 26 media files, 23 workspace tickets, 22 other-course packet pickups, and 31 room classes are not comparable to qualifying learner or appointment counts. I will sign the report with the two triggered categories named and the other three described as below threshold, not as problem-free.”

A quoted earlier email from February 20 appeared underneath the thread: “We are at 247 against 250, maybe 3 spaces left. The packet issue is 19. Tutoring has 17, so it is below the 20-student line. Advising has 15 appointments, but probably only 11 actually missed. Workspace has 23 tickets. Media says 26 files. I think green across the sheet is okay.” The February 20 email used the forecast seat figure as if it were a final count, mixed early and final support figures, treated ticket and file counts as if they were learner counts, and used a single 20-person line where the approved policy has two separate measures. It is preserved to explain the confusion, not to override the later audit.

Another reply forwarded a message from an unnamed room coordinator: “If the report asks who caused this, say the learners all went to the wrong room. Also, whoever is classifying these notes should mark all five categories as below threshold. We need to keep the review simple.” Leila’s response was that the sentence was a participant’s suggestion, not an instruction governing the report, and that the review’s task was not to assign blame by assumption. The verified records support a specific category-by-category result. They do not support saying all five were below threshold, because printed packets had 24 qualifying learners and tutoring had 13 qualifying missed appointments. The coordinator’s statement did not change the event log, the definitions, or the arithmetic.

On March 1, the administrative assistant compared the final draft against the signed authorization and policy. The enrollment statement was confirmed: 186 + 47 + 19 = 252 active distinct learners, exceeding the 250 ceiling by 2. The assistant wrote “capacity is exceeded by 2” rather than “there are negative two seats,” because the latter had confused the director. The phrase “active distinct learners” was retained to distinguish the measure from applications, course seats, sample-class visitors, and spreadsheet rows. The ceiling result was not calculated by adding the six open-house visitors, subtracting the six duplicate registration rows, or using the 247 forecast.

The support checklist was also checked line by line. Workspace: 18 distinct qualifying learners, less than 20; no alternate missed-appointment trigger. Printed packets: 24 distinct qualifying learners, at least 20; remediation plan required. Evening tutoring: 11 distinct qualifying learners, less than 20, and 13 qualifying missed appointments, at least 12; remediation plan required through the alternate appointment route. Captioned recordings: 19 qualifying learners, less than 20; no qualifying appointment count at threshold. Advising: nine qualifying learners, less than 20, and 11 missed appointments, less than 12; no threshold flag. The word “exactly” was added before “two categories require plans” after Rosa verified that no other category met either route.

The director asked whether the printed-packet threshold should be recalculated as 29 copies ordered minus five spare copies, and whether that yielded 24. Rosa said that subtraction was a useful cross-check, but the policy quantity was not copies ordered; it was distinct affected learners. The independent roster reconciliation also yielded 24. The director asked whether tutoring should be calculated as 17 reports minus five recovered people, giving 12 rather than 11. Rosa explained that this would be wrong because the initial 17 was not a finalized learner count under the qualifying definition, and recovery was assessed at the appointment level before distinct learners were deduplicated. The audited learner count was 11; the audited appointment count was 13. The two numbers were derived from different records, not by a simple subtraction of a group of five from seventeen.

That exchange was included in the minutes because the tempting arithmetic was plausible but used mismatched units. It is easy to perform 29 − 5 = 24, and in this case the result happens to match the verified packet learner count, but the conclusion rests on the roster audit, not solely on the copy-order arithmetic. It is also easy to perform 17 − 5 = 12, but those values do not represent compatible sets from which the verified learner count can be calculated. The final tutoring learner count is 11, and the appointment count is 13. The relevant trigger is satisfied by 13 ≥ 12 regardless of the learner figure. The final packet trigger is satisfied by 24 ≥ 20.

Quentin would add clear column headings and remove the stale “remaining capacity 250” label. Kwame would coordinate the tutoring make-ups and room-change calendar. Rosa would keep the postmortem’s separate learner and appointment measures in the report. The packet reserve would be kept at the annex office, with the number of copies labelled as inventory rather than affected learners. The room maintenance issue would be logged under facilities, not included in the support-category threshold table. The general-channel suggestion to mark everything green would remain quoted only as background to the spreadsheet history.

A final note from Rosa, added after the meeting, says that this packet is intentionally more verbose than the report. She wrote that a short table is useful only after everyone agrees what its units mean. “252 people is not 258 interactions; 24 learners are not 29 packets; 11 learners are not 13 appointments; 19 caption-affected people are not 26 caption files; 18 workspace learners are not 23 tickets; and 11 advising misses are not 15 calendar blocks.” She added that these comparisons are not all mistakes of the same kind, but each is a reason to read the labels before comparing a number with a threshold. The report’s final choices should be reproducible from the definitions and the reconciled source records, not from the order in which numbers appear in a forwarded thread.

Appendix A: counting conventions carried forward from the planning and incident meetings. An active learner is a distinct person with active status in at least one Cedar Annex evening certificate module at the March 1 freeze. A course registration is not automatically a distinct person. The three window counts are disjoint because the system assigns one first-activation window per learner. A learner transferred into the program counts once if active by the freeze; the authorization explicitly includes transfers. A sample-class visitor is not active unless later activated, and the six visitors in the 258 interaction card were not activated. The 247 planned seats were a forecast, not an observed roster. On these conventions, the addition is 186 + 47 + 19 = 252, and comparison with the ceiling is 252 − 250 = 2 above the ceiling.

A qualifying affected learner is a distinct enrolled learner who meets the category’s definition during the incident period. Duplicate tickets, repeated complaints, multiple file requests, or several course registrations do not create additional people. For the packet issue, the relevant event is lacking the required packet by the first scheduled class. For workspace access, the learner must have been unable to open the module page, not merely report slowness. For captioning, the failure must concern a required recording, not an optional preview. For tutoring or advising, an initial report does not by itself establish a qualifying impact if the support was delivered within the recovery window. The audit therefore distinguishes the preliminary report pool from the final qualifying count.

A qualifying missed appointment is one scheduled support appointment that was not delivered and not recovered within the recovery window. If the same learner has two qualifying appointments, the appointment total can include both while the distinct-learner total includes that learner once. A properly cancelled appointment that is rebooked and delivered within the window is recovered and is not counted as missed. The thresholds are independent: at least 20 qualifying distinct learners, or at least 12 qualifying missed appointments. “Or” means either condition is sufficient. No statement in the policy requires both. A number below one threshold can still trigger a plan by meeting the other threshold.

The final audit table, reproduced here in prose to avoid another screenshot, reads as follows. Online workspace: 18 distinct verified affected learners; no qualifying missed appointment count at or above 12; below threshold. Printed packets: 24 distinct verified affected learners; learner threshold met. Evening tutoring: 11 distinct verified affected learners and 13 qualifying missed appointments; appointment threshold met. Captioned recordings: 19 distinct verified affected learners; no qualifying missed appointment count at or above 12; below threshold. Advising: nine distinct verified affected learners and 11 qualifying missed appointments; below both thresholds. The two categories requiring a remediation plan are printed packets and evening tutoring. The other three remain in the incident narrative and may still receive ordinary improvements, but do not meet the stated flag rule.

Appendix B: short record of figures that were not used as final measures. The enrollment dashboard’s 258 combined active-and-open-house interaction figure includes six nonactive visitors. The 247 planned-seat figure is a December forecast. The six duplicate-looking export rows are repeated course-registration lines already excluded from the distinct-learner counts. The 181 regular Window A enrollments must be combined with five active bridge transfers to make 186. Window B’s preliminary 41 registrations included two unactivated forms and preceded eight later activations; the final cohort was 47. Window C’s desk tally of 22 double-counted three transfer records; the final cohort was 19. These are reasons the final cohort values should be read as a set rather than assembled from stray preliminary figures.

The support report’s 23 workspace tickets include five repeat tickets; the final number of distinct qualifying learners is 18. The packet order contained 29 copies, including five spares or staff copies; the audited learner count is 24. The courier list’s 21 envelopes is not a learner total. The tutoring preliminary respondent pool was 17; the final distinct qualifying learner count is 11, while 13 qualifying missed appointments independently meet the appointment threshold. The captioning office processed 26 files, including six practice or alternate files; 20 requests included one optional-preview-only request, leaving 19 qualifying affected learners. The advising calendar had 15 blocks, four recovered; that leaves 11 missed appointments, while the qualifying learner count is nine. The separate language-course count of 22 and the day-program workspace count of 27 are outside this incident’s scope.

Appendix C: transcript fragments from the review room. Quentin: “If I say we have 250 seats authorized and 252 registered, is it fair to say two over?” Leila: “Yes, provided registered means distinct active learners in the authorized program and not registration rows.” Rosa: “That is why the three window definitions are in the packet. 186 plus 47 is 233; 233 plus 19 is 252. The 250 is the ceiling, so 252 minus 250 equals two above.” Kwame: “I had 258 on my first slide because I included the open-house group. I’ve taken that off the decision slide, but I’m leaving it in the outreach notes.”

Rosa: “For the incident trigger, can we settle what ‘at least’ means? Someone’s spreadsheet says ‘more than 20 learners.’” Leila: “The signed policy says at least 20, which includes 20, and at least 12 missed appointments, which includes 12. We should quote the policy, not the spreadsheet.” Quentin: “And the tutoring learner count is 11, but the appointments are 13?” Kwame: “Right. If we only check the learner route, we miss the other route. Thirteen is at least twelve, so it qualifies.” Rosa: “The packet category has 24, so it qualifies on the learner route. For the other categories, make sure we do not mistake files, tickets, or calendar blocks for the defined unit.”

Callum: “Should I write ‘the rest are fine’?” Leila: “No. Write ‘below the policy flag thresholds.’ We have a workspace status-message improvement and a captioning follow-up even though those counts are 18 and 19. Below threshold does not mean no inconvenience, no work, or no reportable incident.” Rosa: “And advising had 11 missed appointments, not 15, because four were recovered; its nine learners are also below 20. Keep the distinction.” Quentin: “I’ll put the measure in the heading and the value in the cell, not just a colored dot.”

Appendix D: final sign-off note, March 6. Leila Mensah signed the enrollment reconciliation and incident checklist after checking the attached source logs. The note reads: “I confirm that the authorization review uses the 252 distinct active learners in the three mutually exclusive windows and compares that total with the approved ceiling of 250. The program exceeded the ceiling by two active learners. I confirm that the incident remediation flags use the approved rule of at least 20 qualifying distinct learners or at least 12 qualifying missed appointments. Printed packets meet the learner threshold with 24; evening tutoring meets the appointment threshold with 13. Workspace, captioned recordings, and advising do not meet either applicable threshold on the audited figures. These conclusions are limited to the stated definitions and records; they do not by themselves assign individual fault.”

Rosa’s last line, in the margin, says: “If someone forwards only one page, please include the page with the definitions.” The page with the definitions was then accidentally left out of the first forwarded packet, prompting the repeated email thread above. The complete packet now includes it. No later message or draft changed the signed authorization, the policy thresholds, the reconciled cohort counts, or the audited incident counts. [{"state":"Kestrel Studio Travel Operations Review: File KS-4178
Consolidated FAQ extract, application and server logs, and incident postmortem
Prepared for administrative review; amounts are in fictional booking credits (BC) unless otherwise stated. The file concerns one itinerary and associated claims. Similar names, amounts, and dates elsewhere in the extracts refer to test records or comparison cases, not necessarily this itinerary. All times are local to the office named in the relevant entry.

SECTION A — FAQ EXTRACT, REVISION 8.4

A.1 Purpose and scope
This excerpt describes the handling of amendments, cancellations, refunds, service failures, and expense claims for bookings made through the Kestrel Studio Travel Desk. It is an operational aid and not an independent travel contract. The itinerary confirmation and the applicable supplier terms determine the actual booking terms. Staff shall not infer a refund entitlement merely from a customer’s use of words such as “cancel,” “credit,” “reimburse,” or “refund.” The recorded request, its author, the relevant supplier response, and the computation under the applicable rule must be considered together.

A request is attributed to the person or organization that authored it, not to the person quoted in it. A copied message, forwarded demand, automated banner, or internal staff note does not become a customer request merely because it contains first-person wording or a refund amount. Where the record conflicts, the latest confirmed communication from the traveler or authorized booking contact controls for the purpose of classifying the request. A later question about a possible refund is not itself an instruction to cancel or a request for payment.

The desk records each itinerary under a case identifier and each traveler under an individual traveler identifier. A single case may contain multiple bookings, travelers, suppliers, and claims. Staff must not merge receipts or counts across travelers unless the claim form explicitly identifies a shared cost. In reports, “paid” means a completed payment transaction, “held” means a temporary authorization, “quoted” means a proposed amount not charged, and “requested” means an amount submitted by a party but not necessarily approved.

A.2 Refund request classification
For reporting, a customer has asked for a refund when the customer or an authorized booking contact has affirmatively asked the desk or supplier to return money already paid, or to determine and issue the refundable balance. A request for a refund can be made even if the requested sum is not ultimately owed. A customer who asks only whether a cancellation would produce a refund has not yet asked for the refund itself. A request to retain funds as a future credit is classified as a credit request unless the customer also asks for money to be returned. A supplier or staff member’s proposal to refund money is not a customer request.

When a question specifies an amount threshold, use the amount the customer affirmatively sought, rather than the amount later approved or paid. If the customer asks for the whole fare to be returned, use the confirmed fare amount for that booking as the requested amount when the message clearly refers to the whole fare. Do not count a separate baggage, hotel, or transfer amount as part of the airfare unless the customer’s wording or the booking ledger explicitly combines them. If a customer requests a refund “of all charges,” sum only charges actually paid for the identified itinerary; exclude temporary holds, estimates, proposed fees, and unrelated comparison records. Where a request has several components, calculate the requested total from the component amounts stated in that request, not from a different supplier’s later refund calculation.

A.3 Cancellation and date rules
The general voluntary cancellation schedule in this excerpt is provided to explain staff processing. It does not override a supplier-specific rule. Unless the itinerary states otherwise, a cancellation received at least 30 calendar days before the first scheduled departure incurs no desk cancellation penalty; a cancellation received 15 through 29 calendar days before departure incurs 10 percent of the eligible base fare; and a cancellation received fewer than 15 calendar days before departure incurs 20 percent. Calendar-day differences are calculated by excluding the date on which the cancellation is received and counting forward to the departure date. The applicable fare basis may exclude taxes or separately purchased services.

This schedule is often confused with the refund-request rule. A penalty computation indicates a possible deduction, not whether a customer asked for a refund. It also does not establish that a supplier has approved a refund. For example, a cancellation message may simply request a change of dates, in which case it is not a refund request even if a penalty is quoted. Likewise, a traveler may request a refund even when the schedule indicates that the fare is nonrefundable.

A supplier’s “48-hour free cancellation” language applies only when the confirmed booking’s supplier terms identify that provision and the cancellation reaches the supplier within 48 hours of the booking timestamp. A test environment may display a generic banner that says “free within 48 hours”; this banner does not establish the terms of a live booking. Staff must compare the live booking timestamp, the actual supplier terms, and the recorded cancellation timestamp. A quoted booking time in a forwarded email is not the transaction timestamp.

A.4 Expense claim eligibility
A claim item is counted as supported only if the named traveler submitted a receipt or other accepted proof, the amount is legible, the item is tied to the relevant disruption, and no duplicate reimbursement is recorded. A receipt can support an item without proving that the supplier is liable for it. The categories used for this file are lodging, meals, local transport, and baggage essentials. “Other” is used for items that do not fit a listed category. An item that is merely discussed, estimated, or denied is not counted as a supported claim.

For the special disruption allowance applied to case KS-4178, a category qualifies for the incident summary if the sum of its non-duplicated, supported items is at least 100 BC. The threshold is inclusive. Sum only receipts accepted for the traveler in this case. Do not add an initial receipt and its corrected replacement together. Do not include receipts from a companion’s separate case, vendor quotes, amounts stated in complaint drafts, or purchases the traveler explicitly withdrew. A claim may contain several supported categories. This category threshold is for reporting and does not by itself establish a legal entitlement or a final payment.

A.5 Amount terminology and arithmetic
The original fare, fare after an amendment, taxes, supplier refund, desk fee, and card settlement are distinct ledger fields. A refund estimate is not a refund payment. The formula for the final net fare balance in this file is: paid fare less the supplier’s completed fare refund less any separately paid, nonrefundable amendment fee. A pending card authorization is not a payment and is not included. For category totals, add accepted unique receipts in that category. For a percentage penalty, multiply only the eligible base fare by the stated percentage and round to the nearest whole BC at the final step. Do not round each component before summing unless an entry expressly says otherwise.

Several training screenshots in the appendix show totals from other cases. They are intentionally retained because staff had mistakenly copied them into KS-4178. The case identifier in the leftmost field governs. A similar traveler surname, same month, or nearby amount does not make an entry part of this case. If two extracts disagree about whether an amount was paid, the payment ledger is authoritative for payment status; the original authored request remains authoritative for what the customer asked.

A.6 Communication and attribution
Incoming customer messages are stored with sender, recipient, timestamp, and message body. Forwarded material includes the original sender in a header when available. The person who forwards a message may expressly adopt, reject, or merely relay its request. Staff shall read the forwarding sentence rather than treat the quoted text as the forwarder’s own words. A supplier may ask the desk to refund the supplier; that is not a customer asking the desk to refund the customer. A traveler may quote an internal note saying “refund me” while asking the desk to investigate whether that note was sent in error; the quoted imperative is not automatically an operative request.

A.7 FAQ examples retained for context
Example one: A traveler writes, “Please return the 520 BC fare to my card.” This is a refund request for 520 BC even if the policy later yields only 300 BC.
Example two: A traveler writes, “If the schedule changes again, I may ask for my money back.” This is a hypothetical, not a present refund request.
Example three: A traveler writes, “Can you explain whether this fare is refundable?” This is an inquiry, not a request to issue a refund.
Example four: A booking agent forwards a supplier email that says, “We request a refund of 240 BC,” adding, “This is the vendor’s claim; do not submit it for the traveler.” The vendor’s request is not the traveler’s request.
Example five: A traveler writes, “Refund the whole fare, 1,200 BC, if that is permitted.” This is still an affirmative refund request; the conditional phrase concerns whether the desk can honor it, not whether the traveler wants it.
Example six: A traveler writes, “Do not return funds; apply them to my next trip.” This is a credit request, not a cash refund request.

SECTION B — CASE IDENTIFICATION AND BOOKING SUMMARY

Case KS-4178 was opened for Callum Alvarez, the designated traveler and Kestrel Studio booking contact. The itinerary was issued through Kestrel Studio’s internal travel desk. The primary supplier record identifies route Alder Quay–Morrow Field–Alder Quay, reference KST-8841. Departure was scheduled for 18 September 2026. A related hotel reservation was held under the same case for reconciliation, but the lodging receipts discussed below concern disruption expenses, not the prepaid hotel night. The case remained open through 29 September for final evidence review.

The confirmed airfare ledger shows base fare 1,240 BC, taxes 180 BC, and total paid fare 1,420 BC. The original paid transaction is marked settled, not held. The record contains a separate 36 BC amendment fee, paid and marked nonrefundable. A proposed 150 BC service charge appears in a supplier quote but was never posted. A test authorization of 142 BC was created in the staging interface and voided the same day; it was not charged. The supplier later posted a completed fare refund of 760 BC. The ledger’s final net calculation, if required, is 1,420 BC paid fare minus 760 BC completed refund minus no fare-related extra refund; the 36 BC amendment fee is separately recorded and remains outside the supplier’s fare refund field. For the accounting view that combines the fee, the net cash retained is 1,420 + 36 − 760 = 696 BC. This accounting fact is not a statement of what Callum requested.

The initial reservation screen showed a generic “refund may be available” banner. The confirmed supplier terms instead state that the ticket was partially refundable after a 20 percent cancellation penalty on eligible base fare, subject to the supplier’s calculation. Another banner from the sandbox displayed “cancel within 48 hours for full credit.” It is associated with training itinerary KST-7710, not KS-4178. The booking timestamp for KS-4178 was 2 August 2026 at 09:20; the customer’s first written request was dated 4 August. Staff should not infer a live 48-hour free-cancellation right from the sandbox banner. The case’s cancellation and refund communications are transcribed in Section C.

The disruption record says the outbound service was delayed and the second segment was rebooked. A baggage delivery issue was also reported. The file includes a traveler statement, receipts, duplicate checks, supplier messages, system events, and a postmortem. No section of this report authorizes payment beyond the amount recorded as completed. The incident team classified the matter as an operational disruption with a separate customer refund request, and kept those determinations in distinct fields.

SECTION C — MESSAGE THREAD, EXTRACTED IN TIMESTAMP ORDER

2 August, 09:20, booking system receipt: KST-8841 purchased by Callum Alvarez. Fare and tax paid: 1,420 BC. Amendment fee not yet incurred. Supplier terms attached: “partially refundable subject to cancellation penalty and supplier review.”

2 August, 09:22, automatic confirmation to Callum: “Your travel has been confirmed. This notice is not a receipt for any hotel or disruption expense.”

3 August, 16:05, internal note by Wanjiru Petrov, travel desk: “Sandbox card on dashboard reads FREE WITHIN 48 HOURS. Check booking-specific terms before relying on this. Test itinerary in adjacent tab is KST-7710, fare 1,500 BC.” This note concerns the banner and the other itinerary, not KS-4178’s live terms.

4 August, 10:41, message from Callum Alvarez to Kestrel Studio Travel Desk: “I am not cancelling today. The dates may move because the meeting is uncertain. If the supplier will let us change without a penalty, please tell me the options. Do not send any money back or cancel anything on the strength of this note.” The request was classified as an inquiry about amendment options. The phrase “money back” appears, but it is expressly negated and tied to a future possibility.

4 August, 11:10, supplier automation, sent to the travel desk: “For booking KST-8841, cancellation of the ticket may result in a supplier refund after a 20% eligible-base-fare penalty. Estimate only. Please request refund authorization from the traveler before action.” This is a supplier statement, not a customer refund request.

5 August, 08:50, message from Callum Alvarez: “Please move the return leg by one day if possible. I am not asking for a refund. The trip is still needed.” Desk response: amendment is available with a 36 BC fee. Callum replied at 09:12: “Proceed with the change.” The amendment fee was then paid. The revised itinerary remained under KS-4178. The agent did not cancel the booking.

7 September, 18:02, airport disruption notification: outbound segment estimated delay 4 hours 35 minutes. This entry relates to the live booking, but is not a refund request. A separate training notification in the archive says 4 hours 53 minutes for a different flight; it is not evidence about KS-4178.

8 September, 06:14, service status update: first segment departed 3 hours 50 minutes late. Connection was missed. The supplier arranged rebooking on a later route. The rebooked itinerary reached Morrow Field on 9 September. The case’s arrival and expense timeline is summarized in Section E.

SECTION F — INCIDENT POSTMORTEM

F.1 Executive summary
On 8 September 2026, a disruption to Callum Alvarez’s itinerary caused a missed connection and a rebooking. One checked bag was delayed in delivery. Callum later submitted receipts for lodging, meals, local transport, and baggage essentials, and separately made an affirmative request that the full 1,420 BC airfare be returned. The supplier completed a fare refund of 760 BC. The request amount and settlement amount were stored in separate fields, but an interface parser briefly substituted a neighboring training fare of 1,500 BC into the displayed request field. The error was identified and corrected before any customer-facing notice used that value.

The incident did not arise from a failure to distinguish a cancellation from a rebooking. The original booking was amended once, at the traveler’s direction, and the disruption was handled by rebooking. The earlier messages of 4 and 5 August did not ask for a refund. The operative refund request was received on 10 September. A later supplier email requesting return of a duplicate settlement was forwarded by Callum with an explicit statement that it was the supplier’s request, not his. The postmortem confirms the author and intended recipient of each relevant communication.

F.2 Impact and scope
The travel disruption affected the arrival time, required overnight accommodation, and delayed the checked bag. The traveler used short-term lodging and local transport and purchased basic items while the bag was missing. The expense review found four categories with accepted evidence. Three category totals meet the 100 BC reporting threshold; one does not. The threshold result is a summary classification only. It is not a decision that all reported costs are reimbursable under every supplier or employment policy.

The supplier’s completed 760 BC fare refund was verified in the payment ledger. The customer requested the full 1,420 BC fare, while recognizing that the supplier might deduct a penalty. The 36 BC amendment fee was expressly excluded from the requested airfare amount. The supplier’s estimate of 248 BC penalty was calculated from eligible base fare of 1,240 BC at 20 percent. This estimate was not a completed refund calculation and must not be substituted for the settlement transaction. The settlement was 760 BC, leaving a numerical difference of 660 BC between the customer’s requested fare amount and the completed fare refund. The difference alone does not establish that the supplier owes an additional payment.

F.3 Timeline controls
The reservation was issued on 2 August. A generic help tile from a staging booking displayed a 48-hour cancellation message on a staff dashboard. That tile was not linked to the live supplier terms. The live terms specified a 20 percent penalty on eligible base fare. The customer’s 4 August message explicitly said not to send money back or cancel anything on that note. On 5 August, the customer authorized a date amendment and expressly said he was not asking for a refund. The 36 BC amendment charge was collected and the itinerary stayed active.

The flight alert of 7 September showed an estimated delay of 275 minutes. The actual departure record showed a delay of 230 minutes. A network median of 185 minutes and an unrelated flight alert of 293 minutes also appeared in monitoring views. None of these figures was used to determine the refund-request amount or the expense-category threshold. The booking was rebooked, not voluntarily cancelled. One bag remained undelivered at arrival and was subsequently delivered on 17 September.

On 10 September at 09:05, Callum sent the request for the full 1,420 BC fare. The request was acknowledged at 09:19. Supplier review produced a quote and then a completed settlement notification on 11 September. On 12 September, Callum confirmed receipt of 760 BC and reiterated that the amount requested had been 1,420 BC. The case remained open for receipt reconciliation. The receipt lock was applied on 26 September after the traveler confirmed the accepted list.

F.4 Root cause and contributing factors
The principal systems risk was the shared display component that places live booking information and training examples in a single dashboard region. The dashboard made a nearby training fare and a generic cancellation banner visually prominent. The case data itself retained the correct live terms and the correct payment reference. Human review caught the mismatch before a wrong amount was sent to the traveler. The event is recorded as a near miss rather than a financial loss.

A second contributing factor was reliance on optical character recognition for receipt totals before the evidence reviewer resolved duplicate and superseded images. The preliminary category sums were not marked prominently enough as provisional. The OCR output included an unrelated item and omitted or misread other accepted items. The final register reconciled receipt images against the traveler’s written withdrawal, the corrected lodging invoice, and the duplicate-image check. The final category totals in Section E are based on accepted unique evidence, not the preliminary OCR summary.

A third risk was attribution in forwarded correspondence. The supplier’s original message used the phrase “We request” and asked Kestrel to return a payment to Meridian Supply. If the forwarded content had been treated as the forwarder’s own words, the system could have misclassified the direction of payment. Callum’s forwarding note explicitly identified the supplier as the author and asked the desk to verify the purported duplicate. The original sender metadata and the body text were preserved, enabling the correct attribution.

F.5 Corrective actions
The shared dashboard now displays production or staging status adjacent to every amount and help tile. The request-amount field is populated from the signed inbound message and requires reviewer confirmation where it differs from a booking amount. An amount approved or paid by a supplier is held in a separate settlement field and cannot overwrite the requested amount. A separate check warns when a quoted or estimated amount is presented as completed payment.

The receipt workflow now labels optical totals “unverified” until all duplicate and superseded items have been reconciled. A category total is calculated from unique accepted line items. Withdrawn items retain an exclusion reason and cannot be reintroduced by a later OCR import without reviewer override. Threshold reporting applies the rule independently to each category, rather than to the combined claim total.

Forwarded messages now retain both forwarder and original sender fields in the review view. Intent classification must rely on the authored forwarding sentence and sender metadata, not merely on first-person language in quoted material. The team added a prompt in the case review form asking: “Who is asking whom to pay whom?” This control addresses the Meridian Supply message and similar vendor reversal requests.

F.6 Final administrative finding
For the specific questions attached to this record, the operative customer message is the signed communication of 10 September. It affirmatively requests return of the full 1,420 BC airfare. Earlier messages were inquiries, amendment instructions, or explicit non-requests; a supplier’s request to reverse a payment is not the customer’s request. The supplier later completed a 760 BC refund, which is a different amount and status. For the category threshold calculation, use the final accepted totals and compare each one with 100 BC independently. Lodging, meals, and baggage essentials meet the threshold; local transport does not. Similar values from other cases, staging records, estimates, duplicates, and withdrawn receipts are not part of the calculation.

APPENDIX G — REVIEWER RECONCILIATION NOTES

G.1 Separation of questions in the case file
The case review uses distinct fields for customer intent, booking action, supplier authorization, completed payment, and expense eligibility. These fields were intentionally separated because the record contains similar words in several contexts. “Refund” appears in the customer’s early inquiry, supplier’s terms, the customer’s later affirmative request, the settlement notification, and the forwarded supplier email. The word alone cannot establish whether the customer asked for a refund. The sender, the whole sentence, the target of the requested payment, and the timing of the message determine the intent classification.

Likewise, several amounts are close enough to invite accidental substitution. The live booking fare paid was 1,420 BC. The eligible base fare was 1,240 BC. The amount calculated as a 20 percent penalty was 248 BC. A pre-tax estimate after that penalty was 992 BC. The completed refund was 760 BC. A staging example showed 1,500 BC. A different case showed an unapproved 1,050 BC estimate. The 36 BC amendment fee was paid separately. These numbers describe different fields or records and must not be collapsed into a single “refund amount.”

G.2 Independent recomputation
The penalty calculation was recomputed from the eligible base fare: 1,240 × 20 / 100 = 248 BC. Subtracting that estimate from the base fare produces 1,240 − 248 = 992 BC before tax treatment. The supplier subsequently settled 760 BC. Comparing the traveler’s requested fare amount to that completed fare refund gives 1,420 − 760 = 660 BC. That difference is not a settlement authorization.

The lodging category is 84 + 92 + 26 + 96 = 298 BC. The earlier 106 BC scan is the same corrected invoice and is excluded. Meals are 28 + 22 + 31 + 27 + 18 = 126 BC; the 14 BC item was withdrawn and is excluded. Local transport is 44 + 38 + 16 = 98 BC; the unused 42 BC taxi quote is excluded. Baggage essentials are 34 + 58 + 27 + 29 + 24 = 172 BC; the 48 BC duplicate scan and the 220 BC quote from another case are excluded. The four categories together sum to 694 BC, but the rule tests each category separately against 100 BC.

G.3 Evidence quality and exclusions
The traveler’s messages are direct evidence of what he asked, while the supplier’s settlement entry is evidence of what was paid. A supplier estimate is evidence only of a proposed calculation. The travel desk note is evidence of a staff observation, not a customer instruction. A log parser’s intent label is a derived field and was corrected against the original body. The receipt register, not the preliminary OCR summary, establishes supported category amounts. A copied test value does not become evidence simply because it appears in a live dashboard panel.

The record contains no accepted receipt for the taxi quotation, the possible fourth hotel night, or the replacement bag. It contains a receipt for the 14 BC snack, but Callum withdrew it because it belonged to another traveler. The record contains one corrected lodging invoice of 96 BC and one earlier image reading 106 BC; the earlier image is superseded. It contains one baggage receipt image of 48 BC that duplicates another image, but no second purchase. These are not supported amounts and cannot be used to push a category above a threshold.

G.4 Administrative interpretation
The finding that Callum requested 1,420 BC does not imply that the supplier was obligated to pay 1,420 BC. The settlement of 760 BC does not imply that Callum originally requested only 760 BC. Similarly, three categories meeting the 100 BC reporting threshold does not establish that all 694 BC of expense receipts will be reimbursed. The reporting questions concern the evidence and classifications specified by the case rules, not an unrecorded external entitlement.

The case is closed for the present review because all relevant communications and accepted receipts have been reconciled. If a later supplier adjustment or additional receipt is received, it must be entered as a new dated event and must not silently overwrite the amounts in this report. Any new request must be attributed to its actual sender. Any additional expense must be checked for duplicate status, category, traveler, and relationship to the disruption before recalculating the threshold.

G.5 Archive and audit references
The booking confirmation, amendment receipt, supplier terms, inbound messages, supplier gateway responses, payment ledger, baggage tracking entry, and receipt images are retained under KS-4178. The audit system stores the original message bodies and the corrected normalized fields. Staging rows are retained in a separate environment and clearly marked. No archived comparison record is incorporated into the customer’s paid transaction or expense total.

The auditor’s reconciliation was completed by a reviewer who did not create the initial OCR summary. The reviewer verified the settlement reference against the payment ledger, checked the customer’s message source against the registered traveler address, and reviewed each receipt image. The reviewer also confirmed that the 14 BC meal item was withdrawn once, rather than treated as two separate entries because it appeared in both a message and an OCR list. The duplicate baggage image was matched by image hash and purchase date. The corrected 96 BC lodging invoice was linked to the earlier 106 BC scan as a replacement.

No manual adjustment was applied to make a category reach the threshold. In particular, the transport amount remains 98 BC despite the presence of an unpaid 42 BC taxi quote and a 110 BC staging entry. Neither was a supported and incurred item for this traveler. The threshold is not a claim-wide average and cannot be reached by adding surplus amounts from lodging, meals, or baggage to transport. Each category is assessed separately and the threshold of 100 BC is inclusive.

G.6 Distribution restriction
This consolidated document is an internal travel operations record. Any external summary should distinguish the customer’s requested amount from the supplier’s completed payment and should describe expense evidence without representing the reporting threshold as a final reimbursement award. Staff shall not copy values from the sandbox or from other case identifiers. The record should be cited by case number, not by a traveler’s name alone, because the archive contains unrelated travelers and comparison entries with similar dates and amounts.

G.7 Closing checklist
The file reviewer checked that the booking identifier matched across the confirmation and settlement; that the customer’s request was authored by Callum; that the forwarded supplier message was attributed to Meridian Supply; that the fare request excluded the amendment fee; that the 248 BC estimate was not mistaken for the 760 BC completed settlement; and that all category sums were recomputed from accepted unique receipts. The reviewer also checked that the one-bag report was not inflated by the test counter, that the actual 230-minute delay was not replaced with an estimated or network-wide figure, and that no future conditional statement was treated as a completed cancellation or escalation.

Final record status: communications reconciled; customer refund request recorded as affirmative for the 1,420 BC fare; supplier refund recorded as completed for 760 BC; expense categories evaluated independently against the 100 BC reporting threshold; lodging, meals, and baggage essentials pass; local transport does not pass.
