[{"state":"Granite Analytics developer-tooling weekly meeting notes, Monday morning, assembled by Esi Tanaka. This is the full scratchpad from the meeting, including the bits people added afterward because the call ran long and everyone kept remembering one more thing. The group was talking about the build dashboard, the test runner, release notes, and a few unrelated chores. Nothing here is a formal customer commitment; it is just the team's notes. Esi opened by saying that the dashboard rollout was going well overall and that it was useful to have a single place to see jobs across repositories. Jonas Haddad said the small improvements had been easier to review than the larger redesign, and Aiden Petrov agreed that keeping each change narrow had made the rollout less nerve-racking. The team did not decide to replace its existing source-control host, and nobody proposed shutting down the nightly test environment.

The meeting began with a quick recap of the previous week's action items. The status page now links directly to a failed job's log section rather than opening the log at its first line. That change was merged after review, and Esi said the jump links are especially helpful when a test job emits a great deal of setup output. Jonas thanked the person who caught a case where an empty log made the jump link look broken. The team fixed that by showing a small explanation when there is no matching section. They discussed whether the explanation should say “no failure detail found” or “this job has no failure detail,” and settled on the shorter text. This is already shipped; it is not a proposal waiting for approval.

Aiden gave the runner update. The Linux runner pool is healthy, and its queue is generally short. There is one intermittent delay when several container-image builds start at once, but Aiden has not yet confirmed whether the cause is image download contention or a runner scheduling issue. He asked the group not to call the delay a regression in the dashboard, because the same delay appears when the dashboard is not open. Esi wrote down “investigate burst queue” as an action item. They have not decided to purchase more machines. A separate Windows runner update was that a certificate renewal reminder was delivered to the team inbox; the certificate is still valid and no build has failed because of it.

The test summary was similarly mixed but mostly positive. A few test suites have become faster after the team stopped repeating a large fixture setup in every test. The reduction is noticeable on the integration lane, while the small unit-test lane was already quick. Jonas said a chart made the improvement look larger than it was because its vertical axis started above zero. He asked for a clearer chart before anyone shared the screenshot outside the team. The chart is a draft, not a published performance claim. Nobody said the tests had been removed or that the suite had been disabled. The team still wants the integration coverage, and the notes explicitly say not to trade away coverage just to make the dashboard look green.

There was a brief discussion of documentation. Esi said that new repository owners often miss the short guide explaining how to connect a project to the dashboard. The guide exists, but the link is buried in the general developer-tools index. The proposed action is to add a direct link to the setup page and include one screenshot showing where the repository token is entered. The token itself should never be copied into the screenshot. Aiden volunteered to review the wording, and Jonas said he could check that the screenshot uses a test repository rather than a real project. The group did not decide to publish a public tutorial; the first audience is internal engineers.

The release checklist came up next. It currently asks the release owner to verify that the main branch is green, confirm the changelog entry, and check that the rollback instructions are current. Esi asked whether checking the package signature should be explicit. Jonas said signing is already part of the release job, but the checklist should still have a visible confirmation field so a person can notice if that job was skipped. They agreed to add the field. They did not agree to make the checklist itself a blocking automated gate, because the new field needs a little trial use first. The meeting notes should not be read as saying that unsigned packages were discovered; no such incident was reported.

An idea about notifications took longer than expected. The current system can post build status to a chat channel, but messages sometimes arrive in a noisy batch after a short service interruption. Aiden suggested grouping repeated failures for the same commit into one message. Esi was in favor of testing the idea in a sandbox channel. Jonas worried that grouping could hide a change in failure details, so the group listed “include a link for every affected job” as a requirement. Nothing was implemented during this meeting. The note “notifications are broken” was crossed out and replaced with “batching is noisy during recovery”; the service continues to post messages. A separate request to send a message for every passing job was rejected as too noisy for the main channel.

The team also reviewed some small interface feedback gathered from colleagues. One engineer wanted the job duration displayed in minutes and seconds rather than only seconds. Another wanted the branch name to remain visible when scrolling down a long job page. A third said the retry button was easy to find. These comments came from internal colleagues in a short usability session, not from a paying customer. The team recorded the first two as possible usability improvements and marked the retry-button comment as positive feedback. There is no customer refund request, pricing dispute, or request to cancel a subscription in these notes.

Esi summarized a couple of straightforward housekeeping changes. The dashboard's repository filter now remembers its selection while moving between the overview and job list. The label “default branch” has replaced an older label that some people misunderstood as meaning “most recently active branch.” The change only affects wording; it does not change which branch is built. Jonas confirmed that the help text now says the dashboard reads branch settings from the connected repository. Aiden reminded the group that if a repository has not granted access, the dashboard cannot show its jobs. That is an access limitation, not a service outage.

A short agenda item concerned local developer setup. New hires have reported that the sample configuration uses an obsolete name for a runner field. Esi has a change ready that updates the example and adds a sentence explaining that the sample secret is fake. Jonas is checking that the sample can run without reaching the production service. The team wants the example to be safe to paste into a local test project. The change is awaiting review, so the notes do not claim it is already released. They also recorded that nobody should paste actual signing keys into chat or meeting notes.

The participants considered the next dashboard release. They want to include the empty-log explanation, remembered repository filter, and revised branch label, because all three changes have already passed review. The chart redesign and notification batching idea are not in the release scope. Aiden asked whether a small label fix could be bundled too, but the label was already in the reviewed change set. Esi read back the scope so nobody would mistake a discussion item for a committed feature. The release is still planned for the usual weekly window, but no exact date was promised in these notes. If a blocking issue appears, the team will move it rather than rush an unreviewed change.

The conversation then wandered to test ownership. Some teams have a clear owner for each repository's integration suite, while others rely on whoever last touched the test. Jonas said the dashboard should show an owner field, but only if it can point to a maintained team directory rather than a free-text field that quickly becomes stale. Esi noted that the directory integration is not ready. The group agreed to gather examples and revisit the question next week. They did not assign ownership to a named individual, and they did not decide to block builds when an owner is missing.

Aiden described a harmless warning in one container job. The warning says a cache entry could not be reused, after which the job downloads the required files and completes. The cache is an optimization; a cache miss is not a test failure. The group agreed to track the warning separately from red build failures so the dashboard does not overstate the number of broken jobs. Jonas asked for a tooltip that explains this distinction. The tooltip is a small proposed change, and Esi will draft language. The notes specifically distinguish the cache warning from the earlier burst queue delay: one is a recoverable cache miss and the other is a queue wait worth investigating.

There was a product-review-style recap of feedback from an internal pilot, added to the meeting document by Esi after the call. The pilot group liked having the run summary at the top of the job page. Several people said the links to individual failing tests saved time. Two people asked for longer retention of raw logs, but the current retention policy is unchanged while the team estimates storage costs. One pilot participant said, “I love clicking through five screens just to find the one failed test,” which everyone understood as sarcasm, but Esi left the quote out of the formal feedback tally and added a note to improve navigation. Another participant said the search field was easy to spot. The written, non-sarcastic feedback recorded as positives is the summary-at-top and failing-test links; the group did not count the sarcastic remark as praise for extra clicks.

The team discussed an alert about a scheduled maintenance window. The alert belongs to a separate internal dependency, not the dashboard. The dependency team expects a brief read-only period, and Granite Analytics' dashboard should continue showing previously collected job results during it. New results might arrive later than usual. Esi asked the team to avoid describing that as data loss. Jonas added that if the maintenance lasts longer than planned, they will post an update in the engineering channel. The maintenance has not started, and the notes make no claim that it already caused a failed build.

A tiny accessibility discussion followed. The current status colors are accompanied by text labels, so the state is not communicated by color alone. A keyboard user reported that the focus outline on the repository selector is faint. The team agrees the outline should be more visible and assigned a design follow-up. A separate suggestion to make every control larger was not adopted; the group wants to first check the affected control at normal zoom and with keyboard navigation. No one said the dashboard is unusable, and no accessibility audit has been completed as part of this meeting.

Esi read out the action list near the end of the call. Aiden will investigate burst queue timing and bring back evidence about whether it is scheduling or image downloads. Jonas will test the updated sample configuration and review the safe screenshot. Esi will draft the cache-miss tooltip and find the shortest path to the setup guide. The group will ask the directory team about a maintained owner field. These are assignments, not completed work. The only completed items mentioned in this section are the already merged jump-link behavior and the filter and label changes included in the upcoming release candidate.

The meeting ended with a reminder about the release candidate review. Reviewers should check that links point to the intended job and that text labels remain visible with the status color. They should not paste secrets into screenshots, and they should verify the changelog and signature field. Jonas said the new release candidate is not yet approved. Aiden replied that he would review it after the queue investigation, but nobody made his review a prerequisite. Esi thanked everyone and said the next meeting would begin with the open items, not with a claim that all issues had been fixed.

Appendix: small observations copied from the shared agenda. The build overview is useful when someone wants a quick snapshot. The log jump links make long output easier to inspect. The setup guide needs a more direct link. The filter now remembers its selection. The revised branch wording is clearer. The integration suite still matters even when a dashboard chart is being polished. The cache warning is recoverable. The notification batching idea needs a sandbox test. The Windows certificate reminder is not a failed build. The repository owner field remains unresolved. The sample secret is intentionally fake. These are concise reminders of the discussion, not new decisions or extra feature commitments.

Appendix: parking-lot items. The team might later compare log retention options, review how the owner directory could be displayed, and ask the pilot group whether the navigation changes help. No owner or deadline was assigned for the retention comparison. The group will not add passing-job notifications to the main channel. No one asked for a refund, and no paid account was discussed. These details were kept in the scratchpad because people sometimes revisit them after a release, but they should not be mistaken for approved work.

Appendix: the shared document had a few rough notes that Esi cleaned up. “Green is good?” was changed to “show the textual status as well as color.” “All the tests are slow” was corrected to “some integration setup used to repeat.” “No logs” was corrected to “one empty-log case had no matching section.” The corrections matter because the rougher phrases could make the situation sound broader than it is. The team has not reported that every test is slow, that logs are generally unavailable, or that the status colors are the only signal.

Appendix: in the final chat exchange, Jonas asked whether he should post the pilot feedback in the public product forum. Esi replied that it is internal usability feedback and should remain in the internal planning document for now. Aiden asked whether the release note could mention the filter and link behavior. Esi said yes, once the release candidate is approved. Jonas responded that the changelog draft can be prepared but not published early. The distinction between drafting and publishing was repeated so a copied sentence would not imply that the release has already gone out.

The notes end with the week's broad impression: the team has a useful working dashboard, a few focused improvements are ready or under review, and several worthwhile ideas still need evidence or a design pass. The meeting included praise for the job summary and test links, but it also included concerns about queue delay, discoverability, log retention, and notification noise. It was an ordinary planning conversation, with some positive feedback and some unresolved details, rather than a formal customer escalation.","questions":[{"type":"multilabel","instruction":"Which improvements shipped?","candidates":[{"id":"log_jump_links","description":"Log jump links"},{"id":"remembered_filter","description":"Remembered repository filter"},{"id":"branch_label","description":"Revised branch label"},{"id":"notification_batching","description":"Grouped notifications"}],"target":["log_jump_links","remembered_filter","branch_label"],"hard_cases":["multi_positive","long_state","evidence_middle"],"notes":"The jump links are merged; filter and label changes passed review. Notification batching remains an idea."},{"type":"multilabel","instruction":"Which feedback was positive?","candidates":[{"id":"summary_top","description":"Run summary at top"},{"id":"failing_test_links","description":"Links to failing tests"},{"id":"extra_clicks","description":"Extra navigation clicks"},{"id":"larger_controls","description":"Larger controls"}],"target":["summary_top","failing_test_links"],"hard_cases":["multi_positive","long_state","evidence_middle"],"notes":"Pilot users explicitly liked the summary and failing-test links; the extra-click quote was sarcastic."},{"type":"multilabel","instruction":"Which tasks were assigned?","candidates":[{"id":"queue_investigation","description":"Investigate burst queue"},{"id":"sample_config_review","description":"Review sample configuration"},{"id":"cache_tooltip","description":"Draft cache tooltip"},{"id":"owner_directory","description":"Ask about owner directory"}],"target":["queue_investigation","sample_config_review","cache_tooltip","owner_directory"],"hard_cases":["multi_positive","long_state","evidence_end"],"notes":"The read-out action list assigns all four follow-ups."}]},{"state":"Foxglove Analytics developer tooling incident review and product feedback notes, written in a deliberately informal voice by Quentin Haddad. The document combines the team's postmortem conversation with a small product-review recap because the same people were already on the call. It is not a customer-support transcript and does not describe refunds or billing. The incident concerned delayed CI status updates after a maintenance event in a job-result relay. Builds ran, but the dashboard sometimes showed an older state for a while. The team wants to describe the scope accurately, so the notes keep separating what was observed from what people guessed while the graphs were loading.

Quentin opened with the plain-language summary: during the incident, the relay accumulated a backlog and dashboard status updates arrived late. The underlying jobs continued to execute. The most visible symptom was a job page showing “running” after its runner had already completed. The page eventually updated when the relay caught up. There was no evidence that the job output was erased, and the team did not find a case where the relay changed a failed test into a passing one. A few colleagues initially thought the dashboard had lost results, but the timeline review did not support that conclusion. The incident was about freshness of status, not loss of stored logs.

The first report came through the internal engineering chat. Hiro Mensah posted a screenshot of a completed job that still appeared to be running. Xiu Mensah replied that another repository showed the same stale state. Quentin asked them to include the job links, not just screenshots, so the team could compare timestamps. Aiden was not involved in this review; the notes refer to a different team's meeting elsewhere and should not be blended with this one. The first two links were from separate repositories, and both jobs had completed successfully at their runners. A third report was a genuine failed test, but its failure was unrelated to the relay delay. That unrelated red job is mentioned here because the status color made the incident channel busier than the actual scope warranted.

The event timeline starts with a scheduled maintenance task on the relay's backing store. The maintenance completed, but a connection pool setting reverted to its conservative default during the service restart. That setting did not stop the relay from accepting every event, but it reduced how quickly it could drain accumulated events. A burst of CI completions arrived while the pool was running with fewer active connections. The relay's queue depth rose, and status events were processed later than usual. The runner fleet itself remained healthy. The maintenance was not a failure of the dashboard's repository filter, nor was it caused by the job-log jump links.

The on-call person noticed the growing queue after comparing the relay's oldest pending event with the dashboard's last update. The difference was a few minutes and continued to increase. The on-call person first suspected a runner slowdown because several job pages looked stuck. That hypothesis was checked against runner completion records and rejected: the runners had completed their work promptly. The decisive evidence was that relay events were waiting after the runners had already reported completion. The team is recording this distinction because “slow CI” is a tempting shorthand, but it would point future responders at the wrong component.

The immediate mitigation was to restore the intended connection-pool setting and restart the relay workers one group at a time. The team avoided restarting all workers simultaneously because doing so would have made the backlog harder to observe and could have interrupted active processing. Once the configuration was restored, the workers drained the queue and the dashboard caught up. No manual rewriting of job statuses was needed. The on-call person checked a sample of successful and failed jobs against their runner records, and the statuses agreed after recovery. The team did not disable CI, delete queued events, or ask repository owners to rerun completed jobs.

The postmortem review noted that monitoring had been present but not sufficiently direct. There was an alert for relay errors, and that alert did not fire because the relay was functioning slowly rather than returning an elevated number of errors. There was a dashboard showing queue depth, but it was not part of the on-call's primary view. A person had to open a second panel and compare it with the job-status chart. The team agreed that the backlog age should have its own alert, since a queue that is steadily processing but falling behind is still operationally important. That alert is planned; it was not already active during this incident.

The group also discussed whether the alert should trigger on a fixed queue size. Quentin pointed out that a large but rapidly draining queue can be harmless, while a small queue containing very old events can indicate a stuck worker. The better first measure is the age of the oldest event, with queue depth as context. They did not set a numerical threshold in this document because the team wants to examine ordinary peak traffic first. The notes therefore do not establish a specific minutes-based alert limit. The team will propose a threshold after collecting representative measurements and reviewing it with the on-call rotation.

A separate discovery was that the maintenance checklist described how to restart the relay but did not ask the operator to verify the connection-pool value afterward. The checklist is being updated to include a configuration check and a quick observation of queue behavior after maintenance. Hiro volunteered to write a draft, and Xiu offered to review it with someone who did not participate in the incident. The checklist change is not yet complete. The team explicitly wants a second-person review rather than relying only on the people who already know which setting reverted.

The cause was not a single careless action. The maintenance task completed according to its runbook, and the default setting was valid for ordinary traffic. The problem was that the restart behavior did not preserve the tuned value, while the monitoring emphasized error rates rather than freshness. The tuning value had originally been changed after earlier load tests, but its purpose was not written into the maintenance checklist. The postmortem avoids naming an individual as responsible; the action is to make the configuration durable and visible. The team will also add a small test that checks the effective pool setting after a restart.

The product-review portion of the call covered how engineers noticed the stale status. Several pilot users said the job summary was helpful when they needed to see the latest result quickly. They also liked the direct link from a failure count to the corresponding test output. One person said that the dashboard's compact layout made it easy to scan a repository's recent runs. These are positive comments about the interface, not evidence that the incident was harmless. During the incident, the same compact summary could also show stale data, which is why freshness needs to be communicated clearly.

One comment about the “live” badge was not a compliment. A pilot user wrote, “Fantastic, a live badge that takes a coffee break whenever the relay does.” Quentin understood the remark as sarcastic criticism of stale updates. The team listed the underlying request as a visible “updated at” time next to the status and a clear indication when the data is behind. The group did not interpret the comment as praise for delayed updates. The wording in the feedback appendix preserves the quote only to explain why the requested freshness indicator matters.

The team discussed a proposed small interface change: show the last event time near the current job state, and display a subtle delay notice if updates are older than the usual range. The design needs to avoid suggesting that the runner itself is still active when only the dashboard update is delayed. Quentin suggested separate labels for runner execution and dashboard synchronization. Hiro agreed that users should be able to tell which system is waiting. Xiu asked whether the notice might create noise during ordinary short delays. They agreed to mock up the text and test it with internal users before committing it to a release.

The group did not decide to hide all “running” states, because that would remove useful information when a runner really is still working. Nor did they decide to label every delay as an incident. They want a cautious design that explains what is known and avoids overclaiming. For example, if the runner has completed but the relay event is pending, the page can say that the result is awaiting synchronization. If the runner is genuinely still executing, the existing running state can remain. The team needs reliable data to distinguish those cases, so the mock-up depends on the relay event timestamps.

The support channel produced no direct customer billing request. One engineer asked whether users who saw old status data should be offered additional service time. Quentin said that was not a customer request in the conversation and that any commercial discussion would need a separate review. There is no refund, credit, or cancellation request recorded here. Another message asked whether the team should notify repository owners. The team decided to post an internal status summary and update the incident record; it did not send a broad external notification because the review had not established customer impact beyond the internal pilot and named repositories.

The recovery section records the verification steps. The team compared runner completion times with relay processing times, checked that the queue returned to its usual range, and opened representative job pages to confirm that their displayed states matched the stored event sequence. They inspected both a successful job and the unrelated failed test so that recovery would not accidentally mark every job green. The stale pages updated without users refreshing them manually, although a refresh was useful for one browser that had kept an old page view. No test results were edited. The remaining work is preventive, not a correction of corrupted data.

The action list has four main items. First, make the connection-pool tuning durable across relay restarts. Second, add monitoring for the age of the oldest pending event and put it in the on-call view. Third, extend the maintenance checklist with a post-restart configuration and queue check. Fourth, run a restart test that verifies the effective pool setting. Quentin will coordinate the monitoring review, Hiro will draft the checklist change, Xiu will review the operator steps, and the platform group will handle the restart test. These are assigned follow-ups; the notes do not say they are finished.

A fifth idea is to design the “updated at” and synchronization-delay indicators. It is a product follow-up, not an incident-mitigation action. The team will first make a mock-up and ask pilot users whether the distinction between runner state and relay state is understandable. They will not ship the wording solely on the strength of one sarcastic comment. The review should include a normal fast update, a delayed relay event, and a genuinely long-running job, so the labels are tested against distinct situations.

The retrospective also captures what went well. The on-call person compared runner records with relay records instead of assuming the visible job page was authoritative. The team had enough event timestamps to reconstruct the sequence. The mitigation could be applied without stopping the runner fleet. The internal chat reports included links that made it possible to compare repositories. The event queue eventually drained without manual status edits. These points are positive observations about response and recovery, not claims that the alerting or maintenance process was already adequate.

What could be better: the queue-age signal should have been easier to see, maintenance should preserve or verify the tuning value, and the dashboard should distinguish a completed runner from a delayed status update. The team also wants the incident summary to make clear that no logs were lost. Those are three different improvements: monitoring, operational procedure, and user-facing communication. The planned work is deliberately small enough to review independently. The group does not propose a wholesale replacement of the relay or the dashboard.

The team reviewed nearby changes to avoid accidentally attributing unrelated work to the incident. A repository filter improvement had been released the prior week. A separate setup guide was being revised. Neither caused the relay queue to grow. A log-retention discussion was also ongoing, but the incident did not involve log expiration. The failed integration test in the report was caused by a test assertion and remained failed after the relay caught up; it was not evidence that the relay had changed the job result. These distinctions were added because the timeline had several adjacent topics and a quick scan could conflate them.

A short appendix lists the positive pilot feedback in plain terms: job summary at the top, direct links to failing test output, and compact recent-run layout. The same appendix lists requested changes separately: visible update time, a stale-data indication, and clearer separation between runner execution and dashboard synchronization. The sarcasm about the badge is included as a complaint signal, not a positive feature vote. The group did not treat the request for clearer status as a request to remove status information.

Another appendix is the rough operational timeline. Maintenance begins; the relay restarts; the effective connection pool returns to its conservative default; completions arrive in a burst; pending events accumulate; the on-call sees old job states; runner records confirm that jobs completed; configuration is restored; workers drain the backlog; job pages catch up. The sequence is based on logs and timestamps. It does not assert that the exact same pattern will recur on every maintenance event. The team intends the restart test to verify the configuration behavior before relying on the procedure again.

The final discussion returned to language. Quentin proposed that the incident title say “delayed CI status updates,” rather than “CI outage,” since builds continued to run. Hiro agreed that the narrower title was more accurate. Xiu wanted the summary to mention the stale “running” display because that is what users encountered. They settled on wording that says runners completed normally while dashboard updates lagged. The title avoids implying that no CI work happened, and the summary avoids implying that all job pages were unaffected.

The meeting ended with no new customer action and no additional remediation beyond the listed work. The team will check the monitoring proposal at the next operations review and bring the interface mock-up to the pilot group. The document's overall conclusion is that the service recovered, results remained intact, and a combination of configuration durability, queue-age monitoring, and clearer freshness cues should make a repeat easier to detect and understand. [{"state":"Typed-up shop note, invoice packet, and incident postmortem — kindly retain as one record

Prepared for the small works team at Morrowvale Fabrication, with considerable thanks to everyone who took the trouble to assemble the papers. The packet concerns a single order for Larkspur Dental, routed through Harbor Logistics, and one production incident. The note was found beside the dispatch board; the invoice and the incident report were filed behind it. Names and figures below are fictional shop records. Please excuse the length: the original folder contained several copies of forms and a number of useful, if rather repetitive, annotations.

HANDWRITTEN-STYLE NOTE, TYPED UP BY THE OFFICE

Monday, 7 April. Please be so kind as to keep the blue folder together. Larkspur Dental order LD-418 was promised for dispatch today, but that does not mean the carrier has collected it. The carrier slot is Tuesday morning. We should be most grateful if nobody writes “delivered” on the customer copy until the signed receipt is returned. The parts are packed in crates A and B; the calibration certificate is in the clear sleeve, not taped to the lid.

I counted the pieces again because the first tally was made while the saw was being cleaned. Crate A should contain 24 guide collars and crate B should contain 16. The customer ordered 40 in total. The inspection table shows 24 passed from the first batch and 17 passed from the second batch, but one of those 17 is only a setup sample and has not been accepted for shipment. Thus the accepted shipment count should be 24 plus 16, not 24 plus 17. Please do not confuse the sample with a saleable piece; the sample is marked with a white paint dot and is in the quality cabinet.

The invoice clerk has written down a deposit of $680.00. That is a payment received, not an extra charge. The customer’s signed order says the remaining balance is to be billed after dispatch. It would be extremely kind to check whether the freight charge is included before anyone tells the customer a grand total. In the estimate, freight was shown separately as $84.00. There is also an old note about a possible $48 rush fee, but the production manager crossed out that fee before accepting the order. It is not payable. The shop should not charge it merely because a previous order had a rush fee.

There were 3 small cartons of packing material on the bench, but those are shop supplies and not part of LD-418. A handwritten “3” near the order number is the carton count, not a quantity of parts. The outer crate tare weights are 12 lb and 14 lb; those are not product weights. The scale slip gives gross weights of 86 lb and 72 lb, with the empty crates accounting for the tare. The carrier bills on the quoted flat freight amount for this order, not by adding the gross weights to a money figure.

At 3:15, Sven said the thread gauge was reading a little tight. He did not say the collars were all defective. The gauge was cleaned and checked with its certified master; it then read within the tolerance on the drawing. The first three parts were measured again, with diameters 18.02 mm, 18.01 mm, and 18.03 mm. The drawing calls for 18.00 mm plus or minus 0.05 mm. Those values are in tolerance. Please be very polite if explaining the check; the customer has already waited for an answer and we should not make a simple inspection sound like a crisis.

There is a separate lot of 12 spacer rings for Bluefin Outfitters on the neighboring rack. Those rings cost $7.50 each and are not part of the Larkspur Dental invoice. The packing slip for Harbor Logistics also lists two reusable pallets at $15 each as returnable property. Those values must not be included in the sale subtotal, and the pallets are not a fee if they come back as agreed.

The office copy says the order is “40 parts, 2 crates, 1 certificate, balance due after dispatch.” That wording is correct. It does not say 41 parts, even though a production entry records 41 pieces processed; the extra piece was the setup sample described above. It does not say 42 parts, even though one early pencil note added the crate count to the piece count. Kindly ignore that arithmetic.

INVOICE — DRAFT REVISION 3, REVIEWED BEFORE POSTING

Seller: Morrowvale Fabrication, small batch machining and finishing shop
Customer: Larkspur Dental
Order: LD-418, guide collars, customer drawing LD-GC-9
Invoice date: 7 April
Dispatch planned: 8 April, subject to final sign-off
Currency: USD

Line 1. Guide collars, accepted sale quantity 40, unit price $32.50, extended line amount $1,300.00.
Line 2. Deburr and protective finish, 40 units at $4.25, extended line amount $170.00.
Line 3. First-article measurement record, one service at $96.00, extended line amount $96.00.
Line 4. Freight, one flat quoted charge at $84.00, extended line amount $84.00.

Merchandise and service subtotal before freight: $1,566.00.
Freight: $84.00.
Total before deposit: $1,650.00.
Deposit received on 28 March: $680.00.
Balance due after dispatch: $970.00.

The arithmetic as intended is 40 multiplied by $32.50, which is $1,300.00; 40 multiplied by $4.25, which is $170.00; then $1,300.00 plus $170.00 plus $96.00 equals $1,566.00; add the $84.00 freight to reach $1,650.00; subtract the previously received $680.00 to leave $970.00. The deposit is shown as a credit against the amount due, not as an additional sale line. No tax is charged on this internal draft because the customer exemption certificate was recorded as valid for this order under the shop’s stated accounting procedure. That statement is for this invoice only; it is not a general claim about tax treatment for other customers.

Invoice clerk’s margin note, typed exactly: “Please check line 2. A scratch-pad version says 40 x $4.25 = $160, but the multiplication should be $170. Do not silently carry the scratch-pad number forward.” The $160 figure is not an approved price or a negotiated discount; it resulted from a clerk’s arithmetic slip. A different loose page says “finish allowance $10,” but that page belongs to order BO-209 for Bluefin Outfitters and has no bearing on LD-418.

Invoice clerk’s second margin note: “The $96 measurement record is one service, not 96 pieces and not $9.60. The $84 freight line is a flat order charge. A prior invoice used $48 freight for a smaller parcel; that is not this carrier quotation.” The bill of lading for this order refers to two crates, but crate count does not multiply the flat freight. Similarly, a handwritten weight entry of 158 is in pounds, not dollars. The gross weights are 86 lb and 72 lb, summing to 158 lb; the tare weights, 12 lb and 14 lb, sum to 26 lb, leaving a combined net load of 132 lb. None of those weights changes the quoted $84 freight line.

The customer’s purchase order lists 40 collars at the agreed unit price, not 41. The production traveler lists 41 processed because one was reserved as a setup sample. The sample was retained by the shop, was not accepted as merchandise, and is not billed. The dispatch slip lists 40 accepted pieces. The quality stamp is present on each of those 40 pieces. The traveler’s “41” is included here because a reviewer might otherwise mistake it for the invoiced quantity.

For clarity, the obsolete first invoice draft showed the finish line as 40 x $4.25 = $160.00 and a total of $1,640.00 before deposit. That draft also accidentally omitted the measurement record. Neither figure is the approved revision 3 total. The correct revision has the $170 finish line and the $96 measurement service. Adding those to the $1,300 merchandise line and $84 freight gives $1,650 before deposit. A note at the foot of the obsolete draft saying “rounding difference: $10” was not an authorized credit. The revision history records it as an arithmetic correction only.

A separate order summary in the accounting system includes a $200 deposit from Larkspur Health on order LH-077 and a $680 receipt from Larkspur Dental on LD-418. These are two different customers and two different orders. The $200 must not be substituted for the LD-418 deposit. Another search result shows an unpaid balance of $970 on a previous job for Harbor Logistics; that is coincidentally the same number as the balance calculated on this draft, but it is not a payment on LD-418. The current invoice balance comes solely from this invoice’s $1,650 total less this order’s $680 deposit.

The unit price of $32.50 was confirmed by the signed quotation dated 18 March. A quote from January showed $31.00, but it expired before the order was placed. The current quote specifically states 40 pieces and $32.50 each. The customer asked whether the old rate could still be used; the shop politely explained that the signed March quotation controls. No credit has been promised for the difference between the expired and current rates. The handwritten figure $1,240 in the file is 40 times the expired $31.00 rate, not the current merchandise amount. It is a plausible-looking distractor, but not the amount on this approved invoice.

The line item descriptions have been checked against the order acknowledgement. “Deburr and protective finish” is a per-piece service and is applied to the 40 accepted pieces. It does not apply to the setup sample. “First-article measurement record” is one charge for the measurement document. Freight is charged once. The invoice does not contain a second handling charge, a pallet rental, or the $48 rush fee. The customer is not being billed for rejected work or for internal inspection labor beyond the stated one service.

The draft was checked by two staff members, but that does not make every earlier version reliable. The source of truth for the amounts is the revision 3 line list printed above. The receipt log confirms the $680 deposit cleared on 28 March. The bank fee of $2.50 recorded in the payment ledger is a cost borne by the shop, not an amount to add to the customer invoice. The customer sent exactly $680.00. The invoice balance does not become $972.50 by adding the bank fee, and it does not become $967.50 by subtracting that fee from the customer’s credit.

INCIDENT POSTMORTEM — PACKING AND FINAL COUNT

Incident reference MP-24-17. Written with apologies to the customer and with thanks to the staff who reconstructed the timeline. This postmortem is included to explain why the packet contains several count entries that differ. It is not a report of a lost shipment: the shipment was held before carrier collection, and no customer property was damaged.

Summary. During final packing for LD-418, the dispatch operator read the 41-piece production traveler and initially prepared a label for 41 collars. The quality clerk noticed that the setup sample was still present in the traveler count. The operator stopped before sealing the second crate, the sample was removed from the dispatch staging area and returned to the quality cabinet, and the final packed count was 40 accepted collars. No extra item left the shop. The first draft of the invoice also contained an arithmetic error in the finish extension. That error was caught during review and corrected in revision 3 before posting.

The incident is categorized as a near miss in paperwork and count control, not as a shipment shortage, overage, or product failure. The customer was informed that the dispatch would occur one day later than the first informal estimate because the final documentation needed checking. The signed order did not include a penalty for that one-day adjustment. The carrier reservation remained available for Tuesday morning. The customer did not cancel the order and did not ask to return anything.

Timeline, 4 April. At 08:10, the first operation logged 20 blanks cut from bar stock. At 09:05, a second bar was cut for 21 blanks, giving 41 pieces processed in total. The production traveler used the word “processed,” which includes the setup sample. At 10:20, one piece was set aside to establish the tool offset and verify the gauge. That piece was identified with a white paint dot. At 11:40, the remaining pieces went through deburring. The operator’s note “all 41 through machine” refers to machine processing, not all 41 being approved for sale.

At 13:15, the quality clerk counted 40 pieces as accepted and recorded one sample retained. The count was repeated at 13:42 by another clerk. The repeated count was 24 pieces in crate A plus 16 pieces in crate B, for 40 pieces total. The preliminary packing worksheet had copied “41” from the traveler into a box labeled “quantity prepared.” That box was not the final shipped quantity. A later supervisor annotation changed the wording to “41 processed; 40 accepted and packed; one sample retained.” The annotation was made before the carrier label was printed.

At 15:10, the first draft invoice used the correct merchandise amount, $1,300.00, but entered $160.00 for the finish line. The clerk’s scratch calculation multiplied 40 by 4 and omitted the remaining quarter dollar per unit. The approved unit rate remained $4.25. Forty times $4.25 is $170.00. The difference between the erroneous extension and the correct extension is $10.00. The invoice reviewer noted that the finish line was short by $10 and returned the draft. This was a billing-paperwork error caught before transmission, not a discount, credit, or customer overpayment.

At 15:36, a review of the measurement service showed that the first draft had omitted the $96.00 line. The omission was also corrected in revision 3. The revised total before deposit was therefore not the obsolete draft’s $1,640.00. Starting from the corrected line items: $1,300.00 plus $170.00 plus $96.00 plus $84.00 equals $1,650.00. The difference from the obsolete $1,640.00 draft is $10.00 for the corrected finish extension and $96.00 for the restored measurement service, a total increase of $106.00. This comparison is stated to prevent someone from treating the old draft as the approved bill.

At 16:05, the accounts clerk confirmed the receipt of the customer’s $680.00 deposit. The balance on the revised invoice was calculated as $1,650.00 minus $680.00, or $970.00. A preliminary email template had copied a $200 deposit from the neighboring Larkspur Health account. That template was not sent. The account name and order reference were corrected, and the ledger entry for LD-418 still showed $680.00 received. The $200 was a separate customer payment and was not used in the balance calculation.

At 16:30, the packing supervisor confirmed that the flat freight quotation was $84.00. A lookup of the prior small-parcel job displayed $48.00 and initially caused confusion. That prior quotation related to another shipment. The current carrier confirmation for LD-418 says one flat charge of $84.00 for the two crates. The two crate weights were recorded for the carrier’s paperwork, but the quotation did not specify a per-pound price. Staff therefore did not calculate freight by multiplying 158 pounds by any rate, and did not add a second $84 charge for the second crate.

At 17:00, final labels were held pending review of the paperwork. The customer was given a courteous update that the shop was verifying the accepted quantity and invoice. The update did not say a refund had been approved. No refund was due because the deposit had not exceeded the approved invoice total. No additional charge was collected during the hold. The order remained active and was dispatched after the paperwork was corrected.

Root cause. The production traveler and the packing worksheet used different meanings for “quantity.” The traveler meant pieces that passed through the production steps, including one setup sample. The packing record meant accepted saleable pieces. The two forms did not initially make that distinction sufficiently visible. Separately, the invoice clerk used a rough multiplication and did not independently recalculate the finish extension before saving the first draft. The corrected revision was reviewed against the signed quotation and the accepted quantity.

Contributing conditions. The sample was physically similar to the saleable parts and its paint dot was small. A number written as “41” appeared in both the traveler and the preliminary worksheet, which made copying it easy. The neighboring order had a $200 deposit, a $48 freight entry appeared in the old file, and a separate Bluefin Outfitters note had a $10 allowance. Those items were visually close in the shared folder. They did not apply to LD-418, but their proximity increased the chance of a clerical mix-up. The invoice form also placed “subtotal” near “balance,” making it possible to read the pre-deposit amount as the amount still due.

The team does not regard any of those contributing conditions as a reason to bill an unapproved figure. The signed quotation, current carrier confirmation, receipt log, and accepted-count sheet were the records used to resolve the discrepancy. The shop has thanked the people who found the errors and apologizes for the extra review. The customer was not asked to pay the obsolete draft amount, and no evidence shows that the obsolete draft reached the customer. The first revision remained internal.

Containment. The shop placed a yellow “sample retained” tag on the setup piece and moved it to the quality cabinet. The dispatch count was independently repeated. The preliminary invoice was marked “superseded” and kept only for audit history. The accounts clerk checked the customer name and order number against the receipt entry. The carrier charge was checked against the current confirmation rather than an older job. Staff were asked, very politely, not to erase the record of the first draft, because preserving the correction history makes later reconciliation easier.

Corrective action 1. Traveler forms will have separate boxes for “processed,” “accepted,” “sample retained,” and “packed.” Staff are asked to enter all four figures where relevant. For this case, the completed example would read: processed 41; accepted 40; sample retained 1; packed 40. A supervisor must verify that accepted plus retained equals processed when a sample is taken. The form will not assume that the processed count is the sale quantity.

Corrective action 2. Invoice software will show quantity, unit price, and calculated extension in separate columns. The user must confirm that quantity multiplied by unit price equals the extension before saving. A second person will review any manually entered total. For the LD-418 line, the check is 40 x $4.25 = $170.00, not $160.00. The check is intentionally written out because the earlier arithmetic error was small enough to look plausible.

Corrective action 3. The accounting screen will display the deposit against the same customer and order reference as the invoice. A payment from another customer will remain visible only in that other customer’s ledger. The review checklist will state: total before deposit, less deposit actually received for this order, equals balance due. For LD-418, $1,650.00 less $680.00 equals $970.00. The checklist will also warn that a balance on an unrelated account may coincidentally have the same amount and is not evidence of payment on this order.

Corrective action 4. Freight quotations will be attached to the relevant order rather than filed only under carrier name. A flat charge must not be converted to a weight-based charge unless the carrier’s quotation expressly gives a weight rate. The current order uses $84.00 once. The old $48.00 charge and the shipment weight totals will remain in the record for context, but will be labeled as non-applicable to the current invoice.

Corrective action 5. Obsolete amounts will be marked as superseded in large type. The $1,640.00 pre-deposit amount from the initial draft is not approved. The revision 3 total is $1,650.00 before the deposit, and the balance is $970.00 afterward. The shop will keep both numbers in the audit trail rather than deleting the first entry; the labels must make their different status clear.

Verification plan. For the next five small batch invoices, the office manager will sample the line extensions, check the deposit against the order-specific receipt, and compare accepted count with packed count. The manager will record the result and any correction. A successful review requires all line extensions to match quantity times price, all credits to be attached to the correct customer, and no retained sample to be included in the sale count. The check is about arithmetic and record matching, not a requirement that future orders use the same prices or quantities as this one.

Customer communication record. At 17:12, the shop sent a polite note saying: “We are very sorry for the delay in confirming the paperwork. We have checked the accepted count and revised the invoice before sending it. The order remains scheduled for the Tuesday collection. We shall be pleased to answer any question.” The customer replied at 17:26: “Thank you. Please send the final copy when ready; we still need all 40.” The customer did not request a refund, did not agree to 41 pieces, and did not say that the shop should charge the old January price. The customer’s phrase “all 40” refers to the order quantity, not to the number of processed pieces including the sample.

The quality clerk’s separate comment, “That was a wonderfully clean count,” was intended sincerely: the second count matched the accepted quantity. Another staff member jokingly wrote “our arithmetic is magnificent” beside the obsolete $160 line, but the remark was sarcastic and is not a verification. The approved arithmetic is the calculation in revision 3. The comment does not change a line amount or create a credit.

The incident review also compared several nearby numbers to avoid mistaken conclusions. The signed quote’s $32.50 current unit price gives $1,300.00 for 40 collars. The expired $31.00 rate gives $1,240.00, but it is not current. The per-piece finish charge yields $170.00. The obsolete extension was $160.00. The one-time measurement service is $96.00. The current freight is $84.00, while $48.00 belongs to an earlier shipment. The total current invoice before deposit is $1,650.00. The received deposit is $680.00. The resulting balance is $970.00. These amounts should not be intermixed merely because they occur in the same folder.

No further nonconformance was identified. The measured samples were 18.02, 18.01, and 18.03 mm, each within the stated 17.95 to 18.05 mm acceptance interval. The setup sample was retained, not rejected for a dimensional defect. The 40 packed collars were accepted. The total packed count of 40 agrees with the 24 plus 16 crate count. The invoice quantity of 40 agrees with the accepted shipment, and the billed per-piece lines apply to those 40 only. The measurement service and freight are each billed once, as shown.

The shop would be grateful if any future copy of this packet preserves the order number in the subject line. A file search for “Larkspur” alone can return records for Larkspur Dental and Larkspur Health, whose deposits and balances are unrelated. A search for “Harbor” may return the carrier paperwork or a separate Harbor Logistics customer account. The customer in this packet is Larkspur Dental; Harbor Logistics is the carrier for the shipment. The names appear close together in the folder but do not reverse those roles.

For completeness, the final dispatch record gives 2 crates, 40 accepted collars, 1 measurement certificate, and 1 invoice. It does not give 41 saleable collars. The separate carrier paperwork lists 158 lb gross weight and 132 lb net product load. The packing materials, returnable pallets, shop supplies, sample, and other customers’ goods are excluded from the invoice lines. The final signed carrier receipt will confirm collection, but at the time this report was written it had not yet been returned. The shop therefore records the shipment as prepared and scheduled, rather than claiming receipt by the customer.

Closing note. We appreciate the patience shown by the customer and the careful attention of the team. The purpose of recording the obsolete values is to explain the correction, not to offer them as alternatives. The accepted count, current quote, current freight confirmation, and order-specific deposit are the governing figures for this particular packet. Please use them with thanks.

RECONCILIATION APPENDIX — FIGURES TRANSCRIBED FROM SOURCE RECORDS

A. Signed quotation, 18 March: 40 guide collars at $32.50 each; deburr and protective finish $4.25 per accepted piece; one first-article measurement record $96.00; freight to be charged at the carrier’s confirmed flat amount. The quotation contains no rush fee. Its validity date precedes the order acceptance date by enough time that the January quotation is irrelevant; the customer accepted the March quotation. This appendix repeats the terms so that the invoice reviewer need not infer a unit price from a previous job.

B. Customer purchase order, 20 March: quantity 40; drawing LD-GC-9; destination Larkspur Dental receiving area; desired dispatch during the week of 7 April. The purchase order does not list the setup sample as an item. It asks for a measurement record and says freight will be shown separately. The order includes no line for pallets, cartons, shop supplies, or expedited service.

C. Receipt record, 28 March: customer payment received $680.00, allocated to order LD-418. The payment was not $680 per crate or per part; it is one deposit total. The receipt is not a second invoice charge. The bank’s $2.50 processing cost is recorded on the shop expense side. The balance calculation uses the received customer credit, not the bank cost.

D. Accepted quantity record, 4 April: crate A, 24; crate B, 16; total accepted, 40. Sample retained, 1. Production processed, 41. The arithmetic relationship is 40 accepted plus 1 retained equals 41 processed. The sample remains at the shop. No line on the invoice charges for it, and no crate contains it.

E. Draft invoice arithmetic: line 1, 40 x $32.50 = $1,300.00. Line 2, 40 x $4.25 = $170.00. Line 3, one x $96.00 = $96.00. Line 4, one x $84.00 = $84.00. Add all four line amounts: $1,300 + $170 = $1,470; $1,470 + $96 = $1,566; $1,566 + $84 = $1,650. Subtract the $680 received: $1,650 - $680 = $970 balance due. All calculations are in dollars, with no rounding needed.

F. Obsolete draft comparison: its finish line of $160 was $10 below the proper extension. It also omitted the $96 measurement line. Thus the obsolete pre-deposit total of $1,640 is $106 below the correct pre-deposit total: $10 plus $96 equals $106; $1,640 plus $106 equals $1,746, which would not be right if the starting obsolete total were treated as already including all the other lines. The record explains the apparent mismatch: the obsolete $1,640 total was built from $1,300 merchandise, $160 finish, and $180 combined for the remaining entries, where the clerical sheet incorrectly bundled measurement and freight. Revision 3 separates the entries and shows $96 plus $84, totaling $180. Correcting only the finish line therefore takes $1,640 to $1,650; the measurement was already represented in that particular obsolete total under the bundled $180 figure. A different first worksheet omitted measurement altogether and showed $1,544 before deposit. That worksheet was not the $1,640 invoice draft. The two obsolete sheets must not be conflated.

G. Freight and weights: current flat freight is $84.00. Two gross weights are 86 lb and 72 lb, so gross total is 158 lb. Crate tare weights are 12 lb and 14 lb, so tare total is 26 lb. Net load is 158 lb less 26 lb, or 132 lb. No quoted per-pound amount appears on the current carrier confirmation. The current freight amount is not calculated by multiplying either 158 or 132 by any currency rate.

[{"state":"Copperleaf Studio | Internal developer tooling policy page and FAQ excerpt | revision 6.4

This page is copied from the internal engineering portal. It contains the rules in force for the deployment window described below, a short FAQ, and a clipped CI operations digest. The export is terse; several labels were typed by hand and may contain typos. Times are UTC. The project uses build-minute units, not wall-clock minutes, unless a line explicitly says otherwise. The page is retained with the run record so an operator can reconcile the gate decision without opening another system.

POLICY: MONTHLY RUN BUDGET

Each project has a monthly allowance of 1,000 billable build-minute units. A run's billable amount is the sum of its Linux units and Windows units after the applicable multipliers. Linux units have multiplier 1.0; Windows units have multiplier 1.5. The source fields in the usage table are raw minutes. For example, 20 raw Windows minutes count as 30 billable units. Do not round individual run totals; the input values are whole minutes and multipliers produce whole or half units. Add billable units across completed runs for the project and calendar month. A cancelled run contributes only the units it consumed before cancellation, as recorded in the table. A queued or merely planned run contributes zero.

A project is over budget only if its month-to-date billable total is greater than 1,000. A total of exactly 1,000 is within budget. A customer can request a budget review at any total, but a request does not alter the calculation. Shared organization totals are not project totals. The policy applies separately to each project key; do not combine projects just because the owner or repository is the same. Retries count when the table lists their consumed units. A retry is not free merely because it followed a failed job.

A listed adjustment is a credit, not a usage amount. Subtract approved credits from the project's month-to-date usage. A pending credit is not approved and must not be subtracted. No adjustment appears in the table below. The allowance shown is the project's only monthly allowance. There is no carryover from a previous month and no multiplication of the allowance by the number of workflows.

POLICY: PARALLEL JOBS AND RETRIES

Parallel jobs are billed by their own raw platform minutes. If a Linux job ran for 14 minutes while a Windows job ran for 14 minutes, the billable total would be 14 + (14 x 1.5), not 14 minutes and not 28 raw minutes. Use the actual rows, not the elapsed duration of the overall pipeline. A retry row is separate from the attempt that it retries. If a retry was never started, it has no usage. If the retry started and ran, its listed raw minutes count even when its final status is failed.

The pipeline summary's “duration” field is wall-clock elapsed time and must not be used as a substitute for summed billable units. The summary may include waiting time, queue time, and overlap between parallel jobs. A run digest sometimes shows a rounded usage estimate; use the detailed raw-minute table when available. A developer's local timer is not a billing record. The authoritative data in this export is the usage table below.

POLICY: PROJECT KEYS

The key `api-gateway` belongs to Copperleaf Studio's customer-facing gateway repository. The separate key `docs-preview` belongs to its documentation preview project. The same organization has both keys. Do not transfer minutes between them. A staging workflow can run against either key, depending on the explicit project key in its row. The key, not the workflow's descriptive name, determines the allowance used. An operator may make a typo in a free-text note, but the project key column is the one used for this report.

The value “sample” in a log comment is not a project key. Rows marked “dry run” still count if the usage table gives raw minutes; dry run describes the code path, not whether the platform consumed resources. Rows with status “not launched” and zero minutes are not billable. This distinction is included because the web interface uses the word “run” for both a queued item and an executed job.

The summary panel captured at 09:10 displayed “about 900” for api-gateway, a rounded estimate generated before the final two rows were ingested. That summary is informational only and is not an additional usage row. The final table above is complete through September 30 at 23:59 UTC. No October rows belong in this calculation.

A team message says “we probably used 30 there” but gives no correction to the recorded 13 and 8. For this export, the detailed table and explicit key are controlling. The docs-preview allowance is also 1,000 units, but its calculation is outside the api-gateway question.

FAQ EXCERPT: HOW TO READ THE GATE

Q: Does the CI gate use elapsed pipeline time?
A: No. It uses the sum of the billable job usage for the project. Overlapping jobs do not cancel one another, and queue time does not create usage. Apply the platform multiplier to each raw row and then add the results. The top-level wall-time label is there to help estimate developer wait, not to decide whether the monthly budget has been crossed.

Q: Does a failed job count?
A: If the platform started it and recorded nonzero raw minutes, yes. A failed attempt and a started retry are both counted. A retry that appears only in a plan, with zero recorded raw minutes, does not count. Check the usage rows instead of assuming retries are free.

Q: The dashboard says “under one thousand.” Is that conclusive?
A: Not if the dashboard value is rounded or stale. Apply the written threshold to the exact month-to-date sum. A value exactly equal to the allowance is within budget; one unit above is over. Do not infer a precise total from “about,” “roughly,” or a rounded dashboard badge.

Q: Is each workflow given its own allowance?
A: No. The allowance belongs to the project key. Several workflows that use api-gateway share that project's monthly pool. A workflow title, branch name, or owner does not create another pool.

Q: Can docs-preview absorb a few api-gateway minutes?
A: No. They are separate projects even though they belong to one organization. Keep their totals separate. Do not put the preview rows into api-gateway's sum, and do not use api-gateway's usage to decide the preview project's budget status.

Q: How do I handle a cancelled run?
A: Count its recorded consumed minutes. Do not count the unused planned remainder. There is no cancelled row in the api-gateway table above, but the rule is included to prevent an operator from treating every cancelled workflow as either all-or-nothing.

Q: The engineer wrote that there were “only 900-ish minutes.” Which value should I trust?
A: Do not treat raw minutes as billable units, and do not treat an estimate as the source of truth. Linux and Windows have different multipliers. Use the row-level data and the project key. A rough statement could refer to raw minutes, a stale snapshot, or elapsed duration.

Q: Does a dry run always cost zero?
A: No. The label describes the workflow's intention. If an executed job has raw usage in the authoritative table, include it. Only an unstarted item with no recorded use contributes zero under this policy.

OPS DIGEST, COPIED FROM THE SEPTEMBER REVIEW

08:09 — Release operator: the browser stage had two platforms in the older matrix, but this month's table records the actual Windows minutes only. Use listed rows; don't reconstruct an old matrix.
08:11 — Finance sync: reminder that Windows is 1.5 units per raw minute. Several people keep adding its raw value directly. This note is a reminder, not another usage item.
08:16 — Build operator: docs-preview has its own key. I see 13 Linux and 8 Windows in its small table. Not relevant to the gateway sum.
08:22 — Reviewer: monthly cap is 1,000, strictly greater means blocked. Exactly 1,000 is still okay. Please don't translate “over” into “at or above.”
08:26 — Build operator: our duration tile says 7h 42m, but that is elapsed across the month view and not the resource sum. The data table is the billable record.
08:31 — Release operator: retry G-112 used 22 Linux minutes. It is a distinct row, not a replacement for G-111.
08:36 — Reviewer: no adjustment row in this export. A hypothetical credit mentioned in chat is not an approved credit.
08:40 — Build operator: I did not include the docs project while exporting api-gateway. Keys are shown in the first column of the full report; this excerpt has already been filtered to gateway except for the separate note above.

For clarity, the final API table is a deliberately compact extract from a larger audit packet. The other pages in that packet discuss runner labels, cache behavior, test sharding, artifact retention, branch protection, and alert routing. They do not change the multiplier or allowance. In particular, a cache hit can make a test faster without changing the raw-minute value already recorded; a workflow's number of tests is not a billing unit; the number of contributors does not multiply the project allowance; and a branch's protected status does not exclude its usage.

The run IDs G-105 and G-105R are shown together because an earlier export incorrectly displayed only the successful retry. The failure remains a charged attempt. G-111 and G-112 provide a second example of the same rule. A successful final pipeline can therefore include billable use from failed attempts. Conversely, the number of status changes in a dashboard is not a substitute for adding the raw-minute rows. The table explicitly says whether a row is Linux or Windows, so no platform must be guessed from the workflow name.

The report's “raw minutes” column is not already weighted. The multiplication rule is applied once, not twice. In particular, do not read the word “Windows” as meaning that the listed amount has already been increased. Do not multiply Linux usage. Do not apply the multiplier to a whole pipeline after combining platform rows; that would incorrectly weight Linux minutes too. The recommended method is row by row: leave each Linux number unchanged, multiply each Windows number by 1.5, then sum the billable amounts.

The table uses whole-minute entries. Consequently, the billable total can include half-unit results when a Windows row has an odd raw number. A half unit is valid and must not be rounded away. There is no per-run ceiling or rounding rule. The policy's greater-than comparison is applied to the unrounded project sum. Although all Windows raw values in this extract happen to be whole numbers, their weighted values are exact, and a final total should be written as an exact number rather than “about” a number.

An operator note at the bottom of the portal says “run count 20, about 1,000 minutes” and is not a claim that every run has equal cost. The table has twenty rows, but counting rows cannot establish the monthly billable sum. Some rows are Windows and some Linux, and their values differ. The summary badge should not be used to infer a total from the run count. The policy question is decided from the detailed records and arithmetic, not from the number of workflow entries.

FAQ EXCERPT: REPORTING A RECONCILIATION

When filing a reconciliation, state the project key, month, raw rows included, multiplier method, any approved credit, and resulting comparison with the allowance. Do not describe the project as over budget merely because a warning was triggered; warnings can be configured to appear at 90 percent. A warning is not the same as the policy gate. The gate uses the exact threshold on the complete usage record.

If two exports disagree, check whether one is a stale snapshot, whether one is showing a different project key, and whether one omits retries. This page identifies the final export through the last UTC minute of September. No later correction is attached. An export that says “about 900” predates two table rows and rounds the display. There is no basis here for replacing an exact sum with that approximate phrase.

The details are preserved for an operator who needs to answer one simple question: did the api-gateway project exceed its monthly allowance? The answer must be based on the rules and the exact rows above. Neither the comment about docs-preview, the duration tile, the stale badge, nor a hypothetical credit changes the computation. The final page is intentionally repetitive because prior reconciliations have mixed raw and weighted minutes. Read the platform field carefully, include each listed attempt once, and compare the total with 1,000.

APPENDIX: AUDIT CHECKLIST

1. Confirm the month. The table is September, not a rolling 30-day window.
2. Confirm the project key. The principal table is api-gateway.
3. Use all rows for that key, including failed attempts and retries with recorded use.
4. Keep docs-preview separate.
5. Convert Windows raw minutes at 1.5 and Linux at 1.0.
6. Add the converted amounts without rounding.
7. Subtract only approved credits; none are listed here.
8. Compare with 1,000 using the strict greater-than rule.

The checklist is not a second policy and does not create additional usage. It is included as an audit aid. The exact total should be reproducible from the table. The assistant reviewing this export should answer from the evidence supplied here, not from a remembered dashboard value, a typical usage pattern, or an assumption about how many minutes a normal pipeline takes.

A sample arithmetic note in the portal says: “If a project had 10 Linux minutes and 10 Windows minutes, billable use would be 10 + 15 = 25.” This example is explanatory and is not a row in the September table. Another sample says “a project at 1,001 is over, while one at 1,000 is not.” Those examples restate the rules; they should not be added to the actual project total.

The report is marked complete. All displayed run rows have the project key api-gateway, except where the prose explicitly identifies docs-preview as a separate-key example. No record is marked as an approved credit. The current month ends at 23:59 UTC on September 30. The reviewer does not need external information, an account login, or a second report to perform the comparison. Use only the exact listed usage and stated conversion rules.

The final confirmation field is blank because the gate decision has not yet been entered. A blank confirmation does not mean that usage is zero, and it does not imply that the project passed or failed. It simply means the reviewer has not recorded the result. The question below asks for the consequence of the policy calculation, not whether someone has already clicked the gate control.

APPENDIX: COMMON MISREADS

“Windows 38” means 38 raw minutes, not 38 billable units. “Retry passed” does not erase the failed attempt before it. “About 900” is a stale, rounded badge, not a certified total. “Twenty runs” is a count, not an amount. “Separate preview project” means its minutes are not added to api-gateway. “Exactly 1,000 is within budget” means the threshold is strictly greater than 1,000. Each statement should be applied only to the relevant issue; none changes the facts in the detailed table.

A note from an earlier draft mistakenly said “multiply all work by 1.5.” That draft was superseded before this revision. The current rule is platform-specific: Linux 1.0, Windows 1.5. The old phrase is reproduced here only as a historical correction and is not the applicable rule. No number in the detailed table has been pre-adjusted. If a reconciliation uses the old blanket multiplier, it will not follow the current policy.

The run list is complete, not a sampling. The phrase “compact extract” describes the compact audit packet and not omitted api-gateway runs. The separate docs-preview figures are the only non-gateway figures mentioned, and they are expressly segregated. There are no hidden rows to estimate, no prorating by days, no allowance increase for a release, and no waiver implied by a green status. The computation is therefore a direct conversion-and-addition exercise followed by the stated threshold comparison.

END OF EXPORT

A run is within its artifact quota when the total retained artifact size is less than or equal to the stated run quota. It exceeds the quota only when the retained total is greater than the quota.
