16:51 UTC — Build engineer: I see the badge at roughly 500. Could be safe if it rounds down, but there are two late entries.
17:04 UTC — Storage reviewer: use retained-only ledger; the badge snapshot is earlier than the final index.
17:13 UTC — Release operator: the failed manifest attempts were temporary and discarded. I confirm the retry outputs shown as retained should stay in the sum.
17:21 UTC — Intake bot: no separate quota per package. Form field says run quota, 500 MiB.
17:33 UTC — Build engineer: the dashboard's package count is four. It is not four files and it is not a MiB value.
17:49 UTC — Storage reviewer: equality is allowed under the FAQ. Compare the exact total, not the rounded badge.

The handoff notes do not add further artifacts. They restate which source controls the calculation and identify two plausible misreadings: treating a rounded display as exact and treating package count as size. The detailed ledger enumerates all retained rows. The full log gives the discarded attempts so they can be excluded rather than accidentally added. Each listed retained amount is already in MiB.

The run quota is evaluated after the final retained ledger has synchronized. It is not evaluated at the time of the first package upload, nor is it an average across the month. The date and time in the form identify the run, but the decision requires no duration arithmetic. No other run's artifact usage is included. The project can have other runs, but the quota field on this form says this is a per-run limit. The question asks only whether this specific run exceeded it.

The relevant rows can be grouped for checking, but they must all be counted: alpha has its Linux, Windows, and symbol entries; beta has the same three plus retained provenance; gamma has the same three plus retained manifest; delta has the three listed platform and symbol entries. The discarded manifests are not additional retained rows. This grouping is only an aid; summing the actual rows is the authoritative method. Do not infer equal sizes across packages or omit metadata because it is not a package archive.

No other retention adjustment, credit, compression ratio, exclusion, or per-platform cap is stated in this submission. The stated quota is 500 MiB and the ledger entries are already expressed in that unit. The exact total should therefore be compared directly to 500. A total of 500 would be within quota under the FAQ; the phrase “exceeded” requires a total strictly greater than 500. The rounded dashboard badge cannot settle a close comparison.

APPENDIX: FIELD DEFINITIONS

“Package name” is the distinct release component label, such as alpha or beta. “Artifact row” is one retained output with a listed size. “Retained” means it remains in the run's stored output set for the quota calculation. “Discarded” means it was not retained and is excluded. “Run quota” means a single aggregate size limit for all retained output rows associated with this run. “Dashboard badge” is a display estimate and is not authoritative when an exact ledger is available.

A metadata artifact remains an artifact for quota purposes even if it is not installable by a user. A debug-symbol file remains an artifact even if the release package is smaller without it. A retry's retained output is counted just like any other retained output. No distinction in the FAQ excludes those categories. The only explicit exclusion here is a discarded temporary upload. The ledger already labels which entries are retained, so the reviewer need not decide retention from file type or status history.

The form submission is complete enough to make the requested determination: the run key, single quota, retained sizes, unit, and final ledger status are supplied. The open text includes estimates and a conditional aside, but neither replaces the attached records. A reviewer should calculate the sum, compare it with the exact threshold, and leave unrelated facts such as package count and final green status out of the arithmetic.

END OF SUBMISSION EXPORT

[{"state":"Permit and benefits portal operations log, weekly digest, and FAQ notes

This is the kind of weekly operations digest that starts as a server log and then wanders into notes from the people who keep the permit and benefits portal running. It is copied from the fictional Alder Borough service desk, and everything in it refers to the same review week unless a line gives another date. The team likes to leave context in the log because someone inevitably asks six weeks later why a number moved by a few dollars. The portal handles parking permits, street-vending permits, and a small heating-support benefit. It does not make final decisions about eligibility; it records submissions and routes them to staff.

Monday, 08:02: The intake service started normally. There were 18 parking-permit applications, 7 street-vending applications, and 5 heating-support applications in the morning queue. The screen showed 30 items total. The nightly counter had shown 28, but two draft applications were completed after midnight and before the daily snapshot. No one should treat a draft as a submitted application. The log has a separate field called completed_at for that reason. A useful reminder from the on-call person: a number in a banner is not necessarily the number of approved permits, and a queued application is not an approval.

Monday, 08:17: The fee calculator test ran on a sample parking permit. The annual base charge was $24 and the processing charge was $6, so the displayed total was $30. This is a test record, not a real application. The test also checked a reduced-fee example: a $24 base charge less a $4 reduction, plus the same $6 processing charge, yields $26. The log had a misleading nearby line from an old test that said “$24 + $4 + $6 = $34”; that old line tested a surcharge, not a discount. The currently active setting is reduction, and the calculator output was $26.

Monday, 09:05: Uma Petrov called about a heating-support application she submitted on the portal. She said the confirmation page displayed “received,” and asked whether that meant she had already been granted support. The clerk explained that the status is only a receipt acknowledgement. Her application was still awaiting review. Uma mentioned an amount of $480 from a draft household budget, but that amount was not an award and was not entered as one. The call note was filed under “status question,” not “payment issue.”

Monday, 09:41: A permit clerk tested a household discount for a fictional sample applicant. The published calculation shown in the FAQ is a $40 base charge, minus a $10 qualifying reduction, plus a $5 processing charge. The total is $35. The tester initially expected $45 because the line item “reduction” looked like another fee when viewed quickly. The clerk reopened the form and checked the minus sign. The service log records the final expected total as 35. No account was charged in this test.

Monday, 10:16: Application QP-1182 was submitted for a parking permit. Its status moved from “draft” to “received.” The fee field showed $30, using a $24 base charge and a $6 processing charge. The same log page displayed an unrelated $36 total from a street-vending permit example, which uses a $30 base charge and a $6 processing charge. The two records were adjacent because the staff member was checking both screens. The $36 amount does not belong to QP-1182.

Monday, 11:03: The support queue had 12 cases at opening. Four were resolved, and 3 new cases arrived before lunch. The simple arithmetic gives 12 - 4 + 3 = 11 open cases. One dashboard widget briefly showed 15, but that was the count of all cases handled during the morning, not the count still open. A staff member wrote “queue looks bigger than it is” in the chat. The exported queue file later confirmed 11 unresolved cases.

Monday, 12:22: The portal accepted a fictional street-vending permit fee test. The base fee was $30, the city-neighborhood discount was $8, and the processing fee was $6. The active rule subtracts the discount before adding processing, so $30 - $8 + $6 = $28. A nearby sample from a different permit type showed $38, which was the undiscounted $32 base plus $6 processing. Neither the number 38 nor the other permit type changes the test result of 28.

Monday, 13:10: A staff meeting began in the little room next to the call center. The notes are pasted here because the service desk always asks for the decision after a meeting. The group agreed that the portal should keep three separate labels: received, in review, and approved. People keep saying “my permit is in” when they mean that the application was received, so the FAQ will repeat that receipt is not a decision. The clerk will avoid saying “approved” until a decision record exists. A warm cup of tea was spilled on the first page, which explains the odd smudge in the archived copy, but the relevant numbers are still legible.

Meeting note, 13:18: The weekly permit summary has 20 parking applications, 9 vending applications, and 6 benefits applications. The total is 35 applications received during the reporting period. These are intake counts, not completed decisions. Of the 20 parking applications, 12 were approved, 3 were declined, and 5 remain in review; those three subtotals add to 20. The vending figures were 4 approved, 2 declined, and 3 in review, totaling 9. The benefits figures were 2 approved, 1 declined, and 3 in review, totaling 6. The facilitator said that the total number of approvals is 18, since 12 + 4 + 2 = 18. Someone had written 17 in a draft table by leaving out the two benefit approvals. The corrected figure is 18.

Meeting note, 13:32: The staff discussed whether to put “about 20” or the exact number of open cases in a banner. They decided to show 11 open cases when the query returns 11. The case report for the week began with 12, added 3, and closed 4, so the count was 11. A second report showed 19 cases touched by staff; that number includes closed cases and should not be used as the open count. The group decided not to round the queue count just to make the banner look tidier.

Meeting note, 13:47: The benefit team reviewed a practice calculation for a heating-support applicant. The monthly gross amount entered was $1,200. The rule in this particular practice worksheet allows a standard deduction of $150 before the comparison figure is displayed. The resulting comparison figure is $1,050. This exercise is not a policy decision about any real resident and does not say whether the applicant qualifies. One person guessed $1,350 after adding the deduction instead of subtracting it; that is the wrong operation. The worksheet’s highlighted output was 1,050.

Meeting note, 14:05: A clerical check found four applications with missing attachments, two with an unreadable address, and one that had both problems. For a simple count of applications with at least one of those two problems, the correct calculation is 4 + 2 - 1 = 5. The overlap must not be counted twice. A draft spreadsheet displayed 6 because it added the two categories without removing the one overlapping case. The finalized note says five distinct applications need some follow-up. The list itself stays restricted to authorized staff.

Meeting note, 14:29: The group looked at a fictional fee waiver example. The usual total charge for the sample permit was $35, and the waiver covered $15. The remaining amount due was $20. A nearby line in the old handbook listed a $25 waiver for a different program, but that amount was not the one used in this example. The finance clerk repeated that a waiver is subtracted from the charge; it is not added to it. The sample was included to make sure the calculator did not accidentally display $50.

Tuesday, 07:58: The daily job reported 14 newly submitted parking applications and 8 newly submitted street-vending applications. The intake count for those two types is 22. Two additional heating-support records were drafts saved but not submitted, so the total submitted count for the three categories is still 22, not 24. A note attached to the job says to count only records with status received or later. Drafts are useful to applicants and staff, but they do not appear in the submitted total.

Tuesday, 08:31: A data-check script compared a displayed amount with the underlying fee components. In test record Z-44 the base fee is $32, the discount is $7, and processing is $5. The proper result is $30. The value $44 came from a stale screen that added the discount and processing to the base charge. That screen was refreshed after the test. The current log line reads expected=30 and displayed=30. The sample record is not tied to an actual resident.

Tuesday, 09:12: The FAQ editor pasted a draft paragraph into the portal. It says: “A receipt is not a permit approval. If you see received, we have the application, not a final decision.” Under that paragraph, the editor listed a typical processing example: 5 business days for intake review plus 2 business days for document indexing, a total of 7 business days of listed handling steps. This is an estimate of those two steps only, not a promise that all decisions happen in seven days. The editor added a note to keep the phrase “listed steps” so people do not confuse it with a guaranteed decision deadline.

Tuesday, 09:55: The automated alert count came through as 6 delayed alerts in the morning and 5 in the afternoon. The total delayed alerts for the day was 11. The dashboard’s total of 16 was the number of alerts sent, including five on-time messages. Staff should not report 16 as delayed. The log viewer shows the on-time and delayed fields separately, which is handy when people are not staring at the same dashboard tile.

Tuesday, 10:38: A resident asked how the annual parking charge was calculated. The agent used a plain example: $24 base, $6 processing, and no reduction equals $30. The resident’s own file was not open in the training environment, and the agent did not claim that the example amount applied to the resident. The FAQ says fees can differ by permit type, so this is an illustration rather than an individualized quote. The agent made a point of saying “example total,” because a call note from last month had treated an example as though it were a confirmed charge.

Tuesday, 11:26: The permit staff recorded 8 completed reviews in the morning and 7 in the afternoon. The number completed that day was 15. A separate line showed 17 records handled, because two were returned for missing material rather than completed. The reporting definition says “completed review” means approved or declined, not simply opened or touched. In the end-of-day table, 9 approvals and 6 declines add up to the 15 completed reviews. Nobody needs to infer that all 15 were approvals.

Tuesday, 12:03: The clerk checked three ways of explaining a waiver. One example was a $40 fee with a $10 waiver, leaving $30. Another was a $30 fee with a $5 waiver, leaving $25. A third was a $28 fee with no waiver, leaving $28. The notes are deliberately repetitive because the same minus sign got lost in an earlier draft. The portal’s active fee display uses the remaining amount due, not the amount waived and not the pre-waiver charge.

Tuesday, 13:14: The service counter was busy, so a staff member copied a short FAQ into the team chat. It explained that benefit applications have three possible status descriptions: received, in review, and decision recorded. The text also said that a displayed household amount is not necessarily a monthly payment. The team has no authority to convert an intake estimate into an award merely because it appears next to a dollar sign. For the training example in that FAQ, an estimated monthly cost of $900 and a listed credit of $120 produce a net example cost of $780. The estimate is only an illustration; no benefit award is stated.

Tuesday, 14:02: The reconciliation job found 10 parking applications received, 6 vending applications received, and 4 benefit applications received in the selected batch. There were 20 applications in the batch. Five were approved, three declined, and twelve still awaiting a decision; 5 + 3 + 12 = 20. A nearby export row contained 21, the number of documents attached to the batch, because one application had two documents. Applications and attachments are different counts, and the report’s application total is 20.

Wednesday, 08:10: A staff note says the portal is “mostly behaving, which is the sort of praise that makes the server suspicious.” The server did not become suspicious, of course; the phrase was a joke after a quiet overnight run. There were 3 sign-in retries by staff and 2 by applicants, for 5 total retries. The retries did not create duplicate applications. The duplicate detector found zero duplicate submissions in that run. The log also has a historical total of 8 retries from the prior day, which should not be mixed into the Wednesday count.

Wednesday, 08:44: A practice case for the heating-support FAQ used an example monthly amount of $1,500 and a sample household contribution of $400. The difference, $1,100, is the example amount after contribution. The example does not say that a person with those figures qualifies. A second nearby example used $1,600 and $450, yielding $1,150. The page labels them Example A and Example B; only Example A was copied into the training note. The clerk added commas to make the amounts easier to read, not because any underlying figure changed.

Wednesday, 09:30: The caseworkers compared two ways of counting follow-ups. Three applicants were missing a proof-of-address file, and four were missing a signature. One applicant was in both groups, so the number of distinct applicants needing either item was 3 + 4 - 1 = 6. The desk calendar had seven reminder slots because one applicant needed a second reminder. Reminder slots are not unique applicants. The finalized note refers to six applicants, while the calendar may still show seven slots.

Wednesday, 10:12: An old FAQ screenshot said the application charge was $22. The current example on the live FAQ is $24 base plus $6 processing, or $30. The screenshot is clearly marked archived and predates a change to the example. Staff agreed not to answer a current fee question from the archived screenshot. For training purposes, the live example’s arithmetic is $24 + $6 = $30. This does not mean every permit has the same charge; the live FAQ says to check the relevant permit type.

Wednesday, 11:07: The phone system showed 14 callers waiting at the start of the shift. Five calls were answered, and two callers disconnected before speaking to anyone. The number still waiting after those events was 7. The supervisor’s separate “calls handled” count was 5; disconnected callers are not part of that count. A chart that displayed 16 was counting calls received plus transferred calls and was not a queue-size measure. The shift handover uses the remaining-waiting count of seven.

Wednesday, 12:40: The benefits FAQ was reviewed by a clerk who prefers examples, so it now includes an example of a $60 monthly utility bill with a $15 listed credit. The net example bill is $45. In the margin, an older draft says a $10 credit against a $60 bill leaves $50; that arithmetic is also correct but belongs to a different example. The adopted paragraph uses $15 and $45. It does not promise that a person will receive a credit of $15.

Wednesday, 13:26: A quality-check report sampled 25 records. Twenty-one had all required fields, and four had at least one blank field. Those counts add to 25. Within the four incomplete records, two were missing a contact number, one was missing a preferred-language field, and one was missing both. The number of records with a missing contact number is two, not three, because the overlap does not create another record. The report uses separate field-level counts and a distinct-record total; the staff note warns not to add the field counts and call the result a record count.

Wednesday, 14:11: The public FAQ excerpt was pasted into the log for reference: “A fee reduction lowers the permit charge. A processing charge may still apply. A submitted application is not automatically approved.” Beneath it is the current basic example: base $32, reduction $7, processing $5, total $30. A search result still displays a former example of $32 plus $5, or $37, because it has not been refreshed. The FAQ itself is current and the search result is marked for update. The log does not treat $37 as the current reduced example.

Thursday, 08:05: The morning batch included 9 new parking applications, 5 new vending applications, and 3 new benefits applications. The total was 17. The status count later in the morning showed 8 approved, but that was not a total application count. One of the new parking applications was still incomplete and remained a draft, so it was excluded from the 9 submitted parking applications shown in the batch report. A separate screen showed 10 parking records because it included that draft. The submitted application total stays 17.

Thursday, 08:53: The support team looked at a benefit practice calculation. An illustrative eligible expense was $720, and an illustrative household contribution was $180, leaving $540 under the example calculation. A nearby note about a different case used $700 and $200, also leaving $500. The practice worksheet in the current session is the first one, and its output is 540. The figures are fictional and are not an eligibility determination or promise of payment. The clerk wrote “difference, not sum” beside the calculation after a new trainee briefly added the two values.

Thursday, 09:34: A portal status report showed 16 applications received, 10 in review, and 6 with a decision recorded. These are mutually exclusive statuses in this report, so their total is 32 applications. The activity dashboard displayed 38 because it counted six status changes in addition to the 32 records. For a question about the number of applications represented by the three status groups, use 32; do not add activity events as though they were applications. The reporting page has a footnote explaining that a record can generate several events.

Thursday, 10:18: The clerk tested a combined charge for a fictional vendor permit. The base fee was $45, a reduction of $12 applied, and processing was $7. The total due was $40 because 45 - 12 + 7 = 40. A line in a nearby browser tab showed $52, which was the base plus processing before applying the reduction. The log screenshot captured both tabs, leading to a question about which result was active. The test result panel was the active one and showed $40.

Thursday, 11:02: The team received a note from the document-indexing group: 13 files were indexed in the morning and 9 in the afternoon, for 22 files. This is a document count, not an application count. The application system associated those files with 18 applications. Four applications had two files each, while the others had one. A dashboard tile showing 22 is accurate for files; it is not a statement that 22 separate applications were received.

Thursday, 12:36: One FAQ draft asked, “How many days do the two sample steps take altogether?” The sample says intake review takes 4 days and indexing takes 3 days. The combined listed duration is 7 days. This is a training example and the live portal does not promise that every case follows those exact durations. Another paragraph about a different service says 10 days for decision review; that is not one of the two steps in the sample calculation. The editor left both paragraphs but separated them with headings.

Thursday, 13:20: A staff huddle reviewed the permit-fee display. The rule is that the reduction is taken from the base charge, and the processing amount is added afterward. For the current sample, the base is $50, reduction is $15, and processing is $8. The resulting amount is $43. In an old comment, someone wrote $73 by adding all three figures. That comment is retained to explain the bug report, not as the right fee. The test page now displays $43.

Friday, 08:11: The weekly queue started with 15 open applications awaiting staff review. Six received a decision on Friday morning, and two new applications entered the review queue. The open count became 11. The math is 15 - 6 + 2 = 11. A separate metric showed 17 actions, including the six decisions, two new records, and nine document checks. Actions are not open applications. The team’s Friday handover note uses 11 as the remaining queue count.

Friday, 09:02: The FAQ editor asked whether a paragraph should say that three support programs share the same dollar limit. The answer in the source material was no: the three sample limits were $100, $125, and $150, and they are examples for separate programs. Their sum is $375, but the sum is not a single limit. The editor kept the figures in a comparison table and added a note that a person should read the row for the program they are asking about. The log records no combined benefit limit.

Friday, 10:25: A test report looked at a parking application with a $36 base charge, a $9 reduction, and a $6 processing charge. The calculated total is $33. The test also displayed a nearby unmodified permit example at $42, which is $36 plus $6. A trainee read the $42 from the neighboring card and thought the reduced total was 42, but the current test card clearly shows $33. No real payment was taken during the test.

Friday, 11:50: The public FAQ excerpt was approved with friendly, slightly chatty language: “We have your application when it says received. We have not decided it just because the screen has that word.” A small fee example follows: a $28 base charge, less a $5 reduction, plus a $4 processing charge, comes to $27. A separate example below shows $28 plus $4 equals $32 when no reduction applies. The first example is explicitly headed “with reduction,” and the second is headed “without reduction.”

Friday, 13:05: The weekly count of completed decisions was 14 approvals and 6 declines, for 20 completed decisions. There were 12 applications still awaiting a decision. Together, these figures describe 32 applications in the selected report: 20 decided plus 12 pending. The intake report showed 34 submissions because two were withdrawn before entering the decision queue. The report definition excludes withdrawn records from the selected decision-queue total. Staff agreed to quote 32 when asked about that queue, and 34 when asked about submissions received.

Friday, 14:42: End-of-week note from the portal team: the FAQ is not a decision letter, sample amounts are not personal awards, and the status label “received” means only that the service has received a submission. The small arithmetic examples were checked twice because the team was tired and because a minus sign can be an oddly powerful character. The active examples currently in the FAQ are $24 + $6 = $30; $40 - $10 + $5 = $35; and $32 - $7 + $5 = $30. The status and fee examples are included to make the public pages easier to understand, not to create a new eligibility rule.

FAQ excerpt, retained below the logs: For a parking permit, check the current fee table for the permit type. If a listed reduction applies, subtract it from the base charge, then add any processing charge shown for that permit. For a benefit, the portal may show an estimate or a received status before a staff decision is complete. An estimate is not an award. A submission receipt confirms that the application reached the service; it does not confirm approval. If you see a sample calculation, it is only a sample. For example, a base of $30, a reduction of $8, and processing of $6 produce $28. Do not add the $8 reduction as though it were a fee. If the screen and the current fee table disagree, contact the service desk and quote the permit type, not a guessed total.

FAQ editing note: the team debated whether a long explanation might make people stop reading, then added two more paragraphs anyway. One says the weekly report may count applications, documents, calls, or actions, and those are different units. A number can be perfectly correct and still answer the wrong question. Another says application status is recorded per application, while a document index count is recorded per file. The final note says there is no need to calculate a resident’s personal benefit from these training examples. Staff should refer the person to the appropriate program team. The editor also left a reminder that dates, amounts, and status labels should be read together with their headings, because the neighboring column may describe a different program or a different period.

The portal log finished the week without a service outage. The team’s weekend handover says the test environment has no real resident records, the examples above are fictional, and all the numerical examples are self-contained. The central lesson for staff is not complicated: count the thing the question asks about, use the operation named in the current rule, and do not let a nearby number from another row sneak into the answer. The team’s long weekly note is a little rambling, as usual, but the same message appears in the FAQ and in the logs. These notes come from the fictional Brookmere District office, where the staff manage local permits and a modest household-support benefit. They were assembled from a talkative meeting recorder, a few FAQ drafts, and the application counter’s daily log. The recorder has a habit of preserving side comments like “the printer is thinking about it,” so the document is longer than the actual decisions require. All names, amounts, and cases in this document are fictional training examples. Nothing here is an individual eligibility decision. The office uses the word application for a submitted record, not a saved draft, and staff are expected to say whether a number describes applications, documents, decisions, or dollars.

Monday meeting, 09:00: Viktor Fischer opened by asking everyone to stop calling every green screen “approved.” The portal uses three labels: received, under review, and decision complete. A receipt means the form reached the service. It does not mean a permit was issued or a support payment was authorized. The group agreed that this distinction belongs in the public FAQ, even though the phrase has appeared in earlier drafts. The clerk’s coffee was cold, the meeting room clock was four minutes fast, and neither circumstance changes how the status labels work.

Monday meeting, 09:12: The sample parking fee currently used in staff training is a $36 base charge, a $9 reduction, and a $6 processing charge. The total after applying the reduction and processing charge is $33. Someone had typed $51 into a slide by adding all three numbers. That was corrected before the slide was circulated. A separate sample with no reduction is $36 + $6 = $42. The meeting record says to use $33 for the reduced example and $42 only for the no-reduction example. These are sample fees, not a promise that every permit costs either amount.

Monday meeting, 09:26: The applications received last week were 16 parking permits, 8 vendor permits, and 5 household-support forms. That gives 29 submitted applications. The counter log separately shows 3 saved drafts that were never submitted. Drafts are not added to the 29. A dashboard tile showed 32 records because it included the drafts, and the staff agreed that the tile should be labeled “records including drafts” if it remains visible. The meeting’s official submitted count is 29.

[{"state":"To: Department Manager
From: Farid Rahman, course administration
Subject: This term’s registration mess and the corrections I have actually made

I am sending this because the dashboard keeps showing a cheerful green banner while the people doing the work are fielding the same avoidable complaints every hour. The banner says “All course services operating normally.” That is not what students are experiencing, and it is not what the records say. Please read the attached status report, the pasted working sheet, and the policy extract before anyone sends another message claiming that the problems have been resolved. I have marked what is confirmed, what is still pending, and what people merely assumed from an old email. I am angry about the time wasted, but I am not going to inflate the numbers or turn a student’s guess into a confirmed fact.

This is a status update for the manager, not a request to change the rules. The policy extract is included because staff have been quoting different versions of it. The spreadsheet paste is from the registration desk’s working copy, not the public dashboard. It contains repeated rows and comments, so the row count is not the number of unique cases. Where a student has two distinct problems, both are listed. A note saying “fixed” means a staff member recorded a correction; it does not necessarily mean the student confirmed that the correction solved everything.

My own confirmed actions this week are limited. I corrected the room assignment on the course page for Studio Methods after the timetable office confirmed the change. I restored Bao Petrov’s access to the course site after checking the enrollment record. I also sent Xiu Lindqvist the required advising appointment link after the earlier message went to an obsolete address. Those are three separate administrative actions. I did not issue refunds, waive tuition, promise a grade change, or approve any exception to the attendance policy. Please do not repeat the claim in the hallway note that I “signed off on every request.” I did not.

The immediate student-facing problems in the notes are not all the same kind of problem. Some are about a place in a course, some concern access to materials, some concern a room or time, and some concern how a fee was shown. A student mentioning a fee does not prove that the student was overcharged. A student asking whether a deadline can be moved does not mean the deadline was moved. Likewise, an employee’s assurance that “we’ll look into it” is not evidence that the requested action has already happened.

Working summary, as of the last review: Farid’s registrar export lists the students who contacted the office; the desk sheet lists issue categories; the course-site audit lists access changes; and the timetable office’s note is the authority for room assignments. These sources are not interchangeable. The copied dashboard is stale and should not be used to contradict a dated registrar record. I have left the original comments in the paste below because removing them would conceal why some cases were reopened.

STAFF STATUS NOTES

Monday, 08:10 — I found a queue of messages that had been marked “answered” because an automatic acknowledgement went out. That is not an answer. Several students were still waiting for a person to address the actual question. I asked the desk not to use the acknowledgement count as a resolution count.

Monday, 09:00 — The course page for Studio Methods displayed Room 214, although the approved schedule said Room 241. The timetable office confirmed that 241 was correct. I changed the page and asked the front desk to replace its printed sign. The sign was changed before noon. The old room remained in a saved PDF for part of the day, so some students may have seen both versions.

Monday, 10:35 — Bao Petrov reported that the course site rejected his login. The enrollment record showed active status, but the site’s roster had not refreshed. I checked the record with the registrar, then restored access. Bao later confirmed that he could open the course materials. This is an access problem with a documented correction, not a missing enrollment.

Monday, 11:20 — Xiu Lindqvist said the advising appointment link in the first message did not open. The earlier email contained a link to last term’s scheduling page. I sent the current link and received a reply confirming that the appointment page loaded. The appointment itself is not yet shown as booked, so I have not described it as booked.

Monday, 13:40 — Several students asked whether the lab-fee line included a materials kit. The published fee schedule describes a lab fee and separately describes optional replacement materials. The question is understandable because the portal compresses the labels, but a question about what a fee covers is not evidence of a duplicate charge.

Tuesday, 08:25 — The desk received reports that one section looked full even though seats appeared to be open in the instructor’s planning sheet. The planning sheet is not the enrollment system. A planned seat is not a released seat. Staff must check the registrar record before telling anyone that a place is available.

Tuesday, 09:15 — I reviewed the reopened cases. One student’s first message asked how to request a deadline extension. The follow-up said, “I have not submitted an extension request yet.” The desk correctly left the request status as “information provided,” rather than “extension approved.”

Tuesday, 10:00 — An angry note in the shared queue read, “Great, another portal that remembers everything except my registration.” The sentence is sarcastic. It should be categorized as a registration complaint, not as praise for the portal. The student’s record was checked, and the registration did appear in the registrar system; the portal display was delayed. Staff should distinguish the student’s display problem from an absent registration.

Tuesday, 11:45 — A forwarded message from an instructor said, “Farid has asked us to waive the lab fee.” The original message, when opened, said, “A student asked whether Farid can explain the lab fee.” I did not ask for a waiver. The forwarded summary reversed who made the request and overstated what was requested. I have not changed a fee record.

Tuesday, 14:10 — The admissions desk reported that some students used the wrong form for a course change. The old form asks for a course code but does not ask whether the student wants to leave the current section. Staff must not infer a withdrawal from a request to change sections. A submitted change form remains pending until an authorized registrar action is recorded.

Wednesday, 08:30 — I checked the room signs against the timetable office’s confirmed list. The Studio Methods correction is complete. The design lab sign still needs replacement; it is not part of my confirmed correction because the timetable office has not yet verified the room. Do not merge these two cases just because both mention a room.

Wednesday, 09:50 — A student said, “I would have paid the fee yesterday if the portal had shown the right label.” This is a hypothetical statement about a past action, not confirmation that the student paid. The payment ledger, not the student’s imagined alternative, determines whether a payment is recorded.

Wednesday, 12:05 — The portal team confirmed that the fee label will be reviewed. That is a review, not a refund and not a fee waiver. The student who raised the label issue has not asked me to return money in the message I reviewed. Staff should not record a refund request merely because a fee is mentioned with frustration.

Wednesday, 15:30 — An instructor asked whether the office could reserve two seats for students who had contacted advising. I replied that the office cannot treat an inquiry as an enrollment and that the registrar must record a seat assignment. Neither student was described as enrolled in that section in the records checked that afternoon.

Thursday, 08:15 — The course-site access report showed that Bao Petrov’s access had been restored. The same report showed a separate student with no active course-site account because that student had not completed enrollment. Staff should not copy Bao’s resolution note onto the other record.

Thursday, 10:40 — I reviewed a message that said, “I’m not saying the room notice was wrong; I’m saying the notice on my phone was different from the door sign.” The student is reporting a discrepancy between two displays. This wording does not establish that the official schedule changed twice. The dated timetable record is still the source for the approved room.

Thursday, 13:00 — The section capacity was updated after the registrar confirmed that one seat had been released. The released seat was assigned through the normal queue. It was not a reserved seat for anyone who had merely asked about availability. The earlier planning sheet should not be used as proof of a student’s enrollment.

Friday, 09:20 — I received a report that a student’s advising appointment was missing. The calendar showed no appointment. The student had received a link and confirmed the page opened, but had not completed the booking. Sending the link and booking the appointment are different actions. The case remains open until the student books or asks for help.

Friday, 11:00 — The desk corrected two labels in the working sheet. One case had been placed under “refund” because the student asked what a fee was for. The student’s message did not request returned money. The other had been placed under “withdrawal” because the student asked to move sections; no withdrawal request was made. These corrections are why category totals in yesterday’s export differ from today’s.

Friday, 15:15 — I sent this report to prevent a fresh round of confident but inaccurate summaries. If the manager needs a brief account for the weekly meeting, use the confirmed entries in the current sheet and do not copy the green dashboard banner. I want the record to reflect the problems students actually reported, not the problems a template assumes they reported.

PASTED WORKING SHEET — REGISTRATION DESK

Columns: Case reference | Message summary | Confirmed issue category | Current status | Evidence source | Desk comment

R-401 | “The course is full online, but I was told there might be space.” | Section availability inquiry | Checked; no seat assigned at time of review | Registrar seat list | Planning sheet is not a release notice.

R-402 | “My password works everywhere except the course page.” | Course-site access | Restored after active enrollment verified | Site audit and registrar record | Student confirmed access afterward.

R-403 | “Could someone tell me why this line is called a lab fee?” | Fee-label explanation | Information sent; not a payment correction | Published schedule | No request for money back in reviewed message.

R-404 | “I need to switch from the morning group to the afternoon group.” | Section-change inquiry | Pending; registrar form required | Student message | Does not state a request to withdraw from the course.

R-405 | “The sign says 214, the corrected page says 241.” | Room information discrepancy | Page and sign corrected for Studio Methods | Timetable confirmation | Keep prior PDF attached to the record.

R-406 | “I can’t open the advising link you sent.” | Advising-link problem | New link sent; page-load confirmation received | Email exchange | Appointment not confirmed as booked.

R-407 | “If my work shift changes, I may ask for an extension.” | Possible future extension inquiry | No extension request submitted | Student message | Conditional; do not mark request approved or submitted.

R-408 | “I have paid the fee, but I don’t recognize this label.” | Fee-label question | Payment ledger checked separately | Student message and ledger | Label question alone does not show duplicate payment.

R-409 | “Great, another site that hides the course I registered for.” | Portal display complaint | Registration found in registrar system; display delay reported | Registrar record and portal screenshot | Sarcasm; not a compliment.

R-410 | “Farid wants the fee waived,” as summarized in forwarded note | Misattributed fee request | No waiver request from Farid found | Original and forwarded emails | Original asks for an explanation; forwarded summary is inaccurate.

APPENDIX A — EXTRACT FROM THE CURRENT COURSE ADMINISTRATION POLICY

Version noted by the registrar: current term, revision 4. The portal banner may continue to display revision 3 until its scheduled refresh. Staff must use the current dated extract for decisions and must not treat a portal headline as a substitute for the complete rule. Where the policy gives a threshold, staff should check the recorded facts against the threshold. Where a rule requires a form or a named official’s confirmation, an email acknowledgement or informal assurance is not a substitute for that requirement.

Section 1. Enrollment and section changes. A student is enrolled only when the registrar record shows active enrollment in the named course. A course-site account, a planning spreadsheet, a wait-list message, or an instructor’s intention to add a student does not by itself establish enrollment. A student who asks to move between sections remains in the course unless an authorized withdrawal is separately recorded. A request to change sections is pending until the registrar records a decision. A seat appearing in an instructor’s planning document is not released until the registrar’s seat list shows it as available. When a seat is released, assignment follows the existing queue; a message of interest does not reserve a seat.

Section 2. Withdrawals. A question about how to withdraw is an information inquiry, not a withdrawal request. A conditional statement such as “I will withdraw if the schedule changes again” is not a submitted request. A withdrawal request is recorded when the required registrar form is received. Receipt of the form means the request was submitted; it does not mean the withdrawal was approved or establish its effective date. Staff must not infer a withdrawal from a section-change request, a request to leave a lab list, or a complaint about a course. The registrar’s dated status is authoritative when an automatic acknowledgement or stale dashboard conflicts with it.

Section 3. Course-site access and materials. Active enrollment is a prerequisite for course-site access, but the two records are separate. An active enrollment does not prove that the site works. A site login working does not prove enrollment in a particular course. Course page visibility, downloadable slides, and a reading link are separately checked services. A student who can open the course page may still lack a particular file; a student who can download a file may still report that the course page is missing. Staff should record each distinct reported problem without copying one resolution onto another case. A link that opens the wrong week or wrong course is a link problem even if the link itself loads.

Section 4. Timetable and room communications. The timetable office’s confirmed dated schedule determines the approved room and meeting time. The course page, printed sign, reminder email, saved PDF, and instructor message are useful displays, but if they conflict, staff should verify against the confirmed schedule. Correcting one display does not prove that every other display has been corrected. Room and time are separate fields. A correct room does not establish that the time is correct, and a correct time does not establish that the room is correct. A request to check a time is not evidence that the time is wrong; a student’s direct report of a discrepancy should be logged and checked rather than silently treated as a confirmed schedule change.

Section 5. Attendance. The instructor maintains the attendance record. A student’s report of an absence, late arrival, or mark discrepancy should be recorded as reported until checked. Under the ordinary rule, each group of three recorded late arrivals counts as one absence. A partial group does not count as a whole absence. If an applicable exception is documented under Section 9, qualifying late arrivals are not included in that calculation. Asking how the attendance rule works is not itself an attendance event. A late arrival is not automatically an absence unless the applicable rule and instructor record say so. Staff should not add a mark based solely on an angry message or remove one solely because the student disputes it.

Section 6. Fees and payment records. The published schedule lists the course fee and any separately listed materials charge. The sum of the listed amounts is the schedule total. The schedule and the student’s ledger must be compared before an overcharge is described as established. A question about a fee label is not a claim of duplicate payment. A student’s statement that an amount “looks doubled” is a report requiring a ledger check. Two settled ledger entries for the same charge may support a duplicate-payment finding; a bank-screen image or an unexplained portal display alone may not. A request for a fee explanation, a report of a possible overcharge, and a request for money back are distinct categories. A refund request does not mean that a refund has been approved. A conditional statement that the student might request a refund if a future review confirms an error is not the same as confirmation of the error or completed refund action.

Section 7. Communications and status. An automated acknowledgement confirms receipt of a message only. It does not show that a staff member answered the question, that a correction was made, or that a request was approved. A case may be closed only after the recorded action addresses the issue that was actually raised. If a message contains several distinct requests or complaints, each should be tracked. If one item is resolved and another remains open, the whole message must not be marked resolved. Staff should preserve source messages when a forwarded summary changes who asked for what or makes a request sound more definite than the original. The original text and the authoritative administrative record take precedence over an inaccurate paraphrase.

Section 8. Grades and records. Grade changes are made by the authorized instructor under the relevant course procedure. A question about whether a grade can change is not a grade-change request. A report that two displayed numbers differ is a discrepancy to check, not automatic proof of which number is correct. Attendance records and grade entries are separate. Correcting one does not correct the other. Staff should record what the student asked to have checked, identify the supporting source, and avoid promising an outcome before the responsible office has reviewed it.

Section 9. Listed exceptions and documentation. An exception applies only where the policy text expressly includes the category and the required supporting confirmation is present. If the policy expressly excludes a category, an otherwise relevant circumstance does not override that exclusion. Where instructor confirmation is required, a student’s account alone is not sufficient. If the record states that the instructor has confirmed the qualifying circumstance and the policy does not exclude it, the case may be routed for application of the exception. Routing is not itself a final decision unless the policy names that routing step as the decision. Staff must distinguish “may qualify,” “documentation received,” “exception applies under the text,” and “exception implemented.”

Section 10. Use of this extract. This appendix is an extract for the cases in the accompanying status report. It is included to prevent staff from treating old portal language, informal chat, or a partial spreadsheet as controlling. It does not authorize staff to assume facts absent from the records. If a question is unanswered by this extract, ask the responsible office instead of guessing. Students may be angry, sarcastic, brief, or imprecise; staff should capture the intended administrative issue without treating sarcasm as praise or a hypothetical as a completed action. Notes should identify which evidence was actually checked.

APPENDIX B — WORKING TRACKER METADATA AND REVIEW NOTES

The pasted rows above were exported from a desk working copy at 16:05 on Friday. The export includes historical examples used to teach new desk staff how not to collapse distinct categories. It is not a live list of one student’s entire history. Case references are fictional administrative references created for this status report. Repeated examples are intentional because staff have repeatedly misclassified similar language in opposite ways. A matching word in a student message does not, by itself, settle the category. For example, the presence of the word “refund” can appear in a denial, a hypothetical, an actual request, or an inaccurate forwarded summary. The presence of “withdraw” can appear in a process question, conditional statement, submitted form, or explicit denial. The presence of “wrong” can refer to a student’s report rather than a verified administrative finding.

The tracker’s status column is deliberately conservative. “Requested” means the student asked for something. “Pending” means the responsible system has not recorded a final action. “Checked” means a staff member compared the named evidence. “Resolved” should be used only when the specific issue was addressed. A note that someone sent an email is evidence of sending an email, not evidence that a student received a usable link, booked an appointment, gained access, or agreed that the underlying problem was solved. A student’s confirmation is useful evidence for the student-facing outcome, while system records remain necessary for official enrollment, payment, timetable, and attendance status.

There are known limitations in the working sheet. Some messages arrived as screenshots with cropped headers. Some email threads contain forwarded summaries that omit the original question. The front desk’s printed sign log is updated by hand, and a correction may appear there later than on the course page. The payment ledger is available to finance staff but not to every registration desk worker. The advising calendar can show a link visit without showing a completed booking. The instructor’s attendance record may be updated after a student contacts the office. These limitations explain why certain cases are marked “review requested” rather than “confirmed,” and why a report of a problem is not always the same as a verified institutional error.

Review procedure used for this report: first, identify the student’s own words rather than relying on a forwarded paraphrase; second, separate each request or complaint; third, identify which source can confirm the fact; fourth, note whether a policy threshold or condition must be applied; fifth, record what is known and what remains unverified. If a report names several problems, do not force it into only one category to make the dashboard easier to read. If it names one problem and says other items are correct, do not add those other categories just because they appear elsewhere in the thread. If it raises an uncertain possibility, preserve that uncertainty.

A few examples from this week illustrate the point. The student asking why a fee label changed did not thereby request a refund. The student who said the fee had been charged twice and asked for the money back did make a refund request, even though finance still has to check the ledger. The student who said, “I might ask for a refund if the review finds an error,” made a conditional statement, not a report that an error was already confirmed. The student who wanted a new section explicitly said they did not want to leave the course; that is not a withdrawal. The student who asked how to drop the course had not submitted a withdrawal form. The student with a receipt for a submitted form had made a request, but the receipt alone did not prove approval.

The same care applies to several administrative services. A student may report both missing slides and a broken reading link; those should remain two material-access items. A student may report that the room is wrong but the time is right; that should not become a general timetable-error claim. A room notice can be wrong while the official schedule is right, or the official schedule itself may require checking. The presence of an old PDF is a plausible explanation for a discrepancy, but staff still need to check the current authority. A student may say a page works while a particular resource does not. A login issue and an enrollment issue are not interchangeable. A current active enrollment can coexist with failed access; an operational login can coexist with an inactive course enrollment.

Managers reviewing counts should remember that rows are examples and categories, not necessarily unique students or resolved cases. Rows R-402 and R-415 contrast an active student whose site access was restored with a record where enrollment was not active. Rows R-403, R-422, and R-423 contrast a fee explanation, an explicit refund request, and a conditional refund statement. Rows R-404, R-413, R-417, R-418, R-443, and R-445 distinguish a section-change inquiry, an explicit non-withdrawal, a process question, a submitted form, a future conditional statement, and a documented request. Rows with room and time combinations are likewise separate examples, not sequential updates to one student’s timetable. Do not sum every example row and present it as a count of live student complaints.

The angry tone in several quoted messages is not a reliable indicator of which office owns the case. Frustration about a portal can describe a registration display problem, a site login problem, a missing file, or simply a delayed refresh. “Great, another portal that remembers everything except my registration” is not praise. “This is the most helpful system ever” may be sincere or sarcastic depending on the surrounding text; the desk should inspect the message rather than mechanically assign sentiment. Anger also does not establish that a charge was incorrect, that a staff member made a promise, or that an exception has been approved. It should prompt careful reading, not a shortcut.

At the time this report was prepared, the manager asked for a concise tally of issues that had actually been raised in the source messages. I have not converted every historical teaching row into a live count. The live review concerns the specific status notes above: access restoration for Bao, a corrected Studio Methods room display, a corrected advising link for Xiu, unresolved explanation requests about fee labels, several section inquiries awaiting registrar action, a display discrepancy in the portal, and a small number of cases sent to finance or instructors for confirmation. The exact number in each category should come from the current live export, not from this illustrative paste.

I am frustrated that we have spent hours correcting summaries that could have been accurate the first time. The remedy is not another slogan saying that the queue is green. The remedy is to use the right source, keep separate requests separate, and say plainly when we do not yet know. I have corrected the items I could verify and routed the rest. Please do not tell students that a pending request is approved, that an explanation is a refund, that an automatic acknowledgement is a resolution, or that a question is a completed action. I expect the next manager update to reflect the actual records and the student’s actual words.

Short version, without treating the short version as a decision: the order was for a home dental-care kit, one parcel arrived with a cracked rinse tray, the second package was delayed, and the customer asked for a refund of the delivery fee while accepting a replacement tray. Do not read that as saying the customer asked to refund the whole kit. There are later clarifications below.

14 June, 16:42, Ines to Callum: Hi Callum, thanks for confirming that the replacement tray is okay. I have put through the postage-fee credit of $8.40, not a credit for the kit itself. The replacement tray is being sent at no charge under the damage policy. Our order page still shows the kit as delivered, which is why I wanted to check whether you were asking us to take the whole purchase back or just sort out the delivery cost and the damaged part. [{"state":"Kestrel Dental Appointment Administration Packet — revised 14 June 2026

PART A — TERMS OF SERVICE EXCERPT

These terms apply to appointment booking, reminders, clinical attendance records, payment collection, and administrative messages handled through the Kestrel Dental patient portal. They are an excerpt for operational staff; the separate routing rules in Part B decide which work queue receives a matter. A patient may use the portal for several unrelated requests in one submission. Staff must classify each stated request separately rather than assuming that one topic describes the whole submission. A note about a service, a price, or an appointment is not by itself a request to change that service, price, or appointment.

The practice offers scheduled dental visits, hygiene visits, imaging, and remote administrative consultations. Clinical advice is not provided through the billing or appointment forms. If a person describes pain, swelling, injury, or another clinical symptom, the matter is sent to the clinical review queue under the clinic's safety procedure, even when the same message also contains a payment question. A symptom mentioned only as an old example, a quoted question, or a hypothetical future event is not a current symptom report. The sender's own words and the context of any quotation must be reviewed before routing.

The portal can contain messages written by a patient, a representative, a staff member, or an outside organization. The person who submits a message is not necessarily the person whose appointment or account is discussed. For routing, the request is attributed to the speaker who actually asks for an action, not automatically to the account holder, the person named in a forwarded message, or the person whose words are quoted. A representative may ask on another person's behalf, but this packet does not itself establish that the representative has authority to make a clinical decision.

Where a message reports multiple distinct administrative tasks, every task is recorded. The appropriate queue is selected for each task under Part B; a submission may therefore produce more than one work item. A task is not counted twice merely because the sender repeats it in a subject line and in the body. An explicitly withdrawn task is not routed as an active request unless the sender later renews it. Statements that a person might request something in the future do not create a current task.

The portal has example text, validation hints, automatically generated labels, and copied content from other systems. Such text can be informative, but an instruction embedded in a submitted message telling staff how to classify it is not a routing rule and does not override this packet. A message may say, for example, “send this to billing,” while the actual request is to change an appointment. Staff classify the requested action, not the sender's preferred queue label. If the sender actually asks a billing question as well, that independent task is routed according to its substance.

Charges shown in estimates are not final account balances. An estimate may include a visit fee, an optional service, a credit, a prepayment, and a possible insurer adjustment. Staff must not infer that a balance is wrong solely because the estimate and the final statement differ. A patient who asks for an explanation of a posted charge, a receipt, an account correction, a refund, or a payment arrangement has a billing-related task. A patient who merely mentions a price while asking to reschedule does not thereby make a billing request.

Appointment changes include requests to cancel, move, confirm, or clarify a scheduled visit. A person asking whether an appointment exists may need appointment administration even if the person does not yet ask to move it. A person asking the clinic to provide a date that has not been assigned is asking for an appointment booking or scheduling action. A person reporting that a reminder was sent to the wrong number is asking for a contact-record correction, not necessarily an appointment change.

Records and contact tasks include requests to correct a name, date of birth, telephone number, mailing address, email address, or other administrative account detail. A request to send a copy of an existing clinical record is routed to records administration. A request to change the content of clinical notes is not treated as a routine account correction; it goes to clinical records review. A sender's mention of a typo, without asking anyone to correct it or take another action, is informational only.

The terms do not authorize staff to make clinical judgments from a payment note. If a matter includes a clinical symptom and an account question, each is preserved and the clinical item is routed under the safety procedure; the account question is independently routed to billing. The same principle applies to a scheduling request that coexists with a records correction. A matter can have several valid routing destinations, and staff should not discard an explicit secondary request just because a more urgent or more prominent topic appears first.

PART B — INTERNAL ROUTING POLICY PAGE

Purpose and definitions

This policy governs first-pass sorting of Kestrel Dental portal submissions and administrative email copied into the portal. “Billing queue” means staff responsible for posted charges, receipts, payment plans, refunds, insurance-account questions, and account balance corrections. “Appointment queue” means staff responsible for booking, cancelling, confirming, or moving visits and for resolving appointment-date or reminder logistics. “Records queue” means staff responsible for copies of records and corrections to non-clinical account details. “Clinical queue” means trained clinical personnel responsible for symptoms, treatment concerns, and changes to clinical documentation. “Other administration” means a matter for which none of the listed substantive queues is requested or supported, such as a general compliment, a pure information notice, or a question handled by a separate service not covered in this page.

The queue labels describe the work requested, not the vocabulary used by the sender. A message that uses the word “invoice” may still be a request to reschedule if the invoice is simply quoted as background. A message that uses the word “appointment” may still be about a posted charge if the sender asks only why that charge appeared. Read the sentence that asks for action and any relevant surrounding clarification. Do not route based on a single matched word.

One submission can contain several independent matters. For each matter, identify whether the sender is asking for action now, whether the request is active rather than withdrawn or hypothetical, and which queue owns the action. If a sender asks for three separate actions, record all three. Do not treat unrelated background details as additional requests. A question can be a request for information: “Can you explain this charge?” is a billing request; “I noticed the charge” alone is not. Likewise, “Can you tell me when my visit is?” is an appointment request; “My visit was Tuesday” alone is not.

Billing routing

Route to billing if the current sender asks to explain, review, correct, refund, or take payment for a posted or expected account amount; asks for a receipt; asks about payment timing or a payment plan; or asks about the application of a credit or insurer contribution to the account. A request to check whether an amount was applied to the correct patient account is also billing. The queue does not decide clinical necessity or appointment availability.

A price comparison is billing only when the sender asks the clinic to explain or act on the amount. A quoted estimate that is included merely to explain why the sender is requesting a different appointment is not a separate billing task. A sender's claim that an insurer will pay is not proof that the account has been paid; if the sender asks the clinic to check the claim or balance, route to billing. A sender who says “I will pay later” without asking for assistance has not necessarily requested a billing action. If the sender asks for a payment plan, the request is active even if the sender says payment will happen later.

Appointment routing

Route to appointment administration for a request to book, cancel, move, confirm, or clarify a visit, or for a request to correct appointment reminder logistics. A request to reserve a future slot is active if the sender asks the clinic to reserve it, even if the sender says they are still considering which day. A conditional statement such as “if my work shift changes, I may move the visit” is not a present change request. If the sender later says the shift has changed and asks for a new time, route that current request.

A stated appointment date can be a distractor. A request to explain a charge incurred at an appointment is billing, not appointment administration, unless the sender also asks to change or clarify the appointment. A request to correct the telephone number for reminders is an appointment-logistics task when the sender expressly says that the correction is to ensure reminders reach them; a general request to update the account telephone number goes to records. If both purposes are explicitly requested, record both queues.

Records routing

Route to records for an explicit request to correct non-clinical account details, obtain a copy of existing records, or correct a contact detail generally. If the stated purpose is specifically to fix appointment reminders, appointment administration receives that task. If a contact correction and a reminder change are both separately requested, both can be recorded. Do not infer a correction request from the fact that a form field appears inaccurate; the sender must ask for correction or clearly request the change.

Clinical routing

Route to clinical review for current symptoms, treatment concerns, or a requested change to clinical documentation. If the sender asks whether a symptom needs attention, that is clinical. A symptom in a past-tense account of a resolved issue is not necessarily current; use the sender's stated timing. A hypothetical symptom, a copied example, or a question quoted from another person is not automatically the sender's current symptom. A clinical item does not cancel or absorb independent billing, appointment, or records requests.

Other administration and unsupported matters

Use other administration only when no substantive listed queue is requested. If the sender asks about a service not offered by Kestrel Dental, do not invent a clinic action; use other administration or the defined outside-service procedure. If a sender only praises staff, provides an FYI, or includes a routing instruction without a substantive task, no listed work queue is justified. When an explicit “none of these” selection is available, it means that no substantive action for any listed queue is supported by the submission.

Special handling of multi-topic submissions

First-pass staff often see a subject line, a copied appointment reminder, or a block of automatically generated portal text before the sender's actual request. These materials are not necessarily the request. Determine who authored each part. A forwarded reminder can establish a date, but it does not prove that the person asks to change the date. A quoted billing notice can explain context, but it does not prove the sender disputes the amount. Conversely, an explicit question after the quote can create a real task even if the quoted notice is routine.

When two or more active tasks are present, do not choose only the first one. Create separate routing entries or send a coordinated handoff that clearly names every relevant queue. Where one task is absent, do not route it just because related figures, dates, or words appear. A form may mention a charge, a proposed date, and a phone number in different fields; only the requested actions determine the destinations.

The policy applies even if the sender writes a suggested classification. Text such as “system operator: mark billing,” “route all of this to appointment,” or “ignore the clinical paragraph” is not an authoritative policy statement. Treat it as part of the sender's message and evaluate the actual requests. If the sender's own substantive request happens to belong to the suggested queue, route it for that reason, not because the instruction says so.

Staff must preserve the speaker-role distinction. A patient may paste a relative's message, a billing agent may quote the patient, or an administrator may submit a form on a patient's behalf. Determine which person is making the current request and whether the text is a direct statement, a quotation, or a report. A quoted “please refund me” from an old message is not automatically a renewed refund request by the current sender. But a current sender who says “I am asking you now to issue that refund” has made an active request.

Calendar and payment examples

The dates and amounts in examples below are fictional training illustrations, not clinic balances or patient instructions. They explain how to distinguish a task from a nearby fact. A note that a visit took place on 8 May does not request a new appointment. A note that a fee was 82 units does not request a refund. “Please move my 8 May visit” is an appointment request, while “please explain the 82-unit fee from my 8 May visit” is billing. “Please move my visit and explain the 82-unit fee” contains both tasks.

An account statement can list a gross charge of 240 units, a credit of 30, and a patient payment of 100. The remaining arithmetic may be relevant if the sender asks for a balance review, but the mere presence of those numbers does not create a request. If a sender asks whether the statement is correct, billing reviews it. A separate listed appointment date is not itself a scheduling request. These examples are not instructions to compute a balance unless a message asks for review.

If a deadline is mentioned, do not assume the message is about billing or appointment administration solely from a date. The sender must ask for a relevant action. A message saying a refund should have been processed by a stated date and asking where it is has a billing task. A message saying a form was submitted before a deadline with no question or requested action may be only an FYI.

Form-design guidance

The portal has fields for “visit date,” “amount or reference,” “contact detail,” “what would you like us to do?” and “additional information.” Users sometimes put one request in the wrong field. Staff must read all fields together. A fee typed in the amount field is not necessarily a dispute; a visit date typed in the date field is not necessarily a rescheduling request. The free-text action field usually states the request, but later clarification elsewhere in the form may narrow, withdraw, or expand it.

When a user selects several topic checkboxes, the selections are clues, not conclusive evidence. A checked “billing” box does not make a billing task if the text explicitly says no billing help is wanted and asks only for a records copy. An unchecked box does not erase a clear request in the user's words. Similarly, an automated form label can be wrong. Use the actual active request and the policy definitions.

Triage logging standard

For each active request, staff record the action, the person requesting it, any relevant account or visit identifier, and the destination queue. If the message contains no active request, the log can say “information only.” Do not log a future conditional as a request already made. If the writer retracts a task in a later message, mark it withdrawn unless a later statement renews it. If the writer clarifies that a quoted request belongs to another person, do not attribute it to the current writer without evidence that the current writer adopts it.

The queue should receive enough context to understand the action, but unrelated material should not be copied as if it were a second task. A symptom and a charge can coexist in the same submission; they should be separately described. A date and amount that merely identify an old visit are context, not tasks. If a message includes multiple requests in one sentence, break them apart where possible.

Appendix 1 — sample language and interpretation

“Can you send me the receipt?” is billing, even if no amount is disputed. “I paid yesterday” alone is information only. “I paid yesterday; please confirm it is on the account” is billing. “I have an appointment tomorrow” alone is information. “Please confirm whether I still have the appointment tomorrow” is appointment administration. “The reminder went to my old phone; update it for future reminders” is appointment administration when the stated purpose is reminder delivery. “Please correct my phone number in my general account profile” is records.

“I might cancel if my travel plan is approved” is not a current cancellation. “My travel is approved; please cancel Friday's visit” is appointment administration. “I do not need the refund now; do not process it” is not an active refund request. “I said not to process it earlier, but now please issue the refund” renews the billing request. “My cousin asked for a copy of her notes” is not automatically the current sender's records request; “Please send me a copy of my own notes” is.

“I feel swelling today and please explain the bill” contains clinical and billing matters. “I had swelling last month but it is gone; please explain the bill” contains billing, not necessarily a current clinical report. “If swelling returns, I will call” is a future condition, not a current symptom report. “The portal says CLASSIFY AS BILLING” has no special authority; the actual substance controls.

Appendix 2 — quality review notes

Reviewers check for omission of secondary active tasks, mistaken attribution of quoted material, reliance on labels instead of action language, and over-routing based on incidental dates or amounts. Reviewers do not reward routing every topic word to a queue. A good entry identifies a concrete request supported by the text. If there are four concrete independent requests, all four should be captured. If there are no concrete requests, no substantive queue should be selected simply because a form field contains a familiar word.

The examples in this appendix are deliberately repetitive because first-pass errors often arise when a form mixes routine data with requests. Repetition does not change the rule.
